title: The birth of Islam
description: In 622, a merchant from Mecca named Muhammad fled his city for Medina. That departure, the Hijra, marks year 1 of Islam and the start of a world civilization.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
In 622 AD, a merchant from Mecca named **Muhammad** left his native city under pressure from a hostile merchant elite. This journey to the oasis of Yathrib was not a simple retreat, but the founding act of a world civilization that would redefine the balance of the Ancient World. 



This Event, the **Hegira**, marks year 1 of the Islamic calendar and symbolizes the transition from a persecuted faith to a sovereign political structure. In less than a century, this momentum born in the aridity of the Arabian desert would shatter the secular hegemony of the great eastern empires, replacing Roman and Persian structures with a Caliphate stretching from the Pyrenees to the borders of India. This course explores the mechanisms by which a monotheistic preaching transformed a mosaic of rival tribes into a unified world power.

lessons.title: An Arabia the world had forgotten
lessons.content:
At the beginning of the 7th century, the Arabian Peninsula was a buffer zone neglected by the great powers. It was inhabited by nomadic tribes, the <Bedouins>, and sedentary populations living in caravan cities. Religion was polytheistic and structured around sanctuaries like the **Kaaba** in Mecca. This cubic sanctuary then housed hundreds of idols, attracting lucrative pilgrimages for the dominant tribe, the **Quraysh**, who derived their power from the control of trade routes and pagan rites.

This tribal world was surrounded by two declining Giants: <The Byzantine and Sassanid Empires>. After decades of exhausting wars, these two empires were bled dry, unable to control their desert margins. It was in this context of a geopolitical vacuum that **Muhammad ibn Abdallah**, born around 570, began to receive what he presented as divine revelations in 610, in the cave of **Hira**. The message preached radical monotheism and social justice that threatened the established order.

By attacking the cult of idols, Muhammad directly threatened the economy of Mecca based on pilgrimage. His first disciples, including his wife **Khadija** and his cousin **Ali**, suffered increasing persecution. Faced with the hostility of the Meccan elites, the survival of the small community became impossible without external support, thus preparing the ground for a saving exodus.

{The Kaaba contained about 360 idols at the time of Muhammad - one for each day of the lunar Arabic calendar. Muhammad destroyed them all in a single day upon his victorious return.}

lessons.title: 622: the Hijra changes everything
lessons.content:
The year **622** marks a fundamental rupture for nascent Islam. Threatened with death, Muhammad accepted the invitation of the inhabitants of Yathrib, an oasis located to the north, who were seeking an arbitrator to settle their internal conflicts. 

[Medina Prophet's Mosque]

Thus began the **Hegira**: the transition from persecution to sovereignty. In Medina, Muhammad's status changed. He was no longer just a prophet; he became a head of state, a legislator, and a general. He drafted the <Constitution of Medina>, a revolutionary edict that organized coexistence between different clans, including Jewish tribes, defining for the first time the <Ummah>. This community of faith replaced clan solidarities with a single religious and political allegiance.

This period was marked by an armed struggle against Mecca. Muhammad used the strategy of <razzias> to weaken Meccan caravans, thus cutting off the economic resources of his adversaries. Several major clashes forged the community's discipline. The battle of **Badr (624)** was experienced as a miracle by Muslims who, though outnumbered, defeated the army of Mecca. Despite a setback at **Uhud (625)**, the victorious resistance during the **Siege of Medina (627)**, also called the Battle of the Trench, definitively established his authority. The force of the religious message was now allied with formidable military effectiveness.

{Before the Hegira, the city of Medina was called Yathrib. It was renamed 'Madinat al-Nabi' (the city of the Prophet), which gave rise to the current name of Medina.}

lessons.title: 630: the triumphant return
lessons.content:
In **630**, the balance of power shifted definitively. Muhammad marched on Mecca with an army of **10,000 men**. Aware of its helplessness, the city surrendered without major resistance. Muhammad then showed sharp political sense: instead of massacring his former persecutors, he proclaimed a general pardon, facilitating a peaceful transition.

He entered the **Kaaba** to break the idols, consecrating the place to the one God, Allah. This clemency encouraged the mass conversion of Arab tribes, who saw Islam's success as a sign of divine favor. At Muhammad's death in **632**, almost the entire Arabian Peninsula was unified under a single authority for the first time in its History.



Power then passed to the **Caliphs**, the successors of the Prophet. Under the command of the first two, **Abu Bakr** and **Umar**, unification transformed into a lightning external expansion. Profiting from the weakness of neighboring empires, Arab armies seized **Syria**, **Iraq**, and **Egypt**. Local populations sometimes welcomed the conquerors as liberators from the fiscal pressure of Byzantium.

{The first man to have performed the call to prayer (muezzin) in Mecca was Bilal, a former slave of Ethiopian origin, symbolizing the equality of believers preached by the new message.}

lessons.title: The roots of a civilization
lessons.content:
The expansion of Islam was not only territorial, it was structural and administrative. The conquerors established the status of the <Dhimma>, allowing Christians and Jews to keep their religion in exchange for the payment of a specific tax, the <jizya>. This relative religious tolerance facilitated the institutionalization of the new Arab authority in regions weary of Byzantine religious persecution.

The Arabic language quickly became the cement of this nascent empire, serving as an administrative and liturgical tool. The conquerors inherited administrative structures from ancient empires which they adapted, creating an unprecedented cultural crossroads between Greek, Persian, and Indian thought. This Movement also integrated a moral and spiritual dimension, the <jihad>, which stimulated both the effort of inner construction and the defense of the empire.

Islam radically transformed the Relationship with the World of the 7th century. What began as an isolated revelation in a cave ended up redrawing the map of the Ancient World, creating a space for the movement of goods and ideas stretching across three continents, thus marking the end of Late Antiquity.

{During the conquest of Egypt, the Arabs were so impressed by the urban planning of Alexandria that they chose to found a new capital, Fostat, which would later become Cairo, so as not to alter the ancient city.}

|| In only 22 years (610-632), Muhammad transformed a monotheistic message into a unifying political force, laying the foundations for an empire that would dominate the world stage for centuries.||

quiz.question: What does the Hijra represent in 622?
quiz.explanation: The Hijra is the departure of Muhammad, threatened with death in Mecca, towards the oasis of Medina. This date becomes year 1 of the Muslim calendar.
options: Muhammad's departure from Mecca to Medina
The first revelation received by Muhammad
The capture of Mecca by the Muslims
The death of Muhammad in Medina

quiz.question: Who controlled trade around the Kaaba before Islam?
quiz.explanation: The Quraysh, the dominant tribe of Mecca, drew their power from pilgrimage and trade around the polytheist Kaaba.

quiz.question: True or false: after taking Mecca in 630, Muhammad massacred his former persecutors.
quiz.explanation: Muhammad, on the contrary, grants a general pardon, which facilitates the rallying of Arab tribes to Islam.

quiz.question: In what year did Muhammad die, leaving Arabia unified under one authority?
quiz.explanation: Muhammad died in 632, only ten years after the Hijra, when almost all of Arabia was unified.

quiz.question: Put these events in Muhammad's life in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four dates (622, 624, 630, 632) mark the twenty years in which Muhammad went from threatened prophet to head of a state unifying Arabia.
items: The Hijra: departure to Medina
The Battle of Badr
The capture of Mecca
The death of Muhammad

quiz.question: What is the Dhimma established by the Muslim conquerors?
quiz.explanation: Dhimma is the protected status which authorizes “people of the Book” to maintain their religion upon payment of jizya.
options: The status allowing Christians and Jews to keep their religion against a tax
The name of the Muslim calendar
The court charged with judging infidels

quiz.question: Which two great empires were exhausted by their wars around Arabia in the 7th century?
quiz.explanation: The endless wars between Byzantium (Eastern Roman Empire) and the Sassanid Persians created a geopolitical vacuum from which Muhammad's new message took advantage.

quiz.question: What is the Umma, founded by Muhammad in Medina?
quiz.explanation: The Umma replaces traditional tribal solidarities with a community based on shared faith.
options: The community of believers, which goes beyond blood and clan ties
The name of the Muslim calendar

title: Urban II's call and the First Crusade
description: In November 1095, at Clermont, Pope Urban II made a call that sent tens of thousands of Europeans toward Jerusalem. The Crusades were born.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: In November 1095, in the heart of Auvergne, Pope **Urbain II** delivered a speech whose echo would resonate for centuries. This moment marks the birth of the **Crusades** Movement, an unprecedented phenomenon of collective mobilization where spirituality meets geopolitics. By calling on Western Christians to come to the aid of the East, the papacy was not merely responding to a military threat; it was reinventing the Concept of holy war and durably modifying the relations between the Latin world, the Byzantine Empire, and Islam. This course explores the roots, deployment, and consequences of this major rupture of the High Middle Ages.

lessons.title: Byzantium calls for help
lessons.content:
Since the 7th century, the city of Jerusalem had been under Muslim rule, but Christian pilgrimages remained permitted there. However, the precarious balance of the region was shattered by the meteoric rise of the **Seljuk Turks**. This nomadic people converted to Sunni Islam gradually replaced Arab caliphal authority with a formidable warrior power. The tipping point occurred in **1071**, during the **<Battle of Manzikert>**. Turkish forces annihilated the army of Byzantine Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes there, thus opening the gates of Anatolia.

[Seljuk Turks Battle of Manzikert]

Deprived of its main sources of recruitment and supply, the **Byzantine Empire** sank into a deep crisis. Faced with the Seljuk advance that now threatened Constantinople, Emperor **<Alexios I Komnenos>** made a historic decision: he set aside his differences with the West, born from the recent **<Schism of 1054>**, and sent ambassadors to the Pope to request military aid. For Urban II, this request was providential. It offered him the opportunity to restore the unity of Christendom while asserting the primacy of the See of Rome over the Eastern Churches.

Beyond geopolitics, 11th-century Western Europe was suffering from internal tensions. The **<Peace of God>**, established by the Church, attempted to limit the violence of the knightly class. The crusade then appeared as an elegant solution: channeling the warrior fire of knights and landless younger sons toward an external cause, thus transforming social predators into "soldiers of Christ.".

{In 1071, the Byzantine emperor was captured by Sultan Alp Arslan who, instead of executing him, treated him with honors before asking him what he would have done in his place, illustrating the mutual respect between leaders of the time.}

lessons.title: Clermont: “God wills it!”
lessons.content:
On **November 27, 1095**, during the **<Council of Clermont>**, Urban II addressed a crowd that far exceeded the circle of ecclesiastics. His speech was a masterpiece of rhetoric. He dramatized the persecutions allegedly suffered by Eastern Christians and sacralized the journey to Jerusalem by granting a **<Plenary indulgence>**. This promise of total remission of sins transformed the expedition into an armed pilgrimage, capable of erasing the most atrocious crimes committed by feudal lords.

[Council of Clermont 1095]

Enthusiasm was lightning-fast. The rallying cry **"God wills it!"** spread like wildfire. To signify their commitment, volunteers sewed a red cloth cross onto their right shoulder, a gesture that gave birth to the verb "to take the cross". However, this flame of fervor quickly escaped the Pope's control. Even before the great lords were ready, a motley crowd of peasants, women, and the poor set off.

This first wave, known as the **People's Crusade**, was led by charismatics such as **<Peter the Hermit>**. Lacking any logistics or discipline, it crossed Europe in chaos, sometimes engaging in looting and massacres of Jewish populations, before being almost entirely decimated by the Turks upon arrival in Anatolia. This tragic failure demonstrated that mystical fervor cannot substitute for military strategy.

lessons.title: From Antioch to Jerusalem
lessons.content:
The true military power, the **Barons' Crusade**, did not set out until August 1096. It brought together the most powerful lords of the time, such as **Godfrey of Bouillon**, his brother Baldwin of Boulogne, or the formidable Norman **<Bohemond of Taranto>**. These troops, seasoned and well-equipped, did not constitute a single army but a coalition of national contingents. For the Greeks in Constantinople, the arrival of these "western Barbarians" was experienced as a second invasion, forcing Emperor Alexios I to demand oaths of vassalage from them.

The campaign was a logistical ordeal. The crusaders had to cross deserts, face famine and internal dissension. The turning point occurred during the siege of **Antioch** (1097-1098), a city reputed to be impregnable. Its fall allowed the crusaders to open the road to the south, but at the cost of extreme suffering. Finally, in June 1099, the survivors reached the walls of Jerusalem. After a month of fierce siege, they entered the city on **July 15, 1099**.

The victory led to a bloodbath: chronicles of the time recount that blood flowed up to the horses' ankles in the Temple district. This massacre durably marked the Muslim collective memory. To sustain this victory, the crusaders did not all return to Europe but founded the **Crusader States**. Godfrey of Bouillon, refusing to wear a crown of gold where Christ wore a crown of thorns, took the more modest title of **<Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre>**.

{Godfrey of Bouillon was so strong that legend claims he sliced a camel in two with a single sword stroke during a battle against the Seljuks.}

lessons.title: A lasting divide
lessons.content:
The capture of Jerusalem was not the end, but the beginning of an era of permanent contact and conflict. The establishment of **Frankish colonies** in the East forced Europeans to adapt to a local culture far more refined than their own. Unique military orders were born to ensure the protection of pilgrims, such as the **<Templars>** or the Hospitalers. Paradoxically, these warrior-monks would become pivots of international trade and finance between the two shores.

Politically, the unification of Muslim forces under the aegis of **<Saladin>** would lead to the retaking of Jerusalem in 1187, triggering new crusades including that of the famous Richard the Lionheart. In two centuries, eight major expeditions followed one another. If the initial military objective ultimately failed in 1291 with the fall of Acre, the cultural impact of these exchanges was immense: the West rediscovered Greek science preserved by the Arabs and introduced new Technical and agricultural products.

The legacy of Urban II's call is therefore double. It forged the identity of a Europe capable of mobilizing under a Common banner, but it also dug a gulf of mistrust between monotheistic religions, whose resonances are still felt in contemporary geopolitical tensions.

|| In 1095, a 20-minute speech by Pope Urban II in Clermont mobilized the West for a 3,000 km armed expedition, resulting in 1099 in the capture of Jerusalem and the creation of the Crusader States. ||

quiz.question: What event occurred at the Council of Clermont in November 1095?
quiz.explanation: At the Council of Clermont, on November 27, 1095, Urban II called on Western Christians to go and liberate Jerusalem, in exchange for forgiveness of their sins.
options: Pope Urban II calls for crusade to liberate Jerusalem
The Crusaders found the Latin States of the East

quiz.question: What event pushed the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Comnenus to ask the pope for help?
quiz.explanation: In 1071, in Mantzikert, the Seljuk Turks crushed the Byzantine army and opened Anatolia, pushing Alexios I Comnenus to petition Rome.
options: The defeat of Mantzikert against the Seljuk Turks
The capture of Jerusalem by the Muslims

quiz.question: True or false: the “poor people's crusade” led by Peter the Hermit was a disciplined army that reached Jerusalem without difficulty.
quiz.explanation: Without discipline or supplies, this troop of poor people plundered in their path and was decimated in Anatolia before reaching Jerusalem.

quiz.question: What does Urban II promise to those who go on crusade?
quiz.explanation: Urban II promises a plenary indulgence: total forgiveness of sins for those who take the cross.
options: Full forgiveness of the penalties due to their sins
Land guaranteed in the Holy Land
A salary paid by the Church

quiz.question: True or false: after the capture of Jerusalem, Godfrey of Bouillon proclaimed himself king of the city.
quiz.explanation: Godfrey of Bouillon refused the title of king and preferred to be called Avowed of the Holy Sepulchre, protector of the tomb of Christ.

quiz.explanation: These milestones range from 1071 to 1187: the Byzantine defeat precedes the pope's appeal, which precedes the capture and then recapture of Jerusalem.

quiz.explanation: Jerusalem fell on July 15, 1099, after the expedition left in 1096 and the siege of Antioch.

quiz.question: Which Muslim sultan recaptures Jerusalem in 1187?
quiz.explanation: In 1187, Sultan Saladin recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders, restarting the cycle of the Crusades.

quiz.question: In what year did Saint-Jean-d'Acre, the last bastion of the Latin States of the East, fall?
quiz.explanation: The fall of Saint-Jean-d'Acre in 1291 marks the end of the Latin presence in the Holy Land.

title: The sack of Rome by the Visigoths
description: In August 410, Alaric's Visigoths looted Rome for three days. For the first time in eight centuries, an enemy army walked into the Eternal City.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
In August 410, the unimaginable happened: Rome, the "Eternal City," fell. For the first time since the sack by the Gauls in 390 BC, nearly eight centuries earlier, foreign troops forced open the gates of the city that gave its name to the greatest power of Antiquity. Led by King **Alaric**, the Visigoths seized riches accumulated over generations.

[Sack of Rome 410 Alaric]

This Event was not a simple operation of military predation; it was a civilizational earthquake. Although Rome was no longer the effective center of political decision-making for the Empire, it remained its spiritual, cultural, and symbolic heart. The rape of this sanctuary revealed to the entire world the agony of an imperial system that was believed to be invincible, precipitating a deep reflection on the end of a world and the foundations of the emerging Christian culture.

lessons.title: An empire draining away
lessons.content:
At the dawn of the 5th century, the Western Roman Empire was in a state of advanced decomposition. Political instability, marked by frequent usurpations, had exhausted public finances. The border regions, once protected by disciplined legions, were now porous transit zones. To cope with the lack of soldiers, the Empire systematized the use of the **Roman foedus**, integrating entire peoples to defend its borders in exchange for land and subsidies.

Faced with increasing insecurity, the centers of power migrated. Rome, symbolically powerful but strategically indefensible, was abandoned. In 402, Emperor **Honorius** moved the court to **Ravenna**, a city in Emilia-Romagna. This choice was purely defensive: located in the middle of impassable lagoons and marshes, Ravenna was a natural fortress accessible by the Adriatic Sea, allowing an easy escape to Constantinople in the event of disaster.

While the Emperor shut himself away in his palace of mosaics, the city of Rome was left to its own fate. Its senatorial aristocracy continued to lead a lavish lifestyle, totally disconnected from military reality. However, imperial authority had become a fiction: the real masters of the game were now generals of Barbarian origin who commanded the regular troops, creating permanent tension between the Roman civil elites and the Germanized military circles.

{A famous anecdote tells that upon hearing of the fall of "Rome," Emperor Honorius panicked, believing it was his favorite chicken that he had named so. He was, it is said, relieved to learn that it was "only" the city.}

lessons.title: Alaric, a disappointed Roman
lessons.content:
The sack of 410 was not the result of savage hatred against Rome, but of a negotiation that tragically failed. **Alaric I** was not an invader foreign to Latin culture: he was a high-ranking officer trained in the Roman army, having served under Emperor Honorius during the Battle of the Frigidus. His destiny was linked to the waves of refugees pushed by the incursion of <The Huns> into Eastern Europe.

Alaric did not seek to destroy the Empire, but to have his people enter it in a legal and stable manner. He demanded lands in Noricum (present-day Austria) and an official title of generalissimo. Faced with the contemptuous indecision of the court of Ravenna, Alaric used Rome as a means of pressure. He besieged the city twice between 408 and 409, lifting the blockade in exchange for tons of gold and pepper. Finally, driven to his limit by the betrayals of Honorius, he resolved to the final assault.

[Alaric king Visigoths]

On **August 24, 410**, the Salarian Gate was opened from the inside. The looting lasted three days, but it was singularly orderly. Alaric, a Christian of <Arian> confession, imposed strict rules on his warriors. They had to respect the asylum of churches, notably the Saint Peter and Saint Paul basilicas, and spare the lives of civilians sheltering there. This relative moderation, although violence and fires were real, underscores the Visigoth leader's desire to behave as an heir to Rome rather than a destroyer.

{According to a famous legend, Alaric died shortly after the sack. To hide his body and his immense treasure, his men supposedly diverted the course of the Busento River in Calabria before restoring the riverbed over the burial site.}

lessons.title: The shock and The City of God
lessons.content:
The psychological impact of the fall of Rome was phenomenal. For contemporaries, the city was much more than a town: it was the scale for measuring time and the World. From Palestine, <Saint Jerome> cried out: "In a single city, the entire universe has perished". The pagans, still numerous in the aristocracy, immediately accused Christianity of having weakened the Empire by abandoning the ancient protective gods.

It was to answer these accusations that the Bishop of Hippo, **Saint Augustine**, wrote his masterpiece: **"The City of God"**. In this founding text, he distinguished the "earthly city" (human empires like Rome), doomed to vanish, from the "heavenly city" (the Church), which is eternal. By decoupling the fate of Christianity from that of the Empire of Constantine, Augustine gave Christians the intellectual tools to survive the collapse of political structures.

Even if life resumed its course in Rome after the Visigoths departed for the south, imperial prestige was annihilated. The image of decline was there, concrete. Aurelian's walls had been breached, proving that the provinces were henceforth at the mercy of the great Germanic federations. The sack of 410 acted as a signal for the <Vandals> and the <Franks> who realized that the West was a prey ripe for conquest.

lessons.title: The turn toward the Middle Ages
lessons.content:
The brutal death of Alaric in 410 deprived the Visigoths of their charismatic leader, but did not stop the reshaping of Europe. His successors eventually settled in Aquitanian Gaul, creating an autonomous kingdom that foreshadowed the feudal mosaic of the Middle Ages. Rome would suffer a much more violent sack in 455 by the <Vandals>, coming from Carthage, marking a further step in urban decay.

The final agony occurred in **476**, when the leader of the <Heruli> Germanic auxiliaries, **Odoacer**, deposed the young emperor **Romulus Augustulus**. This gesture ended the line of Western Emperors. Odoacer made a symbolic act of submission by sending the imperial regalia back to Constantinople. In doing so, he recognized that legitimate authority now resided in the East, where the Roman Empire, which we now call the Byzantine Empire, would endure until 1453.

The sack of 410 remains, however, the major memory rupture. It marks the shift of a civilization centered on the Roman Mediterranean toward a fragmented medieval Europe. The Visigoths, far from being the terminators of classical culture, would become its transmitters in Hispania, blending their Germanic traditions with Roman Law and the Christian faith, thus initiating the slow transition toward the medieval order.

{The artistic term "Gothic" was invented during the Renaissance as an insult: Italian scholars judged this medieval art so barbarian that they falsely attributed it to the Goths who had sacked Rome.}

|| In 410, Rome fell for the first time in 800 years - looted for only 3 days by Visigoths who had served in the Roman army.||

Rome had just been destroyed by fire
The Roman Senate had expelled him from the city
He wanted to get closer to Constantinople

A tax paid by the provinces to Rome

quiz.explanation: Faced with the pagans who accuse Christianity of having weakened Rome, Augustine responds in The City of God that earthly empires pass away, but that the Church remains.

quiz.explanation: These stages range from 402 to 476: the withdrawal to Ravenna precedes the Visigoth sack, then the more destructive Vandal sack, until the end of the Western Empire.

Sack of Rome by the Vandals

quiz.explanation: The sack of Rome by the Visigoths took place in August 410, a shock to the entire ancient world.

quiz.question: In what year was the last Western Roman emperor deposed?
quiz.explanation: In 476, the leader Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, ending the Western Roman Empire.

title: The coronation of Charlemagne
description: On Christmas Day 800, in Rome, Pope Leo III placed a crown on Charlemagne's head. The West had an emperor again, and Europe had a model that would last.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
On Christmas Day 800, in the heart of Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, a symbolic gesture permanently altered the geopolitical balance of the West: Pope **Leo III** placed a golden crown on the head of **Charles I**, known as **Charlemagne**, King of the Franks and the Lombards. This act was not merely a simple religious ceremony of circumstance; it marked the birth of the **Holy Roman Empire**, an entity that claimed to restore the imperial authority lost since the fall of Rome in 476.

On this winter morning, Europe definitively left behind the instability of the first Barbarian monarchies to enter an era of centralization and imperial ambition. This coronation, whose staging sparked historical debates, crystallized the growing tensions between the spiritual power of the Church and the temporal power of sovereigns. Beyond the prestige of the title, this Event laid the administrative, cultural, and monetary foundations of a coherent space that foreshadowed the outlines of modern continental Europe.

lessons.title: Forty years of conquest
lessons.content:
**Charlemagne** (742-814) inherited the Frankish kingdom in **768**. While the beginning of his reign was marked by a fragile cohabitation with his brother Carloman, the latter's premature death in 771 left him free to engage in unprecedented territorial expansion. For more than forty years, Charles acted as an tireless warlord, leading campaigns on all fronts to stabilize and enlarge his domain, transforming a tribal kingship into a true continental power.

The most emblematic and relentless conquest remained that of the **Saxons**, located in the northeast of the kingdom. Launched in **772**, this series of campaigns would last **thirty years** and be characterized by extreme violence. To subdue these pagans, Charlemagne used force but also forced conversion to Christianity, considering religion as an indispensable tool for political unification. At the same time, he intervened in Italy where he overthrew the <Lombard> dynasty in 774, annexing their territory and taking their crown. He continued his expansion by subduing **Bavaria** and crushing the <Avars>, a formidable horse-riding people, on the plains of the Danube.

To the west, his expeditions in **Spain** against the Muslims in 778, although marked by the ambush of the <Roncevaux Pass>, allowed him to secure his borders. At its peak, the Carolingian Empire covered approximately **1.1 million km²**, encompassing almost the entirety of Christian Western Europe. This immense territorial mass, however, required an approach other than simple armed force to avoid implosion, pushing Charles to devise a more permanent administrative structure.

{Charlemagne measured approximately 1.84 meters, an exceptional height for his time when the male average was around 1.65 meters, which reinforced his natural aura as a leader.}

lessons.title: Governing and teaching people to read
lessons.content:
Aware that the sword alone could not maintain the cohesion of such a territory, Charlemagne initiated a policy of profound reform, often described as the **Carolingian Renaissance**. The stakes were two-fold: to Christianize the populations and to train an elite capable of leading the state apparatus. To administer his provinces, he relied on a hierarchy of <Counts> and bishops, but he innovated above all by systematizing the mission of the **<missi dominici>**. These royal inspectors ensured a direct link between the palace of Aachen and remote regions, guaranteeing the application of royal orders.

The intellectual component was led by the English scholar **<Alcuin of York>**, who directed the palatine school. The objective was to restore classical Latin and to train literate clerics. This desire for administrative clarity led to a graphic revolution: the creation of **Carolingian minuscule**. This round and regular calligraphy replaced illegible regional scripts, facilitating communication throughout the empire. It is the direct ancestor of our modern lowercase printing types.

This Period also saw a colossal effort to safeguard ancient culture. Monasteries became centers of intense copying, allowing an immense part of Latin Literature to survive through the centuries. On the economic front, Charles imposed the **<Silver denarius>**. By replacing gold—which had become rare and too precious for daily trade—with silver, he created a stable and uniform currency that stimulated exchange within his borders.

{To ensure his laws were understood, Charlemagne required that official texts be read publicly to the people on market days or after mass.}

lessons.title: Christmas 800: an ambiguous coronation
lessons.content:
The consecration of Charlemagne as emperor was the result of a convergence of interests between the Frankish monarchy and the papacy. In 799, Pope **Leo III** was the victim of a violent assault in Rome by the local aristocracy, who accused him of immorality. Weakened, he fled to Charles, who intervened militarily to restore the sovereign pontiff. As a sign of gratitude, but also to establish his own authority, the Pope prepared the restoration of imperial dignity in the West.

During the Christmas Mass, as Charles rose from his prayer, Leo III placed the crown on his head and acclaimed him as **"Emperor of the Romans"**. Although the Event appeared planned, the biographer Eginhard claimed that Charlemagne was displeased with how the ceremony unfolded. This discomfort was likely not feigned: by placing the crown on the sovereign's head himself, the Pope suggested that imperial power emanated from the Church. This precedent would establish a centuries-long tension between spiritual and temporal power.

This act also confirmed an irreversible geopolitical rupture with the **Byzantine Empire**. Constantinople indeed considered that only its sovereign was the legitimate heir to Rome. By claiming to restore the empire in the West, Charlemagne created a second pole of power and affirmed the independence of Latin Christendom. Europe thus found its own center of gravity, distinct from the East, laying the foundations for a distinct Western identity based on the Roman heritage and the Catholic religion.

{Charlemagne's full title after 800 was: "Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, governing the Roman Empire".}

lessons.title: A broken empire, a living idea
lessons.content:
The dream of a universal Christian empire did not survive long after its founder. Upon Charlemagne's death in 814, his son Louis the Pious managed with difficulty to preserve unity. However, in the next generation, succession quarrels between his three sons—Lothair, Louis the German, and Charles the Bald—plunged the empire into civil war. This conflict led to the **Treaty of Verdun (843)**, an act that definitively redrew the map of the continent.

The treaty divided the empire into three parts: **Francia occidentalis** (the core of France), **Francia orientalis** (the core of Germany), and **Lotharingia**, a fragile central territory extending from the North Sea to Italy. This fragmentation weakened central power to the benefit of local aristocracies, fostering the emergence of feudalism. Yet, Charlemagne's legacy remained vibrant. The administrative framework of counties would survive, as would the idea of a Europe united by a shared culture and religion.

Although physically dismembered, the prestige of the imperial title endured through the **Holy Roman Empire**, which lasted until 1806. Charlemagne, for his part, entered legend to become the "Father of Europe." He is today claimed as a common ancestor by several European nations, symbolizing the golden age of a lost Latin and Christian unity that founded our current institutions.

|| On December 25, 800, by restoring the imperial title in the West, Charlemagne created a unified political and cultural structure that, despite its division as early as 843, defined the outlines of modern Europe. ||

title: Magna Carta
description: In June 1215, John Lackland set his seal to a charter forced on him by his barons. Over the centuries, a feudal text became the symbol of law standing above the king.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: In June 1215, the meadow of Runnymede became the Theatre for an unprecedented face-off between a contested monarch and a revolted aristocracy. The King of England **John Lackland**, cornered by military and financial setbacks, was forced to affix his seal to the **The Magna Carta (1215)**. This document, born in haste to avoid a civil war, has become over the centuries the universal symbol of the limitation of arbitrary power. Although its immediate application was a failure, its symbolic reach laid the foundations of modern constitutionalism, affirming for the first time that no one, not even the sovereign, is above the Law.

lessons.title: John Lackland on the brink
lessons.content:
**John I of England**, better known as **John Lackland**, succeeded his brother Richard the Lionheart in 1199. His reign opened with a series of geopolitical catastrophes that eroded his Legitimacy. In 1204, he suffered a humiliating defeat against <Philip II Augustus>, losing most of his continental possessions. This <loss of Normandy (1204)> deprived the crown of essential revenues and humiliated the Anglo-Norman nobility.

To attempt to reconquer his lands, John imposed unprecedented fiscal pressure. He diverted the tools of the <feudal system> to his advantage, demanding exorbitant taxes like scutage (a sum paid to avoid military service) and multiplying arbitrary fines. His suspicious temperament led him to take the families of his barons hostage to guarantee their loyalty, flouting ancestral customs that bound the King to his vassals.

The crisis became total when John opposed the papacy over the appointment of the Archbishop of Canterbury. In 1213, Pope **Innocent III** pronounced his excommunication. Isolated diplomatically, ruined by the failure of the Battle of <Bouvines> in 1214, the King faced a coalition of barons who no longer saw him as a protective suzerain, but as a tyrant. Armed insurrection became inevitable, leading the rebels to seize London in May 1215.

The nickname "Lackland" does not come from his defeats against the French, but from the fact that as the last son of Henry II, he had not received a land appanage at birth, unlike his brothers.

lessons.title: Runnymede, 63 clauses
lessons.content:
Faced with the threat of deposition, John agrees to negotiate. The parties meet on **June 15, 1215** on neutral ground, the meadow of **Runnymede**, located between the royal fortress of Windsor and the rebel camp at Staines.

[Magna Carta 1215 manuscript]

The document sealed that day contains **63 clauses**. Although drafted to resolve immediate issues (forest management, fishing rights, weights and measures), it is deeply influenced by Archbishop **Stephen Langton**, who seeks to codify the liberties of the Church and subjects.

Two clauses stand out for their philosophical scope. **Clause 39** is undoubtedly the most famous: it provides that no free man can be arrested or stripped of his property without a **"lawful judgment of his peers"**. It lays the foundations for what would become judicial independence. **Clause 40**, for its part, forbids the king from "selling" or "delaying" justice, ending the common practice of demanding bribes to obtain a royal hearing.

However, the Great Charter is not a democratic text in the modern sense. It is primarily addressed to "free men", which excludes the vast majority of the population then composed of serfs. Originally, it was a feudal peace treaty aimed at restoring a balance between central power and the privileges of the aristocracy.

lessons.title: From failure to myth
lessons.content:
The legal validity of the 1215 Magna Carta was exceptionally brief. As early as August, John asked the Pope to annul the text, claiming it had been signed under duress. The Pope granted his request, declaring the charter "null and void of all validity for ever". Civil war, known as the **First Barons' War**, then broke out immediately.

Paradoxically, the survival of the document is due to the death of John in 1216. His successor, the young **Henry III**, then nine years old, reissued the text in an abridged form to appease the rebels and consolidate his throne. Under his long reign, the charter was confirmed several times, gradually integrating into the English legislative corpus. It lost its character as a peace treaty to become a stable legal reference.

Yet it was in the 17th century, during the struggle against Stuart absolutism, that the charter acquired its mythical dimension. Jurists like **Edward Coke** rediscovered it and reinterpreted its medieval clauses to make it the ancestor of parliamentary liberties. It was at this time that the idea took root that the Magna Carta guarantees inalienable rights for every citizen, transforming a feudal parchment into a founding act of British democracy.

 There is no single "original" copy of the 1215 charter, but several copies sent simultaneously to the counties; only four survive today.

lessons.title: A worldwide legacy
lessons.content:
The influence of the Magna Carta extends far beyond the borders of England. During the colonization of America, British settlers took the principles of the charter with them, considering them part of their legal heritage. In 1787, the **American Founding Fathers** drew heavily from this text to draft the Constitution and the <Bill of Rights>. The Concept of <habeas corpus> is its direct emanation.

In the 20th century, following the horrors of the Second World War, the Magna Carta served as a moral reference. <Eleanor Roosevelt> explicitly mentioned it during the drafting of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948, calling it the "Great International Charter for all mankind". It thus shifted from the status of a class contract (the barons against the king) to that of universal protection against state arbitrariness.

Despite its respectable age, the charter remains technically in force in English Law, although only three of its clauses have not been repealed by modern legislation. Its importance today is less legal than symbolic: it serves as a reminder that consensus and Law are the only ramparts against absolutism. It remains the foundation on which the edifice of Western civil liberties rests.

 In 2006, a copy of the Magna Carta traveled aboard the space shuttle Endeavour for a 12-day mission in orbit around the Earth.

quiz.explanation: Faced with taxes, hostages and arbitrary fines imposed by John Lackland to reconquer his lands, the barons rebel and impose a text limiting his power.
options: To limit royal arbitrariness: taxes, hostages and abusive fines
To finance a new crusade in the Holy Land

quiz.explanation: In 1204, John Lackland lost Normandy to Philip II Augustus, a setback which weakened him permanently.

quiz.explanation: Clause 39 establishes the principle that no free man can be arrested or imprisoned without due trial of his peers.
options: No free man can be arrested without a judgment of his peers

quiz.question: True or false: The Magna Carta of 1215 granted equal rights to all inhabitants of the kingdom, including serfs.
quiz.explanation: The text of 1215 is mainly addressed to “free men”; the serfs, peasants tied to the land, do not benefit directly.

quiz.explanation: John obtained the annulment of the text by the Pope in August 1215, which reignited the conflict with the barons.
options: John Lackland has the text annulled by the Pope and the civil war resumes
The king is deposed by the barons

John Lackland goes into exile in France

quiz.explanation: In 1214, the defeat of Bouvines, where Philippe Auguste defeated a coalition including England, isolated John Lackland.
options: The sack of London by the barons
The revolt of the northern barons

quiz.explanation: These stages go from 1204 to 1216: the loss of Normandy precedes the defeat of Bouvines, then the signing of the charter and its reissue by Henry III.
items: Loss of Normandy against Philippe Auguste
Defeat of Bouvines

quiz.explanation: King John Lackland placed his seal on the Magna Carta in June 1215, in Runnymede Meadow.

quiz.question: How many clauses are in the text of the Magna Carta of 1215?
quiz.explanation: The document drawn up under the influence of Archbishop Stephen Langton has 63 clauses.

title: The Black Death in Europe
description: Between 1347 and 1353, bubonic plague killed 30 to 60% of Europeans. A health catastrophe that shook medieval society and sped up the shift into a new world.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Between 1347 and 1353, Europe was struck by an unprecedented catastrophe that would redefine the very structures of Western civilization. The **Black Death**, caused by the bacterium **Yersinia pestis**, fell upon a population already weakened by decades of famine and climate disruptions linked to the start of the <Little Ice Age>. In less than a decade, the epidemic killed between **30 and 60% of the population** of Europe, representing approximately 25 to 50 million victims.

This collective trauma was not just a major health crisis; it acted as a true accelerator of history, shaking the foundations of the feudal system and paving the way for a new social, economic, and intellectual organization. This course explores the dynamics of this pandemic, from its distant origins in the Asian steppes to its paradoxically transformative consequences for the survivors.

lessons.title: From Asia to Italy
lessons.content:
The epidemic finds its source in the steppes of Central Asia, where the bacterium circulates naturally in wild rodents. Its transition to humans and its global spread were favored by the <Pax Mongolica>, a Period of imperial stability that ensured the safety of caravans over long distances. As early as the 1330s, outbreaks appeared in China before following the flow of goods along the <Silk Road>.

The shift toward the Mediterranean basin took place in Crimea, in the Genoese trading post of <Caffa>. While the city was besieged by Mongol troops from the <Golden Horde>, the latter, decimated by the disease, reportedly used their siege engines to hurl infected corpses over the ramparts. The Italian merchants, fleeing the city by sea to return to Europe, carried the invisible bacillus with them.

In **October 1347**, twelve Genoese galleys docked at the port of **Messina**, in Sicily. The sailors on board were dying, displaying strange dark swellings. Despite the rapid expulsion of the ships by the authorities, the malady had already spread onto the quay. Within a few months, the plague moved up the Italian peninsula and entered the Kingdom of France via Marseille at the beginning of 1348.

[Black Death burial medieval plague]

{The siege of Caffa in 1346 is often cited as one of the first documented examples of biological warfare, although historians debate the actual impact of this macabre bombardment compared to the natural spread by rats.}

lessons.title: A medicine with no answers
lessons.content:
Fourteenth-century medicine, imprisoned by the dogmas of Antiquity, proved totally powerless against the violence of the infection. Doctors relied on the Works of <Galen> and the <Miasma theory>, thinking that the disease was transmitted by corrupted odors or astral influences. In reality, the primary vector was the **black rat** flea (<Xenopsylla cheopis>). When the epidemic killed the rats, the hungry fleas turned to the human host.

The most common form was the **bubonic plague**, characterized by the appearance of **buboes**: monstrously swollen lymph nodes. If the bacteria invaded the bloodstream, it caused **septicemic plague**, leading to blackish skin necrosis that left a lasting mark on the collective imagination as the **Black Death**. Without treatment, the mortality rate of these forms was around 80%.

[plague doctor mask beak]

A even more lightning-fast variant appeared during the winter months: the **pneumonic plague**. Unlike other forms, it was transmitted directly from person to person through droplets of saliva. The infection of the lungs was then systematically fatal within 24 to 48 hours. This duality of transmission explains the speed of spread within medieval urban centers, characterized by high proximity and chronic lack of hygiene.

lessons.title: Fear, flagellants, pogroms
lessons.content:
Faced with the scale of the disaster, traditional social structures faltered. Death struck all layers of society indiscriminately, from peasants to prelates, fueling an unprecedented spiritual crisis. The Movement of the <Flagellants> appeared, groups of fanatics traveling through cities and whipping each other to appease divine wrath. Piety shifted into a dark and obsessive form, illustrated by the **Dances Macabre** in art.

Scientific incomprehension pushed populations toward irrational violence. <Pogroms against Jews (1348-1349)> multiplied, notably in the Rhône valley and the cities of the Holy Empire. Jewish communities were accused, under torture, of having poisoned wells to destroy Christendom. Despite the efforts of Pope <Clement VI> to protect Jews through papal bulls, tens of thousands of people were massacred by crowds in search of culprits.

The fear of contagion also broke the most intimate bonds. The Florentine writer <Boccaccio> described in his Work how fathers abandoned their sons and wives their husbands. This temporary dehumanization bears witness to the state of shock of European civilization, where Institutions of charity and neighborhood were no longer enough to contain the daily horror.

{While the plague ravaged Avignon, Pope Clement VI remained seated between two giant fires in his apartments to 'purify the air'. Luckily, this suffocating heat kept the fleas at distance, which allowed him to survive.}

lessons.title: After the dying, the turning point
lessons.content:
From 1353, the pandemic receded after having taken almost half of Europe. While the demographic shock was immense, it paradoxically caused a spectacular improvement in the fate of the survivors. The **labor shortage** became the engine of economic change. For the first time, the value of manual labor exploded. Lords were forced to increase wages and reduce corvées to retain their peasants.

In Western Europe, this dynamic led to a massive decline in **serfdom**. Workers, having become Rare and therefore precious, could now play the competition between seigneurial domains. This redistribution of wealth stimulated domestic consumption and forced owners to innovate technically to compensate for the lack of hands, laying the foundations for the agricultural and mechanical progress of the following Period.

On the intellectual level, the failure of religious and medical authorities before the scourge favored a critical spirit. People began to prioritize direct observation and experimentation over old sacred texts. By releasing immense inheritages and creating an urgent need for Reconstruction, the Black Death, in a cruel but decisive way, cleared the ground for the flowering of the **Renaissance**.

{The word 'quarantine' comes from the Italian 'quaranta giorni' (forty days). It was the duration of isolation imposed by the city of Ragusa (Dubrovnik) and then Venice on ships suspected of plague, an effective empirical measure because it exceeded the incubation cycle of the bacillus.}

|| Between 1347 and 1353, the Black Death killed 30 to 60% of the European population, causing an unprecedented demographic collapse that paradoxically accelerated the end of feudalism and the rise of the Renaissance. ||

title: Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War
description: In 1429, a 17-year-old peasant girl persuaded the Dauphin to hand her an army. Within months, Joan of Arc turned around a war France seemed to have lost.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
In **1429**, while the kingdom of France seemed doomed to disappear under English domination, a **17-year-old** peasant girl from Domrémy emerged on the Politics stage. In just a few months, **Joan of Arc** managed to convince the heir prince to entrust her with an army, reversing the course of a century-old conflict.

[Joan of Arc portrait]

Her odyssey, though brief, marked a definitive turning point in the **Hundred Years' War**. She did not only transform the military situation but redefined French royal **Legitimacy** by relying on a fervor born from medieval <providentialism>. This course analyzes how this charismatic figure was able to transform an announced debacle into a sovereign reconquest.

lessons.title: A France cut in two
lessons.content:
The **Hundred Years' War** (1337-1453) was not a monolithic block, but a succession of dynastic crises pitting the Plantagenets (Kings of England) against the Valois (Kings of France). At the dawn of 1429, the French situation was catastrophic, marked by unprecedented territorial and political fragmentation. The country was fractured by a civil war pitting the <Armagnacs>, supporters of French Legitimacy, against the <Burgundians>, allies of England.

The <Treaty of Troyes (1420)> dealt the final blow to Valois sovereignty. King Charles VI, weakened by mental illness, disinherited his son, the Dauphin **Charles VII**, in favor of the English king **Henry V**. Upon the death of both sovereigns in 1422, the young Henry VI of England was proclaimed King of France and England in Paris. Charles VII, whom his enemies mocked as the "little king of Bourges," controlled only a fraction of the territory south of the Loire.

In **1428**, the noose tightened dangerously around the last French possessions. The English besieged **Orléans**, the strategic city closing off access to the south of the country. If the city fell, the path to Bourges would be open and Charles VII's Legitimacy would definitively collapse. It was in this context of total despair that Joan, claiming to be invested with divine will, left her native Lorraine to join the court.

lessons.title: From Domrémy to Chinon
lessons.content: From Domrémy to Chinon: the providential mission

lessons.title: Orléans, Reims, then the fall
lessons.content: {During her examination at Poitiers, royal matrons had to verify her virginity: at the time, it was believed that a witch could not be a virgin, as she would have necessarily concluded a carnal pact with the devil.}

lessons.title: Martyr and memory
lessons.content:
Joan's arrival in Orléans in **May 1429** caused a massive psychological shock. In just **nine days**, she broke a siege that had been dragging on for seven months. Her presence on the ramparts and her strategy of direct offensive galvanized exhausted French troops. The English, terrified by this "witch" that nothing could stop, began to retreat, seeing in their successive defeats a sign of divine abandonment.

Consolidating her advantage, Joan insisted that Charles VII go immediately to Reims, despite it being located in the middle of territory controlled by the <Burgundians>. On **July 17, 1429**, the Dauphin was crowned King of France. This ceremony radically changed the nature of the conflict: Charles VII was no longer one pretender among others, he became the Lord's anointed. The <Treaty of Troyes (1420)> became void in the face of the symbolic power of the sacred anointing.

Despite this success, the momentum faded in the face of diplomatic realities. Joan failed to retake Paris in September 1429, because the royal court now preferred to negotiate with the Duke of Burgundy to stabilize the kingdom. On **May 23, 1430**, during a skirmish at Compiègne, she was captured by Burgundian supporters. The latter, faithful to their English alliance, sold her to their allies for the colossal Sum of 10,000 livres tournois.

{During her trial, the judges tried to trap her by asking if she was in a state of grace. Joan replied with a theological finesse that stunned the assembly: 'If I am not, may God put me there; if I am, may God keep me there.'}

quiz.question: How old was Joan of Arc when she joined the dauphin Charles in 1429?
quiz.explanation: Jeanne was 17 when she left Domrémy to convince the dauphin to entrust her with an army.

quiz.question: Where did Joan of Arc come from?
quiz.explanation: Jeanne is a peasant girl from Domrémy, in Lorraine.

quiz.question: True or false: the Hundred Years' War pitted the kings of France against the kings of Spain.
quiz.explanation: The Hundred Years' War pitted the kings of England, the Plantagenets, against the kings of France, the Valois, not Spain.

quiz.question: What does the Treaty of Troyes of 1420 provide?
quiz.explanation: The Treaty of Troyes disinherits the Dauphin Charles in favor of the King of England, whose reign is proclaimed in Paris.
options: The dauphin is disinherited in favor of the King of England
Joan of Arc is made a knight
The immediate coronation of Charles VII in Reims

quiz.question: What mission does Jeanne say she received from her voices?
quiz.explanation: His voices order him to lift the siege of Orléans, then to lead the dauphin to the coronation of Reims, the only rite which makes a true king.
options: Lift the siege of Orléans then lead the dauphin to the coronation of Reims
Driving the Burgundians out of Paris

quiz.question: In what year did Joan of Arc raise the siege of Orléans?
quiz.explanation: Joan broke the siege of Orléans in May 1429, in just nine days.

quiz.question: True or false: Joan of Arc killed many enemies with her own hand during battle.
quiz.explanation: Jeanne has never killed an enemy with her own hand; she preferred to carry her banner to lead without shedding blood herself.

quiz.question: Put these events in the life of Joan of Arc in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones go from 1420 to 1431: the treaty of Troyes, then Orléans and Reims in 1429, the capture in 1430 and the execution in 1431.
items: The Treaty of Troyes disinherits the dauphin
Joan lifts the siege of Orléans
The coronation of Charles VII in Reims
The capture of Jeanne at Compiègne

title: The Fall of Constantinople
description: On May 29, 1453, after 53 days of siege, the Ottomans forced the walls of Constantinople. The New Rome fell, and the Middle Ages tipped into a new age.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
May 29, 1453, marks a fundamental break in the History of humanity. After 53 days of a relentless siege, the troops of the young Ottoman Sultan entered **Istanbul** through a breach made in defenses once deemed impregnable.

[Constantinople Theodosian walls]

The city, which had served as a rampart for Christendom and a conservatory for ancient culture for over a millennium, collapsed in a few hours under the blows of revolutionary artillery. This Event did not just signify the disappearance of the **Eastern Roman Empire**; it acted as a geopolitical earthquake that closed the medieval era. By locking down the trade routes to the East, the fall of "New Rome" forced Christian Europe to reinvent itself and turn toward new maritime horizons.

lessons.title: A capital already half dead
lessons.content:
Founded in 330 by Emperor **Constantine I**, the city was for a long time the beacon of European civilization. Its strategic position at the crossroads of Europe and Asia ensured unparalleled prosperity. In the 15th century, however, the **Byzantine Empire** was but a shadow of its former self. Weakened by internal struggles and especially by <The Sack of Constantinople by the 4th Crusade (1204)>, the Empire had been reduced to its capital and a few scattered territories in Greece.

Its population, which once reached 500,000 inhabitants, was no more than **50,000 souls** living amidst ruins and market gardens within its very walls. Faced with this decline, the power of the **Ottoman Empire** never ceased to grow, methodically conquering Anatolia and the Balkans. In 1453, Constantinople was a Christian enclave at the heart of an Ottoman sea, an isolated "city-state" whose survival depended only on its historical prestige and geography.

Despite this destitution, the city retained a major asset: the **Theodosian Walls**. Built in the 5th century, they consisted of a triple line of defense with deep ditches and massive towers. For a thousand years, no attacker had succeeded in forcing this defensive system by land, making Constantinople a fortress reputed to be impregnable, capable of resisting even against armies vastly superior in number.

{Despite the Ottoman encirclement, the Byzantins continued to quarrel over points of theology so pointed that the expression "Byzantine discussion" has remained to designate an endless and useless debate in the midst of mortal danger.}

lessons.title: Mehmed II and the cannon
lessons.content:
In 1451, **Mehmed II** acceded to the Ottoman throne at the age of 19. Unlike his predecessors, he was convinced that only the taking of the "City" would ensure the durability of his empire and his own glory. He prepared the assault with an unprecedented mathematical and technical rigor for the time, aware that the ancient walls would not yield to classic medieval tactics.

[Mehmed II portrait sultan]

The central element of his strategy was the massive use of gunpowder. He hired a metal founder named **Urban**, who designed the "Basilica" for him, a monstrous piece of artillery. This 8-meter long cannon was capable of hurling stone balls of **600 kg** over more than a kilometer. This is one of the first historical examples where artillery technology rendered the strongest medieval fortifications obsolete, changing the nature of siege warfare forever.

The siege officially began on **April 2, 1453**. Mehmed II had a colossal army, estimated at between 80,000 and 200,000 men, including the famous <Janissaries>. Opposite him, Emperor **Constantine XI Palaiologos** could only align **7,000 soldiers**, a significant portion of whom were Genoese and Venetian volunteers. Despite this disproportion of ten to one, the defenders managed to plug the breaches every night with debris of wood and earth, defying the Ottoman artillery for nearly two months.

{Urban's giant cannon was so heavy that it required 60 oxen and 400 men to move it; it heated up so much that it could only fire 7 times a day at the risk of exploding.}

lessons.title: May 29
lessons.content:
Faced with the fierce resistance of the walls, Mehmed II used a stroke of genius to take the city from behind. Blocked by a massive chain closing access to the **Golden Horn** (the city's port), he had a greased wooden path built across the hills of Galata. In a single night, he had 70 of his ships towed by land to put them back into the water behind the chain, thus neutralizing the Byzantine maritime defense.

On **May 29, 1453**, the general assault was launched at dawn on all fronts. The exhaustion of the defenders and a gaping breach in the wall near the Saint-Romanus gate sealed the city's fate. It is said that a small secondary door, the **Kerkoporta**, was inadvertently left open, allowing the first Ottoman detachments to rush into the city enclosure and spread panic among the Christian soldiers.

The last emperor, **Constantine XI Palaiologos**, aware of the imminent fall, removed his imperial regalia and threw himself into the fray to die as a simple soldier; his body would never be formally identified. Faithful to the customs of the time, Mehmed II granted three days of pillaging to his troops before solemnly entering the **Hagia Sophia** basilica, which he ordered to be immediately converted into a mosque. Constantinople then became <Istanbul>, the new capital of a conquering empire.

{A few days before the final assault, a lunar eclipse terrified the defenders: an ancient prophecy claimed the city would never fall as long as the moon, symbol of Byzantium, shone in the sky.}

lessons.title: The shock waves reach Europe
lessons.content:
The consequences of this Event extend far beyond the Mediterranean basin. Immediately, the fall of the city caused an escape of Byzantine intellectual elites toward Italy. This <The Greek diaspora and the Renaissance> allowed for the rediscovery of original ancient texts (Plato, Aristotle) that had been forgotten or misinterpreted in the West, directly fueling the intellectual and artistic center of the Italian peninsula.

On the economic front, Ottoman dominance over the straits imposed heavy taxes on the trade of luxury goods. This control of Eastern trade by a hostile Muslim power pushed maritime nations like Portugal and Spain to finance expeditions into the Atlantic. By seeking a sea route to India to bypass the Ottoman intermediary, European navigators would accidentally transform the map of the World: **Christopher Columbus** would encounter America in 1492.

Finally, the fall of Constantinople consecrated the triumph of political Islam in Southeast Europe, modifying the balance of power for centuries to come. It put an end to the continuity of <Byzantine Law and the Roman heritage> as a living state entity, leaving European nations with the task of claiming its moral and cultural legacy through the emergence of modern states.

|| On May 29, 1453, Constantinople, which had resisted for 1,000 years, fell in a few hours, marking the end of the direct political heritage of ancient Rome and the symbolic beginning of the modern era. ||

title: The Aztec Empire
description: In less than two centuries, the Aztecs built a capital of 200,000 people on a lake. Their empire, founded on tribute and sacrifice, collapsed in two years once the Spanish arrived.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
In the heart of what is today Mexico, the Aztecs achieved an architectural and political feat unprecedented in pre-Columbian history. In less than two centuries, this migrant people built a lakeside capital of **200,000 inhabitants**, surpassing most contemporary European metropolises such as London or Rome. 

Their success was based on a unique symbiosis between cutting-edge hydraulic engineering, a demanding spirituality, and relentless military imperialism. However, this hegemonic power collapsed with disconcerting speed between 1519 and 1521. This course explores the meteoric trajectory of this empire, from its mythological roots to its annihilation through the encounter of two radically different worlds.

lessons.title: From marshland to a capital on the water
lessons.content:
The **Mexica**, the original name of the Aztecs, were initially a semi-nomadic people from a mysterious region named <Aztlán>. Arriving in the central valley of Mexico in the 13th century, they faced the contempt of local populations who were already settled, due to their warlike customs and their status as newcomers.

According to religious tradition, their tutelary god **Huitzilopochtli** had ordered them to settle where they saw an eagle devouring a snake on a cactus. This vision came true in **1325** on a marshy and inhospitable island in Lake **Texcoco**. What seemed to be a land of relegation became the birthplace of **<Tenochtitlán>**. To compensate for the lack of fertile land, the Mexica perfected the **<chinampas>**, extremely fertile artificial islands.

The city's insular isolation quickly became its greatest strength. Linked to the mainland by three monumental causeways and protected by sophisticated dikes against flooding and the lake's salinity, the city transformed into an impregnable lakeside fortress. It became a major commercial crossroads, whose markets, such as that of Tlatelolco, would astound European explorers by their size and organization.

{The Aztecs were unaware of the use of the wheel for transport and possessed no beast of burden; yet, they moved millions of tons of stone to build their pyramids.}

lessons.title: The Triple Alliance and tribute
lessons.content:
The meteoric expansion of Mexica power truly began in **1428** with the formation of the **Triple Alliance**. This strategic coalition united Tenochtitlán with the cities of Texcoco and Tlacopan. Although initially designed as a power-sharing arrangement, this alliance quickly fell under the total domination of the Mexica, who established themselves as the political and military masters of the region.

[Tenochtitlan Aztec city illustration]

The Aztec empire was not a centralized assimilating state, but a confederation of city-states forced to pay a regular **tribute**. The capital thus received astronomical quantities of maize, cocoa, precious metals, and quetzal feathers. This system ensured immense wealth for the nobility but generated deep hatred among the subjected peoples, such as the <Tlaxcaltecs>. This fragile political structure explains why, as soon as the Spaniards arrived, many provinces instantly rebelled.

Aztec domination was a war machine in need of perpetual conquests to fuel its economy and its rites. The empire rested on fear more than on consent, thus creating the conditions for its own downfall when faced with an external power capable of federating these grievances accumulated over decades.

{Cocoa was so precious that beans served as currency: in Tenochtitlán, a rabbit cost ten beans and a slave of good constitution could be worth a hundred.}

lessons.title: Gods, Cortés, and smallpox
lessons.content:
The survival of the world, in Aztec thought, is a precarious balance maintained by blood. According to the **<Five Suns Cosmogony>**, the current sun can only continue its course if it is fueled by human vital energy. This metaphysical necessity justified the sacrifices practiced at the summit of the **Templo Mayor**, the sacred center of the empire.

The arrival of **Hernán Cortés** in 1519 shattered these certainties. The emperor **Moctezuma II** received the Spaniards with fatal hospitality, influenced by ambiguous omens. Despite the discipline of the Aztec army, the invaders possessed decisive technological advantages: steel, firearms, and horses—animals unknown on the continent that caused considerable psychological terror.

However, the most devastating factor remained biological. The Europeans brought diseases such as <smallpox>, against which the Amerindian populations had no immune defense. In a few months, lightning-fast epidemics decimated the ranks of warriors and command structures, paralyzing resistance at the very moment Cortés besieged the capital with the help of thousands of indigenous allies.

{During the 'Noche Triste', the Spaniards tried to flee the city laden with gold; many drowned in the canals of Lake Texcoco because the weight of their loot dragged them to the bottom.}

lessons.title: Mexico City on the ruins
lessons.content:
The outcome occurred in **1521** after a heroic 80-day siege. Starved, deprived of drinking water after the cutting of the Chapultepec aqueduct, and ravaged by disease, **Tenochtitlán** fell to Cortés. The city was systematically dismantled, and its stones were used to build **Mexico City**, the new capital of **New Spain**.

The fall of the empire marked the end of a cultural era, but not the total disappearance of its influence. The agricultural traditions of the **<chinampas>** survive to this day, and the Aztec language, **Nahuatl**, is still spoken by over a million people. The symbol of the eagle and the snake remains the emblem of the modern Mexican nation, testifying to the persistence of an identity born in the marshes of Lake Texcoco.

Aztec history serves as a reminder that a monumental power can collapse if its system of domination is perceived as unbearable by its subjects and if it encounters an unpredictable technological and biological shock. The conquest transformed a brilliant civilization into a founding myth irrigating Latin American culture.

|| The Aztecs built a metropolis of 200,000 inhabitants based on a unique agricultural genius, but their fragile tributary system and smallpox allowed 500 Spaniards to destroy this empire in just two years. ||
