title: The discovery of America
description: On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus reached an island in the Bahamas that he believed was Japan. One navigational error opened the age of globalization.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
On October 12, 1492, after more than two months of uncertainty on the Atlantic Ocean, a sailor aboard the Pinta cried out: "Land!". For the crew, it was the end of growing anxiety; for history, it was the beginning of a global upheaval. **Christopher Columbus**, a Genoese navigator in the service of the Spanish monarchy, had just landed on an island in the Bahamas which he named San Salvador. Convinced he had reached the outskirts of Japan and the riches of Asia, he was still unaware that he had stumbled upon a continent whose existence Europe had forgotten.

[Christopher Columbus portrait]

This monumental geographical misunderstanding, born of a bold but erroneous reading of Greek and Arabic texts, would trigger the brutal encounter of two worlds. This event traditionally marks, for European historiography, the transition from the Middle Ages to the Modern Era. This voyage was not only a technical feat, but the culmination of a geopolitical and religious ambition carried by the Spanish monarchs at the end of the <Spanish Reconquista (1492)>.

lessons.title: A route west, and a very large mistake
lessons.content:
Contrary to a persistent misconception, **Christopher Columbus** was not trying to prove that the Earth is round. As early as the 3rd century B.C., scholars like <Eratosthenes> had not only established the sphericity of the globe but also calculated its circumference with astonishing precision. Columbus's real challenge was economic: to find a direct maritime route to Asia via the **west**. The goal was to access spices, silk, and gold without depending on Muslim intermediaries or taxes imposed by the Ottoman Empire on traditional land routes.

However, his plan rested on a major scientific calculation error. Columbus relied on Arabic estimates of the Earth's circumference, but he confused Arabic miles with Roman miles. He concluded that the Earth was much smaller than it actually is, estimating the distance between the Canaries and Japan at only 4,500 kilometers, compared to nearly 20,000 in reality. Portuguese experts, whom he first approached, detected this flaw and rejected his funding, judging the expedition doomed to starvation in the middle of the ocean.

In the end, it was Queen **Isabella of Castile** who agreed to bet on him. Through the <Capitulations of Santa Fe>, she granted him exceptional privileges: he was appointed **Admiral of the Ocean Sea**, viceroy of the lands to be discovered, and secured **10% of all future profits**. This contract transformed exploration into a highly lucrative state enterprise for the Genoese adventurer.

{To motivate his investors, Columbus claimed that sirens existed, but after seeing some in the Caribbean (actually manatees), he wrote in his journal that they were much less beautiful than in legends.}

lessons.title: 70 days to San Salvador
lessons.content:
On **August 3, 1492**, the expedition left the port of Palos with three ships. Two light and fast caravels, the **Pinta** and the **Niña**, accompanied the **Santa María**, a heavier vessel serving as the flagship. The crew, composed of 90 men, did not consist of convicts but of experienced sailors recruited thanks to the technical support of the **Pinzón** family. These experts in Atlantic navigation were essential for stabilizing a crew terrified by the vastness of the Ocean.

[Santa María caravel ship]

The crossing lasted **70 days**, a period far exceeding Columbus's forecasts. To calm his men's anxiety, the navigator used a psychological ruse: he kept two logbooks. One was real, the second was falsified and showed deliberately reduced distances traveled so as not to frighten the crew about the distance from the European coasts. Despite this, in early October, a mutiny was narrowly avoided thanks to the appearance of signs portending land (birds, floating branches).

On **October 12**, Columbus landed and met the indigenous populations: the **Taínos**. Convinced he was in the Indies, he called them "Indians". This first contact was marked by a total cultural misunderstanding. Columbus saw in them beings devoid of religion and complicated technology, immediately noting their potential docility and the gold jewelry they wore. This predatory gaze foreshadowed future colonial structures.

The return to Spain was a political triumph. Although the wealth brought back was modest (a few nuggets, parrots, and a few captives), the proof that a route was open to the west was enough to launch Spain into an empire race against its Portuguese rival.

{The names *La Niña* and *La Pinta* were only nicknames given by the sailors: the real name of the Niña was the *Santa Clara*, while the Santa María was nicknamed *La Gallega* (the Galician) because she was built in Galicia.}

lessons.title: The Columbian Exchange
lessons.content:
The arrival of the Europeans triggered what is called the **Columbian exchange**, a global biological blending. The Old World discovered the potato, the tomato, maize, cocoa, and tobacco—foods that would revolutionize demographics and consumption habits in Europe. In return, the Spaniards introduced to America wheat, sugar cane, coffee, as well as the horse and livestock, radically altering the ecology and transport methods of the continent.

However, this shock was also the setting for an unprecedented sanitary tragedy. The thousand-year isolation of American populations had prevented them from developing immune defenses against Eurasian viruses. Smallpox, measles, and influenza spread like wildfire. This "microbial unification of the world" caused the death of **50 to 90% of the indigenous population** in barely a century, creating a demographic vacuum that would facilitate territorial conquest.

On the diplomatic front, Spain and Portugal hurried to divide these new opportunities. Under papal arbitration, they signed the <Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)>. This document drew an imaginary meridian line in the middle of the Atlantic: everything discovered to the west belonged to Spain, everything to the east to Portugal. This arbitrary sharing of the world, decided without consulting local populations, laid the foundations of modern colonial empires.

{Although Columbus is credited with the discovery, the Vikings, led by Leif Erikson, had established a colony in Newfoundland about 500 years before him, but this settlement had left no lasting trace in European memory.}

lessons.title: A continent without its discoverer
lessons.content:
Despite four successive voyages, Columbus died in **1506** without ever admitting that he had discovered a new continent. It was the navigator **Amerigo Vespucci** who, by exploring the coasts of South America, scientifically understood that it was a "Mundus Novus" (New World). In 1507, the cartographer Martin Waldseemüller named this territory "America" on his universal map, definitively anchoring the Florentine explorer's first name in world geography.

Columbus's figure is today the subject of critical re-examination. Long celebrated as a messianic hero, he is now also perceived as a brutal administrator. His government of Hispaniola was marked by such violence toward the indigenous people and his own colonists that he was sent back to Spain in chains during his third voyage. His downfall illustrates the complexity of a man at the hinge between medieval mystical fervor and the Renaissance appetite for power.

Beyond the individual, the year 1492 marks the true beginning of **globalization**. The influx of silver extracted from American mines would boost the European economy but also trigger massive inflation. The center of gravity of world trade definitively shifted from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic. Europe, once on the periphery of the great silk roads, became the central pivot of a trade system now encompassing the four continents.

|| Christopher Columbus died in 1506 convinced he had reached Asia: his monumental error nevertheless united two hemispheres and triggered an irreversible biological, economic, and human upheaval. ||

title: The storming of the Bastille
description: On July 14, 1789, a Paris crowd stormed a fortress that held only **7 prisoners**. That act became the symbol of the French Revolution.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
On July 14, 1789, a crowd of angry Parisians stormed the **Bastille**, an imposing medieval fortress that dominated the east of the capital. Although the event is celebrated today as the trigger of modern democracy, it was initially part of a climate of panic and state bankruptcy.

[Storming of the Bastille 1789]

{On July 14, 1789, the Bastille contained only 7 prisoners: 4 forgers, 2 madmen, and a libertine aristocrat. It was less a dreaded prison than a political symbol—but symbols can change everything.}

Far from being a massive release of political prisoners, this act constituted a brutal break with royal authority. To understand how a simple riot for gunpowder became the founding act of the **French Revolution**, this event must be placed in the context of a monarchy at its breaking point, unable to reform itself in the face of an unprecedented economic crisis.

lessons.title: France on the edge of bankruptcy
lessons.content:
In 1789, the kingdom of France was going through a systemic crisis. Finances were exhausted, mainly due to the colossal cost of the **American Revolutionary War**, where France supported the insurgents against England. Faced with the impossibility of raising new taxes without the consent of the kingdom's representatives, **Louis XVI** resolved to convene the **Estates-General** in May 1789.

[Estates-General 1789 France]

This assembly, which rested on the system of the **Ancien Régime and the three estates**, immediately blocked any reform: the clergy and the nobility refused to lose their fiscal privileges. The **Third Estate**, representing the vast majority of the nation, refused this blockage. On June 17, it proclaimed itself the **National Assembly**, asserting that sovereignty now resided in the nation and no longer in the person of the king.

On June 20, during the famous **Tennis Court Oath**, the deputies swore not to separate until they had drafted a constitution. 

[Tennis Court Oath painting]

The king's response was ambiguous. While he seemed to give in officially, he secretly massed **30,000 soldiers**, mainly foreign regiments judged to be more docile, around Paris. The firing on July 11 of **Jacques Necker**, the extremely popular Finance Minister perceived as the only one capable of resolving the famine, acted as a spark. For Parisians, it was the signal of an imminent royal coup.

lessons.title: Muskets first, then gunpowder
lessons.content:
On July 12 and 13, Paris falls into insurrection. The toll gates - where taxes on goods were paid - are burned and gunsmith shops looted. The population desperately seeks means to defend itself against royal troops. On the morning of July 14, a crowd of several thousand people takes over the Hôtel des **Invalides**. They seize about **32,000 rifles**, but one item is missing: gunpowder.

Rumor has it that this powder was transferred to the **Bastille**. This fortress, although militarily obsolete, embodies royal absolutism through the use of the **<lettre de cachet>**. The prison governor, the Marquis de **Launay**, has a reduced garrison composed of Swiss soldiers and war invalids. He begins negotiations with delegations from the permanent committee of the Hôtel de Ville, but refuses to hand over the powder.

Tension rises. Around 1:30 PM, attackers manage to enter the first courtyard. In the confusion, shots break out. The governor orders to fire, causing **98 deaths** among the protesters. This massacre transforms a supply demonstration into a fierce military siege. Thanks to the arrival of mutinous soldiers from the French Guard and their cannons, the insurgents force the fortress gates in the late afternoon. De Launay surrenders to avoid total bloodshed before being lynched and beheaded by the crowd.

lessons.title: When a revolt becomes a revolution
lessons.content:
The fall of the Bastille causes an immediate shockwave. On the morning of July 15, the Duke of La Rochefoucauld-Liancourt wakes **Louis XVI**. To the King asking: "Is it a revolt?", the Duke replies with a mythical phrase: "No Sire, it is a revolution". Ironically, the King had noted the word "Nothing" in his diary on the date of July 14, referring only to his hunting record, empty-handed that day.

The King is forced to back down. He recalls **Necker**, withdraws his troops from the capital, and visits Paris on July 17 to accept the **tricolor cockade**, associating the white of the monarchy with the blue and red of the city of Paris. It is a de facto recognition of popular sovereignty. The news of the taking of the Bastille crosses France at lightning speed, often distorted by word of mouth.

In the provinces, this narrative merges with tensions related to famine to create **The Great Fear**. Peasants, fearing an aristocratic plot and the intervention of brigands, arm themselves and attack castles. They do not seek to kill nobles, but to burn the **terriers**, those documents listing manorial rights and feudal debts. This peasant uprising will force the Assembly to vote for the **abolition of privileges** during the night of August 4, 1789, legally ending medieval society.

lessons.title: From July 14 to a national holiday
lessons.content:
The demolition of the Bastille begins the day after July 14. It is organized by the entrepreneur **Palloy**, who transforms the fortress stones into souvenir objects (sculpted models, medals) distributed throughout the country. This project symbolizes the desire to leave no trace of royal arbitrariness. A year later, on July 14, 1790, the **Fête de la Fédération** celebrates national unity on the Champ-de-Mars, in the presence of the King, to mark the first anniversary of the taking of the fortress.

However, July 14 did not immediately become the national holiday we know. It was necessary to wait for the **Third Republic**, in 1880, for this date to be officially engraved in Law. The choice of July 14 by the 1880 deputies was strategic: it allowed for the celebration of both the revolutionary rupture of 1789 and the national reconciliation of 1790.

{The entrepreneur Palloy, in charge of the demolition, had dominoes carved from the fortress stones and offered a set to Louis XVI's son, the Dauphin, so the child could 'play with the remains of despotism'.}

Beyond the anecdote of the 7 prisoners, the Bastille remains the universal symbol of the victory of liberty over oppression. It marks the transition from a world of obedient subjects to a world of citizens equal before the Law, a principle engraved in the **Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen** of August 26, 1789.

|| By taking the Bastille on July 14, 1789, to seize gunpowder, the people of Paris transformed a financial crisis into a revolution, causing the final collapse of the feudal system. ||

title: Napoleon's strategy at Ulm
description: In October 1805, Napoleon surrounded and captured **60,000 Austrians** in two weeks, with almost no major battle. Ulm showed the power of speed.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
In October 1805, **Napoleon Bonaparte** achieves what military historians consider the "masterpiece of movement warfare." In the space of two weeks, the Emperor of the French manages to encircle and capture an entire Austrian army of **60,000 men** without needing to fight a single major pitched battle.

[Napoleon Bonaparte portrait]

This demonstration of strength, known as the **Ulm campaign**, marks a turning point in the art of war: victory no longer depends solely on the brutal clash of masses on the battlefield, but on speed of movement, secrecy, and logistics. It perfectly illustrates the transition from the classical strategy of the 18th century to Napoléonic Modernity.

lessons.title: Austria attacks too soon
lessons.content:
In 1805, European geopolitics shift. **Napoleon I**, crowned Emperor for less than a year, threatens the balance of power. Facing his growing hegemony, England, unable to land on the continent, uses its financial power to form the **Third Coalition**. It allies with the Austria of Emperor **Francis II** and the Russia of Tsar **Alexander I**.

Impatient, Austria decides to go on the offensive even before its Russian allies have reached the theater of operations. **General Mack**, an officer with rigid tactical conceptions, moves his army of **70,000 men** into Bavaria. His objective is to lock the passage to Vienna by settling in **Ulm**, a fortified position he deems impregnable.

Mack, however, commits a fundamental error of analysis. Convinced that the French will emerge from the <Black Forest> from the west to head up the Danube in a conventional manner, he takes no steps to protect his flanks or his rear. Meanwhile, the Russians led by **Kutuzov** are still hundreds of kilometers to the east, slowed down by a difference in calendars between the allied nations.

{The Russian army used the Julian calendar, which was 12 days behind the Gregorian calendar used by the Austrians, causing logistical confusion that isolated General Mack at Ulm.}

lessons.title: Marching faster than the enemy
lessons.content:
While Mack waits for him in the Danube valley, Napoleon executes his secret plan. He abandons his project to invade England and pivots the **Grande Armée**, stationed on the English Channel coasts, toward the heart of Germany. This movement is made possible by a major structural innovation: the <Napoleonic Army Corps>.

Contrary to the armies of the Ancien Régime which marched in a single massive block, the Grande Armée is divided into seven autonomous corps. Each has its own infantry, cavalry, and artillery, allowing them to take parallel routes without congestion. On September 25, 1805, these 210,000 men cross the Rhine. Napoleon then uses his genius for disinformation: he orders Marshal **Murat** to make demonstrations of force with his cavalry in front of Mack, simulating an imminent frontal attack.

While Mack's attention is fixed on the west, the army corps of **Bernadotte, Davout, Soult, Ney, and Lannes** execute a monumental forced march to the north. They bypass Austrian positions in a huge arc. Marching nearly 30 kilometers a day, the French soldiers arrive east of Ulm in record time.

This successful flanking maneuver is devastating. On October 7, the French cross the Danube behind Mack's army. The latter suddenly finds himself cut off from his communication lines with Vienna and his Russian allies. The "Ulm trap" has closed.

lessons.title: An army that surrenders without a battle
lessons.content:
Considered trapped, **General Mack** desperately tries to break the encirclement by launching a few skirmishes, notably at **Elchingen**, but French operational superiority crushes these timid attempts. **Marshal Ney** distinguishes himself by seizing the heights overlooking the city of Ulm, making any defense impossible.

[Battle of Ulm 1805 surrender]

On **October 17, 1805**, realizing the futility of continuing the fight, Mack surrenders. The official surrender is a humiliating spectacle for Austria: 27,000 soldiers lay down their arms before the Emperor. In the following days, the remnants of the routed Austrian army are captured by the <Grande Armée> launched in pursuit, bringing the total Austrian losses to **60,000 men**.

Napoleon defeated a major European power while sacrificing very few of his own men. For the French army, this victory belongs to the soldiers' legs as much as to their courage. The Emperor demonstrated that the concentration of forces on the adversary's nerve centers (their supply lines) allows for the annihilation of an army even before it can deploy for combat.

{After the surrender, Napoleon invited the Austrian officers to dinner. General Mack, dejected, introduced himself with these words: "Here is the unfortunate Mack," to which the Emperor politely replied while returning his sword.}

However, the Emperor's joy is short-lived. The very same week of this triumph, he receives news of the <Battle of Trafalgar>, where the British fleet decimated the French navy, permanently denying him mastery of the seas.

lessons.title: The road opens toward Austerlitz
lessons.content:
The fall of Ulm leaves the road to **Vienna** completely open. French troops enter the imperial capital on November 13, 1805, without meeting serious resistance. But the war is not over, as the remnants of the Austrian army have joined the Tsar's Russian forces. Napoleon must strike a decisive blow before exhausting himself in a war of attrition in Central Europe.

The brilliance of the Ulm maneuver would serve as a model for all military History. The theorist **Carl von Clausewitz** later analyzed this campaign as proof that the extermination of the enemy begins with their strategic paralysis. The peak of this campaign occurs on **December 2, 1805**, during the Battle of Austerlitz. Napoleon seals the fate of the coalition using the same principles: speed, surprise, and exploitation of the psychological weaknesses of his adversaries.

The 1805 campaign will be remembered as the year Napoleon ruled the continents, while England ruled the oceans. This duality would force the Emperor to seek other ways to defeat London, notably through the future <Continental System>.

|| In October 1805, Napoleon captures 60,000 Austrian soldiers at Ulm without fighting a single decisive battle, proving that maneuver and speed are worth as much as frontal combat. ||

title: The Battle of Waterloo
description: On **June 18, 1815**, in a single rainy day in Belgium, Napoleon's empire collapsed. Waterloo closed the Hundred Days and opened a century of monarchical order in Europe.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: On June 18, 1815, under a heavy sky and on ground soaked by the previous day's storms, the fate of Europe is played out in the plains of Belgium. **The Battle of Waterloo (1815)** marks the final act of the Napoleonic epic, where the French army faces a heterogeneous coalition led by the Duke of Wellington and Marshal Blücher. This confrontation is not just a colossal military clash; it represents the final collapse of the First French Empire and the birth of a new geopolitical balance that would stabilize the continent for nearly a century. In a single day, the figure of **Napoleon**, who had dominated the World with his tactical genius, sees his charisma shattered by a series of strategic errors and implacable Allied coordination.

lessons.title: The return from Elba
lessons.content:
After Napoleon's first abdication in **April 1814**, the fallen Emperor is exiled to the island of Elba. During this absence, the victorious powers meet at the **<Congress of Vienna>** to redraw the map of Europe and restore the Bourbon monarchy. However, Napoleon perceives the fragility of the **Restoration** and decides to attempt a daring return. On March 1, 1815, he lands east of Antibes with a handful of men.

This return, remembered in History as the **Hundred Days**, is a triumphal march toward Paris. The troops sent by Louis XVIII to stop him rally to him one after another. Leaving Grenoble, Napoleon declares: "The Eagle will fly from steeple to steeple until the towers of Notre-Dame". Without bloodshed, he retakes the Tuileries, but immediately finds himself confronted by a coalized Europe that declares him **"outlawed"**. For the Emperor, the only way out is a lightning military victory.

[Napoleon return from Elba 1815]

{Napoleon never met the Duke of Wellington before Waterloo. Although the two men felt mutual hatred and admiration during years of war in Spain, the Belgian battlefield was their one and only face-to-face.}

Napoleon's objective is clear: destroy the Anglo-Dutch forces of **Wellington** and the Prussian troops of **Blücher** before they manage to join forces. This is the very essence of his so-called **<central position>** maneuver, aiming to defeat separately two enemies whose combined strength would be invincible.

lessons.title: Two days earlier: Ligny and Quatre Bras
lessons.content:
On June 16, 1815, two days before the final confrontation, the campaign begins favorably for France. Napoleon defeats the Prussians at the Battle of **Ligny**, forcing them to retreat, while **Marshal Ney** contains the British at **Quatre-Bras**. However, despite this victory, Napoleon makes two major errors in judgment.

On one hand, he does not order Ney to crush Wellington at the opportune moment, allowing the latter to retreat to a solid defensive position on the **Mont-Saint-Jean** plateau, near Waterloo. On the Other hand, he believes the Prussians are permanently out of the fight. He then detaches Marshal **Grouchy** with 33,000 men - nearly a third of his army - to pursue the fugitives and prevent their return.

{Some historians attribute part of Napoleon's lack of responsiveness on the morning of June 18 to an acute crisis of hemorrhoids that supposedly prevented him from staying in the saddle to direct his usual reconnaissance.}

On the morning of June 18, the state of the ground is catastrophic after torrential rains. Napoleon decides to delay the attack until 11:30 AM to let the ground dry, hoping to facilitate the movement of the **<Grand Battery>**. This delay of a few hours will prove fatal: it offers Blücher the time necessary to reorganize his Prussian columns and march toward the sound of the guns instead of fleeing eastward.

lessons.title: The day that broke the Empire
lessons.content:
The battle begins with a diversionary attack against the farm of **Hougoumont** and a powerful assault on the British center at **La Haye Sainte**. Cavalry charges by the French, led by the fiery **Marshal Ney**, follow one another with heroic but desperate fury. Facing them, Wellington's army maintains iron discipline, forming into infantry **<Square>s** - geometric structures of soldiers bristling with bayonets that the cavalry fails to break.

While victory still seems possible for Napoleon, the first Prussian columns of Blücher appear on his right flank around 4:30 PM. Napoleon hopes until the end for Grouchy's arrival, but the latter, scrupulously respecting his initial orders, remains far from the battlefield. In a final gesture of despair, Napoleon commits the **Imperial Guard**, the elite corps of his army reputed to be invincible.

For the first time since its creation, the Guard retreats under British fire. This unexpected withdrawal breaks the morale of the French troops. The cry "The Guard is retreating!" spreads, triggering a general panic. The French army disintegrates and the retreat turns into a bloody rout, while Wellington and Blücher finally meet at the **Belle-Alliance** inn.

lessons.title: The final exile and the Europe of kings
lessons.content:
After the tragedy of Waterloo, Napoleon abdicates for the second time on **June 22, 1815**. Exiled this time to the island of **Saint Helena**, in the heart of the Atlantic Ocean, he will die there in 1821, leaving behind a France exhausted but transformed. The defeat at Waterloo seals the fate of the French Revolution exported by arms and inaugurates the triumph of conservative diplomacy.

The remodeling of the continent at the **<Congress of Vienna>** imposes the principle of monarchical **<Legitimacy>** against liberal and national aspirations. Europe is now framed by a solid alliance between Russia, Austria, and Prussia. Buffer states are created, such as the Kingdom of the **Netherlands**, to contain any future French expansion. While this system harshly repressed liberties, it paradoxically succeeded in establishing the "European Concert," a balance of power so stable that no general war would ravage Europe until 1914.

|| Waterloo (June 18, 1815) marks the final end of Napoleon I: despite the boldness of the Hundred Days, effective Allied coordination and French tactical errors, including the delay of the attack and the absence of Grouchy, lead to the fall of the Empire and a century of monarchical peace in Europe. ||

{The word "merde," attributed to General Cambronne in response to the summons to surrender at Waterloo, became so famous that it is still called the "mot de Cambronne" today. However, the officer always denied having said it.}

title: The Paris Commune
description: From March 18 to May 28, 1871, Paris governed itself for **72 days**. The experiment ended in the Bloody Week, a crackdown that left a lasting mark on French memory.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
From March 18 to May 28, 1871, the French capital experienced one of the most singular and tragic political experiments in its history: the **Common**. For 72 days, Paris established itself as an autonomous city, defying the legal government and experimenting with a direct democracy with a social vocation. This popular uprising did not arise from nothingness; it was the product of national humiliation, a winter famine, and a deep social divide between a radicalized working world and a conservative province. This revolutionary parenthesis ended with the **Bloody Week**, a repression of unheard-of violence that left a lasting mark on the French collective memory.

[Paris Commune barricades 1871]

lessons.title: After the defeat and the siege
What the Commune tried
lessons.content:
On **March 26, 1871**, elections were organized to appoint the council of the Common. On **March 28**, the Paris Commune was officially proclaimed on the Place de l'Hôtel de Ville amidst immense fervor. This new power intended to be a federation of autonomous communes, rejecting state centralism in favor of direct popular sovereignty. The council brought together workers, artisans, journalists, and intellectuals from various currents: Blanquists, Jacobins, or members of the **<Workers' International>**.

In less than three months, the Common legislated urgently to relieve working-class misery and lay the foundations of a new society. On the social level, it decreed the remission of unpaid rents, the abolition of night work for bakers, and the prohibition of employer fines on wages. Above all, it encouraged **self-management** by handing over workshops abandoned by their owners to worker cooperatives. 

On the political and symbolic level, the Work was revolutionary: it proclaimed the **separation of Church and State** (34 years before the Law of 1905), established secular and free schooling, and decreed the destruction of the **Vendôme Column**, a symbol of Napoleonic imperialism. Women played a central role in this effervescence, such as **Louise Michel**, creating discussion clubs and actively participating in the defense of the city, although they did not officially obtain the national right to vote.

[Paris City Hall Commune 1871]

lessons.title: The Bloody Week
lessons.content:
The Communard experience lived under the constant threat of the "Versaillais". Thiers, strengthened by the diplomatic support of the Prussians who released prisoners of war to reinforce his ranks, launched the final assault on **May 21, 1871**. This was the beginning of the **Bloody Week**, one of the fiercest repressions in European history. Versailles troops entered Paris through the Porte de Saint-Cloud and progressed eastward, district by district, barricade after barricade.

[Bloody Week 1871 Paris]

Violence was paroxysmal. In response to the summary executions of Communards by the regular army, radicalized insurgents shot hostages, including the Archbishop of Paris. In a gesture of despair as much as military strategy, major buildings were set on fire: the **Tuileries** Palace, the Court of Auditors, and the **Hôtel de Ville** were devastated by flames. The fighters of the Common, nicknamed the **Fédérés**, retreated step by step.

The final act took place in the **Père-Lachaise** cemetery, where the last 147 fighters were shot against a wall that would become the **Mur des Fédérés**. On May 28, the last barricade fell. The toll was terrifying: between **10,000 and 30,000** people were killed in seven days, not counting the thousands of deportations to the penal colonies of New Caledonia that followed the re-establishment of moral order.

lessons.title: A myth that lasts

title: The Belle Époque
description: Between the end of the war of 1870 and August 1914, Europe believed in progress. Electricity, world's fairs, brand-new art movements, and the cracks that led to catastrophe.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The **The Belle Époque (1871-1914)** refers to the Period of relative peace and cultural abundance extending from the end of the <Franco-Prussian War> (1871) to the outbreak of the <First World War> (1914). This name, carrying a powerful nostalgic charge, evokes a European golden age marked by an unshakable faith in progress, science, and reason.

[Paris Universal Exhibition 1900]

For the wealthy classes and the rising bourgeoisie of Western Europe, these four decades represent a parenthesis of unprecedented prosperity, monetary stability, and major technological innovations. However, this brilliant facade conceals social rifts and geopolitical tensions that would eventually lead the continent to a brutal rupture in August 1914.

lessons.title: When technology changed daily life
lessons.content:
The Belle Époque is structurally driven by the **second industrial revolution**. Unlike the first, centered on coal and steam, this one relies on new energies: **electricity**, **oil**, and advances in **chemistry**. These discoveries do not remain confined to laboratories but are rapidly exported into daily urban life, radically modifying the public space.

In a few decades, electricity illuminated metropolises, allowing for the extension of nightlife and the appearance of new transportation such as the electric tramway or the metro, inaugurated in Paris in 1900. Meanwhile, the **internal combustion engine** revolutionized distances with the first Benz automobiles (1885) and the pioneering flights of the Wright brothers (1903). Communication also accelerated thanks to Bell's **telephone**. 

The **1900 Universal Exhibition**, which gathered 50 million visitors in Paris, became the symbol of this technical and cultural domination. The French capital established itself as the center of the World, where the budding **cinema** of the Lumière brothers and the popular entertainment of the **Moulin Rouge** participated in a permanent effervescence. This confidence in man was theorized by the **positivism** of **Auguste Comte**, who postulated that science holds the key to all of humanity's problems.

[Eiffel Tower 1889]

{The term "The Belle Époque (1871-1914)" was only coined after 1914, in contrast to the horror of the trenches, to designate a lost paradise that contemporaries of the time did not name as such.}

lessons.title: Behind the scenery
lessons.content:
Behind the brilliance of the Parisian boulevards and the fashionable salons, the Belle Époque is a Period of violent contrasts. Prosperity was the privilege of a bourgeois minority, while the vast mass of workers suffered the full brunt of industrial capitalism's excesses. The working day often rose to **10 or 12 hours**, without real social protection against accidents or illness. Urban misery, marked by insalubrity, fueled growing class tensions.

This domination also played out on a global scale through colonialism. European powers, seeking new markets and raw materials, carved up the World. The **<Berlin Conference> (1884-1885)** institutionalized this division, fixing arbitrary borders on the African continent. Europe then perceived itself as invested with a "civilizing mission", justifying a violent exploitation of colonized territories.

On the domestic political level, stability was just as precarious. In France, the **<Dreyfus Affair>** tore society into two irreconcilable camps, revealing the power of anti-Semitic and nationalist currents within the Republic. This climate of tension shows that, despite the veneer of modernity, European societies remained crossed by deep hatreds and persistent archaisms.

quiz.question: What affair tore the French Republic apart during the Belle Époque, around a Jewish officer wrongly convicted of espionage?
quiz.explanation: Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish officer, is wrongly convicted of espionage: the affair reveals virulent anti-Semitism and lastingly divides France.

quiz.question: What scientific discovery by Albert Einstein, published in 1905, revolutionized the conception of space and time?
quiz.explanation: Einstein published the theory of Relativity in 1905, challenging classical notions of space and time.

quiz.question: In what year does the Universal Exhibition open in Paris, which attracts 50 million visitors?
quiz.explanation: The Universal Exhibition of 1900 attracted 50 million visitors and made Paris a global showcase of progress.

quiz.question: What event in June 1914 triggered the spiral that ended the Belle Époque?
quiz.explanation: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, triggered the game of alliances which led to the First World War.
options: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo
The fall of the French government
The fire at the Eiffel Tower
The signing of a Franco-German treaty

quiz.question: How many hours per day did workers often work during the Belle Époque?
quiz.explanation: Behind the windows of progress, workers often work 10 to 12 hours a day, without real social protection.

quiz.explanation: These milestones span from 1871 to 1914 and trace the rise and then the brutal end of the Belle Époque.

Construction of the Eiffel Tower
Paris Universal Exhibition

title: The Battle of Verdun
description: For **299 days**, French and German armies tore each other apart around Verdun. **700,000** casualties for almost no ground gained: the symbol of the horror of the trenches.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
In 1916, at the heart of the First World War, two industrial powers faced off for **299 days** within a restricted perimeter of a few dozen Square kilometers. The Battle of **Verdun** was not just a military confrontation; it represented the pinnacle of total war where Technique was put at the service of mass destruction. With a terrifying human toll of **700,000 dead or wounded**, this confrontation has become the universal symbol of the horror of Trench warfare and human resilience in the face of the deluge of fire.

[Battle of Verdun trenches 1916]

lessons.title: The German plan: bleed France dry
lessons.content:
At the beginning of 1916, the conflict bogged down in <Trench warfare>. The German general **Erich von Falkenhayn** then conceived an operation of an unprecedented nature: the objective was not a strategic breakthrough to win the war, but a radical war of attrition. His plan, summarized by the expression "bleeding France white", aimed to attack a transit point that the French army could not abandon for reasons of national prestige.

[General Falkenhayn portrait]

Verdun, a stronghold surrounded by hills and forts, was chosen as this "man-grinder". The offensive began on **February 21, 1916**, with an operation named <Gericht> (the court). For nine hours, an unprecedented artillery barrage pounded the French lines with **1,200 cannons**. The firepower was such that the landscape was literally leveled. 

The first days were disastrous for the defenders. **Fort Douaumont**, the keystone of the defense, fell to the Germans almost without a fight on February 25. This Event caused a political earthquake in Paris: the loss of this symbol made the defense of Verdun imperative, thus cruelly validating Falkenhayn's calculation that France would throw all its forces into it.

{The sound of the artillery shelling at the opening of the battle was so powerful that it was audible as far as the Vosges, more than 150 kilometers from the front.}

lessons.title: Pétain, the Sacred Way and the rotation of troops
lessons.content:
Faced with imminent collapse, general **Philippe Pétain** was appointed to head the sector. His military vision focused on two pillars: the power of artillery and logistics. He understood that to hold out, the front had to be supplied with men and ammunition at all costs, despite the city's geographical isolation.

This saw the birth of the **"Sacred Way"**, the only departmental road linking <Bar-le-Duc> to Verdun. To maintain this vital umbilical cord, Pétain organized an incessant flow: nearly **6,000 trucks** circulated every day, or one vehicle every 14 seconds. In the event of a breakdown, the vehicle was immediately pushed into the ditch so as not to break the chain.

[Voie Sacrée Verdun trucks]

At the same time, Pétain implemented the <Noria> system. Unlike the Germans who let their divisions exhaust themselves on the spot, he organized a rapid rotation of troops. This strategic decision had a major sociological consequence: **70% of the French army** would fight at Verdun at one point or another during the conflict. This battle thus became a collective national experience, touching almost every family in France.

The French resistance also relied on a stubborn defense of every meter of ground. The tragic episode of the **Bayonet Trench** (where soldiers were said to have been buried alive by a bombardment, their rifles sticking out of the ground) illustrates, although partially mythologized, the extreme violence suffered by the infantry.

lessons.title: The hell of the guns, for almost nothing
lessons.content:
From the summer of 1916, the intensity of the battle shifted. The opening of the <Battle of the Somme (1916)> by the Allies forced the German staff to divert part of its resources to another front, thus relieving the pressure on Verdun. The French then went on the offensive to retake the lost ground.

Under the impetus of general **Robert Nivelle**, French troops reconquered Fort Douaumont in October, then Fort Vaux. The battle officially ended on **December 18, 1916**. The assessment was bitter: after ten months of dantesque fighting, the front lines had almost returned to their initial position.

The environmental impact was such that the term lunar landscapes is often used to describe the battlefield. Millions of shells churned the earth so deeply that the topography was altered. Certain areas, saturated with unexploded ordnance and gas, are classified as **<Red Zones>**, permanently unfit for agriculture or habitation.

The final toll bears witness to the absurdity of the clash: about **370,000 French** and **330,000 Germans** fell or were mutilated. For the first time in history, the majority of losses were due to <Heavy artillery of the Great War>, dehumanizing the combat and transforming the soldier into mere raw material for the war industry.

lessons.title: From the ossuary to the handshake
lessons.content:
After 1918, Verdun established itself as an absolute <Location> of memory. The **Douaumont Ossuary**, inaugurated in 1932, houses the remains of **130,000 French and German soldiers** mixed together, as they were impossible to identify. The monument, whose cloister measures 137 meters long, overlooks a national cemetery of 16,000 graves, illustrating the scale of the sacrifice.

However, Verdun was able to evolve from a symbol of national hatred to a symbol of peace. The climax of this transformation took place on **September 22, 1984**. During an official ceremony, French President **François Mitterrand** and German Chancellor **Helmut Kohl** spontaneously held hands in front of the ossuary. This powerful gesture sealed the <Franco-German reconciliation> and placed Verdun at the heart of European construction.

Today, the site is a global center for peace. It serves as a reminder that the battle was not just a clash between two nations, but the shipwreck of a civilization. The remains, the disappeared villages, and the forests planted on the old craters serve as a permanent lesson on the dangers of exacerbated nationalism.

{The village of Fleury-devant-Douaumont was taken and retaken 16 times in two months, before being totally wiped off the map. It is one of the 9 'villages who died for France', which still have an honorary mayor today although they no longer have any inhabitants.}

|| Verdun (1916): 299 days of total industrial war, 700,000 losses for zero territorial gain and the birth of the symbol of <Franco-German reconciliation>. ||

quiz.question: What is the code name given by the Germans to their offensive against Verdun in 1916?
quiz.explanation: The operation bears the name Gericht, “the tribunal”, chosen by General Falkenhayn.

quiz.question: Why did German General Falkenhayn choose Verdun precisely for his offensive?
quiz.explanation: Falkenhayn wants to “bleed France dry” by drawing it into a battle of attrition on a place that it cannot give up defending.
options: Because France cannot abandon it without losing face, which allows it to bleed dry
Because Verdun is the military capital of France
Because Verdun is the least defended city on the front
Because the British are stationed there

quiz.question: For how many days did the Battle of Verdun last, from February 21 to December 18, 1916?
quiz.explanation: The battle lasted 299 days, one of the longest of the First World War.

quiz.question: True or false: Fort Douaumont, key to French defense, fell after heroic resistance lasting several weeks.
quiz.explanation: Fort Douaumont fell on February 25, 1916, almost without a fight, only four days after the start of the German offensive.

quiz.question: What is the role of the Sacred Way during the Battle of Verdun?
quiz.explanation: The Voie Sacrée connects Bar-le-Duc to Verdun: nearly 6,000 trucks travel there every day to maintain supplies.
options: Supply Verdun with men and equipment from Bar-le-Duc
Connect Verdun to the Maginot line
Transporting German prisoners to the rear

quiz.question: What does the troop rotation system, the Noria, put in place by Pétain allow?
quiz.explanation: Thanks to the Noria, the divisions are relieved regularly, so that around 70% of the French army fights at Verdun at one time or another.
options: Rotate divisions quickly to limit time spent at the front
Replace French soldiers with colonial troops only
Concentrate a single division during the entire battle

quiz.question: Approximately how many men, French and Germans combined, were killed or wounded during the Battle of Verdun?
quiz.explanation: The battle caused around 700,000 casualties in total, around 370,000 French and 330,000 Germans.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Battle of Verdun and its memory in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones range from the opening of the German offensive in February 1916 to the Franco-German reconciliation of 1984.
items: Opening of the German bombardment
Fall of Fort Douaumont
The Allied Somme offensive relieves Verdun
End of the Battle of Verdun
Handshake between French and German leaders in front of the ossuary

quiz.question: What does the handshake between François Mitterrand and Helmut Kohl in Verdun in 1984 symbolize?
quiz.explanation: This gesture in front of the Douaumont ossuary makes Verdun a symbol of peace between France and Germany.
options: The signing of a new military treaty
The inauguration of the European Union

title: The Russian Revolution
description: In less than eight months, Russia went from the rule of the tsars to the rule of the Bolsheviks. 1917 invented a model that would divide the world for decades.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The year 1917 marked a major civilizational rupture that would divide the <World> into two blocs for a large part of the 20th century. In less than eight months, Russia went from a thousand-year-old autocracy to a radical political experiment led by a disciplined revolutionary <avant-garde>. This shift was not just a simple popular uprising; it was a complex process where the collapse of an archaic regime under the weight of the Great War left a power vacuum that the Bolsheviks, led by Lenin, would fill with a mixture of opportunism and organized force.

[Russian Revolution 1917 <Petrograd>]

lessons.title: A Russia out of breath
lessons.content:
At the beginning of 1917, the Russian Empire was a colossal power with feet of clay. Engaged in the <First World War> since 1914, the country was unable to sustain the industrial and logistical effort required by a modern conflict. The Russian army, despite its courage, had already lost **1.7 million soldiers**, and mutinies were multiplying in the face of officers often perceived as incompetent.

On the home front, the situation was dramatic. **<Petrograd>** (today's Saint Petersburg) suffered from blatant shortages of flour and coal. **<Tsar Nicholas II>**, a mystical and autocratic sovereign, persisted in exercising undivided personal power, refusing the reforms demanded by the **<Douma>**. His decision to personally take command of the troops at the front in 1915 had a fatal political consequence: he was henceforth held solely responsible for military defeats.

[Tsar Nicholas II portrait]

The isolation of power was aggravated by the influence of Tsarina **Alexandra**, whose devotion to the healer monk **<Rasputin>** fueled the wildest rumors of treason and debauchery. In December 1916, the assassination of the latter by aristocrats failed to save the throne; on the contrary, it demonstrated that even the traditional supporters of the monarchy had shifted into opposition. The regime was no more than a facade ready to collapse.

{The poison (cyanide) used to assassinate <Rasputin> reportedly failed to kill him because the sugar in the cakes it was slipped into neutralized the effect of the product.}

lessons.title: February: the end of the Romanovs
lessons.content:
The revolution broke out in **February 1917** (according to the **<Julian calendar>**), not over a political slogan, but for bread. The women workers of <Petrograd> took to the streets, joined by strikers. The decisive turning point occurred when the garrison regiments, initially charged with repressing the crowd, **fraternized with the protesters**. Deprived of armed force, **<Tsar Nicholas II>** was forced to abdicate on **March 2, 1917**, ending **300 years of reign by the House of Romanov**.

An unstable balance then set in, known as **"double power"**. On one side, the Provisional Government, composed of liberal deputies, sought to transform Russia into a parliamentary democracy. On the other, the **<Petrograd Soviet>**, a council of workers and soldiers, held real authority over factories and barracks.

The head of government, **Alexander Kerensky**, made the historical error of keeping Russia in the war out of loyalty to his French and British allies. This obstinacy disconnected legal power from the deep aspirations of the people: immediate peace, bread, and land redistribution. This gap offered a historical opportunity to the most radical revolutionaries.

lessons.title: October: Lenin takes power
lessons.content:
Exiled in Switzerland, **Vladimir Lenin** understood that Russian instability was a unique chance for the world revolution. Germany, hoping to destabilize its Russian enemy, organized his return in a **"sealed train"** benefiting from diplomatic immunity. Upon his arrival in <Petrograd> in April 1917, Lenin rejected any collaboration with the government and published his **<April Theses>**, summarized by the punchy slogan: **"Peace, Bread, Land"**.

[Lenin portrait]

The Bolsheviks armed themselves and organized the **<Red Guards>**, a workers' militia. Under the impetus of Lenin and the <Technique> organization of **<Leon Trotsky>**, the insurrection was set for the night of **November 7, 1917** (October 25 in the Russian calendar). Contrary to the mythological imagery later constructed by Soviet cinema, the seizure of power was a surgical coup d'état.

Strategic points (bridges, stations, telegraphs) were occupied without a shot being fired. The **Winter Palace**, seat of the government, fell almost without resistance. Kerensky fled, and Lenin announced to the Congress of Soviets that all power was now in the hands of the Bolsheviks. This was not the end of the violence, but the beginning of a bloody **civil war** that would pit the "Reds" against the "Whites" (partisans of the Tsar or the republic) until 1922.

{During the taking of the Winter Palace, the insurgents discovered the Tsars' immense wine cellars. It is said they had to post guards in front of the bottles to prevent the revolution from sinking into general drunkenness.}

lessons.title: The birth of the USSR
lessons.content:
The success of the Bolsheviks rested on their ability to transform a social revolt into a centralized state machine. To ensure the survival of the new regime, they did not hesitate to use brute force. The **Cheka**, a secret <politics> police created in December 1917, inaugurated the practice of terror to eliminate opponents. The imperial family paid the price: in July 1918, <Tsar Nicholas II>, his wife, and his children were executed in a cellar in Yekaterinburg to prevent them from serving as a symbol for the White armies.

On the international level, Russia signed the separate peace of **<Brest-Litovsk>** in 1918, losing immense territories to Germany, but gaining the time necessary to stabilize domestic power. The foundation of the **<USSR>** (Union of Soviet Socialist Republics) in 1922 confirmed the birth of the first state claiming to apply **<Marxism-Leninism>**.

The <Russian Revolution> of 1917 would long remain the absolute model for the proletarian seizure of power for revolutionary movements worldwide (China, Cuba, Vietnam). It demonstrates that a determined and hierarchical minority can seize the destiny of an immense country during a major structural breakdown.

{In 1918, to catch up with the West, Russia went directly from January 31 back to February 14. The Russians thus technically never lived the first thirteen days of February 1918!}

quiz.question: What sparked the February 1917 revolution in Russia?
quiz.explanation: The February revolution started with demonstrations for bread in Petrograd; the workers take to the streets and the garrison fraternizes with them.
options: Protests linked to bread shortages in Petrograd
A military coup organized by Lenin
The total defeat of the Russian army against Germany
An attack against Tsar Nicholas II

quiz.question: How many years had the Romanov dynasty reigned when Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917?
quiz.explanation: The abdication of Nicholas II on March 2, 1917, put an end to 300 years of reign of the Romanov dynasty.

quiz.question: True or false: after the abdication of Nicholas II, a single power clearly rules Russia.
quiz.explanation: A “double power” was established: the Provisional Government on one side, the Petrograd Soviet, a council of workers and soldiers, on the other.

quiz.question: What slogan summarizes the program that Lenin launched in his April Theses?
quiz.explanation: Upon his return in April 1917, Lenin called for “Peace, Bread, Land”, a program which directly responded to popular expectations.

quiz.question: How did Lenin manage to return to Russia in 1917?
quiz.explanation: Germany, which wants to weaken its Russian enemy, organizes Lenin's return from exile in a “leaded train”.
options: In a sealed train organized by Germany, which hopes to weaken Russia
By a secret agreement with the Tsar

quiz.question: Who organized, alongside Lenin, the Bolshevik insurrection of October 1917?
quiz.explanation: Leon Trotsky, an outstanding organizer, prepared with Lenin the insurrection which overthrew the Provisional Government.

quiz.question: Put these events of the Russian Revolution in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones range from the fall of Tsarism in February 1917 to the founding of the USSR in 1922.
items: Abdication of Nicholas II
April Theses of Lenin
Capture of the Winter Palace
Peace of Brest-Litovsk
Birth of the USSR

quiz.question: What is the Cheka, the Bolshevik political police, putting in place?
quiz.explanation: The Cheka launched terror against opponents of the new power, particularly after the Bolshevik takeover.
options: A policy of terror against opponents

quiz.question: What ideology founded the USSR, born in 1922?
quiz.explanation: The USSR is the first state built on Marxism-Leninism, which combines the ideas of Marx and the method of Lenin.

title: The Great Depression
description: On **October 24, 1929**, Wall Street collapses. Within three years **25%** of Americans are out of work, and the crisis opens the way for political extremism in Europe.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
On **October 24, 1929**, a <Date> engraved in history as **Black Thursday**, the <New York> Stock Exchange experienced a collapse of unheard-of violence. This financial earthquake did not remain confined within the walls of Wall Street; it metastasized into a total economic paralysis that would be named the **<The Great Depression (1929)>**.

[Wall Street Crash 1929]

This <Event> marked the end of an era of insolent growth and the beginning of a decade of global misery. In the space of three years, the world gross domestic product collapsed by 15%, while unemployment reached dizzying heights, affecting **25% of Americans** and destabilizing fragile European democracies. To understand <The Great Depression (1929)> is to analyze how a speculative rush could precipitate the <World> toward an unprecedented social disaster.

lessons.title: The Roaring Twenties and the bubble
lessons.content:
After the <First World War>, the United States entered a <Period> of exceptional prosperity called the **"Roaring Twenties"**. Driven by technical innovation (automobile, radio) and access to credit, American society engaged in frenetic **<mass consumption>**. This euphoria naturally extended to the financial sector: between 1920 and 1929, the **Dow Jones** index multiplied by six, completely disconnecting market value from the actual health of companies.

[Roaring Twenties jazz 1920s]

The engine of this bubble was **<Purchasing stocks on margin>**. This mechanism allowed small savers to acquire shares by providing only a fraction of their value, with the rest being lent by brokers. As long as prices rose, the system seemed infallible. However, as early as 1928, warning signs appeared: industrial production stagnated and agricultural prices fell due to chronic **<overproduction>**, as wages no longer rose fast enough to absorb the goods produced.

{On the day of the crash, the panic was such that at the Chicago stock exchange, brokers symbolically hanged a wooden stork that served as the market mascot, accusing it of having brought misfortune instead of prosperity.}

Stock market speculation then became a headlong rush. Investors ignored that the market was **<overvalued>**. When the first doubts set in in October 1929, the machine jammed: the need to repay loans contracted for **<Purchasing stocks on margin>** forced players to sell at the same time, precipitating a free-fall in prices.

lessons.title: From the crash to the collapse of the banks
lessons.content:
On **October 24, 1929**, the bubble burst for good. Eleven million sell orders were placed in a single day, causing a widespread panic. On **October 29**, or "Black Tuesday," the fall accelerated. The debacle was total: in a few days, 30 billion dollars evaporated. Between 1929 and 1932, the market lost **89%** of its initial value. But the real drama lay in the contagion to the banking system.

[unemployed queue Great Depression]

Banks, having lent massively for speculation, found themselves with irrecoverable debts. At the same time, terrified savers rushed to the counters to withdraw their savings, causing **<bank runs>**. Lacking sufficient liquidity to meet the demand, **9,000 American banks** went bankrupt between 1929 and 1933. The disappearance of these **<Institution>**s led to the loss of deposits for millions of households, instantly ruining part of the middle class and drying up credit sources for industry.

{During <The Great Depression (1929)>, ruined Americans hitched horses to their cars to save on gas. These hybrid vehicles were ironically called "Hoover Cars," after President **<Herbert Hoover>** who was judged responsible for the crisis.}

The absence of credit and the collapse of demand caused a chain reaction: factories closed, production dropped by **46%**, and mass unemployment set in. Without a welfare state to support them, millions of people found themselves on the streets, depending on soup kitchens.

lessons.title: The crisis reaches Europe
lessons.content:
Thanks to Europe's dependence on American capital, the crisis crossed the Atlantic in record time. The United States repatriated their loans invested in the <Reconstruction> of Europe, suffocating countries like Austria and Germany. The mechanism of the **<Gold standard>** played a role here as a transmission belt: to protect their gold reserves, central banks raised interest rates, which further slowed global economic activity.

Faced with the catastrophe, governments initially opted for **<deflation>** policies, seeking to lower wages and prices to restore competitiveness. This was a crushing failure that only worsened social misery. In Germany, the hardest-hit country, unemployment jumped to **30%**, or 6 million people. This economic despair became the breeding ground for political radicalism.

The Nazi Party of **Adolf Hitler** exploited this distress to discredit the **<Weimar>** Republic. The link is direct: the Nazis' electoral successes followed the curve of rising unemployment precisely. In **January 1933**, Hitler came to power, promising bread and work to a people humiliated by famine. <The Great Depression (1929)> thus shattered the liberal order born after 1918 and paved the way for a new global conflict.

lessons.title: Roosevelt and the New Deal
lessons.content:
The election of **<Franklin D. Roosevelt>** in 1932 marked a major ideological turning point. By launching the **"New Deal"**, Roosevelt broke with liberal **<laissez-faire>**. The State became the central actor in the economy through a **<recovery>** policy. He regulated the banking system with the **Glass-Steagall <Law>** (1933) to prevent deposit banks from playing the stock market, and launched major public works to provide jobs for the unemployed.

However, despite these efforts, the economic recovery remained slow and fragile during the 1930s. The United States experienced a relapse in 1937. Paradoxically, it was the entry into a total war economy after the attack on **<Pearl Harbor>** in 1941 that would definitively absorb unemployment through an unprecedented industrial mobilization.

<The Great Depression (1929)> left a lasting legacy. It imposed the idea that the State must intervene to stabilize the economic cycle and protect citizens against market hazards. This crisis remains today the absolute reference for central bankers during contemporary stock market crashes.

|| After the crash of 1929, unemployment affected 25% of Americans in 3 years, the Dow Jones lost 89% of its value between 1929 and 1932, and the crisis directly favored Hitler's rise to power in 1933. ||

quiz.explanation: The American stock market lost approximately 89% of its value between 1929 and 1932.

quiz.question: What are the “bank runs” that hit American banks after the crash?
quiz.explanation: Panicked customers rush to withdraw their money, causing around 9,000 US banks to fail.
options: Waves of customers withdrawing their money in panic
Mandatory audits imposed by the State

quiz.question: Put these events of the Great Depression in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: The crash of October 1929 led to a chain of bank failures, then the crisis paved the way for Hitler and the New Deal response, both in early 1933.
items: Black Thursday on Wall Street
A wave of bank failures in the United States
Hitler's rise to power in Germany
Roosevelt's launch of the New Deal

quiz.explanation: To maintain their gold reserves, European central banks raise their interest rates, which further worsens the recession.
options: The gold standard, which pushes central banks to raise their interest rates
The gold franc, the single European currency

quiz.question: Who took advantage of massive unemployment in Germany to come to power in January 1933?
quiz.explanation: With 30% unemployment in Germany, Hitler exploited popular despair against the fragile Weimar Republic.

quiz.question: What policy did Franklin D. Roosevelt launch to respond to the crisis?
quiz.explanation: Elected in 1932, Roosevelt launched the New Deal: major works, banking regulation and the start of social protection, to revive the economy.

title: The Battle of Stalingrad
description: From the summer of 1942 to February 1943, Germans and Soviets killed each other in the ruins of a city on the Volga. Stalingrad became the turning point of the Second World War.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
From the summer of 1942 to February 2, 1943, the world had its eyes fixed on a devastated strip of land along the Volga. The **battle of Stalingrad** represented not just a clash between two military powers, but the psychological and material tipping point of the Second World War. In the charred ruins of an industrial city, the Wehrmacht, previously deemed invincible, met a Soviet resistance ready for any sacrifice. With a toll exceeding **one million deaths**, this confrontation remains the deadliest battle in human history.

[Battle of Stalingrad ruins]

lessons.title: Hitler goes after the oil of the south
lessons.content:
In the spring of **1942**, after the failure of the direct offensive on Moscow the previous winter, Hitler redefined his priorities. He launched **<Case Blue>**, a massive offensive targeting the **south of the USSR**. The stakes were vital: to seize the oil of the **Caucasus** to fuel the Reich's tanks and suffocate Stalin's war economy.

In this plan, the city of **Stalingrad**, a major railway and port hub on the Volga, was initially only a secondary objective for flank protection. However, the symbolic dimension quickly took precedence over strategy. For Hitler, taking the city bearing the name of his rival was an ideological necessity; for Stalin, defending it became a matter of national survival. General **<Friedrich Paulus>**'s **6th Army**, the spearhead of the Wehrmacht, was diverted from its route to the oil wells to conquer this pile of bricks and steel.

The first bombardments by the <Luftwaffe> in August 1942 transformed the city into a lunar landscape of craters and skeletons of buildings. But far from breaking the defenders' morale, these ruins offered the Soviets thousands of ideal hiding spots for a fierce resistance.

{ Hitler was so certain of his victory that he had already printed invitations for a celebration banquet at the prestigious Hotel Lux in Stalingrad.}

lessons.title: Fighting house by house
lessons.content:
Faced with German technological power, Soviet general **Vasily Chuikov** imposed a brutal tactic to compensate for the inferiority of his troops: **"hugging"**. By keeping his soldiers within 30 meters of the enemy lines, he rendered German artillery and aviation ineffective, as the latter feared hitting their own men.

The battle fragmented into a multitude of micro-combats for every floor, every cellar, every sewer. The Germans bitterly called this struggle the **Rattenkrieg** (rat war). **Pavlov's House**, a simple four-story building, was transformed by Sergeant Pavlov and a handful of soldiers into an impregnable fortress. They held out for **58 days**, which is more time than the whole of France resisted the German invasion in 1940.

Industry did not stop: in the **Dzerzhinsky** tractor factory, workers continued to manufacture tanks under the bombs. The vehicles left the editing lines without paint and, for lack of transport personnel, the workers themselves drove them directly to the front, just a few hundred meters away. Stalin radicalized the defense with **Order 227**, summarized by the scathing slogan: **"Not a step back"**, punishing any unauthorized retreat with death.

lessons.title: The pincers that closed the trap
lessons.content:
While Paulus wore down his divisions in the rubble, General **Georgy Zhukov** secretly prepared a large-scale response. He identified the structural weakness of the German deployment: the flanks of the 6th Army were guarded by ill-equipped and poorly motivated allied troops (Romanians, Italians, Hungarians).

On **November 19, 1942**, the Soviets launched **<Operation Uranus>**. In four days of lightning breakthroughs, the two jaws of a giant pincer closed at Kalach-on-the-Don. The 6th Army, or about **300,000 men**, was totally encircled in a pocket of resistance called the "cauldron".

Hitler categorically refused any breakthrough attempt to save his troops, ordering Paulus to hold his ground. The aerial resupply promised by <Hermann Göring> was a total failure: the planes only managed to deliver a fraction of the tons of food and ammunition needed. Hunger, typhus, and a particularly harsh winter, with lows of **-30°C**, finished breaking the German resistance.

{ During the siege, the Soviets used psychological warfare by broadcasting the ticking of a clock over loudspeakers, followed by a message reminding that a German soldier died every 7 seconds in the USSR.}

lessons.title: The surrender that changed the war
lessons.content:
On **January 30, 1943**, in a desperate gesture, Hitler named Paulus **field marshal**. Since no officer of this rank had ever surrendered in German military history, it was a clear inducement to suicide. Paulus refused this useless sacrifice and surrendered on **February 2, 1943**.

Of the 300,000 men initially encircled, only **91,000 survivors** left for the prisoner camps in Siberia. The shock was immense: for the first time, Nazi propaganda had to admit a total defeat. In Germany, three days of national mourning were declared, while hope changed sides throughout occupied Europe.

Stalingrad marked the exhaustion of Germany's strategic reserves and the irresistible rise of the **Red Army**. The initiative passed definitively into the hands of the Allies. The city became the symbol of the victory of will over technical superiority, but at a terrifying human price: the reconstruction of the city would take decades, and the bones of soldiers from both sides continue to be exhumed from the soil of the Volga even today.

{ During the battle, the Soviets used "anti-tank dogs" trained to carry explosives under enemy tanks. However, as they had been trained with Russian tanks running on diesel, they often sought to hide under Soviet tanks instead of German gasoline-powered tanks.}

|| Stalingrad (1942-43) is the turning point of the war: the annihilation of the German 6th Army marks the end of Nazi invincibility during the deadliest battle in history. ||

Systematically retreat to the other side of the Volga

quiz.explanation: The Pavlov House resisted German attacks for 58 days, becoming a symbol of Soviet resistance.

quiz.explanation: Order 227, on the contrary, imposes “Not a step back”, prohibiting any withdrawal without an order.

quiz.explanation: On November 19, 1942, Operation Uranus closed its grip on the poorly defended German flanks and surrounded around 300,000 men.

quiz.explanation: Operation Uranus encircles around 300,000 German and allied troops in the Stalingrad pocket.

quiz.explanation: Hermann Göring, head of the Luftwaffe, promised an airlift which failed, leaving the surrounded troops to die of hunger and cold.

title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
description: On **August 6, 1945**, an atomic bomb flattened Hiroshima. Three days later, Nagasaki. The Second World War ended, and the nuclear age began.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
On **August 6, 1945**, at 8:15 AM, the sky over **Hiroshima** burst with a flash brighter than a thousand suns. In a fraction of a second, a single weapon - the atomic bomb - leveled an entire city, instantly killing between 70,000 and 80,000 human beings. This technological and human trauma was repeated three days later in **Nagasaki**. 

These events do not only mark the end of the **Second World War** in Asia; they seal the birth of the **nuclear age**, a civilizational shift where, for the first time, humanity acquired the technical capacity to destroy itself. Understanding these bombings requires going back to the origins of an unprecedented state secret and analyzing the political gears that led to this radical decision.

[Hiroshima atomic bomb mushroom cloud 1945]

lessons.title: The Manhattan Project
lessons.content:
The genesis of the nuclear weapon dates back to a major fear: that Nazi Germany would be the first to develop this devastating technology. Alerted by a letter signed by **Albert Einstein** (but written by **<Leó Szilárd>**), President **<Franklin D. Roosevelt>** launched the **Manhattan Project** in **1942**. This colossal industrial and scientific effort mobilized about **130,000 people** and absorbed a budget of 2 billion dollars, an astronomical amount for the time.

The project relied on three secret nerve sites. At **Oak Ridge**, uranium was processed; at **Hanford**, plutonium was produced. But the intellectual heart of the project was located in **Los Alamos**, New Mexico. Under the scientific direction of **Robert Oppenheimer** and the military command of <the general> **Leslie Groves**, the greatest physicists of the free world worked in a race against time.

The culmination of this research occurred on **July 16, 1945**. In the lifeless desert of **<Jornada del Muerto>**, the first nuclear explosion in history, code-named **"Trinity"**, pulverized a steel tower and vitrified the sand. Watching the mushroom cloud rise, Oppenheimer, marked by a deep classical culture, thought of the sacred Indian text of the **Mahabharata**: **"I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds."**

[Trinity nuclear test 1945]

{The Trinity test was so powerful that residents more than 150 km away thought they saw the sun rise twice that morning.}

lessons.title: Truman's decision
lessons.content:
Upon Roosevelt's death in April 1945, Vice President **Harry S. Truman** discovered the existence of the bomb with shock. At that time, Germany had already surrendered, but Japan continued the fight with fanatical determination, symbolized by the attacks of the **<kamikazes>**.

The American staff then considered **Operation Downfall**, an amphibious invasion of the Japanese islands. However, projections were terrifying: strategists predicted between **500,000 and one million American losses**, as Japan had mobilized its civilian population for total defense. For Truman, the atomic bomb appeared as a radical way to shorten the war and save American lives.

Beyond the military argument, a diplomatic dimension emerged. The **<Potsdam>** conference revealed growing tensions with the Soviet ally. Using the atomic weapon allowed the United States to assert an incontestable supremacy over the **USSR** before the post-war division of the world. Hiroshima was chosen because it housed an important military command center and its bowl-like terrain allowed for the concentration of the blast effects.

{The city of Hiroshima had been deliberately preserved from conventional bombing so that experts could precisely assess the damage caused by a single nuclear shock wave.}

lessons.title: Two bombs, then surrender
lessons.content:
On **August 6, 1945**, the **B**-29 bomber **Enola Gay**, piloted by Paul Tibbets, dropped **"Little Boy"**, a uranium bomb. The explosion at 600 meters altitude generated a thermal temperature of several million degrees. Bodies at ground zero were instantly vaporized, sometimes leaving only shadows printed on walls. The number of victims rose to **140,000 deaths** by the end of the year, including deaths related to burns and radiation sickness.

With Japan not surrendering immediately, a second strike was ordered on **August 9, 1945**. The second bomber, the **<Bockscar>**, headed toward its primary target, **<Kokura>**, but thick cloud cover forced it to divert to its secondary target: **Nagasaki**. The plutonium bomb **"Fat Man"** caused 70,000 immediate victims there. The same day, the **USSR's entry into the war against Japan** shattered Tokyo's hope for Soviet mediation.

Faced with the total annihilation promised by Truman, Emperor **Hirohito** made an unprecedented decision: he imposed peace on his war council. On **August 15, 1945**, Japanese radio broadcast the **<Gyokuon-hōsō>**. For the first time, the people heard the voice of the one they considered a living god, announcing that the country must "endure the unendurable."

{Tsutomu Yamaguchi survived both atomic bombs: he was working in Hiroshima on August 6, then, despite his injuries, took the train back to his home in Nagasaki, where he was present on August 9 during the second explosion.}

lessons.title: The long shadow of the atom
lessons.content:
The human toll of the bombings remains an open wound. Besides the immediate deaths, tens of thousands of survivors, called **<hibakusha>**, suffered all their lives from deformities, cancers, and intense social stigma. These events raised a profound ethical debate: can the use of a weapon of mass destruction against civilian populations be justified to end a war?

Geopolitically, 1945 marks the beginning of nuclear proliferation. Very quickly, world balance rested on **<Nuclear deterrence>**, a <Concept> where possession of the bomb prevents direct conflict between great powers for fear of mutual annihilation. The **World** entered the **Cold War**, paced by the arms race.

Finally, the Hiroshima experience led to the creation of international pacifist movements and strict regulation of nuclear energy. This moment in August 1945 remains the ultimate warning of science put at the service of destruction, setting the limits of what humanity can inflict upon itself.

|| Hiroshima, August 6, 1945: 80,000 deaths in an instant. Japan surrenders 6 days after Nagasaki - the nuclear era begins. ||

quiz.explanation: The Trinity test, on July 16, 1945, was the first nuclear explosion in history and confirmed that the bomb worked.

quiz.explanation: The Enola Gay dropped Little Boy on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, at 8:15 a.m.

quiz.explanation: The Bockscar initially aimed for the town of Kokura, but clouds prevented it from dropping its bomb, sending it back to Nagasaki.

quiz.explanation: The Soviet entry into war against Japan on August 9, 1945 destroyed the hope of mediation by Moscow.

quiz.explanation: Hiroshima was bombed on August 6, 1945, Nagasaki three days later, on August 9.

quiz.explanation: In a historic speech, Emperor Hirohito announced Japan's surrender on August 15, 1945.

quiz.explanation: The Hibakusha, the survivors, bear physical aftereffects and an ethical debate which still lasts today.
