quiz.explanation: In one month, humanity goes from the first successful nuclear test to the end of World War II in Asia.

title: Rosa Parks and Montgomery
description: On **December 1, 1955**, a seamstress refused to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery. Her arrest launched a **381-day** boycott and changed the civil rights movement.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
On **December 1, 1955**, in Montgomery, Alabama, a 42-year-old seamstress named **Rosa Parks** refused to give up her seat to a white passenger on a city bus. Far more than a simple isolated incident born of physical fatigue, this act of resistance took place in a climate of extreme racial tension and constituted the breaking point of an institutionalized system of segregation.

This individual gesture, immediately transformed into collective action, marked the true start of the modern civil rights movement in the United States. By triggering a massive boycott that lasted over a year, the Black community of Montgomery not only shook the local economy but also propelled onto the world stage a charismatic figure of non-violence: the young pastor **Martin Luther King Jr.**

lessons.title: A South cut in two
lessons.content:
In the mid-1950s, the American South lived under the regime of the **<Jim Crow>** laws. This legislative body, validated by the <Plessy v. Ferguson> ruling of 1896 under the "separate but equal" doctrine, imposed a strict racial segregation in all sectors of social life: from education to public fountains, including hospitals and transport.

In Montgomery buses, discrimination was particularly humiliating. Vehicles were divided into two zones: the front for Whites, the back for Blacks. However, a central "buffer" zone existed: if the white section was full, Black passengers sitting in this zone had to give up their seats. Worse still, the practice often forced Black people to pay their fare at the front, then get off to re-enter through the back door, risking the driver starting without them.

Faced with this oppression, **The NAACP** was looking for a "test case" to challenge the constitutionality of these laws in federal courts. Contrary to popular belief, Rosa Parks was not a chance figure: a seasoned activist, she had discreetly attended training at the <Highlander Folk School>, a training center for civil rights activists. Her profile as a calm, married, and respected woman made her the ideal candidate to embody the moral resistance of an entire community.

lessons.title: The refusal of December 1
381 days without buses
lessons.content:
Maintaining such a long boycott required a paramilitary organization. The Black community of Montgomery, which represented 75% of bus users, set up a vast carpooling system. Hundreds of volunteers used their personal cars to transport workers, while taxi stations owned by African Americans charged reduced rates equal to the price of a bus ticket.

The reaction of the authorities and white supremacists was brutal. Police harassment multiplied, the insurance for carpooling vehicles was canceled, and physical violence broke out. In January 1956, the home of **Martin Luther King** was the target of a bombing. His calm response, calling for the love of enemies in front of the ruins of his home, definitively established his moral authority.

[Montgomery bus boycott 1955]

The boycott weighed heavily on the city's finances. The bus company lost about 65% of its usual revenue, and downtown businesses, deserted by Black customers, suffered massive losses. The conflict moved beyond the local scope to become a national issue, capturing media attention and putting pressure on the federal administration.

lessons.title: The Supreme Court decides
lessons.content:
While the boycott paralyzed the city, the battle was also being played out on legal ground. Relying on the precedent of **<Brown v. Board of Education (1954)>**, which had banned school segregation, The NAACP lawyers took the bus case before the judges. On **November 13, 1956**, the Supreme Court of the United States confirmed that segregation on Alabama public buses was unconstitutional.

On **December 21, 1956**, the boycott officially ended. Rosa Parks and Martin Luther King symbolically boarded a bus and sat in the front. This victory demonstrated the effectiveness of non-violent resistance and direct economic action. Above all, it proved that local laws could no longer ignore the constitutional rights guaranteed by the federal state.

{At her death in 2005, Rosa Parks became the first woman and second African-American figure to receive the honor of having her remains lie in honor under the Capitol Rotunda in Washington, a tribute usually reserved for presidents and military leaders.}

However, the price of this courage was high: Rosa Parks lost her job and received so many death threats that she had to leave Montgomery for Detroit in 1957. This movement was not only the end of a local practice, but the trigger for a decade of struggles that would lead to the <Civil Rights Act of 1964>.

|| The Montgomery bus boycott lasted 381 days (1955-56): it revealed the leadership of Martin Luther King and proved that organized civil disobedience can legally break segregation at the federal level. ||

quiz.explanation: Nine months earlier, high school student Claudette Colvin, 15, had already refused to give up her place, but the activists had not put her forward.

title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
description: In October **1962**, the world spent **13 days** a hair away from nuclear war. Missiles in Cuba, fleets on alert: the Cold War reached its peak.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
In October 1962, humanity brushed against the apocalypse. For nearly **13 days**, the two superpowers of the **Cold War** engaged in an unprecedented nuclear face-off, where every decision could trigger an irreversible chain reaction. This confrontation, born of the installation of Soviet launch pads on the island of Cuba, represents the peak of tension between the Eastern and Western blocs. Missiles were operational, bomber fleets were on maximum alert, and the outcome of the conflict finally depended on the lucidity of a few diplomats and the composure of a single officer in an isolated submarine.

[Cuban Missile Crisis 1962 Kennedy]

lessons.title: Cuba, too close to the United States
October 14: the secret breaks
lessons.content:
On **October 14, 1962**, the secret phase of the crisis comes to an end. A spy plane **U-2** flies over Cuba and brings back photographs revealing the presence of launch pads for <SS-4> missiles. Faced with the fait accompli, Kennedy assembles the **ExComm** (Executive Committee), a restricted group of civilian and military advisors. For six days, in total secrecy to avoid a global panic, this group examines all options: from diplomatic passivity to the immediate invasion of the island.

[U-2 spy plane aerial photography]

Internal tensions are high within the **ExComm**. **general Curtis LeMay**, Air Force Chief of Staff, advocates for a massive air strike to destroy the missiles before they become operational. Kennedy, haunted by the specter of a miscalculation, fears that a direct attack would push the Soviets to invade Berlin or trigger a nuclear response. He eventually opts for a middle ground: the **naval blockade**, administratively renamed a "quarantine" to avoid the word "blockade," which is legally an act of war. On **October 22**, during a dramatic televised address, Kennedy reveals the existence of the missiles to the whole World and demands their immediate withdrawal.

{The man who truly avoided nuclear war was neither Kennedy nor Khrushchev, but Soviet submariner Vasili Arkhipov, who refused to launch a nuclear torpedo on October 27, 1962, against an American destroyer.}

lessons.title: Black Saturday
lessons.content:
Tension reached its peak on **October 27, 1962**, a day nicknamed "Black Saturday." A **U-2** plane is shot down over Cuba by a Soviet surface-to-air missile, killing its pilot. At the same time, in the middle of the Sargasso Sea, the Soviet submarine **B-59** is harassed by practice depth charges dropped by the US Navy to force it to surface. Cut off from all communication with Moscow and convinced that the war has begun, the Russian commander orders the firing of a nuclear-tipped torpedo.

Soviet protocol requires the unanimity of the three senior officers on board for such a launch. While the commander and the political officer favor the attack, **Vasili Arkhipov**, commander of the flotilla, firmly opposes it. His refusal likely saves the planet from a nuclear winter. In parallel, in the diplomatic backstage, Kennedy and Khrushchev seek an honorable way out. 

The secret agreement, negotiated via Robert Kennedy (the president's brother), is concluded: the USSR withdraws its missiles from Cuba under international control, in exchange for which the United States publicly pledges not to invade the island. A crucial clause that remained secret for years: the Americans agree to withdraw their own missiles from **<Turkey>** a few months later.

[Khrushchev Kennedy meeting]

{The "red telephone" between Washington and Moscow, installed after the crisis, is actually a teleprinter - not a telephone. The red telephone only exists in movies.}

lessons.title: After the fear, a little dialogue
lessons.content:
The Cuban Missile Crisis marks a major psychological turning point in the **Cold War**. Having realized they were on the brink of self-destruction, the two Giants begin a phase of relative normalization called **<Détente>**. The need for direct and rapid communication becomes evident, leading to the creation of the direct communication line between the Kremlin and the White House as early as 1963. 

It also marks the beginning of an awareness of the need to limit nuclear weapons. The crisis validates the doctrine of **<Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD)>**: since no one can win, no one must attack. On the political front, Kennedy emerges from the ordeal strengthened, appearing as a statesman capable of combining firmness and restraint. Conversely, Khrushchev, although having obtained the withdrawal of missiles in Turkey, is perceived as having backed down by party radicals. This apparent "weakness" will contribute to his fall in 1964.

The historical importance of this Event lies in the fact that it forced the World to consider the material reality of extinction. If the crisis was resolved by high-level diplomacy, it above all highlighted the fragility of military command systems in the face of chance and individual anonymous heroism, such as that of Arkhipov.

|| In October 1962, a single Soviet submariner prevents nuclear fire: Vasili Arkhipov refuses to validate the firing of an atomic torpedo. ||

quiz.question: Why did the USSR secretly install nuclear missiles in Cuba in 1962?
quiz.explanation: Khrushchev wants to compensate for the Jupiter missiles that the Americans have installed in Italy and Turkey, very close to the USSR.
options: To restore balance in the face of American missiles already installed in Italy and Turkey
To help Cuba defend itself against an imminent invasion by the United States

quiz.explanation: On October 14, 1962, an American U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet missile ramps on Cuban soil.
options: Thanks to photos of a U-2 spy plane, October 14, 1962

quiz.explanation: Kennedy chose a middle path: a naval blockade which he called "quarantine" to avoid the word "blockade", which is equivalent to a declaration of war in international law.
options: A naval blockade, which he calls “quarantine”

quiz.explanation: Black Saturday, on the contrary, is the most dangerous day: a U-2 is shot down and a Soviet submarine is almost ready to launch a nuclear torpedo.

quiz.explanation: Vasili Arkhipov, political officer aboard the B-59, said no even though two other officers had agreed to the shot.

quiz.explanation: The crisis lasted 13 days, from October 14 to 28, 1962, before Khrushchev announced the withdrawal of the missiles.

quiz.explanation: In exchange for the withdrawal of Soviet missiles from Cuba, the Americans secretly agreed to withdraw their own missiles from Türkiye.

quiz.explanation: The doctrine of mutually assured destruction is required: since no one can win a nuclear war, no one should start one.

title: The Algerian War
description: For **eight years**, France fought a war of independence on land it insisted was its own. The Algerian War brought down the Fourth Republic and left lasting scars.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The Algerian War (1954-1962) constitutes one of the darkest and most complex chapters of 20th-century French history. This conflict was not just a struggle for decolonization, but a true civil and identity war fought on a territory that France considered an integral part of its own soil. For eight years, the French state fought a determined nationalist insurgency, at the cost of a major institutional crisis that led to the fall of the Fourth Republic and the birth of the Fifth Republic.

[Algerian War FLN fighters]

This war, long referred to euphemistically as "events" or "law enforcement operations," left deep scars in both societies. It pitted irreconcilable worldviews against each other: that of Algerian nationalism carried by the National Liberation Front (FLN) and that of French Algeria defended by part of the army and inhabitants of European origin. Its outcome redefined France's role on the international stage and permanently transformed the French political landscape.

lessons.title: A French Algeria, on paper
lessons.content:
Algeria occupies a unique place in the French colonial empire. Conquered starting in **1830**, it was not managed as a distant colony, but as an extension of the mainland. From **1848**, it was divided into <French departments>, which means that for the political class of the time, leaving Algeria would be equivalent to amputating France itself. This legal peculiarity explains the state's tenacity and the initial refusal of any political concession to the indigenous populations.

On the ground, the social divide was immense. In **1954**, the population consisted of about **9 million Muslims** and **1 million "Pieds-Noirs"**, Europeans some of whom had been settled for several generations. Despite their status as French citizens, Muslims suffered from flagrant inequalities, notably through the Code de l'Indigénat, which was abolished late. The first sparks of the conflagration date back to **May 8, 1945**. While Europe celebrated the victory over Nazi Germany, nationalist demonstrations in **Sétif** and Guelma were suppressed in a bloodbath (between **6,000 and 45,000** dead depending on sources).

Faced with the impossibility of obtaining reforms through legal means, the **FLN** chose direct action. On **November 1, 1954**, nicknamed **"Red Toussaint"**, the movement triggered about 70 simultaneous attacks across the territory. The Interior Minister at the time, François Mitterrand, responded with absolute firmness: "Algeria is France."

{Unusual fact: Until 1999, the French state legally refused the word "war". They spoke of "law enforcement" operations to avoid granting FLN fighters the status of prisoners of war protected by the Geneva Convention.}

lessons.title: The Battle of Algiers
lessons.content:
From 1956, France engaged in a "total war" with the vote of <special powers>, which allowed the army to take on police powers. The contingent, made up of young military service conscripts, was massively deployed in Algeria. Nearly **400,000 French soldiers** patrolled the country to counter the <guerrilla warfare> tactics of the **FLN**, whose fighters hid in mountainous terrain or blended in with the urban population.

[Battle of Algiers 1957]

In **1957**, the conflict moved to the heart of the capital during the **Battle of Algiers**. To break the bomb-planting networks, general **Massu**'s paratroopers received full powers. While the army won an indisputable military victory by dismantling **FLN** cells, it suffered a devastating moral defeat. To obtain information, the use of **torture** (the "gégène" or waterboarding) became systematic.

This institutionalized practice caused an immense scandal in mainland France. Intellectuals like **Jean-Paul Sartre** or the historian **Henri-Iréneé Marrou** denounced a drift in republican values. France was torn apart: part of public opinion, initially in favor of maintaining French Algeria, began to doubt the <Legitimacy> of a war that corrupted its own ideals.

lessons.title: De Gaulle and the turning point
lessons.content:
The inability of the Fourth Republic to resolve the conflict led to a total political deadlock. On **May 13, 1958**, an insurrection by supporters of French Algeria broke out in Algiers, orchestrated by generals and "pieds-noirs" vigilance committees. Fearing a civil war in mainland France, President René Coty called upon the "providential man", **the general de Gaulle**. The latter returned to power, founded the **Fifth Republic** and strengthened his authority with a new Constitution.

[De Gaulle speech Algeria]

Initially perceived as the savior of French Algeria, De Gaulle quickly realized that maintaining French sovereignty had become an untenable diplomatic and economic burden. In the midst of the period of global decolonization, France was isolated at the <UN>. The general then initiated a spectacular turn toward **self-determination**. This choice was seen as a betrayal by part of the army and the settlers.

This tension led to the <Generals' putsch> in April 1961, an attempted coup d'état to overthrow De Gaulle and stop the independence process. Following the failure of this putsch, the **OAS** (Secret Army Organization) launched a campaign of blind terrorism, both in Algeria and in mainland France, to prevent any negotiation, radicalizing positions just as peace seemed near.

lessons.title: Évian, independence, memory
lessons.content:
The outcome occurred with the signing of the **Evian Accords** on **March 18, 1962**. They provided for an immediate <ceasefire> and the organization of a referendum on the independence of Algeria. "Yes" won with more than 99% of the votes on July 1, 1962. However, the end of official combat did not stop the violence. Bloody score-settling multiplied, particularly affecting the <harkis>, those Muslim Algerians who had fought alongside the French army, victims of fierce repression after the departure of the troops.

The summer of 1962 was marked by the massive exodus of the **pieds-noirs**. Nearly one million people abandoned everything to reach France, often welcomed with suspicion or hostility. It was the end of 132 years of French presence. The human toll was heavy: the **FLN** claimed **1.5 million deaths**, while current historians estimate the number of Algerian victims between 300,000 and 500,000 people, to which are added 25,000 killed French soldiers.

{Did you know? Despite independence, France kept its nuclear testing bases in the <Sahara> (such as in Reggane) until 1966, under secret agreements included in the Evian negotiations.}

|| To remember: <The Algerian War (1954-1962)> ended with the country's independence after eight years of fighting, marking the end of the French colonial empire and leaving a painful memorial legacy linked to torture, the exodus of the pieds-noirs and the fate of the <harkis>. ||

title: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu
description: From **March 13** to **May 7, 1954**, a French army besieged in a valley in northern Vietnam surrendered to the Viet Minh. The defeat ended French Indochina.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: On May 7, 1954, the entire <World> held its breath: in a distant valley of North Vietnam, a European colonial army, despite an apparent technological superiority, had just surrendered to an army of peasant-soldiers. <The Battle of Dien Bien Phu (1954)> does not only represent a French military disaster; it is the tipping point where the colonial era faded before the nationalist aspirations of the Third World in the midst of the **<Cold War>**. From the establishment of the entrenched camp to the agony of the trenches, this course analyzes how the logistical genius of a former history teacher ended seventy years of French presence in Indochina.

lessons.title: Indochina at war
lessons.content:
Since the 1880s, France had exercised its sovereignty over **Indochina**, the pearl of its colonial empire. However, the shock of the <Second World War> weakened this dominance. In **September 1945**, taking advantage of the vacuum left by the Japanese defeat, the communist leader <Ho Chi Minh> proclaimed the independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. France, refusing to lose its status as a great power, tried to restore its authority by force. It was the beginning of the **<Indochina War>**.

The conflict quickly sank into a deadlock. On one side, the **French Far East Expeditionary Corps** (CEFEO) had tanks, planes and elite troops. On the other, the **Viet-Minh** practiced a formidable <guerrilla warfare>. Avoiding frontal clashes, nationalist forces harassed convois and blended into the rural population of <Tonkin>. For French strategists, the challenge was to force this elusive enemy out of the shadows for a decisive battle.

General **Võ Nguyên Giáp**, commander-in-chief of the Viet-Minh, perfectly understood this trap. A former teacher, he theorized a war in three stages: clandestine resistance, mobile <guerrilla warfare>, then a general offensive. In 1953, he felt his army was ready for the final clash. Facing him, the French staff desperately sought a ground to break the communist momentum.

[General Giap Viet Minh]

 General Giap, having never received formal military training, claimed to have learned strategy by reading the accounts of Napoleon's campaigns at the Hanoi library.

lessons.title: The trap in the basin
lessons.content:
In 1953, General **Navarre**, the new French commander-in-chief, conceived a bold operation: **Operation Castor**. The goal was to install an air-land base in the heart of enemy territory, at **Dien Bien Phu**, to prevent the Viet-Minh from invading Laos and to force it to attack a fortified zone. In **November 1953**, thousands of paratroopers jumped into the basin to set up an entrenched camp protected by strongpoints with evocative female names (Béatrice, Gabrielle, Éliane).

The French calculation relied on a logistical certainty: the Viet-minh could never transport heavy artillery through the jungle and the steep mountains. Navarre was convinced that French aviation could destroy any opposing supply attempt. This reasoning ignored the determination of a people on the move and the genius of Giap. 

Under the cover of the forest, an army of shadows set in motion. Tens of thousands of coolies (porters) used reinforced Peugeot bicycles to transport up to 200 kg of equipment each. The cannons were dismantled, hauled by hand onto the ridges overlooking the basin, then camouflaged in bunkers dug directly into the rock, making them invisible to French aviation.

 The bicycles used by the Viet-Minh were so precious they were called "steel horses"; to support the weight of the cannons, the frames were reinforced with bamboo and metal.

lessons.title: 55 days under fire
lessons.content:
On **March 13, 1954**, the trap closed. To the astonishment of the French, a deluge of fire rained down on the camp. From the first hours, Viet-minh artillery destroyed the airstrip, the only vital artery for reinforcements. Colonel **Piroth**, commanding the French artillery, realized his tragic mistake: unable to locate the enemy guns to silence them as he had promised, he committed suicide in his bunker with a grenade.

The siege lasted **55 days** in atrocious conditions. The basin turned into a quagmire of mud and blood under the effect of the <monsoon> rains. The camp was progressively strangled by a network of trenches that the Viet-Minh dug every night to get closer to the French barbed wire. Airdrops became increasingly perilous, and a large part of the supplies fell to the enemy.

Despite the heroism of the CEFEO fighters, many of whom were legionnaires or African skirmishers, the strongpoints fell one after another. France requested a massive aerial intervention from the United States (Operation Vulture), but President **Eisenhower** refused to commit without British support. Isolation was total. On **May 7, 1954**, after final hand-to-hand combat on strongpoint Éliane, the <ceasefire> was sounded.

 On the first day of combat, the French fired 6,000 shells, but Giap's artillery fired 9,000, a firepower that the French staff judged materially impossible for a <guerrilla warfare> army.

lessons.title: The end of an empire
lessons.content:
The fall of Dien Bien Phu was a geopolitical earthquake. For the first time, a national liberation <Movement> defeated a European army in a pitched battle. The day after the fall, negotiations opened on an international scale. The **<Geneva Accords>**, signed in July 1954, confirmed France's departure. Vietnam was temporarily divided at the **17th parallel**: in the North, the communist regime of <Ho Chi Minh>, in the South, a pro-Western regime.

The human toll was heavy: the CEFEO counted more than 2,000 dead and 11,000 prisoners. The latter were taken to re-education camps during a deadly forced march; fewer than 4,000 of them would see France again. This defeat accelerated decolonization in French Africa, notably in Algeria, where the insurrection broke out a few months later in November 1954.

In terms of the **<Cold War>**, France gave way to the United States which, fearing the "<domino theory>" (the successive fall of Asian countries to communism), became increasingly involved in South Vietnam. Dien Bien Phu was therefore not only the end of a colonial war, but the prelude to the American **<Vietnam War>**.

 A tenacious military legend says that the names of the strongpoints (Béatrice, Gabrielle, Éliane...) were chosen by Colonel de Castries in tribute to his multiple mistresses.

|| To remember: <The Battle of Dien Bien Phu (1954)> (March 13 - May 7, 1954) marks the end of French Indochina by the surrender of Navarre's entrenched camp to General Giap, illustrating the victory of popular logistics over a conventional army. ||

title: The Armenian Genocide
description: Between **1915** and **1916**, the Ottoman government organized the deportation and systematic killing of much of the empire's Armenian population.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Between 1915 and 1916, at the heart of the turmoil of the First World War, the government of the Ottoman Empire orchestrates what will remain in History as the first act of systematic extermination of the modern era. Approximately **two-thirds** of the Armenian population living on imperial lands are annihilated by direct massacres and forced deportations.

[Armenian Genocide deportation 1915]

This tragic Event, resulting in the death of **600,000 to 1.5 million people**, marks a fundamental rupture in international consciousness. It forced jurists to invent a new Concept to name the unnamable: <genocide>. This narrative traces the trajectory of an ancestral minority that became, through the force of a radical ideology, the enemy from within.

lessons.title: A minority under pressure
lessons.content:
The **Armenians** constitute one of the oldest Christian populations in Eastern Anatolia, present on these lands long before the Turkish conquest. Within the Ottoman Empire, they are governed by the <millet> system, which grants them religious and cultural autonomy in exchange for a lower legal status and the payment of specific taxes.

In the 19th century, as the empire declines (the "sick old man of Europe"), the rise of nationalisms and pressure from European powers, acting as protectors of Eastern Christians, exacerbate tensions. The Armenians, who demand reforms and more security against looting, begin to be perceived by the central power as a "fifth column" serving Russian interests.

This mistrust degenerates for the first time during the **<Hamidian massacres>** (1894-1896). Under the reign of Sultan **Abdul Hamid II**, large-scale violence claims between 100,000 and 300,000 Armenian victims. These killings, which go unpunished despite Western indignation, create a dangerous precedent.

The rise to power of the **<Young Turks>** in 1908 initially raises hopes for citizen equality. However, within this Movement, a radical branch led by the triumvirate of **Enver, Talaat, and Cemal Pashas** progressively imposes **Pan-Turkism**, an ideology aimed at creating an ethnically homogeneous nation where non-Muslim minorities no longer have a place.

{In 1895, during the Hamidian massacres, the future founder of the Red Cross, Henry Dunant, sent out an alarm call for the creation of a national homeland to protect the Armenians, prefiguring the humanitarian debates of the following century.}

lessons.title: 1915: the machinery of extermination
lessons.content:
The outbreak of the **First World War** in 1914 acts as the final catalyst. The Ottoman Empire allies with Germany and Austria-Hungary. After the crushing Ottoman defeat against the Russians at the **Battle of Sarikamish** in January 1915, the Minister of War, **Enver Pasha**, shifts the blame for the disaster onto an alleged betrayal by Armenian soldiers.

Repression is immediate and methodical. It begins in Constantinople on **April 24, 1915**, with the arrest of over 200 Armenian intellectuals, deputies, and notables, who will be executed. This Date is today that of the worldwide commemoration of the genocide. Deprived of its elites, the Armenian population is disarmed: Armenian soldiers in the Ottoman army are transferred to labor battalions where they are exterminated.

In May 1915, the **provisional Law of deportation** (Tehcir Law) provides a legal framework for the massive expulsion of populations. Under the pretext of moving them away from combat zones, the government organizes the forced transfer of hundreds of thousands of civilians to the Mesopotamian deserts. These transfers take the form of actual "death marches.".

Able-bodied men are generally massacred as soon as they leave the villages by special units composed of criminals released for the occasion. Women, children, and the elderly, forced to march under a leaden sun without food or water, are victims of systematic abuses by guards and local tribes encouraged by the authorities.

[Armenians death march deportation]

{The Austrian writer Franz Werfel immortalized the resistance of a group of Armenians in his novel "The Forty Days of Musa Dagh" (1933); this book became such a powerful symbol of resistance that it was later read clandestinely in Jewish ghettos during the Second World War.}

lessons.title: Deir ez-Zor and the end of a world
lessons.content:
The survivors who reach the end of the deportation columns arrive at rudimentary **concentration camps** located in the Syrian desert, along the Euphrates. The site of **Deir ez-Zor** becomes the final destination of this ordeal. In 1916, the last survivors are systematically eliminated in further mass massacres or die of exhaustion and typhus.

The scale of the crime does not remain secret. Ambassadors from neutral countries, such as American **Henry Morgenthau**, as well as German officers - although allies of the Ottomans - send back terrifying reports describing a calculated attempt at extermination. Morgenthau would speak of a "racial murder.".

The annihilation is almost total in Anatolia: millennial religious structures are destroyed and Armenian property is confiscated by the State or redistributed to Muslim populations arriving from the Balkans. By the end of the war, the Armenian community of the Empire has lost two-thirds of its members, ending three millennia of continuous presence on these lands.

It was the observation of this specific crime that, years later, pushed the jurist **Raphael Lemkin** to forge the <Legal definition of genocide>. It was a matter of filling a legal void to designate the planned destruction of a group because of its very identity.

{After the war, a group of survivors organized Operation Nemesis, a secret mission to assassinate the main leaders responsible for the genocide in exile, including Talaat Pasha, who was killed in Berlin in 1921.}

lessons.title: Memory and recognition
lessons.content:
After the war, the main leaders of the triumvirate flee. Although Ottoman courts condemn them to death in absentia in 1919 for "war crimes", the birth of the Republic of Turkey under **Mustafa Kemal** (Atatürk) is accompanied by a policy of starting from scratch. The Treaty of Lausanne (1923) ignores the Armenian question, sealing the fate of the survivors in a vast <diaspora>.

Even today, the issue of official recognition remains a major geopolitical stake. Modern Turkey recognizes the suffering and massacres within the context of the chaos of the World war, but categorically rejects the term "genocide," contesting the intentionality of the Ottoman State and the number of victims. It practices what historians call State denial.

In the face of this denial, the work of memory has continued tirelessly. Since the 1960s, the Armenian diaspora has campaigned for the World to recognize the historical reality of 1915. In 2021, the United States joined the list of thirty or so countries, including France (since 2001), officially recognizing the genocidal nature of the massacres.

This fight for truth goes beyond the simple Armenian memorial framework; it highlights the importance of studying the mechanisms of mass violence to prevent new crimes against humanity.

|| Between 1915 and 1916, the Ottoman Empire organized the methodical extermination of 600,000 to 1.5 million Armenians, constituting the first genocide of the 20th century, the recognition of which remains a major subject of diplomatic tension today. ||

title: The creation of the UN
description: On **June 26, 1945**, **51** countries signed the Charter of the United Nations in San Francisco. Born from the ashes of the Second World War, the UN set out to spare the world the scourge of war.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
On **June 26, 1945**, 51 countries signed the **UN Charter** in San Francisco, the official birth certificate of a global organization whose primary objective is to save future generations from the scourge of war. Emerging from the trauma of the Second World War, the UN is not just a simple diplomatic alliance; it aims to be a universal legal and moral framework. This colossal project, initially led by the victors of the conflict, attempts to reconcile two often contradictory principles: the sovereign equality of nations and the political dominance of the great World powers.

[UN Charter signing San Francisco 1945]

lessons.title: The failure of the League of Nations
lessons.content:
The idea of <global governance> was not born by chance in 1945. It finds its roots in the first world conflict, when American President **Woodrow Wilson** prompted the creation of the **League of Nations**. Based in Geneva, this organization's ambition was to settle conflicts through law rather than iron. However, despite these laudable intentions, the League of Nations carried insurmountable structural weaknesses within it.

[League of Nations Geneva]

The first obstacle was its lack of universality. Although Wilson was its main architect, the US Senate, eager to preserve United States **Isolationism**, refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles. Without the world's leading economic power, the organization lacked political weight. Furthermore, the League of Nations had no coercive force. It could morally condemn an invasion, but it had no <Blue Helmets> or army to enforce its decisions.

Faced with the rise of fascism and Japan's expansionism in Manchuria then Italy's in Ethiopia, the League of Nations proved powerless. Its de facto dissolution in 1939 marked the end of a diplomatic utopia, but served as a crucial lesson for the designers of the UN: any effective international organization must imperatively include the great powers and have real means of pressure.

{ The League of Nations technically continued to exist officially throughout the Second World War, only being dissolved in 1946 to bequeath its assets and files to the new UN.}

lessons.title: The Security Council and the veto
lessons.content:
Learning the lessons of the past, the drafters of the San Francisco Charter designed a two-headed structure. On one side, the **General Assembly**, where each State has one vote, embodies the global discussion forum. On the other, the **Security Council** acts as the powerful executive body, responsible for maintaining international peace and security. Unlike its ancestor the League of Nations, the UN can vote for economic sanctions and authorize the use of force.

[UN Security Council chamber]

To ensure that the strongest nations do not lose interest in the organization, a mechanism of privilege was established: the **veto power**. The five great victors of 1945 (United States, USSR, United Kingdom, France, and China) became permanent members of the Council. This right allows them to block any substantive resolution, even if it is voted for by the majority of other countries. This was Stalin and Roosevelt's sine qua non for accepting international arbitration.

This political realism has its downside, however. From the end of the 1940s, the **Cold War** transformed the Security Council into a theater of diplomatic clashes. The veto was used multiple times by the Eastern and Western blocs to paralyze actions that threatened their respective interests, sometimes rendering the UN powerless in the face of conflicts indirectly involving the superpowers.

lessons.title: What the UN gets right out of the spotlight
lessons.content:
While the UN's political action is subject to the jolts of diplomacy, its humanitarian and technical action via its **specialized agencies** has transformed the daily lives of millions of people. The "United Nations system" is built around autonomous bodies that deal with global problems transcending national borders. The **WHO**, for example, centralizes global health surveillance and enabled the historic eradication of **smallpox** in 1980, a first in the History of humanity.

Other agencies such as **UNICEF**, dedicated to child protection, or the **UNHCR**, which manages massive refugee flows, make up for State failures in times of crisis. The cultural sphere is not left behind with **UNESCO**, whose objective is to preserve world heritage and promote education to prevent wars at their source. The UN has thus created a network of international solidarity that often operates in the shadow of major political speeches.

These concrete results show that the organization succeeded where the League of Nations had failed: becoming indispensable to the technical functioning of the modern world. Whether for the coordination of telecommunications, civil aviation, or food aid via the **FAO**, the UN is the logistical cement of globalization.

lessons.title: Contested, and still unique
lessons.content:
Today, the UN has **193 members**, almost all the States on the planet. However, it faces a growing crisis of Legitimacy. Its structure, frozen in the immediate post-war period, no longer reflects the current balance of power. Emerging powers such as India, Brazil, or Germany, as well as the entire African continent, challenge the exclusivity of the veto power of the "permanent five".

In addition to these demands for reform, the UN struggles to adapt to new threats that are no longer necessarily wars between States, but asymmetric conflicts, transnational terrorism, or climate change. The organization's operating budget remains derisory compared to its ambitions: about **3 billion dollars** per year, less than the budget of the police department of the city of New York, where its headquarters is located.

{ The land on which the UN headquarters in New York is built is technically not part of the United States. It is an international zone that has its own security force, its own fire department, and even issues its own postage stamps that you can only use from that location.}

Despite these criticisms, the UN remains the unique universal platform for dialogue. Without it, there would be no framework to negotiate global climate treaties or to regulate the law of the sea. It remains an essential crisis buffer, proving that even if it is not the "world government" hoped for by the idealists of 1945, it prevents the world from falling into total anarchy.

|| To remember: Created in 1945 to learn the lessons from the failure of the League of Nations, the UN relies on a powerful Security Council but is often paralyzed by the veto power of the 5 permanent members. While its political role is contested, its action through specialized agencies (WHO, UNICEF) is a historic success in terms of health, education, and humanitarian aid. ||

title: The birth of the EU
description: The European Union grew out of one practical idea: make war between France and Germany physically impossible by tying together coal and steel. Small steps led from **1950** to Maastricht.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The **European Union** was not built by a sudden global treaty, but by a pragmatic strategy of "small steps". Born in the rubble of the Second World War, it initially aimed at a very precise goal: making war between France and Germany not only unthinkable but materially impossible by merging the resources necessary for armaments. From this de facto solidarity, initiated in 1950, flowed a unique economic then political integration in the world, transforming a continent ravaged by nationalisms into a zone of peace and prosperity.

[Franco-German reconciliation Adenauer De Gaulle]

lessons.title: 1950: Schuman, coal and steel
lessons.content:
At the end of the war, the question of control over the Ruhr, Germany's industrial heart, crystallized tensions. **Jean Monnet**, Planning Commissioner, and **Robert Schuman**, French Minister of Foreign Affairs, then devised a revolutionary solution. On **May 9, 1950**, during the <Schuman Declaration>, they proposed to place the entire Franco-German production of coal and steel under a common **High Authority**. 

[Jean Monnet Robert Schuman portrait]

The choice of these two resources was not accidental: at the time, they constituted the foundation of any defense industry. By linking the economies at the base, the project's authors created a structural mutual dependence. This project gave birth in **1951** to the **ECSC** (European Coal and Steel Community), joined by Italy and the three Benelux countries. This was the first time that sovereign States delegated part of their power to a supranational body.

 Initially, Schuman kept his plan so secret that even his own diplomats were unaware of it until the very morning of the official announcement.

lessons.title: 1957: the Common Market
lessons.content:
After the success of the ECSC, the "Six" wished to deepen integration despite the failure of a common army in 1954. They met in Italy on **March 25, 1957**, to sign the **Treaties of Rome**, marking the birth of the **EEC** (European Economic Community) and **Euratom** (atomic energy).

[Treaty of Rome signing 1957]

The objective of the EEC was to create a vast economic space without internal customs barriers. This dynamic relied on the establishment of a common external customs tariff and the launch of structural policies, such as the <CAP> in 1962. This coming together fostered the exceptional economic growth of the "**Thirty Glorious Years**".

The attractiveness of this economic model pushed the Community to open up. In **1973**, the first enlargement integrated the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Denmark. This geographical enlargement modified the nature of the EEC: from a small industrial club, it became a global commercial power capable of carrying weight against the United States and the USSR during the Cold War.

 During the signing ceremony in Rome, the official treaties were not ready in time due to printing delays; the leaders actually signed blank pages for the official photo.

lessons.title: 1992: Maastricht and the euro
lessons.content:
The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 radically changed the geopolitical situation. To anchor a reunified Germany to Europe and stabilize the continent to the East, European leaders accelerated integration. The **Maastricht Treaty**, signed in **1992**, transformed the EEC into the **European Union** (EU).

This treaty relied on three pillars: economic and monetary union, a common foreign policy, and police and judicial cooperation. Above all, it introduced **European citizenship**, allowing Europeans to vote and move freely within the Union. The most spectacular transformation remains the creation of the **euro**. 

Initially a scriptural currency in 1999, the euro physically replaced national currencies on **January 1, 2002**. This transition to a single currency completed the large internal market, eliminating exchange fees and facilitating price comparisons across the continent, despite the budgetary coordination challenges this imposes on member States.

 The bridges represented on the euro banknotes did not actually exist: they symbolized architectural styles without favoring a specific country. However, the town of Spijkenisse in the Netherlands physically built them all in 2011 to reproduce them identically.

lessons.title: Growing wider without dissolving
lessons.content:
Since the 2000s, the EU has experienced unprecedented expansion to integrate former communist bloc countries, bringing the number of members to 28 in 2013. This rapid growth, however, complicated decision-making, leading to the **Lisbon Treaty** (2007) to reform the institutions.

The recent history of the EU is marked by major crises (Greek debt crisis, migration crisis) and an unprecedented historical event: **Brexit**. In 2016, the British voted to leave the Union, an effective divorce in 2020 that highlights the tensions between national sovereignty and community integration.

Today, the EU remains a unique hybrid construction: more than a simple international organization, but not quite a federal State. It must now invent new mechanisms to respond to the challenges of climate change and continental security in the face of new global threats.

|| The EU was born in 1950 with the ECSC to make Franco-German war impossible through industrial integration, evolving from a large common market (1957) to a political and monetary union (1992). ||

 The European flag, with its 12 gold stars, does not represent the number of member countries (which has varied) but symbolizes perfection and unity, in reference to the 12 months of the year and the 12 signs of the zodiac.

title: The Rwandan genocide
description: In **100 days**, between April and July **1994**, hundreds of thousands of Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed in Rwanda. The fastest genocide of the century unfolded in full view of the world.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
In just **100 days**, between April and July 1994, Rwanda is the Theatre of an unprecedented tragedy. Between **500,000 and 800,000 Tutsis** and moderate Hutus are systematically massacred. 

[Rwandan genocide 1994]

This mass massacre is distinguished by its lightning speed and by the staggering inaction of the international community, which watched the extermination of part of its population without intervening militarily to prevent it. This course analyzes the colonial roots of this hatred, the mechanics of the extermination, and the silence of nations.

lessons.title: When identity becomes an ID card
lessons.content:
Rwanda is historically a country in the **Great Lakes** region, characterized by high population density. Its population consists mainly of two groups: the **Hutus** (the majority at around 85%) and the **Tutsis** (around 14%). Before the arrival of Europeans, the distinction between these two groups was not racial in nature but social and economic. A Hutu owning a lot of cattle could become Tutsi, and vice versa.

The **Belgian** colonial administration, under the influence of racial theories of the early 20th century, would freeze these relations. Convinced that the Tutsis were a "superior race" of Nilotic origin, the Belgians decided to rely on them to lead the country. In **1933**, they imposed the **ethnic identity card**, making group membership hereditary and immutable. This measure transformed a fluid social stratification into a rigid caste system.

Approaching independence in **1962**, Belgium performed a strategic U-turn by supporting the Hutu majority. The resentment accumulated for decades by the Hutus then transformed into an ideology of exclusion. A series of pogroms forced thousands of Tutsis into exile in neighboring countries, laying the groundwork for a conflict that only required a trigger to explode.

 In 1933, to assign ethnic belonging, Belgian colonizers used physical criteria like the shape of the nose or, more simply, the number of cows owned: with more than ten head of cattle, one was classified as Tutsi.

lessons.title: A planned extermination
lessons.content:
In the 1990s, the regime of President Juvénal Habyarimana, weakened by a civil war against the rebel army of the <Rwandan Patriotic Front> (RPF), locked itself into Hutu radicalism. The genocide was not a spontaneous explosion of rage, but an operation planned by extremists of the <Hutu Power>. They formed the **Interahamwe**, militias of young civilians trained to kill. For weaponry, the State imported massive quantities of **machetes** from China, an agricultural tool transformed into a weapon of mass destruction.

[machetes Rwanda genocide]

The psychological conditioning of the population was ensured by a fearsome tool: <Radio des Mille Collines>. By broadcasting daily hate messages, it dehumanized the Tutsis by calling them **cockroaches** (inyenzi in Kinyarwanda). The signal for the massacre was given on the evening of **April 6, 1994**: the presidential plane was shot down by a missile. Although the perpetrators of the attack remain uncertain, Hutu extremists immediately shifted the blame onto the Tutsis.

Within the hour, roadblocks were set up across the country. The genocide began with frightening logistics: approximately **8,000 people were killed each day**. The massacre was close-range: it was perpetrated by neighbors, colleagues, sometimes even members of the victims' own families, under pressure or incitement from local authorities.

lessons.title: The silence of the world
lessons.content:
While the extermination was in full swing, the reaction of World powers was strikingly passive. The UN had a force on site, led by <general> **Roméo Dallaire**, but its mandate was strictly limited to observation. Traumatized by the failure of a previous intervention in **<Somalia>**, the **United States** refused to intervene and pressed the Security Council not to qualify the events as a "genocide" - which would legally require action according to the 1948 Convention.

France, for its part, maintained ambiguous relations with the Hutu regime and belatedly launched operation **<Turquoise>**. Although presented as humanitarian, this mission was criticized for allowing those responsible for the genocide to flee to **<Zaire>**. The massacre finally ceased only through the force of local arms, and not through International Law.

The victorious offensive of the **RPF** troops, led by **Paul Kagame**, culminated on July 4, 1994, with the capture of the capital, Kigali. This military success ended the killings but left the country in ruins, with a traumatized population and millions of refugees fleeing the rebel advance. The new power then had to manage the humanitarian emergency and justice in the face of hundreds of thousands of perpetrators.

[Paul Kagame RPF Rwanda]

 The signal triggering the massacres on Radio des Mille Collines was a coded instruction: "Go to work" or "Cut down the tall trees," a cynical reference to the high average height of the Tutsis.

lessons.title: Justice and memory
lessons.content:
In the aftermath of July 1994, Rwanda had to rebuild itself on a field of corpses. The country implemented a judicial system unique in the World: the <Gacaca>. These grassroots courts, inspired by local traditions, allowed for the trial of nearly two million cases between 2005 and 2012, promoting truth and reconciliation at the community level, while the <International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda> (ICTR) handled the high-level planners.

The duty of memory now occupies a central place in Rwandan society. The **Kigali Genocide Memorial**, inaugurated for the tenth anniversary in 2004, serves as a burial site for over 250,000 victims. It reminds the World every year that the genocide was made possible by silence and indifference. Rwanda has since abolished any mention of ethnicity on official documents, promoting a unified national identity under the slogan "Ndi Umunyarwanda" (I am Rwandan).

However, the scars remain deep. Controversies regarding the role of France or the authoritarianism of the regime born of the **RPF** continue to fuel historical debates, making the Rwandan genocide a crucial subject of study for understanding the mechanisms of contemporary political violence.

 To encourage reconciliation, Rwanda turned to sport: the national cycling team, "Team Rwanda," was formed with riders whose families belonged to both sides (Hutus and Tutsis), becoming a global symbol of found unity.

|| In 100 days (April-July 1994), 500,000 to 800,000 Tutsis were massacred in Rwanda by Hutu extremists. Despite warnings from the UN, the international community did not intervene, and only the military offensive of the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) put an end to the massacres.||

title: The fall of the Berlin Wall
description: On the night of **November 9 to 10, 1989**, Berliners tore down with their bare hands the wall that had divided their city for **28 years**. A misunderstanding on live television sped up the end of the Cold War.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The cracks in the Eastern bloc: Summer 1989

The year 1989 marked a structural turning point in the survival of people's democracies. The arrival to power of **Mikhail Gorbachev** in the USSR radically changed the situation. Unlike his predecessors, he refused to use force to keep satellite countries in the Soviet orbit, favoring dialogue and internal reform. This voluntary passivity from Moscow encouraged protests.

The first symbolic blow came from **Hungary**. In May 1989, Hungarian authorities decided to open their border with Austria. It was the first time a real breach appeared in the <iron curtain> since its creation. Thousands of East German citizens on "vacation" in Hungary rushed through this opening to reach the FRG (Federal Republic of Germany) via Austrian territory.

In the GDR itself, social discontent exploded. In Leipzig, weekly protests, the **Montagsdemonstrationen** (Monday demonstrations), grew in scale. Protesters chanted **"Wir sind das Volk"** ("We are the people"), asserting their sovereignty against a sclerotic single party. The regime, led by conservative **Erich Honecker**, hesitated on what course of action to take. By the time he was replaced by Egon Krenz in October, the movement had already become irresistible.

{The wall was officially nicknamed by the Eastern regime the "Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart," claiming it served to prevent Western spies from entering, not to prevent its own citizens from leaving.}

lessons.title: A wall to stop a people
lessons.content:
From the fall of the Wall to the end of a world

The fall of the wall did not just mean the opening of a border; it triggered an ultra-fast political reunification process. Driven by West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, and with the approval of the major powers (United States, USSR, France, and United Kingdom), Germany regained its full sovereignty. Official reunification was proclaimed on **October 3, 1990**.

Beyond Germany, the shockwave was global. 1989 is often called the "miracle year": the communist regimes of Poland, Czechoslovakia (during the <Velvet Revolution>), Bulgaria, and Romania collapsed one after another. The Wall was the cornerstone of the European balance; its disappearance mechanically led to that of the USSR, which was officially dissolved in December 1991.

The fall of the wall thus symbolizes the transition from the era of bipolar confrontation to a new world, carrying the hope of universal democracy. However, it also leaves a complex legacy: the traces of the economic and social division between the former "new states" of the East and the West still persist decades later, a reminder that while a wall can be destroyed in a night, the disparities created over forty years take longer to erase.

|| The fall of the Berlin Wall (November 9, 1989) marks the end of the Cold War. Triggered by a communication error, it led to German reunification as early as 1990 and to the total collapse of the Soviet bloc. ||

{After the fall, a large part of the wall was crushed to serve as fertilizer and rubble for the construction of German motorways.}

lessons.title: The summer everything cracked
lessons.content: Cold War & contemporary world

lessons.title: November 9: Schabowski's mistake
lessons.content:
In just six weeks, from **May 10 to June 22, 1940**, the German army achieved one of the most dazzling military feats of modern history by conquering France, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Luxembourg. This brutal collapse of the leading European military power of the era stunned the world.

The **Blitzkrieg** (lightning war) was not just a series of territorial victories; it represented a conceptual revolution where speed and the disorganization of the adversary counted more than their immediate physical destruction. By breaking the front at a nerve center, the attacker paralyzed enemy decision centers even before reserves could be deployed.

[German tanks Blitzkrieg 1940]

lessons.title: From Berlin to the end of a world
lessons.content:
The execution of Case Yellow and the shock of Sedan

The initial German plan called for a classic attack through the Belgian plain, but General **Erich von Manstein** convinced Hitler to adopt a more audacious strategy: the <Sichelschnitt>. While one army group drew the Franco-British forces North by invading the Netherlands and Belgium, the bulk of the armored forces secretly pushed into the **Ardennes** massif.

The French command, embodied by General **Gamelin**, made the fatal error of judging the Ardennes impassable for tanks. Consequently, this sector was entrusted to poorly equipped reserve troops. On **May 13, 1940**, the divisions of **Heinz Guderian** crossed the Meuse at **Sedan**. The breakthrough was successful: the road to Paris and the English Channel was open.

Once the front was pierced, the panzers did not stop to consolidate their positions; they raced West to cut Allied supply lines. Within a week, the Allied armies engaged in Belgium found themselves encircled, their backs to the sea. This was the beginning of the agony of Dunkirk, where **Operation Dynamo** managed in extremis to evacuate the British Expeditionary Force to England, while leaving the French army alone to face the disaster.

[Dunkirk evacuation beach 1940]

title: Blitzkrieg
description: In **six weeks**, from **May 10** to **June 22, 1940**, the German army conquered France and the Benelux countries. This “lightning war” rewrote the art of war through sheer speed.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
En seulement six semaines, du **10 mai au 22 juin 1940**, l'armée allemande réalise l'un des exploits militaires les plus fulgurants de l'histoire moderne en conquérant la France, les Pays-Bas, la Belgique et le Luxembourg. Cet effondrement brutal de la première puissance militaire européenne de l'époque stupéfie le monde. 

La **Blitzkrieg** (guerre éclair) n'est pas seulement une série de victoires territoriales ; elle représente une révolution conceptuelle où la vitesse et la désorganisation de l'adversaire comptent plus que sa destruction physique immédiate. En brisant le front en un point névralgique, l'assaillant paralyse les centres de décision ennemis avant même que les réserves ne puissent être déployées.

[German tanks Blitzkrieg 1940]

lessons.title: Hit hard, hit fast
lessons.content:
Contrairement à une idée reçue, le terme de Blitzkrieg n'est pas une appellation officielle de la <Wehrmacht> ; il s'agit d'une invention de la presse anglo-saxonne pour décrire l'inexplicable rapidité de l'avance allemande. En réalité, les officiers allemands se réfèrent à la **Bewegungskrieg** (guerre de mouvement). Ce concept repose sur le principe du **Schwerpunkt** : la concentration massive de tous les moyens disponibles sur un point précis et restreint du front pour créer une rupture irrémédiable.

L'innovation majeure des années 1930 ne réside pas tant dans les performances techniques des chars **Panzers** que dans leur emploi tactique. Là où les Français considèrent le char comme un simple appui pour l'infanterie, les Allemands les regroupent en divisions blindées autonomes. Ces unités sont capables d'opérer loin derrière les lignes ennemies, guidées par des communications radio constantes.

Cette offensive terrestre est indissociable d'une domination aérienne totale. Les bombardiers en piqué **Stukas** agissent comme une artillerie volante, ciblant les colonnes de réfugiés et les QG pour semer la panique. Cette coordination étroite entre l'air et le sol, appelée l'**engagement interarmes**, permet aux Allemands de maintenir une pression psychologique insoutenable sur un commandement allié encore marqué par la lenteur de la Première Guerre mondiale.

{Les sirènes hurlantes installées sur les Stukas, surnommées les 'trompettes de Jéricho', n'avaient aucune utilité militaire réelle : elles étaient conçues uniquement pour terroriser moralement les soldats et les civils au sol lors des piqués.}

lessons.title: The sickle cut
lessons.content:
Le plan initial allemand prévoyait une attaque classique par la plaine belge, mais le général **Erich von Manstein** convainc Hitler d'adopter une stratégie plus audacieuse : le <Sichelschnitt>. Tandis qu'un groupe d'armées attire les forces franco-britanniques vers le nord en envahissant les Pays-Bas et la Belgique, le gros des forces blindées s'enfonce secrètement dans le massif des **Ardennes**.

Le commandement français, incarné par le général **Gamelin**, commet l'erreur fatale de juger les Ardennes infranchissables pour des chars. En conséquence, ce secteur est confié à des troupes de réserve mal équipées. Le **13 mai 1940**, les divisions de **Heinz Guderian** franchissent la Meuse à **Sedan**. La percée est réussie : la route vers Paris et la Manche est ouverte. 

Une fois le front crevé, les panzers ne s'arrêtent pas pour consolider leurs positions ; ils foncent vers l'ouest pour couper les lignes de ravitaillement alliées. En une semaine, les armées alliées engagées en Belgique se retrouvent encerclées, dos à la mer. C'est le début de l'agonie de Dunkerque, où l'**opération Dynamo** parvient in extremis à évacuer le corps expéditionnaire britannique vers l'Angleterre, laissant cependant l'armée française seule face au désastre.

[Dunkirk evacuation beach 1940]

lessons.title: The armistice and the appeal
lessons.content:
La seconde phase de la campagne, la bataille de France (plan Rouge), n'est plus qu'une formalité tragique. Privée de ses meilleures divisions perdues dans le Nord, l'armée française s'effondre malgré des actes de résistance héroïques. Le gouvernement fuit la capitale et Paris est déclarée **ville ouverte** le **14 juin** pour éviter sa destruction, permettant aux troupes allemandes de défiler sur les Champs-Élysées sans qu'un coup de feu ne soit tiré.

Face à la débâcle, le traumatisme est tel que la classe politique française se déchire. Le maréchal **Philippe Pétain**, héros de Verdun, accède au pouvoir et demande la cessation des combats. L'**armistice** est signé le **22 juin 1940** à Compiègne. Par un sens aigu de la mise en scène, Hitler impose que la cérémonie se déroule dans le même wagon où l'Allemagne avait capitulé en **1918**, lavant ainsi symboliquement l'« affront » de la Grande Guerre.

Au même moment, une voix isolée s'élève depuis la BBC à Londres. Le **général de Gaulle** lance son appel du **18 juin**, affirmant que la guerre est mondiale et que la France n'a perdu qu'une bataille. Si l'impact immédiat de ce discours est faible sur le territoire occupé, il pose les bases de la **France libre** et du refus de la défaite diplomatique.

{Pour la signature de l'armistice, Hitler a fait briser les murs du musée de Compiègne afin d'extraire le wagon historique et de le replacer exactement à l'endroit précis où la délégation allemande avait dû s'incliner 22 ans plus tôt.}

lessons.title: A double-edged victory
lessons.content:
La victoire de 1940 consacre l'Allemagne comme la maîtresse de l'Europe continentale. Cependant, ce succès foudroyant cache des faiblesses structurelles qui pèseront lourd pour la suite du conflit. La Blitzkrieg est une stratégie de « guerre courte » : elle repose sur des stocks de carburant limités et une logistique qui ne peut s'étendre indéfiniment. 

L'échec de la Blitzkrieg lors de l'invasion de l'URSS en 1941 démontre ces limites. Face à l'immensité géographique russe et à la capacité de mobilisation quasi illimitée de l'Armée rouge, la vitesse allemande s'enlise dans la boue et le froid. La guerre éclair ne peut pas se transformer en guerre d'usure sans une économie de guerre totale, ce que l'Allemagne ne parviendra à mettre en place que trop tardivement.

Sur le plan mémoriel, l'événement de 1940 reste connu sous le nom de l'**Étrange Défaite**, titre de l'ouvrage de l'historien **Marc Bloch**. Il souligne que la défaite française ne fut pas seulement matérielle, mais surtout intellectuelle : le refus de comprendre que le temps des tranchées était révolu face à la rapidité mécanique du nouveau siècle.

{Pour soutenir le rythme effréné de la Blitzkrieg, des millions de comprimés de Pervitine (une méthamphétamine) furent distribués aux soldats allemands, leur permettant de rester éveillés et de combattre sans repos pendant plusieurs jours consécutifs.}

|| En six semaines, la Blitzkrieg combine blindés, aviation et radio pour pulvériser la doctrine défensive française, prouvant que la vitesse et la concentration des forces l'emportent sur la supériorité numérique statique. ||

quiz.explanation: In just six weeks, from May 10 to June 22, 1940, the German army conquered France, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg.
