title: The Marshall Plan
description: In **1947** Europe lay in ruins. The United States offered massive aid to rebuild it, and to hold back communism.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
In June 1947, as Europe sank into an unprecedented economic and social crisis, US Secretary of State **George Marshall** proposed a massive financial aid plan. This initiative, officially named <ERP> (European Recovery Program), went beyond the simple framework of humanitarian assistance.

[Marshall Plan poster American aid]

This project constitutes the largest economic Reconstruction operation in modern History. It is simultaneously the most audacious foreign politics tool of the 20th century, designed to stabilize a continent on the brink of the abyss and durably anchor Western Europe within the democratic bloc.

lessons.title: A Europe out of breath
lessons.content:
At the end of the Second World War, Europe's material toll was catastrophic. Transport infrastructure was destroyed, power grids cut, and great industrial cities were nothing but fields of ruins. The winter of **1946-1947**, one of the harshest of the century, finished exhausting the populations: coal and food shortages caused famines and violent social unrest.

On the accounting side, the situation was just as bleak. **Great Britain** was in a state of virtual bankruptcy, unable to support its Greek allies against the communist guerrilla warfare. In France, industrial production stagnated at **38%** of its 1938 level. This widespread misery provided fertile ground for Marxist ideology. To popularize the plan, the Americans organized a huge poster competition across Europe: over 10,000 designs were submitted to illustrate the idea that Europe's salvation lay in cooperation and aid from the United States. To pay for its first emergency imports before the Marshall Plan, France had to physically ship tons of gold bars from the Bank of France to New York by battleship.

In this climate of despair, national communist parties achieved historic electoral scores, notably in **France** and **Italy**. For the United States, the risk of seeing Europe tilt toward the East through the ballot box became an existential threat. Washington understood that hunger and cold were the best allies of Soviet influence and the expansion of the <Cominform (1947)>.

lessons.title: The American offer, and the Soviet refusal
lessons.content:
On **June 5, 1947**, during a speech at **Harvard University**, George Marshall set out his vision: American aid must not be a mere temporary remedy, but an engine for structural recovery. However, he set a sine qua non condition: Europeans must agree on a global and coordinated Reconstruction plan, rather than requesting scattered bilateral aid.

Initially, the proposal was open to the entire continent, including the USSR and its satellite countries. However, during the **Paris conference** in July 1947, tensions erupted. **Stalin**, fearing that the influence of the dollar would destabilize his control over Central Europe, rejected the offer, calling it economic imperialism. He formally forbade Poland and Czechoslovakia from participating.

This diplomatic confrontation sealed the partition of the continent. Only **16 countries** from Western Europe met to found the **OEEC** (Organisation for European Economic Co-operation). This Institution was responsible for centralizing needs and distributing funds, thus marking the first concrete step toward European economic integration. The amount of aid was calculated to match the deficit in the European balance of payments: it was exactly the Sum required for Europe to continue buying American products without going bankrupt.

lessons.title: How the aid worked
lessons.content:
Between **1948 and 1952**, the United States transferred approximately **13 billion dollars** (more than **150 billion** in today's value). Contrary to popular belief, this aid did not consist solely of suitcases of cash. It mostly took the form of goods: raw materials, machine tools, tractors, and agricultural products.

The mechanism was ingenious: the United States delivered the goods, European governments resold them to their national companies in local currency, and the money thus collected (the "counterpart fund") was reinvested in major infrastructure projects. For the United States, it was a break-even operation: they supported their own full employment by exporting their surplus production to Europe.

The results were meteoric. By 1952, the industrial production of recipient countries exceeded pre-war levels by **35%**. West Germany began its <Wirtschaftswunder> (economic miracle), while France modernized its countryside thanks to American equipment. Beyond the figures, the Marshall Plan introduced American management methods to Europe and fostered the emergence of a society of mass consumption.

lessons.title: A political victory as much as an economic one
lessons.content:
The Marshall Plan was the practical application of the <Truman Doctrine>, aimed at containing Soviet expansionism through economic prosperity. By stabilizing Western economies, it succeeded in weakening the audience of revolutionary Movement groups and legitimizing the capitalist model. It also sealed the transatlantic bond, paving the way for the creation of the Atlantic Alliance a few years later.

On the Politics level, this plan forced former enemies, such as France and Germany, to collaborate within the **OEEC**. By demanding collective management of the aid, the Americans pushed the Europeans toward federalism, thus creating the roots of what would later become the European Economic Community (<EEC>).

In 1953, George Marshall received the **Nobel Peace Prize**, a Rare tribute for a career military officer, highlighting that the stability of the World depends on Reconstruction rather than simple military victory.

quiz.question: Who announced the Marshall Plan in June 1947?
quiz.explanation: In June 1947, American Secretary of State George Marshall announced an unprecedented aid plan to rebuild Europe.
options: US Secretary of State George Marshall

quiz.question: What is the real strategy behind the Marshall Plan, beyond reconstruction?
quiz.explanation: Officially aid for reconstruction, the plan also aims to prevent poverty from pushing Western Europe towards communism, facing the USSR.
options: Preventing poverty from pushing Western Europe towards communism

quiz.question: True or false: Stalin accepts Marshall Plan aid for the USSR and its allied countries.
quiz.explanation: Stalin refuses the offer and forbids Poland and Czechoslovakia from accepting it, cutting the continent in two.

quiz.question: What condition did Marshall pose to the Europeans in his Harvard speech on June 5, 1947?
quiz.explanation: Marshall demanded that Europeans organize themselves around a common plan rather than receiving aid dispersed country by country.
options: They must agree on a common plan, rather than receiving scattered aid
They must repay the aid with interest
They must adopt the dollar as their currency

quiz.question: In what form does American aid mainly arrive in Europe?
quiz.explanation: The aid does not mainly consist of tickets, but of material goods: machines, coal, tractors, food.

quiz.question: True or false: in 1952, industrial production in Western Europe remained below its pre-war level.
quiz.explanation: By 1952, industrial production exceeded pre-war levels by 35%, marking the economic success of the plan.

quiz.question: How many billions of dollars did the United States send to Europe between 1948 and 1952?
quiz.explanation: Between 1948 and 1952, the United States sent approximately 13 billion dollars, or more than 150 billion today.

quiz.question: What organization are the 16 countries of Western Europe creating to distribute American aid?
quiz.explanation: The 16 countries of Western Europe come together in the OEEC, the organization responsible for distributing the funds of the Marshall Plan.

title: The Vietnam War
description: For twenty years the United States poured enormous force into Vietnam to hold back communism. It got bogged down, tore itself apart, and left without winning.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The Vietnam War constitutes one of the darkest and most complex chapters of the 20th century. This conflict, which is at the heart of the **Cold War**, pitted communist North Vietnam against South Vietnam, supported by the Western bloc. For two decades, the United States committed unprecedented technological and financial resources to contain its expansion of communism in Southeast Asia. Yet, despite a display of material power, Washington faced a total stalemate. Between moral trauma, deep division in American society, and transformation of military strategies, this confrontation redefined the balance of power between great powers and national liberation Movement groups.

[Vietnam War American soldiers]

lessons.title: A divided country, then a war that grew
lessons.content:
Following the French defeat during the <Indochina War>, the **Geneva Accords** ratified in **1954** the temporary partition of Vietnam at the **17th parallel**. The North was led by the communist leader <Ho Chi Minh>, while the South fell under the influence of the United States. Washington placed **Ngo Dinh Diem** there, a leader whose authoritarian and corrupt regime harshly repressed his opponents, paradoxically favoring the emergence of an internal resistance.

In **1960**, opponents of the Southern regime, supported by the North, founded the **NLF** (National Liberation Front), pejoratively nicknamed the **Viet Cong** by its adversaries. Fearing that the fall of Vietnam would trigger a regional collapse according to the <Domino theory>, Presidents Kennedy and then Johnson massively increased military assistance.

The breaking point occurred on **August 2, 1964**, during the **Gulf of Tonkin** incident, where North Vietnamese torpedo boats allegedly attacked the American destroyer USS Maddox. Although the reality of the second incident is now questioned by historians, President **Lyndon B. Johnson** used it to obtain the **Gulf of Tonkin Resolution**, a legislative Law giving him full military powers without a formal declaration of war. Starting in **1965**, operation <Rolling Thunder> launched a massive bombing campaign, while the first contingents of Marines landed on the beaches of Da Nang.

{President Johnson reportedly confided in private, a few months after the Tonkin incident: "For all I know, our Navy was shooting at whales that night."}

lessons.title: Why force was not enough
lessons.content:
American involvement reached its peak in **1969** with the deployment of **543,000 soldiers**. The American strategy was based on <search and destroy> and absolute air superiority. Yet, the bombings failed to break the **Ho Chi Minh trail**, a complex network of roads and tunnels used by the North to supply its troops in the South through Laos and Cambodia.

Faced with heavy American weaponry, North Vietnamese general **Vo Nguyen Giap** imposed a war of attrition. His troops avoided pitched battles, preferring harassment, traps, and immersion among the peasant populations. The Americans, unable to identify the enemy in a hostile jungle, resorted to chemical defoliants such as **Agent Orange** to destroy the plant cover, causing health and ecological disasters.

This tactical asymmetry physically and morally exhausted young American draftees. The financial cost of the war exploded, while the number of coffins returning to the United States began to shake the national consensus. Technological superiority clashed with a political determination that the <Pentagon> strategists had not anticipated.

{It is estimated that the U.S. military used more than 80 million liters of chemical herbicides on the Vietnamese jungle, which destroyed about 20% of South Vietnam's forests.}

lessons.title: The shock of the Tet Offensive
lessons.content:
On **January 30, 1968**, during the Vietnamese New Year festival (the **Tet**), communist forces launched a coordinated surprise attack on more than 100 Southern cities, even penetrating the grounds of the American embassy in Saigon. While the **<Tet Offensive>** was a military disaster for the North, which lost tens of thousands of fighters, it constituted a devastating psychological victory.

For years, the American government had assured that victory was near. The images of the offensive broadcast by television—a medium that had become ubiquitous—showed a completely different reality. American public opinion shifted: the anti-war Movement transformed into a massive protest that divided families and university campuses.

Faced with this pressure, Johnson's successor, **Richard Nixon**, began a politics of "Vietnamization" of the conflict, consisting of gradually withdrawing American troops while massively arming the South Vietnamese army. The **Paris Peace Accords in 1973** formalized the total disengagement of American combat forces. Deprived of its protector, the Saigon regime collapsed in two years before the inexorable advance of Hanoi's troops.

lessons.title: The end of the war, and what it left behind
lessons.content:
The tragic conclusion occurred on **April 30, 1975**, during the fall of Saigon. The images of helicopters evacuating diplomats and civilians from the top of the American embassy symbolized the humiliation of the world's leading power. The country was officially reunified under the aegis of the Communist Party in **1976**, and Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.

The human toll was horrific: about **58,000 Americans** perished, but Vietnamese losses (military and civilian) rose to several million. The war left behind a devastated country and a generation of American veterans marked by social rejection and post-traumatic stress. On the diplomatic level, this conflict cooled the interventionist fervor of the United States for more than a decade, a phenomenon known as "Vietnam Syndrome".

The legacy of the war is also cultural and media-based. It was the first televised war in History, where the press played a role of counter-power by revealing atrocities, such as the <My Lai> massacre. It remains today an essential reference for understanding the limits of military power in the face of organized national resistance Movement groups.

|| After 20 years of conflict and the use of 7.6 million tons of bombs, the United States suffered its first major strategic failure of the 20th century in Vietnam, leaving a country reunified under communism and a morally divided America. ||

quiz.explanation: The Geneva Accords of 1954 temporarily divided Vietnam in two at the 17th parallel, with Ho Chi Minh in the North and a regime supported by Washington in the South.

quiz.explanation: According to this theory, if one country falls under communism, its neighbors would follow in cascade, justifying American intervention.

quiz.explanation: This naval incident, the reality of which was privately contested by Johnson himself, served to justify military escalation from 1965.

quiz.explanation: This strategy of seeking and then destroying the enemy is not enough to break the Ho Chi Minh Trail, the northern supply route.

quiz.explanation: In 1969, approximately 543,000 American soldiers were deployed there, without succeeding in breaking North Vietnamese resistance.

quiz.explanation: More than 80 million liters of herbicides destroyed around 20% of South Vietnam's forests.

quiz.explanation: On the ground, the offensive failed for the North, but its televised scale in the United States contradicted the optimistic announcements from Washington.

quiz.explanation: These milestones range from the partition of 1954 to the fall of Saigon in 1975, which sealed the reunification of the country under communism.

title: The Nuremberg trials
description: Between **1945** and **1946**, **24** Nazi leaders stood trial at Nuremberg. For the first time, an international court invented crimes against humanity.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Between November 1945 and October 1946, the city of **Nuremberg**, a former ideological bastion of Nazi rallies, became the Theater for an unprecedented legal Event. For the first time in History, a state did not settle for military victory over its enemy, but chose to judge its leaders before an international civil and military tribunal. This historic trial marks the birth of a global legal conscience in the face of the horror of the extermination camps, enshrining the Concept of **<crimes against humanity>** as an inalienable legal category of <international law>.

[Nuremberg trials defendants dock]

lessons.title: Law instead of revenge
lessons.content:
As the end of the Second World War approached, the fate of high-ranking Nazi dignitaries sparked intense debate among the Allied powers. British Prime Minister **Winston Churchill** initially advocated for summary executions without trial for the main criminals, fearing that a judicial platform would allow them to spread their ideology. For his part, **Stalin** proposed show trials whose outcome, the death penalty, would be decided in advance to satisfy Soviet public opinion.

It was ultimately the Theory carried by the United States and the jurist **Robert Jackson** that prevailed: to restore civilization after barbarism, the Allies had to prove their ethical superiority through a fair trial, based on irrefutable evidence and respect for the rights of the defense. This political will was materialized by the <London Charter> (August 1945), a founding text that defined the operating rules of the **International Military Tribunal** (IMT).

The judges and prosecutors of the four Allied nations (United States, USSR, United Kingdom, France) agreed on four revolutionary counts. In addition to classic war crimes, the tribunal included conspiracy, crimes against peace (premeditated aggression) and, for the first time, **<crimes against humanity>**, targeting the systematic extermination of a people. This legal framework allowed for a shift from a victors' justice to a justice for History.

{The choice of Nuremberg was not only symbolic: it was one of the few German cities that still had an intact Palace of Justice and, above all, an adjacent prison connected by a secure tunnel.}

lessons.title: Evidence facing the accused
lessons.content:
The trial opens with 24 defendants representing the various branches of Nazi power. Among them, **Hermann Göring**, former head of the <Luftwaffe> and Hitler's designated successor, dominates the dock with his arrogance and aggressiveness. He attempts to challenge the court's legality, arguing that a sovereign state cannot be judged by another. Beside him are figures like **Rudolf Hess** or the Minister of Armaments **Albert Speer**, the only defendant to admit a share of responsibility.

[Hermann Göring Nuremberg trial]

Prosecutor Jackson's strategy relies primarily on the methodical administration of documentary evidence. Rather than relying solely on witnesses, the prosecution uses archives meticulously kept by the Nazis themselves. Millions of pages of documents, photographs, and personal diaries are presented as damning evidence of the planned nature of the Holocaust. The trial becomes a living archive of human madness.

The most brutal shock occurs during the screening of films shot by the Allies at the liberation of the camps. Silence falls over the courtroom as images of emaciated bodies and industries of death flicker by. These images transform the perception of the trial: it is no longer about judging a military defeat, but inhumanity established as a system of government. Even some defendants seem to lose their composure in the face of the raw reality of their acts.

lessons.title: A verdict that still counts
lessons.content:
After eleven months of exhausting hearings, the verdict is delivered on **October 1, 1946**. The sentence is nuanced: there are no automatic convictions. The tribunal pronounces **12 death sentences** by hanging, 3 life sentences, 4 prison sentences ranging from 10 to 20 years, and 3 acquittals (to Stalin's great fury). This distinction between the defendants proves that the court examined individual guilt rather than punishing a monolithic bloc.

The trial primarily establishes crucial legal principles that would later be adopted by the UN as the <Nuremberg principles>. The most famous is that of **individual responsibility in international law**: the fact of having acted on orders from a superior does not relieve the individual of criminal responsibility. International law now takes precedence over national law when it comes to protecting the fundamental rights of the individual.

Nuremberg's legacy is immense. It constitutes the first step toward the creation of international criminal justice. However, it would not be until the end of the **Cold War** that these principles would be institutionalized again with the tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda, and then with the creation of the **<International Criminal Court>** (ICC) in 2002.

{Hermann Göring managed to commit suicide the night before his execution by swallowing a cyanide capsule - which no one has ever been able to explain how he obtained despite daily body searches.}

lessons.title: Real advances, and real limits
lessons.content:
Despite its technical success, the Nuremberg trial has been subject to criticism. Some legal scholars see it as a violation of the principle of <non-retroactivity>, since the defendants were tried for crimes that did not officially exist in national penal codes before the war. Furthermore, the absence of judgment on Allied crimes (such as the **Katyn** massacre attributed to the Germans by the Soviets but committed by the latter) has sometimes fueled the idea of double standards.

However, Nuremberg succeeded in its most fundamental gamble: establishing an undeniable historical truth. By forcing Nazi leaders to answer for their actions before the World, the trial prevented the emergence of theories denying the scale of the massacres in the years that followed. It allowed the dismantling of the Nazi ideological apparatus without turning the defendants into martyrs.

Today, the Nuremberg memorial serves as a reminder that law is the only effective rampart against state barbarism. The trial etched in stone that humanity possesses rights that even the most powerful governments cannot trample with impunity, laying the groundwork for the 1948 **Universal Declaration of Human Rights**.

|| The Nuremberg trial (1945-46) invents the crime <against humanity> - for the first time, heads of state are judged by an international tribunal.||

quiz.explanation: Alongside conspiracy, crimes against peace and war crimes already known, crimes against humanity appear for the first time in international law.

quiz.explanation: The lawyer Robert Jackson mainly uses the millions of pages of archives, photos and diaries produced by the Nazi regime itself.

quiz.explanation: Hermann Göring, former head of the German Air Force, stands out for his defiant attitude towards the judges.

quiz.explanation: Twenty-four Nazi leaders representing the regime apparatus are tried before the international tribunal.

quiz.explanation: The verdict distinguishes individual responsibilities: 12 death sentences, 3 life sentences, 4 prison sentences and 3 acquittals.

title: Decolonization: an overview
description: Between **1945** and **1975**, more than **80** countries won their independence. The European empires collapsed and the map of the world changed.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: Between 1945 and 1975, the World experienced an unprecedented geopolitical shift: the almost total disappearance of European colonial empires. More than **80 countries** attained national sovereignty within three decades, redefining the balances of the **Cold War**. This process, far from being a simple transfer of power, resulted from a convergence of factors: the exhaustion of the metropoles after 1945, the emergence of local elites trained in the West, and a new international context hostile to imperialism. Although this Movement marks the end of an era of multi-century domination, it leaves a complex legacy of contested borders and persistent economic dependencies.

lessons.title: Why everything changed after 1945
lessons.content:
The Second World War acted as a powerful catalyst for emancipation. By suffering rapid defeats against the Axis, colonial powers like France or the Netherlands lost their aura of invincibility in the eyes of the colonized. At the same time, the <Atlantic Charter>, drafted by Franklin D. Roosevelt and Winston Churchill in 1941, promised the "right of all peoples to choose the form of government under which they will live." Although Churchill initially limited this principle to Nazi-occupied Europe, African and Asian nationalist leaders seized upon it to denounce colonial hypocrisy.

On the human level, the massive participation of colonial soldiers in the liberating battles in Europe and the Pacific transformed mentalities. These veterans, after having fought for the freedom of others, could no longer accept the status of second-class citizens in their own countries. This awareness was carried by **indigenous elites**, often trained in the universities of the metropoles, who returned home imbued with ideals of freedom, equality, or Marxism.

Finally, the new world order dominated by the United States and the USSR accelerated the process. Both superpowers, for ideological and strategic reasons, rejected the traditional colonial model. Washington saw it as a barrier to free trade, while Moscow denounced imperialism as the highest stage of capitalism. Thus, metropoles ruined by the war found themselves facing international and local pressure that had become unsustainable.

{During the signing of the Atlantic Charter, Roosevelt had to put pressure on Churchill, who was a staunch imperialist and absolutely did not want this text to apply to the British Empire.}

lessons.title: Negotiation here, war there
lessons.content:
The withdrawal of colonial powers does not follow a single pattern, oscillating between pragmatism and bloody repression. The United Kingdom generally favors a **negotiated** approach, aiming to preserve its economic interests via the <Commonwealth>. As early as 1947, **India** and **Pakistan** gain independence, marking the beginning of the end for the British Empire. In Africa, <Kwame Nkrumah>'s **Ghana** becomes the first sub-Saharan British colony to gain independence in 1957, serving as a model for the rest of the continent.

In contrast, France initially tries to maintain its empire through force or late reforms. This resistance leads to traumatic conflicts. The **Indochina War** (1946-1954) ends in a humiliating military defeat at Dien Bien Phu. A few months later begins the **Algerian War** (1954-1962), a divisive conflict that causes the fall of the <Fourth Republic> and only finds its resolution with the Évian Accords. For French Black Africa, the turning point comes in 1960 with the grouped accession of 14 countries to sovereignty during the famous "Year of Africa".

Some decolonizations are marked by total lack of preparation, as in the **Belgian Congo** (1960). Belgium, leaving the territory in just a few months, leaves a country without trained administrative staff, which immediately triggers a civil war and the assassination of Prime Minister <Patrice Lumumba>. Finally, the Iberian dictatorships resist the longest: Portugal only grants independence to Angola and Mozambique in 1975, after the Carnation Revolution.

lessons.title: Bandung, and the voice of the South
lessons.content:
Decolonization gives birth to a new diplomatic force: the "Third World". In 1955, the **<Bandung Conference>** brings together 29 Asian and African countries. For the first time, formerly dominated nations speak with one voice to condemn colonialism and racism. They refuse to be the pawns of the two blocs (East/West) and advocate **non-alignment**.

However, this unitary momentum quickly fades in the face of the realities of the Cold War. Many states fall back into a form of **<Neocolonialism>**, where domination is no longer territorial but financial and technological. External debt becomes a major instrument of political control. Despite these obstacles, Southern countries manage to transform the United Nations, where they become a majority, making development and the fight against apartheid world priorities.

|| Between 1945 and 1975, more than 80 countries gain independence, but arbitrary borders and economic dependence inherited from colonialism still hinder their full sovereignty today. ||

{The term "Third World" was coined in 1952 by French demographer Alfred Sauvy, by analogy with the Third Estate of the French Revolution, to designate this part of humanity, ignored and exploited, which finally wanted to become something.}

title: Apartheid and Mandela
description: For **46** years South Africa organized racial segregation by law. **Nelson Mandela**, after **27** years in prison, helped the country leave it behind without a civil war.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
In 1948, as the world emerged from the Second World War and began to condemn scientific racism, South Africa took a radically opposite direction. For **46 years**, this country legally organized total racial segregation of its population under a regime unique in the world: **apartheid**. 

[apartheid segregation signs South Africa]

This system, far from being a simple set of prejudices, constituted a meticulous state structure aimed at maintaining the domination of the white minority over the black majority. Yet, this regime, once thought immutable, collapsed in the early 1990s without sinking into civil war. This political miracle is inseparable from a figure who became global: **Nelson Mandela**, who, after **27 years** of captivity, became the architect of an unprecedented national reconciliation.

lessons.title: How segregation became the law
lessons.content:
**apartheid** (meaning "separateness" in Afrikaans) was institutionalized by the **National Party** after its victory in the **May 1948** elections. This party represented the interests of the Afrikaners, descendants of Dutch colonists, who feared being overwhelmed by the demographics of the black populations.

The system did not just separate individuals; it classified them. The **Population Registration Act** (1950) required every citizen to be registered according to their ethnic origin: White, Black, Metis, or Indian. This classification determined the entirety of civil rights, from access to employment to the right to vote, strictly reserved for Whites. The **Bantu Education**, established in 1953, completed this framework by offering black students a deliberately low-level education, intended to limit them to subordinate labor jobs.

Geographically, the regime established the <bantoustans>. These territories, occupying barely 13% of the country's surface area, were supposed to become autonomous national homelands for Blacks. In reality, they served to strip black populations of their South African citizenship, transforming them into foreign workers on their own soil. To travel in white areas, Blacks were required to carry a **pass**, an internal permit whose absence led directly to prison.

{The apartheid regime classified the population into 4 categories. The Japanese were officially "Honorary Whites" for trade reasons - South African racism knew how to bow to Japan's economic interests.}

lessons.title: From non-violence to armed resistance
lessons.content:
Faced with this oppression, the African National Congress (**ANC**) organized resistance. **Nelson Mandela**, a lawyer by training born in **1918**, quickly emerged as a charismatic leader. Initially a proponent of non-violence inspired by Gandhi, the movement shifted at the turn of the 1960s.

The breaking point occurred during the <Sharpeville massacre> in March 1960. Police fired on an unarmed crowd protesting against the pass laws, killing 69 people. This event led to the banning of the ANC and convinced Mandela that peaceful struggle had become suicidal against a state that used only force. He then co-founded **Umkhonto we Sizwe** ("Spear of the Nation"), the movement's armed wing, to carry out sabotage actions against the regime's economic and military installations.

[Sharpeville massacre 1960]

Hunted by intelligence services, Mandela was arrested in 1962. During the **Rivonia Trial** in 1964, he narrowly avoided the death penalty and transformed his defendant's dock into a political platform, declaring he was prepared to die for the ideal of a democratic and free society. Sentenced to life imprisonment, he was transferred to the **Robben Island** prison, where he became the most famous political prisoner on the planet while the country sank into internal violence and diplomatic isolation.

{During his time on the run before 1962, Mandela used so many disguises (chauffeur, gardener, cook) to escape the police that he was nicknamed the "Black Pimpernel" by the press, in reference to the famous elusive fictional hero.}

lessons.title: Negotiating the end of apartheid
lessons.content:
In the 1980s, the regime began to crack under the weight of township resistance and global economic sanctions. South Africa was banned from sports competitions and suffered an embargo that suffocated its economy. It was in this context of total crisis that President **F.W. de Klerk**, who came to power in 1989, understood that the survival of Whites depended on the end of apartheid.

On **February 11, 1990**, Mandela was released after **27 years** of detention. His exit from prison, broadcast live worldwide, marked the beginning of an extremely tense transition period. For four years, Mandela and de Klerk led arduous negotiations to define a new constitution. The challenge was immense: reassuring the white minority who feared bloody vengeance, while meeting the aspirations for justice of the black majority.

The first multiracial elections in the country's history were held from **April 27 to 29, 1994**. For the first time, long queues formed in front of polling stations, mixing all skin colors. The ANC won a historic victory and **Nelson Mandela** was elected president with **62.6%** of the vote, forming a government of national unity including his former enemies to stabilize the country.

{To unite the nation after his election, Mandela supported the Springboks rugby team during the 1995 World Cup. By wearing their green jersey, a historical symbol of white dominance, he won the hearts of his former Afrikaner opponents.}

lessons.title: Reconciling without forgetting
lessons.content:
To prevent the country from sinking into a cycle of vendettas, Mandela and Archbishop **Desmond Tutu** promoted the concept of the "Rainbow Nation." The central idea was to prioritize reconciliation over punishment. This ideal was embodied in the <Truth and Reconciliation Commission> (TRC), established in 1995.

The TRC mechanism was revolutionary: it offered amnesty to perpetrators of political crimes committed under the previous regime, on the express condition that they fully confessed their acts publicly. This process of **transitional justice** allowed victims' families to finally learn the fate of their loved ones and allowed perpetrators to reintegrate into national society. Although criticized by some for its leniency, the commission succeeded in its primary goal: preventing South Africa's explosion.

Mandela left power in 1999 after a single term, thereby reinforcing the democratic dimension of the new republic. Despite the legal end of racism, the legacy of apartheid remains heavy, notably through persistent economic inequalities that remain contemporary South Africa's greatest challenge.

{The current South African national anthem is unique in the world: it merges the old anthem from the apartheid era and the ANC resistance song, and its lyrics are sung in five different languages (Xhosa, Zulu, Sesotho, Afrikaans, and English).}

|| To remember: Apartheid (1948-1994) was a system of institutionalized racial segregation by the National Party. Its fall, orchestrated by Nelson Mandela and F.W. de Klerk (1993 Nobel Peace Prize), gave birth to a multiracial democracy founded on the principle of national reconciliation. ||

title: The Cultural Revolution in China
description: Between **1966** and **1976**, **Mao Zedong** launched a purge of extreme violence to take power back. Red Guards, chaos, then the pragmatic turn of **Deng Xiaoping**.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Between 1966 and 1976, China goes through one of the darkest periods in its modern history: the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution. Launched by **Mao Zedong**, this decade of chaos was not a simple ideological reform, but a political and social purge of extreme violence intended to regain absolute personal power. By mobilizing youth against the very structures of the State and society, Mao provoked the persecution of tens of millions of people and the irremediable destruction of an immense part of the Chinese civilizational heritage.

[Red Guards Cultural Revolution China]

lessons.title: After the failure of the Great Leap
lessons.content:
The outbreak of the Cultural Revolution has its roots in the tragic failure of the <Great Leap Forward> (1958-1962). This program of agricultural collectivization and accelerated rural industrialization resulted in an unprecedented economic catastrophe, engendering a devastating famine that caused the death of 15 to 55 million Chinese. Faced with this disaster, **Mao Zedong**'s prestige is severely damaged within the leadership of the Communist Party.

Stepping back from day-to-day affairs, Mao sees a new generation of leaders, described as pragmatists, take the reins of the country to fix the economy. Among them are **Liu Shaoqi**, then President of the Republic, and his ally **<Deng Xiaoping>**. These leaders favor a more technical and less ideological management, a deviation that Mao perceives as a revisionist betrayal threatening the very essence of the revolution.

{To prove his physical strength before launching the Cultural Revolution, 72-year-old Mao Zedong swam in the Yangtze River in July 1966. Propaganda claimed he had covered 15 kilometers in 65 minutes, an impossible world record aimed at showing he was ready for political combat.}

[Mao Zedong portrait]

To regain control, Mao decides to bypass the Party apparatus by addressing the masses directly, and more particularly the youth. In 1966, he publishes his famous **<Dazibao>** - a large-character poster - titled "Bombard the Headquarters". This text accuses Party leaders of being "supporters of the return to capitalism". Through this act of rebellion, unprecedented for a head of state against his own administration, Mao unleashes the forces of chaos to purge the country of its elements judged to be bourgeois.

lessons.title: The fury of the Red Guards
lessons.content:
Responding to the call of their "Great Helmsman", millions of students and high schoolers organize into paramilitary groups: the **<Red Guards>**. Galvanized by the cult of personality surrounding Mao, they are given the mission to destroy the "four olds": old ideas, old culture, old customs, and old habits. Their rallying sign is the famous book compiling the leader's quotes.

[Little Red Book Mao]

Terror sets in in the cities. The **Red Guards** systematically attack anyone representing intellectual or traditional authority. Teachers are humiliated in front of their students, doctors forced to clean latrines, and Party cadres dragged through the streets during **criticism sessions** and forced self-confessions where physical violence is the norm. Wearing Western clothes or owning foreign books becomes a capital crime.

{The Red Guards did not stop at destroying temples; they also attacked daily details considered bourgeois. In 1966, they tried to change how traffic lights worked in Beijing: according to their revolutionary logic, red should mean 'Go' and not 'Stop'.}

National education is paralyzed: schools and universities close their doors for several years. For Mao, ideological purity takes precedence over technical competence. This clean-slate movement leads to an immense generational and cultural rift, the scars of which will permanently mark Chinese social structure.

lessons.title: From chaos to control
lessons.content:
From 1967, the social situation escapes Mao's own control. The various factions of **Red Guards** begin to fight each other violently to prove their revolutionary superiority, bringing some provinces to the brink of civil war. To restore order without disavowing himself, Mao has the <People's Liberation Army> intervene. It ends up reining in the turbulent youth through a radical measure: sending 17 million urban youths into forced exile in remote rural areas to be "re-educated" by the peasants.

{The obsession with Mao's thought affected all fields, including medicine. Newspapers of the time reported that surgeons performed open-heart surgeries while reciting quotes from the Little Red Book to guarantee the success of the operation through ideological force alone.}

The most violent phase of the movement subsides, but political paranoia persists at the top of the State. The struggle for Mao's succession becomes the new challenge. On one side, the radicals led by the **Gang of Four**, including Mao's wife, **Jiang Qing**, who want to continue the permanent revolution; on the other, the survivors of the purges who aspire to stability.

The effective end of this decade of chaos occurs with the death of **Mao Zedong** on **September 9, 1976**. Just a few weeks after his death, the **Gang of Four** is arrested, marking the official stop of the revolutionary experiment. The country emerges from this period bloodless, with a devastated economy and a population traumatized by ten years of denunciation and arbitrary violence.

lessons.title: The reckoning, then the pragmatic turn
lessons.content:
The legacy of the Cultural Revolution is heavy: the human death toll is estimated between **500,000 and 2 million** direct deaths, not counting the tens of millions of lives broken by deportation or disability. In **1981**, under the impetus of survivors of the chaos, the Chinese Communist Party publishes a historic resolution recognizing that the Cultural Revolution was a "grave mistake" attributable to Mao, although his status as father of the nation remains untouchable.

**Deng Xiaoping**, who had been purged twice and forced to work as a mechanic in a provincial factory, establishes himself as the new strongman. Drawing lessons from the isolation and irrationality of the previous period, he launches the policy of opening up and reform. He abandons Maoist utopia in favor of a pragmatism summarized by his famous metaphor: "It doesn't matter if the cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice".

This transition marks the shift from a China obsessed with class struggle to a power focused on economic growth. Nevertheless, the trauma of the Cultural Revolution remains a complex period of Chinese collective memory, often silenced in contemporary public space in order to preserve the regime's image of stability.

|| The Cultural Revolution (1966-1976): A decade of violent purges launched by Mao to regain power, marked by the destructive action of the Red Guards and concluded by the economic pragmatism of Deng Xiaoping. ||

quiz.explanation: This wall poster marks the launch of the Cultural Revolution: Mao declares war on his own administration.
options: The economic policy of the Western powers

quiz.explanation: Armed with the Little Red Book, the Red Guards attack everything that embodies the old culture, humiliating teachers and Party cadres.
options: Destroy the “four old things”: ideas, culture, customs and habits

quiz.question: True or false: from 1967, the different Red Guard factions began to clash with each other.
quiz.explanation: The movement spirals out of control and rival factions kill each other, forcing Mao to call in the army.

quiz.explanation: Around 17 million young city dwellers are sent to the countryside to end the urban chaos caused by the Red Guards.

quiz.explanation: Estimates place the direct human toll between 500,000 and 2 million deaths, not counting the lives shattered by persecution.

quiz.explanation: From Mao's appeal in 1966 to Deng Xiaoping's reforms in 1978, these milestones span a decade of purges followed by an economic shift.

title: The Holocaust: the mechanics of a genocide
description: Between **1941** and **1945**, the Nazi regime organized the murder of six million Jews. The Holocaust was not a sudden burst of hatred. It was a process run by a state.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Between 1941 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the extermination of **6 million Jews**, representing two-thirds of the European Jewish population at the time. This unprecedented crime, designated by the term **Shoah** (a Hebrew term meaning "catastrophe"), was not the product of a disorganized outburst of violence, but a rationalized State process. This genocide is distinguished by its bureaucratic character and its progressive transition from social persecution to industrialized killing, marking a major break in the history of Western civilization.

[Auschwitz-Birkenau entrance gate]

lessons.title: From discrimination to exclusion (1933-1939)
lessons.content:
From Adolf Hitler's accession to the position of chancellor in **January 1933**, the German state apparatus is put at the service of an anti-Semitic ideology. The first phase of persecution is legal and social: it involves "de-assimilating" Jews to exclude them from the national community. The **laws of Nuremberg**, adopted in September **1935**, constitute the foundation of this policy by depriving Jews of their citizenship and forbidding unions with citizens of "German blood".

This legal violence shifts into physical brutality during the **"Kristallnacht"** in November **1938**. This organized <pogrom> across the Reich sees the ransacking of thousands of businesses, the burning of synagogues, and the preventive internment of 30,000 men in concentration camps. On the eve of the war, Jewish life in Germany has become impossible, but the Nazi project is not yet total physical extermination; it is then about forcing mass emigration while seizing the victims' property.

The invasion of Poland in 1939 changes the scale. The Nazis are faced with millions of additional Jews. They then implement a policy of <ghettoization>, particularly in Warsaw and Łódź. Enclosed in unsanitary and overcrowded neighborhoods, Jewish populations suffer appalling mortality due to famine and epidemics, constituting a first stage of indirect destruction.

lessons.title: The invasion of the USSR and the shootings
lessons.content:
The decisive turn toward the "Final Solution" occurs on **June 22, 1941**, with the launch of Operation Barbarossa against the USSR. The war then takes on an ideological and racial dimension of extermination. In the wake of the **Wehrmacht**, mobile SS units named **<Einsatzgruppen>** are charged with eliminating the "enemies" of the Reich: communist cadres and, above all, the entirety of the Jewish populations encountered during the advance to the East.

[Einsatzgruppen execution]

The method, sometimes dubbed "Holocaust by bullets," is of a direct and traumatic violence for the executioners themselves. The commandos round up Jews on the outskirts of towns and villages, force them to dig mass graves before systematically shooting them. Within **18 months**, these mobile groups murder approximately **1.5 million people**. The massacre of **Babi Yar**, near Kyiv, in September 1941, remains the symbol of this phase with **33,771 victims** shot in just two days.

{The massacre at Babi Yar was so rapid that the Nazis did not have time to check if all the victims were dead; the walls of the pit continued to move for several hours under the weight of the freshly moved earth.}

However, this method of killing is judged too slow, too visible, and psychologically taxing for the soldiers. The Nazi authorities then seek a "cleaner" and more anonymous way to continue the extermination on a continental scale.

lessons.title: Wannsee: organizing murder across a continent
lessons.content:
The shift toward industrial extermination is coordinated during the **Wannsee Conference** on January 20, **1942**. Under the aegis of Reinhard Heydrich, 15 high-ranking officials settle the administrative details of the deportation of all European Jews to the East. It is not about deciding on the principle of extermination - already established by Hitler - but about ensuring the cooperation of all administrations (railways, justice, economy) for the logistics of the **"Final Solution"**.

[Wannsee Conference 1942]

This is how the killing centers appear in occupied Poland, such as **Belzec**, **Sobibor**, or **Treblinka**. Unlike classic concentration camps, these places have no detention function: they are designed as real death factories where victims are murdered as soon as they get off the train by asphyxiation in **gas chambers**. The **Auschwitz-Birkenau** complex becomes the nerve center of this system, combining a forced labor camp and an immediate extermination center.

At Auschwitz, a brutal **selection** is carried out on the unloading ramp by SS doctors. A minority of deportees is judged "fit for work" and survives temporarily in inhuman conditions; the vast majority (children, elderly people, pregnant women) is immediately led to their death. This process illustrates the notion of the **<banalité du mal>**, where bureaucrats manage the extermination of a people as if it were a simple transport and stock management problem.

lessons.title: The toll and the duty of memory
lessons.content:
When Allied troops liberate the camps in 1945, they discover the absolute horror of a crime that almost succeeded. Of the **9 million Jews** living in Europe before the war, two-thirds have disappeared. The toll is particularly heavy in Eastern Europe: Poland lost about 90% of its Jewish population, annihilating centuries of Yiddish culture.

Beyond the Jewish people alone, the Nazi regime also targeted the <Gypsies> (Porajmos), homosexuals, the disabled, and political opponents, but the Holocaust remains unique due to its aim for the total, systematic, and biological destruction of an entire people. The Nuremberg trials (1945-1946) would attempt to legally define this horror under the term **crime against humanity**.

The Holocaust deeply transformed world philosophical and legal thought. It forced humanity to question the capacity of technical modernity to produce barbarism. Today, the memory of the genocide is maintained by memorials like <Yad Vashem> in Israel, in order to prevent the return of such ideologies.

{During the trial of Adolf Eichmann in 1961, one of the few survivors of Auschwitz called to testify fainted upon seeing the accused in his glass booth, struck by the terribly ordinary appearance of the man who had organized the death trains.}

|| The Holocaust: 6 million Jews exterminated according to a bureaucratic industrialized system - the Wannsee Conference that organizes it lasts 90 minutes. ||

title: September 11, 2001
description: On **September 11, 2001**, nineteen Al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four planes. The deadliest attack in American history opened the era of the war on terror.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
On Tuesday, **September 11, 2001**, the world shifted into a new geopolitical era. Nineteen terrorists from the Islamist organization **<Al-Qaeda>** hijacked four commercial airliners to transform them into cruise missiles. Two crashed into the **World Trade Center** towers in New York, a symbol of global capitalism, while a third struck the **Pentagon**, headquarters of the American military command. The fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after a heroic struggle by the passengers.

[World Trade Center Twin Towers September 11 2001]

With a death toll of **2,977 people**, it remains the deadliest terrorist attack in history. This Event does not only constitute a human tragedy; it marks the end of the hope for a peaceful 'new world order' after the Cold War and triggers a series of conflicts whose shockwaves still shape the 21st century.

lessons.title: Where did Al-Qaeda come from?
lessons.content:
The September 11 attacks are not an isolated Event, but the culmination of the rising power of a transnational terrorist network. **Osama bin Laden**, a wealthy Saudi heir, founded **Al-Qaeda** in the late 1980s in the wake of the **<Soviet-Afghan War (1979-1989)>**. At that time, he indirectly benefited from logistical and financial support from the United States, via Pakistani secret services, because he was fighting the Soviet occupier.

[Osama bin Laden portrait]

After the Soviet withdrawal, bin Laden changed targets. He denounced the presence of American troops in **<Saudi Arabia>** during the Gulf War (1990) and set himself the mission of striking the West at its heart. During the 1990s, the network multiplied its attempts: a first bomb exploded in the basement of the World Trade Center in **1993**, followed by massive attacks against American embassies in Kenya and Tanzania in **1998**. In the year 2000, the USS Cole, a warship, was targeted in Yemen.

{The 19 hijackers spent approximately $400,000 to carry out their attacks - which caused economic damage estimated at more than $2 trillion between wars, security, and reconstruction.}

Despite these signs, the compartmentalization of American intelligence services prevented a global vision of the threat. The FBI and CIA, not sharing their crucial information on future hijackers already identified, failed to foil the plot in preparation.

lessons.title: The timeline of September 11
lessons.content:
The scenario of the attack relied on precise planning. Between 7:59 and 8:42 AM, four civilian flights took off from the East Coast. within, the terrorists, armed with box cutters, took control of the cockpits. At **8:46 AM**, **American Airlines Flight 11** struck the **North Tower** (WTC 1). As the media began to broadcast images of a presumed accident, doubt vanished at **9:03 AM**: **United Flight 175** struck the **South Tower** (WTC 2) live in front of millions of viewers.

L'attaque est totale. At **9:37 AM**, **American Flight 77** crashed into a wing of the **Pentagon** in Washington, proving that even the heart of the American defense is vulnerable. Chaos was absolute: airspace was closed for the first time in history, and President **George W. Bush** was evacuated by Air Force One. The sacrifice of the passengers on **United Flight 93** at **10:03 AM**, who revolted against the hijackers to prevent the plane from striking either the Capitol or the White House, marked the only partial failure of the terrorist operation.

The visual trauma reached its climax during the collapse of the skyscrapers. Weakened by the kerosene fire which melted the steel structures, the towers collapsed: the South Tower at **9:59 AM**, then the North Tower at **10:28 AM**. New York was covered by a phenomenal cloud of toxic dust, creating an unprecedented scene of urban apocalypse.

lessons.title: The war on terror
lessons.content:
In reaction, the United States declared a 'global war on terror'. In **October 2001**, with the support of NATO, they launched Operation **<Enduring Freedom>** in **Afghanistan**. The objective is twofold: to destroy Al-Qaeda bases and to overthrow the **<Taliban>**, the fundamentalist regime that harbored bin Laden. Kabul fell quickly, but guerrilla warfare took hold for twenty years of conflict.

However, the Bush administration widened its target. In **March 2003**, the United States invaded **<Iraq>** without a UN mandate. The official motive was the possession by **<Saddam Hussein>** of weapons of mass destruction, intelligence that would prove to be false. This intervention lastingly destabilized the region, leading to a civil war and the dismantling of the Iraqi state, which would offer fertile ground for the future emergence of new extremist networks like the Islamic State.

{The fear of flying after September 11 pushed millions of Americans to take the car, resulting in an increase in road accidents of 1,500 additional deaths in one year. The fear of terrorism killed more people than terrorism itself.}

On the domestic front, these wars were accompanied by legal gray zones, such as the opening of the **<Guantanamo>** camp for 'enemy combatants' deprived of classic legal rights. It was not until ten years later, on **May 1, 2011**, that Osama bin Laden was located and executed by special forces during a raid in Pakistan.

lessons.title: A world under surveillance
lessons.content:
The consequences of September 11 radically modify the social contract in democracies. In the United States, the **PATRIOT Act**, passed shortly after the attacks, grants massive surveillance powers to the authorities, reducing the protection of privacy in the name of national security. This model of exceptional legislation spread throughout Europe, reinforcing control over communications and financial transactions.

Air travel was forever transformed by the creation of the **TSA** and the drastic strengthening of security controls in airports. Architecturally, the Ground Zero area in New York has been rebuilt around a memorial and the new One World Trade Center tower, making the site a sanctuary of American resilience. 

The legacy of September 11 is heavy: it is estimated that the wars that followed caused the death of more than 500,000 people (direct and indirect) and displaced millions of refugees. The world now lives under the constant threat of decentralized terrorist networks that use the tools of globalization to fight it.

{More than 300 search and rescue dogs worked at the Ground Zero site. Bretagne, the last surviving dog who served during the searches, passed away in 2016 at the age of 16, honored by a line of honor from the New York firefighters.}

|| To remember: September 11, 2001 marks the transition from a localized threat to a global terrorism led by Al-Qaeda, triggering major military interventions (Afghanistan, Iraq) and a permanent security shift in Western societies. ||

title: Athenian democracy
description: In the 5th century BC, Athens invented a system where citizens governed directly. Selection by lot, an equal right to speak, and exclusion on a massive scale.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
In the 5th century BC, the city of Athens underwent an unprecedented conceptual revolution: it invented <politics> in the modern sense. For the first time in human history, a system was designed so that citizens were no longer the subjects of a monarch, but the sovereign actors of their own destiny. This regime of **direct democracy** was based on the idea that power (kratos) belongs to the people (demos).

Far from being born spontaneously, this organization was the result of two centuries of social tensions and legislative compromises. It transformed the public space into a place of permanent deliberation, symbolized by the nerve centers of the city where religious, commercial, and judicial life mixed.

[Athens Agora ancient ruins]

This Athenian experience, although limited geographically and socially, remains the foundation of Western political thought and an essential reference two and a half millennia later.

lessons.title: Reforms that opened up the city
lessons.content:
Athenian democracy emerged from a state of profound crisis. In the 7th century BC, the city was torn apart by the privileges of the landed aristocracy and the massive debt of the peasantry. **Solon**, appointed archon (leader) in **594 BC**, laid the first cornerstone by abolishing debt slavery. He replaced birthright with wealth right, allowing non-noble citizens to access magistracies. Although he did not yet create democracy, he introduced the idea that the law must apply to everyone.

The real turning point occurred with **<Cleisthenes>** in **508-507 BC**. To end the clan struggles that were paralyzing Athens, he carried out a radical spatial reorganization of Attica. He divided the territory into three zones (city, coast, internally) and created **10 artificial tribes** composed of citizens from these three regions. This geographic diversity broke traditional neighborhood and family loyalties in favor of a new civic solidarity.

Cleisthenes also instituted the **Boule**, or Council of Five Hundred. Each tribe provided 50 members drawn by lot for one year. This council was responsible for preparing the laws that would be debated before the people. Through this structure, Cleisthenes guaranteed that every citizen, regardless of their origin or profession, could actively participate in the city's administrative machinery.

To avoid the return of a tyrant, Cleisthenes established the procedure where the exile of a politician was voted on using a ceramic shard, but a quorum of 6,000 voters was required for the decision to be valid.

lessons.title: How it worked under Pericles
lessons.content:
It was in the middle of the 5th century BC, during the golden age of Athens, that the system reached maturity. Under the influence of **Pericles**, a general re-elected fifteen times, democracy became "radical." The beating heart of the system was the **Ecclesia**, the sovereign assembly of citizens. It met about **40 times a year** on the slope of the **Pnyx**, a hill facing the Acropolis.

The Ecclesia decided everything: it voted on laws, declared war, signed peace treaties, and controlled the city's finances. The fundamental principle was **Isegoria**, the equal right for every citizen to speak at the podium. Voting was generally done by a show of hands, except for serious decisions affecting individuals.

[Pericles bust sculpture]

To make this equality real and not purely theoretical, Pericles introduced the **Misthos**, a daily allowance paid to citizens who sat in the assembly or in the courts. Without this financial compensation, the poorest citizens (artisans, small farmers) would not have been able to leave their work to serve the city. 

Justice was administered by the **Heliaia**, a popular court composed of **6,000 jurors** drawn by lot from volunteers over the age of 30. By multiplying the use of drawing lots for most public functions (except for the military positions of generals, which required technical skills), Athens ensured that no individual could appropriate power in the long term.

lessons.title: A democracy that excluded most people
lessons.content:
Despite the modernity of its discourse on equality, Athenian democracy was a closed democracy, reserved for a privileged minority. To be a citizen, one had to be a man, free, of age, and have completed military service (ephebia). In **451 BC**, Pericles even tightened the conditions: one now had to be born of a citizen father and a mother who was the daughter of a citizen.

Out of a total population estimated at about **300,000 inhabitants**, only a tiny portion (between 30,000 and 50,000 people) enjoyed political rights. Three categories were structurally excluded from the system:

**Women**, who were legally eternal minors under the guardianship of their father or husband. **Slaves**, essential to the economy to free up time for citizens, were considered "animated tools" devoid of any rights. Finally, **metics**, foreigners residing in Athens, paid taxes and served in the army but had neither the right to vote nor the right to own land.

This democracy was therefore a "face-to-face democracy" where equality among peers rested on the exploitation of a huge servile labor force and the systematic exclusion of foreigners and women. It is the paradox of a system that advocated universal freedom while being founded on a strictly hierarchical social structure.

In Athens, if a citizen was not interested in public life, he was called an "idiotes" (private individual), a term that gave rise to the word "idiot" because it was considered that a person uninterested in the common good lacked reason.

lessons.title: Weak points and legacy
lessons.content:
The functioning of the Ecclesia was not without its excesses. The influence of **Demagogues**, skilled speakers using emotion to manipulate crowds, often led the city to disastrous decisions, particularly during the war against Sparta. The philosopher **Plato**, witness to the decline of Athens and traumatized by the death sentence of his teacher **Socrates** in **399 BC**, became the fiercest critic of the regime. For him, democracy was the reign of shifting opinion rather than truth, leading inevitably to anarchy.

Socrates' death illustrates the dark side of popular sovereignty: the assembly, in a moment of religious and political fever, voted for the philosopher's death for "corrupting the youth." This decision remains in history as the classic example of the tyranny of the majority against free thought. 

Yet, despite these flaws, the Athenian model has survived in the global political imagination. It introduced key concepts: the accountability of governors to the governed, equality before the law, and the necessity of adversarial debate. Today, as our representative democracies face crises of legitimacy, the Athenian model of drawing lots and direct citizen involvement is returning to the center of contemporary political reflection.

|| To remember: Athenian democracy (5th century BC) was a system of direct management of power by free male citizens. Based on drawing lots and equality of speech at the Ecclesia, this model excluded 85% of the population but laid the foundations for law and public debate in the West. ||

title: The American Civil War
description: From **1861** to **1865**, the United States tore itself apart: more than **620,000** dead. At the heart of the war, slavery, national unity, and the birth of a stronger federal state.
subject: histoire

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
From **1861 to 1865**, the United States went through the most serious crisis in its History: the **Civil War**. This fratricidal conflict, which opposed the Northern states (the Union) to the Southern states (the Confederacy), transformed a young republic into a modern industrial power, but at the cost of unprecedented human trauma. With more than **620,000 deaths**, this conflict remains the deadliest war ever fought by Americans, highlighting in red-hot iron the questions of national unity and the abolition of a slave system that had become morally and economically anachronistic.

[American Civil War battle]

lessons.title: Two Americas face to face
lessons.content:
In the mid-19th century, the United States no longer formed a homogeneous bloc. The **North** was experiencing a galloping industrial revolution, relying on a salaried workforce, dense urban infrastructure, and a protectionist policy. In contrast, the **South** remained an aristocratic and rural society, whose wealth depended almost exclusively on cotton exports produced by **4 million slaves**.

[slaves American southern plantation]

The fracture is not only economic; it is ideological. The debate centers on the notion of **<States' Rights vs. the federal government>**. Southerners rejected any attempt by Washington to interfere in their 'particular institution', slavery. The election to the presidency of **Abraham Lincoln**, in November **1860**, acted as a spark. Although Lincoln was moderate, he represented the **Republican Party**, which was vigorously anti-slavery.

Without having obtained a single vote in the Southern states, his election was perceived by the Southern elites as a declaration of political war. Even before his inauguration, South Carolina seceded, followed by six other states. Together, they founded the **Confederate States of America** (CSA) in Montgomery, choosing **Jefferson Davis** as president. Their constitution sealed their identity by explicitly guaranteeing the permanence of slavery.

{ Originally, regional identity was so prevalent that people said 'the United States ARE' in the plural. It was only after the war that the use of the singular, 'the United States IS', became standard to designate an indivisible nation.}

lessons.title: Total war, then emancipation
lessons.content:
The armed conflict began on **April 12, 1861** when Southern cannons bombarded **Fort Sumter**, a federal bastion located in South Carolina. This aggression pushed Lincoln to raise an army of volunteers, leading to the secession of four additional states, including Virginia. The war, which many thought would be short, bogged down in unprecedented industrial violence.

On **September 17, 1862**, the Battle of **Antietam** marked a psychological turning point. It was the bloodiest day in American military History, with **23,000 casualties** in just twelve hours. Although the tactical result was indecisive, the failure of the invasion of the North by General **Robert E. Lee** provided Lincoln with the political capital necessary to transform the meaning of the war. On January 1, **1863**, he signed the **<Emancipation Proclamation>**.

This decree radically changed the nature of the conflict: from a war for the simple preservation of the Union, it became a crusade for freedom. Diplomatically, this prevented European powers like the United Kingdom from intervening in favor of the South, as they could not openly support a proslavery cause. Despite this, the Confederacy resisted thanks to the tactical genius of its generals, until the shock of **Gettysburg** in July **1863**. This giant battle, involving more than 160,000 men, definitively broke the Southern momentum.

{ The Civil War saw the birth of the beginnings of modern plastic surgery; surgeons like Gurdon Buck performed the first facial reconstructions on soldiers disfigured by the new types of Minié balls.}

lessons.title: Northern victory, Lincoln's death
lessons.content:
Starting in 1864, the Union mobilized its overwhelming material superiority. General **Ulysses Grant**, appointed commander-in-chief, launched a war of total attrition, accepting heavy losses to exhaust the South's limited human reserves. At the same time, General **Sherman** applied scorched-earth tactics during his famous 'March to the Sea', devastating Georgia to break the morale of civilian populations.

The asphyxiation was total. Cornered, General **Robert E. Lee** was forced to sign the surrender of the Army of Northern Virginia at **Appomattox** on **April 9, 1865**. The North's victory was total, but mourning quickly tarnished the triumph.

[Abraham Lincoln portrait]

On **April 14, 1865**, just five days after the capitulation, Lincoln was assassinated at **Ford's Theatre** by the Southern-sympathizing actor **John Wilkes Booth**. The disappearance of the providential man deprived the nation of its best reconciler just as the **<Reconstruction>** began. In December **1865**, the **13th Amendment** was ratified, constitutionally abolishing slavery throughout the territory. However, the integration of former slaves remained a colossal challenge for the republic purified by blood.

lessons.title: Scars and legacy
lessons.content:
The end of fighting did not mean the end of tensions. The Period of **<Reconstruction>** (1865-1877) attempted to impose civil equality in the militarily occupied South. Real progress was made: African Americans voted and were elected to Congress. But this Period provoked a violent reaction from white supremacists, marked by the creation of the **Ku Klux Klan** in **1865**.

The withdrawal of federal troops in 1877 sounded the death knell for these hopes. Southern states established **Jim Crow laws**, a system of racial segregation that would last for nearly a century. The Civil War therefore created a nation united on the map and freed from legal slavery, but it left a deep social and racial fracture that the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s would only begin to resolve.

On a geopolitical level, the conflict nevertheless forged the tools of the future World power: an overpowered heavy industry, a transcontinental railway network, and a strong, centralized federal State capable of intervening massively in the economy and society.

title: Why is the sky blue?
description: Looking at a blue sky is so ordinary that we forget to ask why. The answer lies in the light of the Sun and in the air we look through to see it.
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Watching the blue sky is such a common act that we forget the incredible physical complexity playing out above our heads. This daily spectacle is not due to an intrinsic coloring of the air, but results from a precise interaction between solar radiation and the components of our atmosphere.

Understanding why the sky is blue means diving into the physics of light and discovering that this same mechanism is responsible for the flaming hues of twilight. It is all a matter of trajectory, particle size, and biological perception.

[sunset red orange sky atmosphere]

lessons.title: White light hides every color
lessons.content:
Light from the sun appears white to us, but it hides a much richer reality: it contains the entirety of the **<visible spectrum of light>**. Like a prism, the atmosphere breaks down this clarity into a multitude of colors, ranging from violet to red. Each color is distinguished by its **wavelength**. Cool tones, like blue and violet, have short, tight waves, while warm tones, like red, stretch into much longer waves.

The space between the sun and our eyes is not an absolute vacuum, but a dense medium filled with **gas molecules**, mainly **nitrogen** and **dioxygen**. These particles are extremely small, much smaller than the wavelength of visible light. This difference in size is crucial: it determines how the rays will bounce off the molecules.

When a solar ray enters the atmosphere, it does not always travel through the air in a straight line. It encounters these molecular obstacles that act as deflectors, sending light energy in an infinity of new directions. This phenomenon is the starting point for the coloring of our celestial dome.

{If one were on the Moon, which has no atmosphere to scatter light, the sky would remain a deep black even in broad daylight, despite the brilliant presence of the sun.}

lessons.title: Scattering: why blue wins
lessons.content:
It was in 1871 that the British physicist **Lord Rayleigh** mathematically theorized this behavior of light. He discovered that a particle's ability to deflect light depends radically on its color. This principle, named **<Rayleigh scattering>**, establishes that short waves are scattered much more intensely than long waves.

[blue sky sunlight scattering atmosphere]

In practice, blue light, with its short wavelength, is hit and scattered by air molecules about **9 times more** than red light. While red rays cross the atmosphere in an almost straight line without being disturbed, blue rays ricochet everywhere. 

This is why, when you look up at a portion of the sky that is not directly in alignment with the sun, you still receive light: it is the blue light that has been scattered in all directions and finally reaches your retina. The sky literally "glows" with this blue scattered by the upper layers of the air.

{The sky on Mars is the opposite of ours: it is often pinkish-orange during the day because the iron dust in its atmosphere scatters light differently, but the sunset there is blue.}

lessons.title: So why not violet?
lessons.content:
A legitimate question then arises: if the shortest waves are the most scattered, why is the sky not violet? Indeed, violet has an even shorter wavelength than blue and therefore undergoes even more brutal scattering. The "physical" sky therefore contains a huge amount of scattered violet.

The answer is not found in the sky, but in the biology of our vision. The human eye captures light thanks to receptors called **cones**. We possess three types of cones, sensitive to red, green, and blue. Our visual system is significantly more efficient at detecting blue than violet. Furthermore, the sun naturally emits a larger quantity of blue photons than violet photons.

Our brain therefore makes a sort of "average" of this diffuse light and renders a characteristic azure blue for us. If we had the vision of certain birds or insects capable of perceiving ultraviolet light, the sky would probably offer us a palette of saturated colors very different from the one we know.

lessons.title: And the red of evening?
lessons.content:
The spectacle of the sunset uses exactly the same physical laws, but changes the distance parameters. At noon, the sun is at its zenith and its light passes through the minimum thickness of the atmosphere to reach us. In contrast, when the sun descends toward the horizon, its rays must travel a **much longer** distance through the dense layers of air before arriving at your eye.

During this long horizontal journey, Rayleigh scattering is so total that almost all blue light is dispersed long before reaching you. It is literally "filtered" by the thickness of the air. What remains of the initial beam are the most resistant and longest wavelengths: reds and oranges.

The more the air is charged with humidity or **aerosols** (small particles of dust or pollution), the more intense the colors can become. These larger particles sometimes cause another type of scattering, <Mie scattering>, which can give the sky a milky appearance or intensify orange hues over vast areas.

|| To remember: The sky is blue because short waves (blue) are scattered 9 times more by air molecules than long waves (red); at sunset, the distance crossed is so great that only red remains. ||

quiz.explanation: Short waves like blue are much more dispersed by air molecules than long waves like red: this is Rayleigh scattering.
