title: The discovery of anesthesia
description: Before 1846, patients were often awake and in extreme pain while surgeons worked. Anesthesia turned an operation into treatment instead of torture.
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: Before the mid-19th century, entering an operating room was akin to passing through the gates of hell. The discovery of anesthesia in 1846 marks a fundamental break, not only technical but also moral, in the history of <sciences>. It transformed the perception of the suffering body and allowed for the rise of complex surgery, once unimaginable. This course explores the transition from "organized terror" to the birth of a rigorous medical discipline that revolutionized humanity's relationship with pain.

lessons.title: Before: speed against suffering
lessons.content:
Before 1846, surgery was performed only as a last resort, in the face of certain death. The lack of pain control imposed a unique constraint on the practitioner: **speed**. A surgeon was not judged on his meticulousness, but on his ability to amputate a limb before the patient sank into a fatal **traumatic shock**. Operating rooms, often located at the top of buildings to benefit from natural light, were designed to isolate screams, while sturdy assistants held down struggling patients.

[surgery without anesthesia 19th century]

{The surgeon Robert Liston was so fast that he once accidentally amputated his assistant's fingers; both the patient and the assistant died of infection, and a spectator died of cardiac shock, making this the only operation in history with a 300% mortality rate.}

At that time, the only recourses were rudimentary sedatives like **alcohol**, **opium**, or **mesmerization** (a form of hypnosis), but none truly succeeded in suppressing the sensation of tearing tissues and bones. The profession of surgeon then required total psychological insensitivity, an "iron hand" capable of ignoring the pleas of the patient. This physiological limit blocked all medical progress: it was impossible to open the abdomen or the thorax on a conscious and agitated patient.

lessons.title: 1846: the day of ether
lessons.content:
On **October 16, 1846**, at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, an experiment definitely changed the course of History. The dentist **<William Morton>**, who had long been looking for a way to extract teeth without pain, organized a public demonstration. He used an inhaler of his invention containing **sulfuric ether**, whose intoxicating properties were known recreationally but never successfully applied to major surgery.

[ether anesthesia first demonstration 1846]

{Before becoming a medical tool, ether was used in student parties called "Ether frolics", where guests inhaled the gas to laugh and stagger, not realizing they no longer felt the blows they gave themselves when falling.}

Before the eyes of an amphitheater filled with skeptical students and doctors, Morton administered the gas to **Gilbert Abbott**. Once the patient was asleep, the surgeon **John Warren** proceeded to excise a vascular tumor in the neck. Unlike the usual scenes of torture, the patient remained still, his breathing calm. Upon Abbott's awakening, who confirmed feeling nothing, Warren declared to the assembly: "Gentlemen, this is no humbug."

This success marks the end of systematic surgical pain. The news crossed the Atlantic in record time. As early as December 1846, Robert Liston himself performed the first amputation under ether in London, exclaiming that this "Yankee dodge" beat everything he had ever known. However, this revolution was not welcomed without friction: some clergy opposed anesthesia, arguing that pain was a necessary divine trial, particularly during childbirth.

lessons.title: Next: chloroform and arguments
lessons.content:
The success of ether immediately triggered a violent battle for the priority of the invention. **Crawford Long**, a country doctor, claimed to have used ether as early as **1842**, but his lack of publication deprived him of World recognition. Meanwhile, **Charles Jackson**, a chemist, claimed to be the real brain behind Morton's idea. This quarrel ended up poisoning the lives of the protagonists, with Morton dying ruined by endless lawsuits to validate his patent.

On a technical level, ether had major drawbacks: it was irritating to the respiratory tract and highly flammable. In 1847, the Scottish obstetrician **James Young Simpson** introduced **chloroform**. More powerful and more pleasantly scented, it quickly became the favorite product in Europe.

{James Young Simpson discovered the virtues of chloroform during a dinner with friends: after inhaling some to test the product, they all woke up the next morning under the dining room table, thus proving the radical effectiveness of the gas.}

Its use was definitively legitimized in 1853 when **Queen Victoria** accepted it for the birth of her eighth child, silencing the last religious objections.

Over the decades, chemical research led to the discovery of less toxic and more precise agents. Medicine then moved from a brutal sleep-inducing technique to a fine management of the state of consciousness, opening the way for modern long-duration surgery.

lessons.title: Anesthesia today
lessons.content:
The discovery of anesthetic gases was only a first step. At the end of the 19th century, the understanding of microorganisms thanks to <Antisepsie (Semmelweis and Lister)> completed the medical arsenal: one could now operate without pain AND without infection. Anesthesia then became a science of monitoring. One no longer merely put the patient to sleep; one learned to monitor their **vital signs** (pulse, breathing).

{The word "anesthesia" was suggested to William Morton by the poet and physician Oliver Wendell Holmes, from the Ancient Greek meaning "absence of sensation"; before that, it was simply called "gaseous preparation".}

The 20th century saw the appearance of **intravenous anesthesia** and muscle relaxants, which allowed for the relaxation of muscles without the need to administer massive and dangerous doses of gas. Today, the anesthesiologist is an indispensable pillar of the operating room. They precisely dose analgesia (pain suppression), narcosis (sleep), and muscle relaxation, ensuring the safety of the patient during interventions that can last more than twelve hours.

Surgery has thus moved from a spectacle of brutal speed to a discipline of surgical precision. Without anesthesia, organ transplants, cardiac surgery, or neurosurgery could never have seen the light of day. It is one of the rare fields where science has succeeded in abolishing a multi-millennial biological fatality.

quiz.question: In what year was the first public demonstration of ether anesthesia in Boston?
quiz.explanation: On October 16, 1846, in Boston, the first convincing public demonstration of anesthesia took place.

quiz.question: Before anesthesia, what were surgeons primarily judged on?
quiz.explanation: Without anesthesia, surgeons were judged on their speed, to limit the patient's suffering.
options: The number of successful operations without anesthetic
Their ability to make the patient speak

quiz.question: What product did William Morton have a patient inhale during the 1846 demonstration?
quiz.explanation: Dentist William Morton makes the patient inhale ether before the operation.

quiz.question: Who is the surgeon operating on the neck tumor during this demonstration?
quiz.explanation: Surgeon John Warren operates on a neck tumor while the patient is on ether.

quiz.question: True or false: During the 1846 demonstration, the patient screamed in pain during the entire operation.
quiz.explanation: The patient does not scream thanks to the ether, which astonishes the entire room.

quiz.question: What other anesthetic product then became popular, particularly in Great Britain?
quiz.explanation: Chloroform then became popular, particularly in Great Britain, alongside ether.

quiz.question: What problem remains to be solved after the discovery of ether, giving birth to a new medical specialty?
quiz.explanation: We must learn to dose, monitor breathing and the heart: this is the birth of anesthesiology.
options: Dose anesthesia without killing the patient, by monitoring breathing and heart
Find a completely painless product for the anesthesiologist
Convince patients to accept the operation

quiz.question: True or false: today, anesthesia can only put the entire body to sleep, never just one area.
quiz.explanation: Today, we can put the whole body or just an area to sleep, using local or regional anesthesia.

title: Darwin's theory of evolution
description: In 1859, Darwin published On the Origin of Species. The core idea: living things change over time through natural selection.
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: In 1859, the publication of **"On the Origin of Species"** by **Charles Darwin** marked a major epistemological break. This text did not just propose that species change over time, an idea already in the making among some naturalists; it offered for the first time a universal, rational, and verifiable explanatory mechanism: **<natural selection>**. By unifying all of the life sciences under a single biological law, Darwin moved humanity from its providential pedestal to place it within an immense common lineage. This course explores the genesis of this revolution, from the deck of the Beagle to the foundations of modern biology.

lessons.title: The voyage that opened his eyes
lessons.content:
In December **1831**, the young **Charles Darwin** embarked on an expedition around the world aboard the **<HMS Beagle>**. His initial mission was cartographic, but the trip quickly transformed into an immense enterprise of collecting geological and biological specimens. During five years of travel, Darwin amassed observations that contradicted the fixist vision of the time, according to which species were created once and for all in their current form.

[Charles Darwin portrait]

It was during his stopover in the **Galápagos Islands** in 1835 that the most famous click in the history of biology occurred. He observed varieties of **<finches>** that were morphologically close, but whose beak shapes varied radically from one island to another. This specialization seemed directly linked to the available food resources: strong beaks for cracking seeds, or thin ones for capturing insects.

[Darwin finches Galapagos beaks]

Darwin then began to doubt the immutability of species. He sensed that these birds shared a common ancestor from the mainland and that they had modified over time to adapt to their respective environments. Back in England in 1836, he would nevertheless take more than **20 years** to formalize his intuitions, aware that his theory would shake the religious and social foundations of Victorian society.

{The captain of the Beagle, Robert FitzRoy, was a fervent creationist who bitterly regretted all his life having involuntarily allowed Darwin to gather the evidence for his theory.}

lessons.title: Natural selection, in plain words
lessons.content:
To structure his thinking, Darwin relied on four implacable logical pillars. The first is **variation**: within a population, all individuals are slightly different. The second is **selection pressure**: the natural environment cannot support the infinite expansion of populations, creating a struggle for survival. 

The third pillar is **adaptive advantage**: in this competitive environment, certain biological traits (running faster, better resisting cold, having a beak adapted to hard seeds) increase the chances of survival and reproduction. Finally, **hereditary transmission** ensures that these advantageous traits propagate from generation to generation.

This process, which Darwin calls **natural selection**, is a blind mechanism, without intention or final goal. Contrary to popular belief, it is not the victory of the strongest, but the survival of the best adapted. Through the accumulation of these micro-changes over millions of years, entire populations are transformed, eventually forming new species. This is what Darwin calls **descent with modification**, drawing the image of a tree of life where all creatures are connected by common ancestors.

lessons.title: A clash of ideas
lessons.content:
Despite the solidity of his work, Darwin hesitated to publish, fearing public disgrace. Everything changed in **1858** when he received a manuscript from a young naturalist exploring Malaysia, **<Alfred Russel Wallace>**. To Darwin's astonishment, Wallace had, independently, reached the same conclusions about natural selection. Under pressure from his scientific friends, Darwin rushed the writing of his masterpiece so as not to lose the priority of his discovery.

The public reaction was violent. The most radical implication of the theory, although Darwin was careful not to make it explicit in his first work, was that the human being is just one animal among others, coming from the same lineage as the great apes. This idea provoked epic debates, like the one in 1860 between Bishop **<Samuel Wilberforce>** and biologist **<Thomas Huxley>**, nicknamed "Darwin's bulldog" for his fierce defense of the theory.

Huxley then embodied the transition of science from shadow to light, refusing to let religious dogmas dictate biological truth. Darwin's theory gradually imposed itself not through ideological fervor, but through its unmatched ability to explain the natural world with an economy of means and a scientific precision never before achieved.

lessons.title: And today?
lessons.content:
Darwin knew nothing of the mechanisms of heredity. He did not know how traits were physically transmitted from parents to children. It would take until the 20th century for the discovery of **<DNA>** and work on **genetics** to fill this void. This fusion between natural selection and genetics is today called the **modern synthesis**. 

Far from being a simple hypothesis, evolution is a fact observed daily. It can be seen in the resistance of bacteria to antibiotics or in the rapid evolution of certain viruses. Darwin's theory transformed biology, once a simple science of cataloging, into a predictive and dynamic science. It teaches us that life is in perpetual flux and that today's biodiversity is the result of a story four billion years long.

|| Darwin revolutionized our vision of the world in 1859 by demonstrating that the complexity of life emerges from a natural and blind process: natural selection. ||

{The expression "survival of the fittest" was coined by philosopher Herbert Spencer to justify social inequalities, a concept that Darwin himself found scientifically dubious.}

quiz.question: In what year did Charles Darwin publish “On the Origin of Species”?
quiz.explanation: Darwin published his major work in 1859.

quiz.explanation: Darwin boarded the ship the Beagle and spent years observing nature around the world.

quiz.explanation: In the Galapagos, Darwin noticed that nearby birds had different beaks depending on their diet, a strong clue.
options: Different beaks depending on their food
Always the same size whatever the bird

quiz.question: What did Darwin call the mechanism by which traits useful for survival spread through a population?
quiz.explanation: Darwin calls this mechanism natural selection: the environment instead keeps what helps to survive and reproduce.

quiz.question: True or false: according to Darwin, individuals “want” to evolve to adapt to their environment.
quiz.explanation: It is not a will: it is a filter, the environment rather keeps the traits that work, without the intention of the individuals.

quiz.question: What other naturalist comes up with ideas close to those of Darwin, which pushes him to publish his book?
quiz.explanation: Alfred Russel Wallace came up with similar ideas, which pushed Darwin to finally release his book.

quiz.question: Why did Darwin's ideas shock 19th century society?
quiz.explanation: Saying that species change, and that humans share a history with other animals, shakes up the religion and society of the time.
options: They challenge the idea that species were created as they are, and bring humans closer to other animals
They prove that the Earth is younger than we thought
They announce the end of traditional agriculture
They call into question the existence of fossils

quiz.question: According to the course, what current example illustrates “live” evolution?
quiz.explanation: The fight against antibiotic-resistant bacteria is an example of evolution that can be observed directly.
options: The complete disappearance of the dinosaurs

title: The Big Bang
description: 13.8 billion years ago, the universe started to expand. This is not a bomb going off in a void: space itself is what grows.
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
**13.8 billion years** ago, the entire universe - all matter, all energy, and space itself - was concentrated in a state of extreme density and temperature. This initial state, which scientists call a <singularity>, marks the beginning of cosmic history.

[Big Bang universe expansion galaxies]

Contrary to a common misconception, the Big Bang does not refer to a single moment of creation, but the cosmological model describing the evolution of the universe since that primordial moment. In a fraction of a second, it began to expand at a dazzling rate. This expansion continues today, continuously shaping the structure of the cosmos and pushing galaxies away from each other.

lessons.title: Not an explosion in a void
lessons.content:
The term **"Big Bang"** is one of the most famous in science, but also one of the most misunderstood. One should not imagine this Event as an explosion of matter spreading into a pre-existing vacuum. In reality, it is space itself that is stretching. Before this moment, there was neither space, nor time, nor matter as we know them. The question "what was there before?" is often considered to be without physical meaning, because time began with this Event.

The origin of the name is paradoxical. The term was coined in **1949** by the British astrophysicist **Fred Hoyle**. Ironically, Hoyle was a fierce opponent of this Theory: he defended the steady-state model, according to which the universe had always existed without major change. By using the expression "Big Bang" during a BBC broadcast, he sought to ridicule the idea of a sudden beginning. Although Hoyle was wrong on the substance, his vivid expression caught the public imagination and remained the official name.

This expansion has no "center". If you imagine the surface of a balloon being inflated, every point moves away from the others without a single point on the surface being designated as the middle of the expansion. This is precisely what happens in our three-dimensional universe.

 Despite his opposition to the Big Bang, Fred Hoyle discovered how stars manufacture complex chemical elements (carbon, oxygen) through nuclear fusion, which would have earned him the Nobel Prize had he not been so controversial.

lessons.title: Three great proofs
lessons.content:
Sciences do not rely on simple suppositions, but on tangible evidence. The first major breakthrough dates back to **1929**, when the astronomer **Edwin Hubble** observed the Movement of distant galaxies. He noticed a systematic phenomenon: the further a galaxy is from Earth, the faster it seems to move away. This proportional link between distance and speed, called Hubble's constant, proves that the universe is not static but in full expansion.

[Hubble deep field galaxies]

The second major proof, and arguably the most spectacular, is the **<cosmic microwave background>**. In **1965**, two engineers, **Arno Penzias** and **Robert Wilson**, working on a telecommunication antenna, picked up a constant background noise, a sleet that came from everywhere at once. After eliminating all possible terrestrial sources, they realized they had just detected the thermal "echo" of the Big Bang. This microwave radiation was emitted 380,000 years after the start of the universe, at the precise moment when light was able to circulate freely for the first time.

 A small part of the "snow" or sleet that you could see on old un-tuned analog televisions comes directly from this cosmic microwave background.

Finally, the abundance of light elements confirms the model. Calculations predict that the first minutes of the Big Bang must have produced about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium. Telescopic observations show exactly these proportions in the oldest gas clouds in the universe, thus validating the Theory of <primordial nucleosynthesis>.

lessons.title: The story in fast-forward
lessons.content:
Modern physics allows us to go back in time with dizzying precision, but it hits an invisible wall: the **Planck Time**, located at **10⁻⁴³ seconds** after the initial instant. Before this threshold, temperature and density are so high that our current laws (general Relativity and quantum physics) are no longer compatible. This is the realm of the unknown.

Just after, the universe goes through a phase of **Inflation**, an exponential expansion in a fraction of a second that makes the universe homogeneous. At **3 minutes**, the temperature drops enough for protons and neutrons to assemble: this is the birth of the first atomic nuclei. However, the universe remains an opaque fog of free electrons that block light.

It takes **380,000 years** for "recombination" to occur: electrons are captured by nuclei to form the first neutral atoms. Light is finally released: it is the emission of the **<cosmic microwave background>**. As for the first **stars**, they only appear about **200 million years** later, ending the "dark ages". Our own solar system is a newcomer, formed only **4.6 billion years** ago, benefiting from matter recycled by generations of long-gone stars.

 If the 13.8-billion-year History of the universe were scaled down to a single calendar year, the Big Bang would take place on January 1st at midnight and the human species would only make its appearance on December 31st at 11:52 PM.

lessons.title: And tomorrow?
lessons.content:
For a long time, cosmologists wondered if gravity would eventually stop the expansion to cause a final collapse. However, a major discovery in **1998** overturned this vision: the **<accelerated expansion of the universe>**. By observing distant <supernovae>, researchers realized that the universe is not just expanding, but doing so faster and faster.

This mysterious force pushing the universe apart is called **dark energy**. It would represent about 68% of the total content of the universe, while ordinary matter (what we are made of) accounts for only 5%. This acceleration suggests that the universe will end in a state of absolute cold and total dilution, a scenario named the **Big Freeze**.

The observable universe, which is the part of space that light has had time to travel to reach us, has a radius of about **46 billion light-years**. This figure exceeds 13.8 billion years because, while the light was traveling towards us, the space between it and us continued to stretch. This immensity reminds us that we are seeing only a tiny fraction of a whole that could well be infinite.

|| The Big Bang, which occurred 13.8 billion years ago, is not an explosion in space but the expansion of space itself, proven by the receding of galaxies and fossil radiation. ||

quiz.question: What is the Big Bang, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: The Big Bang is not an explosion in a pre-existing void: it is space itself which begins to grow, taking matter with it.
options: The expansion of space itself, not an explosion into a void already there

quiz.explanation: British astrophysicist Fred Hoyle coined the term in 1949 to mock the idea, but the nickname stuck.

quiz.explanation: In 1929, Hubble showed that the universe is not static: it is growing.

quiz.explanation: Penzias and Wilson capture the cosmic microwave background, a thermal echo of the young universe coming from all directions.
options: The cosmic microwave background, a radio crackle coming from everywhere
The direct light of the first stars

quiz.explanation: Calculations and observations indicate approximately 75% hydrogen and 25% helium formed during primordial nucleosynthesis.

quiz.explanation: This timeline goes from initial inflation to the formation of the Sun 4.6 billion years ago, through the first cores around 3 minutes and the diffuse background around 380,000 years ago.
items: The inflation phase, just after the beginning of the universe
The formation of the first atomic nuclei
The release of light, at the origin of the cosmic microwave background
The appearance of the first stars

quiz.explanation: Like a balloon being inflated, no point in the universe is the center: all the points move away from each other.

quiz.explanation: Dark energy represents about 68% of the content of the universe, compared to about 5% for ordinary matter.

quiz.explanation: In 1998, the observation of distant supernovas showed that the expansion of the universe was accelerating, attributed to a mysterious dark energy.

That the universe has stopped expanding

title: Why do volcanoes erupt?
description: A volcano is an opening in the Earth's crust. Magma under pressure rises through it and becomes lava. Here is why the Earth “spits.”
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
A volcano is not a simple mountain spitting fire, but a window open onto the thermal and chemical activity of our planet. It is a rupture in the outer structure of the Earth through which magma, a complex mixture of molten rock and gases under high pressure, rises to the surface to become lava.

Understanding this phenomenon requires exploring the depths of the lithosphere and analyzing the titanic forces that drive the heart of the globe to maintain its thermal balance.

[volcano eruption lava]

lessons.title: Under our feet, nothing stands still
lessons.content:
The Earth is not an inert block of rock, but a stack of layers with distinct physical properties. The surface layer, the **crust**, is a rigid shell whose thickness varies from **5 to 70 km**. Below lies the **mantle**, a colossal structure reaching down to **2,900 km** in depth. Although composed of solid rocks (notably peridotite), the mantle behaves in a ductile manner over geological timescales, allowing for the circulation of matter.

This circulation is governed by **convection currents**. Intense heat from the decay of radioactive elements in the Earth's core heats the rocks of the deep mantle. Having become less dense, these rocks slowly rise toward the surface, cool down, then sink back. This cyclic Movement acts as a conveyor belt for <tectonic plates>, causing them to collide or move apart.

It is at the boundaries of these plates that most geological activity is concentrated. When plates move apart at the level of <mid-ocean ridges>, pressure drops sharply, favoring the partial melting of rocks. Conversely, during <subduction>, one plate sinks beneath another, dragging with it sediments and water that modify the mantle's chemistry.

{Some very deep eruptions bring up pieces of the mantle so quickly that they don't have time to transform: this is how diamonds, formed more than 150 km deep, reach the surface intact.}

lessons.title: From magma to eruption
lessons.content:
The **magma** results from the partial melting of mantle or crustal rocks. Contrary to popular belief, rock does not melt solely because it is "hot". Geologists identify three triggers: an **increase in temperature**, a **decrease in pressure** (adiabatic melting), or the **addition of water**. Water acts as a chemical flux, lowering the melting point of surrounding rocks, a crucial process in <subduction> zones.

Once formed, magma is less dense than the surrounding solid rock. It then begins an ascent through failures in the lithosphere, driven by buoyancy. This journey toward the surface is often interrupted in **magma chambers**. These reservoirs located a few kilometers deep serve as storage and chemical differentiation zones.

In these chambers, pressure builds up critically. Gases dissolved in the mixture (water vapor, carbon dioxide) begin to form bubbles as the magma rises, like a carbonated drink being opened. If the cap rock can no longer contain this internal energy, the eruption is triggered.

{The eruption of Tambora in 1815 was so powerful that it cooled the global climate, causing "the year without a summer" in 1816. Catastrophic harvests in Europe and North America led to the worst famine of the 19th century.}

lessons.title: Runny or explosive?
lessons.content:
Not all eruptions look the same; their violence depends directly on the **viscosity of the magma**, which is itself Dicté by its silica content. A magma low in silica (basaltic) is very fluid. It allows gases to escape without resistance, producing **effusive eruptions**. This is the case with Piton de la Fournaise or the volcanoes of **Hawaii**, where lava flows quietly, forming broad shield volcanoes.

In contrast, magmas rich in silica are extremely viscous. Gases remain trapped until the pressure becomes unbearable. The resulting explosion is devastating, projecting ash and <pyroclastic flows>. These **explosive eruptions** are characteristic of Ring of Fire volcanoes, such as **Pinatubo** or Mount **St Helens**.

Volcanoes can also remain "dormant" for millennia before waking up abruptly. The most famous case is that of **Vesuvius** in 79 AD, which buried Pompeii under meters of ash. The record for power, however, goes to **Tambora** in 1815, whose explosion was heard more than 2,000 km away.

|| Volcanoes form where tectonic plates separate or collide - 80% of the world's volcanic activity happens under the oceans.||

lessons.title: Danger, fertile soil, life in the deep
lessons.content:
Volcanism is not just a natural hazard; it is an essential engine of Earth's evolution. Over the long term, volcanoes are the primary architects of the primitive atmosphere through the degassing of volatile compounds. Even today, volcanic ash, rich in minerals, creates exceptionally fertile agricultural lands that attract large populations despite the danger.

However, major eruptions can temporarily modify the solar cycle. Sulfur aerosols projected into the **Stratosphere** reflect sunlight, causing global cooling. This phenomenon generated the "**year without a summer**" following the Tambora episode. Furthermore, certain sites like the Yellowstone <supervolcano> are under constant monitoring, as an eruption at this scale would have systemic planetary consequences.

Finally, underwater volcanism plays a key role in the chemical regulation of the oceans. The <black smokers>, hydrothermal vents located near mid-ocean ridges, host unique ecosystems based on **chemosynthesis** rather than photosynthesis, proving that Earth's geothermal energy can suffice to support life in the total darkness of the abyss.

{The largest known volcano in the solar system is not on Earth but on Mars: Olympus Mons rises 22 km high, nearly three times Everest, because the absence of plate tectonics allowed magma to accumulate in the same Place for millions of years.}

|| TO REMEMBER: Volcanoes expel magma accumulated under pressure in magma chambers, under the influence of tectonic movements and the viscosity of molten rocks. ||

quiz.question: What happens to the magma once it reaches the open air?
quiz.explanation: Once in the open air, the magma that rises to the surface of a volcano becomes lava.

quiz.question: What causes magma to form in a subduction zone?
quiz.explanation: In a subduction zone, the sinking plate carries water that lowers the melting point of rocks, forming magma.
options: Water driven by the plunging plate, which lowers the melting point of rocks
The sudden cooling of the plate which plunges
The total disappearance of the oceanic crust
A sudden drop in atmospheric pressure

quiz.question: True or false: Fluid magma, like that of Hawaii, generally produces explosive eruptions.
quiz.explanation: A fluid magma lets gases escape easily: the eruption is effusive, the lava flows, like in Hawaii or at Piton de la Fournaise.

quiz.question: What determines whether an eruption is more effusive or more explosive?
quiz.explanation: A fluid magma lets the gases escape and flows (effusive eruption), while a sticky magma traps the gases until it explodes (explosive eruption).

quiz.question: How much of the world's volcanic activity takes place beneath the oceans, far from our eyes?
quiz.explanation: About 80% of the world's volcanic activity occurs beneath the oceans, particularly near ridges.

quiz.question: Which 1815 volcanic eruption in Indonesia cooled the global climate and caused “the year without a summer” in 1816?
quiz.explanation: The Tambora eruption in 1815 was so powerful that it cooled the global climate, causing disastrous harvests in 1816.

quiz.question: What are the “black smokers” found near underwater ridges?
quiz.explanation: Black smokers are underwater chimneys that spew hot mineral-rich fluids, around which lightless ecosystems live.
options: Chimneys that emit burning fluids rich in minerals
Ice geysers specific to polar regions
Clouds of volcanic ash on the surface

quiz.question: Which ancient city was buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD? AD?
quiz.explanation: In 79 AD BC, the eruption of Vesuvius, near Naples, buried the city of Pompeii in ashes.

title: How do earthquakes happen?
description: Every year the Earth records hundreds of thousands of earthquakes. Most go unnoticed. A few change whole cities.
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Every year, the Earth records about **500,000 detectable earthquakes**, a few dozen of which are powerful enough to reshape landscapes and cause major structural damage.

[earthquake collapsed buildings urban]

An earthquake is not a random Event, but the brutal conclusion of a long process of energy accumulation. Understanding earthquakes requires exploring the dynamic structure of our planet, from continental drift to the microscopic physics of rock failure under pressure.

lessons.title: Plates that never stop moving
lessons.content:
The Earth's surface is not a rigid and immobile shell; it is divided into a dozen major **tectonic plates** that float on the asthenosphere, a layer of the Earth's mantle with ductile properties. These plates move at a speed of **1 to 10 cm per year**, which corresponds approximately to the growth speed of human fingernails.

[tectonic plates collision]

These movements are governed by convection currents from the internal heat of the Earth. Plates interact primarily at their boundaries in three different ways. In divergence zones, such as mid-ocean ridges, they move apart to make room for new magma. In convergence zones, they collide, often causing **subduction** (one plate dives beneath another) or the formation of mountains.

Finally, they can slide laterally against each other along transform faults, like the famous <San Andreas> in California. It is precisely at these junctions that the vast majority of the world's earthquakes are concentrated, because the fluid Movement of the plates is hindered by the roughness of the Earth's crust.

{If tectonic plates suddenly stopped moving, the Earth would lose its magnetic protection over time, because the Movement of plates is linked to the dissipation of heat from the core which generates our magnetosphere.}

lessons.title: When the fault gives way
lessons.content:
An earthquake occurs along a **fault**, a fracture that separates two rock blocks. In Theory, the Movement of tectonic plates should drive these blocks continuously. However, due to the roughness of the rock surfaces, **friction** is stronger than the force of the Movement. The blocks then stay stuck against each other.

[San Andreas fault aerial view]

Despite this apparent blockage, the tectonic plates continue to push. The rock, although rigid, possesses a certain elasticity. It then deforms slowly, accumulating what sciences call **elastic stress**, much like a bow being pulled tighter and tighter. This preparation stage can last for decades, even centuries.

The rupture threshold is reached when the accumulated energy exceeds the resistance of the fault rocks. The blockage then suddenly gives way: the two blocks slide against each other in a few milliseconds. This elastic relaxation instantly releases the stored energy in the form of **seismic waves**. The precise point of the rupture at depth is the **focus**, while at the surface, the impact is maximal at the **epicenter**.

lessons.title: Measuring the power, fearing the tsunami
lessons.content:
To measure the power of an earthquake, seismologists use the **moment <magnitude scale>** (Mw), which has largely replaced the Richter scale for major events. This measurement is a logarithmic function: a 1-point increase on the scale multiplies the energy released by approximately **32**.

To Date, the most powerful earthquake ever recorded with modern instruments is the **Valdivia earthquake in Chile (1960)**, reaching a magnitude of **9.5**. Such an Event releases energy comparable to thousands of atomic bombs.

When the focus of a powerful earthquake is located under the ocean, the vertical movement of the seafloor suddenly displaces an immense column of water, generating a **tsunami**. These waves, initially imperceptible in the high seas because they are very long, rise violently as they approach the coasts.

The **Indian Ocean tsunami (2004)** illustrates the global reach of this phenomenon: triggered by a magnitude 9.1 earthquake near Sumatra, it traveled thousands of kilometers to strike 14 countries, causing the death of **227,000 people**. This highlights that the danger of an earthquake does not stop at the immediate ground shaking.

{Contrary to a popular belief, a magnitude 0 or negative earthquake exists: the scale is open and measures micro-earthquakes so weak that they are only detectable by ultra-sensitive sensors placed in a laboratory.}

lessons.title: Waves, warnings, and buildings that hold
lessons.content:
Once the fault has ruptured, energy travels through the Earth via different types of waves. The first to arrive are **P-waves** (primary), which compress the rock like an accordion. They are followed by **S-waves** (secondary), which are slower and more destructive, making the ground oscillate perpendicularly to their direction. Finally, surface waves are those that cause the most visible damage to buildings.

Modern sciences do not yet allow the prediction of the exact Date of an earthquake, but they can identify risk zones thanks to fault mapping. Prevention therefore relies on **earthquake engineering**. In countries like Japan, skyscrapers are equipped with **seismic isolators** (Giants shock absorbers or foundations on bearings) that allow the structure to dissipate energy instead of absorbing it.

Educating populations and setting up early warning systems - capable of detecting P-waves and cutting gas networks or stopping trains before the arrival of more destructive S-waves - save thousands of lives every year. Earthquake resilience is as much a matter of geology as it is of technological and social preparation.

|| To remember: Earthquakes arise from the brutal rupture of rocks that have accumulated centuries of elastic stress at the boundaries of tectonic plates. This energy propagates in the form of waves, whose magnitude follows a logarithmic scale where each unit multiplies the energy released by 32. ||

quiz.question: What is a fault that causes an earthquake?
quiz.explanation: An earthquake occurs along a fault, a fracture between two blocks of rock that end up sliding suddenly.
options: A fracture between two blocks of rock
A layer of the Earth's atmosphere

quiz.question: Why don't tectonic plates slide continuously, despite their constant movement?
quiz.explanation: At the boundaries of the plates, the friction of the rocks hinders sliding: the energy then accumulates silently until rupture.
options: The friction of rocks blocks their sliding at the borders
They are held together by the Earth's magnetic field
The Earth's mantle is completely solid and immobile

quiz.question: What is the difference between the focus and the epicenter of an earthquake?
quiz.explanation: Focus refers to the breaking point at depth, while epicenter is the point on the surface just above where the effects are often strongest.
options: The focus is the breaking point at depth, the epicenter is the point on the surface just above
The focus is on the surface, the epicenter is deep
These are two different names for exactly the same point.
Focus measures magnitude, epicenter measures duration

quiz.question: True or false: Each additional degree on the magnitude scale multiplies the energy released by approximately 32.
quiz.explanation: The magnitude scale is logarithmic: each degree multiplies the energy by about 32, so that a magnitude 8 earthquake releases about 1,000 times more energy than a magnitude 6 earthquake.

quiz.question: What is the approximate length of the San Andreas Fault in California, in kilometers?
quiz.explanation: The San Andreas Fault stretches approximately 800 miles along California.

quiz.question: What disaster followed the 9.1 magnitude earthquake near Sumatra in 2004?
quiz.explanation: The 2004 earthquake near Sumatra raised the seabed and triggered a tsunami that struck 14 countries, killing an estimated 227,000 people.
options: A tsunami that hit 14 countries and killed around 227,000 people
A major volcanic eruption in Indonesia
An electrical blackout across the entire Asian continent
Extreme cold snap in Southeast Asia

quiz.question: Put in the order of arrival the different types of seismic waves after the rupture of a fault.
quiz.explanation: After rupture, P waves arrive first, followed by S waves and then surface waves, which cause the most visible oscillations in the ground.
items: P waves, which compress the rock like an accordion
S waves, slower and often more destructive
Surface waves, which cause the ground to oscillate very visibly

quiz.question: What is earthquake engineering used for?
quiz.explanation: Seismic engineering designs buildings with mobile foundations or shock absorbers, capable of withstanding tremors.
options: To design buildings capable of absorbing the energy of tremors
To predict the exact day of a future earthquake
To prevent tectonic plates from moving
To measure the magnitude of an earthquake after the fact

quiz.question: True or false: today we know how to accurately predict the exact day of a major earthquake.
quiz.explanation: We do not yet know how to predict the exact day of a major earthquake; we can only map the risk areas.

title: The Chernobyl disaster (1986)
description: On April 26, 1986, reactor No. 4 at Chernobyl exploded. It is the worst civil nuclear accident in history. Here is what happened, without the sensationalism.
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
On **April 26, 1986**, at 1:23 AM, reactor No. 4 of the **Chernobyl** nuclear power plant in Soviet Ukraine was the scene of the most serious industrial accident of the modern era. This disaster, ranked at level 7 (the highest) on the **INES** scale, released into the atmosphere a quantity of radioactive particles estimated at **400 times more radioactivity** than the Hiroshima bomb. Beyond the immediate human drama, this Event permanently altered our relationship with atomic energy and acted as an accelerator for the fall of the Soviet Union.

[Chernobyl nuclear plant 1986 explosion]

lessons.title: A test that went wrong
lessons.content:
The tragedy originated in a safety test paradoxically meant to improve the resilience of the plant. Engineers wanted to verify if, in the event of a power cut, the **Inertia** of the spinning turbines could provide enough energy to power the cooling pumps during the 40 seconds required to start the emergency diesel generators.

However, a series of delays and administrative pressures pushed the night shift to perform the test under low-power conditions, making the reactor unstable. The core of the reactor, a <Soviet RBMK reactor> type, possessed a dangerous physical characteristic: a **positive void coefficient**. This means that if steam bubbles form in the cooling circuit, the nuclear reaction accelerates instead of slowing down.

When at 1:23:40 AM, the operator activated the **AZ-5** emergency shutdown button, the graphite control rods, supposed to stop the reaction, caused a massive initial power surge due to their defective design. In a fraction of a second, power rose to **30,000%** of its nominal value. The steam pressure then pulverized the **1,000-ton** upper biological shield, exposing the melting core to the open air and projecting highly radioactive debris for kilometers around.

{The reactor burned at such a temperature that it created a corium magma, a nuclear lava nicknamed 'the Elephant's Foot' because of its shape; staying 300 seconds in contact with it in 1986 was fatal in less than two days.}

lessons.title: Denial, evacuation, liquidators
lessons.content:
In the hours following the explosion, the Soviet state apparatus sank into denial. The first **firefighters** dispatched to the scene fought what they believed to be a simple roof fire. Without protective equipment, they handled blocks of **graphite** with their bare hands, unaware that these debris were the very components of the reactor core. Within hours, the first symptoms of **acute radiation syndrome** (nausea, skin burns) appeared.

As radiation sensors went off the charts, official reports minimized the scale of the disaster. The nearby city of **Pripyat**, built for the plant workers, continued its normal life for 36 hours. Children played outside under a rain of invisible ash, while authorities waited for Moscow's approval to act. It was not until the afternoon of April 27 that the 50,000 inhabitants were evacuated in a few hours, leaving behind an entire life.

To extinguish the fire and seal the reactor, the USSR mobilized nearly 600,000 people: the <liquidators>. Among them, helicopter pilots dropped sand and lead onto the gaping core, while soldiers, nicknamed **biological robots**, had a maximum of 90 seconds to clear debris on the roof of the adjacent reactor, as electronic machines failed under the effect of extreme radiation.

[Pripyat abandoned city Chernobyl]

{Some liquidators received a medal showing a drop of blood crossed by alpha, beta, and gamma rays; it is one of the rare military decorations in the world created to reward sacrifice against an invisible enemy.}

lessons.title: Human and environmental consequences
lessons.content:
The consequences of Chernobyl are the subject of intense scientific debate. The radioactive cloud, carried by the winds, crossed Europe as far as France and Scandinavia, depositing **cesium-137** and **iodine-131** on the ground. On the health front, the WHO recognizes about **4,000 cases of thyroid cancer**, mainly in children who consumed contaminated milk. However, the total toll of indirect deaths (future cancers, stress-related diseases) varies according to studies from a few thousand to several tens of thousands.

At the center of the disaster, a <30 km exclusion zone> today offers a striking spectacle. The absence of human activity has transformed this contaminated territory into an open-air laboratory. Contrary to expectations, nature is not dead there: without the pressure of agriculture and urbanization, populations of wolves, elk, and Przewalski's horses are more numerous than before the disaster. The radioactivity induces local genetic mutations, but it turns out to be less deleterious for the survival of species than human presence was.

On a technical level, a first concrete **sarcophagus** was built in haste in 1986 to isolate the reactor. Weakened by time, it was covered in 2016 by the **New Safe Confinement**. This monumental steel structure, designed to last 100 years, was assembled at a distance and then slid on rails to avoid exposing workers to residual radiation from the site.

lessons.title: A political and technical legacy
lessons.content:
Chernobyl is not just a technical accident; it is a geopolitical earthquake. For <Mikhail Gorbachev>, then leader of the USSR, the disaster revealed the systemic flaws of the Soviet Union: bureaucratic secrecy, industrial obsolescence, and disregard for human safety. The Event forced the implementation of **Glasnost** (policy of transparency), indirectly precipitating the fall of the Eastern Bloc.

On a global scale, the accident shattered the myth of infallible nuclear energy. It led to the creation of the **World Association of Nuclear Operators** (<WANO>) to promote the exchange of best practices between countries and prevent such a tragedy from happening again. Many Western countries, following 1986, froze their nuclear programs or accelerated the transition to other energy sources.

The accident remains today an absolute reference in risk management and the psychology of disasters. It reminds us that technological power requires political transparency and flawless scientific rigor so as not to turn against its creators.

|| Chernobyl (1986) released 400 times more radioactivity than Hiroshima - the <30 km exclusion zone> remains uninhabited by man, but wildlife paradoxically thrives there. ||

quiz.question: What test was the night shift of reactor no. 4 carrying out before the explosion?
quiz.explanation: Engineers were testing whether the still-spinning turbines could power the cooling pumps in the event of a power outage, before the diesel generators started up.
options: A safety test on the power supply to the cooling pumps in the event of a power outage
A seismic resistance test of the building
A test of the water quality of the nearby river

quiz.question: What type of reactor, known for its instability at low power, was used in Chernobyl?
quiz.explanation: The water-cooled, graphite-moderated RBMK reactor became very unstable at low power, which contributed to the accident.

quiz.question: True or false: in Chernobyl, the activation of the control rods immediately stopped the chain reaction.
quiz.explanation: Because of their design, the control rods first caused a brief surge before they could stop the reaction, precipitating the explosion.

quiz.question: Approximately how many inhabitants did Pripyat have at the time of its evacuation?
quiz.explanation: Pripyat had around 50,000 inhabitants, evacuated in a few hours on April 27, 1986.

quiz.question: What level does the Chernobyl disaster reach on the INES scale, which ranks nuclear accidents from 1 to 7?
quiz.explanation: Chernobyl reached level 7, the maximum on the INES scale, like Fukushima in 2011.
options: Level 7, the maximum of the scale
There is no scale for this accident

quiz.question: What do we call the hundreds of thousands of people mobilized by the USSR to contain the disaster?
quiz.explanation: Nearly 600,000 people, called liquidators, were mobilized to contain the disaster: pilots, workers, soldiers.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Chernobyl disaster in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: The explosion occurred on April 26, 1986, Pripyat was evacuated the next day, a first sarcophagus was built in 1986, then replaced by a new arch in 2016.
items: A safety test on reactor No. 4 goes wrong and causes an explosion
The town of Pripyat is urgently evacuated
A first concrete sarcophagus isolates the damaged reactor
A huge steel arch covers the entire site

quiz.question: True or false: the exclusion zone around Chernobyl is now home to abundant wildlife.
quiz.explanation: Without agriculture or towns for decades, the exclusion zone sees abundant wildlife developing there: wolves, elk, Przewalski's horses.

quiz.question: Why did a new steel arch cover the site in 2016?
quiz.explanation: The concrete sarcophagus built in 1986 having weakened, it was covered in 2016 by a new arch designed to last around 100 years.
options: The first concrete sarcophagus built in 1986 had weakened
The first sarcophagus was never finished
A new radioactive leak had just been discovered
The Ukrainian government wanted to reopen the plant

title: Why doesn't the Moon fall to Earth?
description: The Moon is falling toward the Earth all the time. It simply misses, every single time. That is exactly what an orbit is.
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Why doesn't the Moon crash into us even though Earth's gravity attracts it irresistibly? The short answer is paradoxical: the Moon is indeed "falling" toward Earth continuously, but it systematically misses it at every moment.

[Moon Earth orbit space]

This dynamic, which defines the very Concept of an orbit, constitutes one of the pillars of classical mechanics. Understanding this fragile balance between free fall and Movement of Inertia means diving into the physics of **Isaac Newton**, who was the first to unify the laws of falling bodies on Earth with those of the Movement of celestial bodies in the sky.

{If you weighed 60 kg on Earth, you would only weigh 10 on the Moon, as its gravity is six times weaker than ours.}

lessons.title: Newton's imaginary cannon
lessons.content:
To make a then-revolutionary Concept accessible, **Isaac Newton** imagined a now-famous thought experiment: a cannon located at the top of a mountain so high that it would exit Earth's atmosphere to free itself from air resistance.

[Newton cannonball orbit thought experiment]

If a ball is fired horizontally with little power, gravity pulls it toward the ground and it describes a quick curve before crashing. If the powder charge is increased, the ball travels a longer distance. However, if a specific velocity is reached, called **Orbital velocity**, a remarkable phenomenon occurs: as the ball falls toward the ground, the surface of the Earth, which is round, curves and drops away beneath it at the same speed.

The projectile then finds itself in a state of perpetual **free fall**. It falls without ever hitting the ground, because its curved trajectory perfectly matches the roundness of the planet. This is precisely the state of the Moon: it possesses enough lateral velocity to transform what should be an impact into an infinite loop.

{Newton's original 1687 manuscript shows a diagram almost identical to those used today by NASA to explain the orbiting of satellites.}

lessons.title: Two forces, one balance
lessons.content:
The Moon currently orbits at an average distance of **384,000 km**. To maintain this balance, its lateral displacement speed is approximately **1 km/s**. This speed is the rampart that prevents it from succumbing to gravitational attraction.

If the Moon stopped dead in its tracks, it would fall vertically and crash into the Earth in a few days. Conversely, if Earth's gravity vanished instantly, the Moon would escape in a straight line into the interstellar void, in accordance with the principle of Inertia. The orbit is therefore the result of a permanent compromise between these two tendencies.

<Newton's universal gravitation> Law teaches us that the force of this attraction depends on the mass of the objects and the distance separating them. The closer a satellite is to Earth, the stronger the attraction, and the higher its speed must be to avoid falling. This is why the **International Space Station** (ISS), located only 400 km up, must fly at **7.7 km/s** (about 28,000 km/h) to stay in orbit, completing a trip around the World in just 90 minutes compared to 27.3 days for the Moon.

This difference illustrates the decrease in gravitational influence with distance, a key Concept for understanding why celestial objects do not all instantly clump together.

lessons.title: The tides push the Moon away
lessons.content:
Contrary to popular belief, the lunar orbit is not a fixed system. It is subject to the influence of <tidal forces>. The Moon's gravity deforms Earth's oceans, creating a "bulge" of water. Since the Earth rotates on its axis faster than the Moon orbits it, this bulge slightly leads the Moon's position.

This shift creates friction that slows Earth's rotation: our days lengthen by about 1.4 milliseconds per century. In return, through a transfer of kinetic energy, the Moon recovers this lost energy and moves away from us. The calculation is precise: our satellite moves away from the Earth by **3.8 cm per year**.

This process has major historical and biological consequences. Several billion years ago, the Moon was much closer, perhaps only 25,000 km away. Tides were then titanic walls of water crashing several times a day on primordial coasts, accelerating erosion and the chemical mixing necessary for the appearance of life.

{Due to this slowing of the Earth, dinosaurs lived on a planet where days lasted only 22 or 23 hours.}

lessons.title: Eclipses, for now
lessons.content:
The progressive distancing of the Moon means that the current configuration of the sky is exceptional. Today, by a fascinating geometric coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times larger than the Moon, but also 400 times further away. This allows the two stars to have the same apparent size in the sky and makes total solar eclipses possible.

However, in about **600 million years**, the Moon will have become so distant that it will appear too small to totally mask the solar disk. Future inhabitants of the Earth (if any remain) will only be able to observe annular eclipses, where a ring of light surrounds the lunar silhouette.

In the very long term, one could imagine the Moon eventually escaping, but this is not the most likely scenario. In about **50 billion years**, Earth's rotation will be synchronized with the lunar orbit: the Earth will always show the same face to the Moon, just as the Moon already always shows us the same face. The system will then be stabilized, unless the Sun destroys the Earth long before during its red giant phase.

{During its red giant phase, the Sun will swell so much that it could swallow Mercury and Venus, and its edge could graze Earth's orbit.}

|| The Moon does not crash because its lateral velocity exactly counterbalances Earth's attraction, creating a perpetual free fall that paradoxically moves it 3.8 cm away per year. ||

quiz.question: Why doesn't the Moon crash into the Earth, even though gravity is constantly pulling it?
quiz.explanation: The Moon is indeed falling towards the Earth, but its lateral speed causes it to continually miss the Earth: this is what we call an orbit.
options: It has a lateral speed which makes it miss the Earth at every moment: it is a permanent free fall
It is held by an invisible magnetic field
Earth's gravity does not act beyond the atmosphere
The Moon does not experience any gravitational pull

quiz.question: What did Isaac Newton imagine to explain the principle of the orbit?
quiz.explanation: Newton imagines a cannon firing a ball horizontally: at a sufficient speed, the ball falls without ever touching the ground, because the Earth curves under it at the same rate.
options: A cannon firing a cannonball from a mountain high enough to escape the atmosphere
A pendulum swinging endlessly in the void
An experiment with two opposing magnets
A balloon filled with helium released at altitude

quiz.question: How far does the Moon orbit the Earth on average, in kilometers?
quiz.explanation: The Moon orbits approximately 384,000 km from Earth.

quiz.question: True or false: if gravity suddenly disappeared, the Moon would travel in a straight line into space.
quiz.explanation: According to the principle of inertia, a body maintains its speed if it is not slowed down: without gravity to hold it back, the Moon would go straight.

quiz.question: What creates tidal forces between the Earth and the Moon?
quiz.explanation: The Moon's gravity pulls harder on the side of the Earth facing it, which deforms the oceans and creates a bulge of water: tides.
options: The Moon attracts the side of the Earth facing it more strongly than the opposite side
The rotation of the Earth on itself
The heat of the earth's core
The solar wind that hits the atmosphere

quiz.question: How many centimeters does the Moon move away from Earth each year?
quiz.explanation: Due to tidal forces, the Moon moves away about 1.5 inches per year.

quiz.question: Why are total solar eclipses possible today?
quiz.explanation: By geometric coincidence, the Sun is both 400 times larger and 400 times farther away than the Moon, giving them the same apparent size in the sky.
options: The Sun is about 400 times larger than the Moon, but also 400 times farther away: both have the same apparent size
The Moon is actually larger than the Sun
The Sun is getting closer and closer to the Earth
The Moon is stationary relative to the Sun

quiz.question: True or false: in the distant future, the Moon will move away to the point where it will no longer be able to cause total solar eclipses.
quiz.explanation: In about 600 million years, the Moon will be too far away to completely hide the Sun: only annular eclipses will remain.

title: Is there life elsewhere in the Universe?
description: Trillions of planets, and yet total radio silence. Science looks for life elsewhere without promising little green men.
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The immensity of the cosmos defies human imagination: the observable universe contains approximately **2,000 billion galaxies**, each home to hundreds of billions of stars. If we apply simple statistical logic, the number of potentially habitable planets numbers in the trillions. Yet, despite this theoretical profusion, we have faced a total radio silence since the dawn of modern astronomy.

[radio telescope SETI]

This apparent contradiction between the high probability of the existence of extraterrestrial civilizations and the total absence of evidence or contact is known as the **Fermi paradox**. This line of questioning is no longer just a matter of science fiction, but a rigorous scientific discipline: **Exobiology**.

lessons.title: What life seems to need
lessons.content:
To search for life elsewhere, scientists first rely on the only known model: terrestrial life. This is based on two fundamental pillars: **carbon chemistry**, capable of forming complex organic molecules, and **liquid water**, which serves as an essential solvent for biological reactions.

The first criterion for a planet to be a candidate for life is its orbital position. It must be located within the **<habitable zone>** of its star. This is a region where the energy flux received allows for the maintenance of a surface temperature compatible with the presence of liquid water. If the planet is too close, the greenhouse effect spirals out of control and the water evaporates; if it is too far away, the water freezes permanently.

Since the **discovery of exoplanets** (planets orbiting stars other than the Sun) in the 1990s, our vision has changed. We now know of more than **5,500**, and the data suggests that almost every star in our galaxy has at least one planet. However, habitability does not mean the presence of life: other factors such as the presence of a protective atmosphere or a magnetic field are crucial.

{There are more stars in the observable universe than there are grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth. Statistically, even a one-in-a-billion probability of life appearing would imply millions of biological centers just in our galaxy.}

To conceptualize this probability, astronomer **Frank Drake** proposed the **<Drake equation>** in 1961. This formula attempts to estimate the number of technologically advanced civilizations in the Milky Way by multiplying various factors (rate of star formation, fraction of habitable planets, probability of the emergence of intelligence). Although unverifiable, it structures the scientific debate.

lessons.title: Oases in the solar system
lessons.content:
There is no need to look toward distant stars to find fascinating environments. Within our own solar system, celestial bodies challenge the idea that life can only exist on a temperate rocky planet. Research is now focusing on the moons of the gas giants.

**Europa**, one of the satellites of Jupiter, is the most serious candidate. Beneath an ice crust several kilometers thick hides a global **liquid water ocean**. This ocean is kept liquid not by the Sun, which is too distant, but by **<tidal forces>**: the colossal gravitational pull of Jupiter deforms the moon, creating internal friction that generates heat.

[Europa moon Jupiter ice ocean]

**Enceladus**, a small moon of Saturn, presents an even more spectacular phenomenon: it ejects geysers of water vapor and organic particles through cracks at its south pole. The **Cassini** probe was able to fly through these plumes and detect silicates and molecular hydrogen, probable signs of hydrothermal activity at the bottom of its ocean. This suggests the existence of chemical energy sources capable of nourishing microbial life without any sunlight.

Finally, **Mars** remains a major subject of study. We know that liquid water once flowed on its surface. Today, robotic explorers are looking for **<biosignatures>** (fossil or chemical traces) proving that life could have appeared there before the planet lost its atmosphere and most of its water.

lessons.title: The great silence
lessons.content:
In 1950, the physicist **Enrico Fermi** raised a question during an informal lunch: if advanced civilizations exist by the thousands, why do we see no trace of them? This is the heart of the paradox: the universe is old (13.8 billion years); a civilization just one million years ahead of us would have had ample time to colonize the galaxy, even at sub-luminal speeds.

Several hypotheses attempt to resolve this "Great Silence." The first is that of the **<Great Filter>**: there would be a stage in evolution (the transition from simple to complex cell, or the invention of self-destructive technologies like the atom) that is almost impossible to clear. Either we have already passed this filter (we are an exception), or it is ahead of us (all civilizations eventually collapse).

Other researchers suggest that we are not communicating on the right channels. The **SETI** program listens to radio waves, but a more advanced civilization might use technologies based on neutrinos or lasers that we cannot yet detect. It is also possible that Earth is deliberately isolated, like a nature reserve, in what is called the **<zoo hypothesis>**.

Finally, the answer could be temporal: on the scale of the universe, civilizations could be like fireflies lighting up and burning out very quickly, without ever shining at the same time to see each other. Intersidereal distances, measured in light-years, impose a communication delay that makes any dialogue almost impossible.

lessons.title: How we search today
lessons.content:
The hunt for life is entering a new era thanks to instruments of unprecedented precision, such as the **James Webb** Space Telescope. It no longer just takes pictures of planets; it analyzes the interaction of light with their atmosphere through **<spectroscopy>**. This technique allows identifying the chemical composition of the air of distant worlds in search of abnormal quantities of oxygen, methane, or ozone.

The discovery of life, even purely microbial, would cause an ontological earthquake. It would prove that the appearance of life is not a unique accident, but a standard biological process of the universe. This would mean that life is written into the laws of physics and chemistry, and is not the result of a miraculous geographical chance.

In the meantime, we continue to send bottles into the cosmic sea. The **Voyager** probes, launched in 1977, carry engraved golden records containing sounds and images from Earth. Although the chances of them being intercepted are almost zero, these objects testify to our fundamental need to leave our cosmic solitude.

{If a civilization located in the Andromeda galaxy were looking at us today with an imaginary ultra-powerful telescope, it would not see humans, but the first ancestors of man 2.5 million years ago, because of the time it takes light to travel.}

|| The universe contains hundreds of billions of planets, making life statistically probable, but the absence of contact (Fermi paradox) suggests that the emergence of technological intelligence is either extremely rare or fleeting. ||

title: What is a black hole?
description: A black hole is not a cosmic vacuum cleaner. It is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: A black hole is a region of space-time where the gravitational field is so intense that the velocity required to escape it, called **escape velocity**, is greater than the speed of light. Long considered simple mathematical solutions from Albert Einstein's **General Relativity**, these fascinating objects are today an observational reality. They are not holes in the literal sense, but concentrations of matter of such density that they deform the very fabric of the universe, creating an invisible boundary beyond which no information can reach us.

lessons.title: When a star collapses
lessons.content:
The genesis of a stellar black hole begins with the death of a massive star, possessing at least **20 to 25 times the mass of the Sun**. For millions of years, such a star survives thanks to a precarious balance between two opposing forces: **gravity**, which seeks to compress everything toward the center, and **radiation pressure** from nuclear fusion, which pushes outward.

When the star has exhausted its nuclear fuel, the radiation pressure stops abruptly. Gravity then takes over without resistance, causing the core of the star to collapse on itself in a fraction of a second. This shock releases phenomenal energy in the form of a **supernova** explosion. If the residual core is sufficiently massive (exceeding the **Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit**), no known physical force can stop the compression.

The matter is then compressed until it occupies a quasi-zero volume, reaching an infinite density: this is the **singularity**. Around this point, **<The event horizon>** forms, a spherical boundary whose radius is proportional to the object's mass. Crossing this limit means definitively leaving the accessible universe.

{If you fell into a black hole, you would undergo "spaghettification": the gravity at your feet would be so much stronger than at your head that your body would be stretched like a strand of pasta before even reaching the horizon.}

lessons.title: Not a cosmic vacuum cleaner
lessons.content:
Contrary to a stubborn misconception, a black hole is not a vacuum cleaner of matter that travels through the universe. Its force of attraction depends solely on its mass and distance. If our Sun were suddenly replaced by a black hole of identical mass, Earth would continue its orbital trajectory without being "sucked in," although we would eventually freeze for lack of light.

Astronomers classify these objects into several categories. Besides stellar black holes, there are giants: **supermassive black holes**. Their mass varies from a few million to several billion times that of the Sun. They sit at the heart of almost all galaxies. In our own Milky Way, this role is held by **Sgr A*** (Sagittarius A-star), a monster of **4 million solar masses**.

Their presence is revealed by the influence they exert on their environment. Matter that gets too close forms an **<accretion disk>**, a ring of gas and dust swirling at speeds close to the speed of light. Friction within this disk heats the matter to millions of degrees, making it extremely bright in the X-ray and radio wave spectrum, which paradoxically allows us to "see" the shadow of the black hole against this luminous background.

lessons.title: 2019: the first image
lessons.content:
For decades, we only had indirect evidence of the existence of black holes. This paradigm changed in **April 2019** thanks to the **Event Horizon Telescope** (EHT) project. Using a technique called <interferometry>, researchers combined data from eight radio telescopes spread across the globe to create a virtual telescope the size of the Earth.

[black hole accretion disk galaxy]

The target was **M87***, the supermassive black hole in the Messier 87 galaxy, located **55 million light-years** away. The revealed image shows an asymmetrical ring of light surrounding a zone of total darkness: the silhouette of the event horizon. This historic shot confirmed point by point Einstein's predictions made a century earlier.

This major advance was completed in **2022** by the first image of our own neighbor, **Sgr A***. In parallel, astronomy entered a new era in **2015** with the detection, by the **LIGO** and **Virgo** observatories, of **gravitational waves**. These ripples in space-time are produced during cosmic cataclysms, such as the merger of two black holes, allowing us for the first time to "listen" to the vibrations of the universe.

lessons.title: Hawking and the slow evaporation
lessons.content:
Black holes are at the heart of modern theoretical physics because they push the laws of nature to their limits. In **1974**, physicist **Stephen Hawking** revolutionized our understanding by demonstrating that black holes are not totally black. Due to quantum effects at the interface of the horizon, they would emit extremely faint radiation: **<Hawking radiation>**.

This discovery implies that a black hole very slowly loses mass over time. If it no longer absorbs anything, it eventually evaporates completely. However, for a stellar-mass black hole, this process would take billions of times the current age of the universe. This concept raises the "information paradox": if an object falls into a black hole and the latter evaporates, what happens to the information stored in the original object? Solving this enigma is one of the greatest challenges in current physics.

Whether through their role as "engines" at the heart of galaxies or their ability to warp time (which flows more slowly near an intense gravity field), black holes remain the ultimate laboratories for testing our understanding of reality. They are the missing link between the infinitely large of Relativity and the infinitely small of quantum mechanics.

|| A black hole forms by the collapse of a massive star and is delimited by the event horizon, a boundary crossed for the first time visually in 2019 with the image of M87*.||
