quiz.explanation: The poem ends with Hector's funeral; the Trojan horse is not there.

title: Oedipus Rex, Sophocles
description: Oedipus wants to save Thebes from a plague. As he investigates, he discovers that he is the guilty man. Sophocles invents the tragedy in which knowing means destroying yourself.
subject: litterature

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
**Oedipus Rex** is considered by **Aristotle** in his <Poetics> as the perfect tragedy. Within a unity of time and action, **Sophocles** stages the dizzying fall of a man who, while seeking the truth to save his city, discovers the horror of his own identity: he is both the son and the murderer of his father, the husband and the son of his mother. The play has lost none of its power after 2,500 years, as it touches on the fundamental paradox of the human condition.

[Oedipus Sphinx ancient Greek relief]

lessons.title: Sophocles and Greek tragedy
lessons.content:
**Sophocles** (496-406 BC) is one of the three great Greek tragedians along with **Aeschylus** and **Euripides**. Of the 120 plays he is said to have composed, only **7 have reached us** in their entirety, including the Theban cycle which comprises <Antigone> and <Oedipus at Colonus>.

His technical contribution to the Theatre is immense. He introduced the **third actor** (<tritagonist>), which allowed for more interactions and more complex dialogues, thereby reducing the omnipresence of the chorus in favor of individual psychology. His figures are no longer monolithic archetypes, but beings gripped by deep doubts, whose nobility lies in their will to understand and act in the face of the unfathomable.

As a civic and religious Institution, tragedy is performed during the **Great Dionysia** before tens of thousands of citizens. The social function of these performances, according to Aristotle, is **catharsis**: a purification of the emotions of pity and terror. By seeing a noble hero fall, the spectator discharges their own destructive passions by proxy.

[Oedipus Sphinx riddle painting]

{ Sophocles was not just an author; he held important political positions in Athens, was a general alongside Pericles, and a priest of the healer god Asclepius.}

lessons.title: The investigation that turns on the investigator
lessons.content:
The action begins in Thebes, struck by a <loimos> (plague). Oedipus, the beloved king who once saved the city by solving the enigma of the **Sphinx**, promises to find the culprit of the murder of the former king, **Laius**. The play presents itself as a police investigation in reverse, where the investigator is himself the criminal.

Tragic irony permeates every word: the more Oedipus curses the anonymous murderer, the more he unknowingly condemns himself. The truth is revealed in stages by the blind seer <Tiresias>, then by shepherds who witnessed the past. We then learn that Oedipus, son of Laius and **Jocasta**, had been abandoned at birth after a fatal oracle. Raised in **Corinth** by King Polybus, whom he believed to be his father, he had fled this city to escape the prophecy (to kill his father and marry his mother).

Fate mocks human resistance: it is on the path of exile, during a simple roadside quarrel, that he kills an old man who is none other than Laius. Arriving in Thebes, he frees the city and receives the hand of the widowed queen, Jocasta. The logic of fate here is circular and implacable: it is the very act of fleeing the prophecy that ensures its perfect realization.

{ In Antiquity, the outcome was not a surprise for the audience, as everyone knew the myth of Oedipus. Tragic pleasure resided not in the "what", but in "how" the hero was going to discover the truth.}

lessons.title: Seeing too clearly, then going blind
lessons.content:
What makes the play extraordinary is the perfect alignment of two major dramatic springs: recognition (<anagnorisis>) and reversal (<peripeteia>). In Sophocles, the moment when Oedipus identifies the culprit coincides exactly with his social and moral fall. Knowledge is not a liberation, but a destruction.

Faced with the unbearable, Jocasta takes her own life. Oedipus, for his part, chooses to gouge out his eyes with the gold brooches of his wife and mother. This act is highly symbolic: he who saw physically was blind to the truth of his blood; having become blind, he finally accesses inner vision and self-knowledge. He then asks for exile, leaving his status as king for that of a <pharmakos> (scapegoat), whose departure must heal Thebes from defilement.

The play explores **hubris**, that disproportionate pride that pushes man to believe he can surpass the gods or escape his destiny through his intelligence. Oedipus, the man who deciphers riddles, did not know how to decipher his own life. Sophocles thus poses the question of responsibility: can one be guilty of crimes committed in total ignorance? The tragedy does not answer, it exposes the fragility of human glory in the face of the cosmic order.

lessons.title: From Freud to our modern whodunits
lessons.content:
The influence of Oedipous Rex spans the centuries. Beyond the text of Sophocles, Oedipus has become a universal figure of the unconscious. However, it is crucial to distinguish the ancient Work from its modern interpretation. **Sigmund Freud** borrowed the myth to name the **Oedipus complex**, postulating a universal desire of the child for the parent of the opposite sex.

For Sophocles, the subject is by no means repressed sexual desire, but the metaphysical question of predestination. The ancient text emphasizes that the hero never desired these acts; he suffered them as a divine curse. Where psychoanalysis sees an internal drive, the Greek tragic poet sees an external force: fatality.

The posterity of the Work also manifests itself in French classical theater (Corneille, Voltaire) and in 20th-century rewritings (Cocteau, Pasolini). All return to this source to question the relationship of man to the Law and to the sacred. The play remains the absolute model of dramatic tension, where every word spoken by the hero builds his own grave.

{ The word "enigma" comes from the Greek <ainigma>. For the Greeks, life itself was an enigma posed by the gods, and Oedipus is the only hero to have solved it twice: facing the Sphinx, then facing himself.}

quiz.question: What plague strikes Thebes at the beginning of the play?
quiz.explanation: Thebes is struck by a plague, and the oracle demands that the murderer of the former king Laius be punished.

quiz.question: What does Oedipus promise the city of Thebes?
quiz.explanation: Oedipus promises to find the murderer of Laius, without knowing that he will find him in himself.
options: Find and punish the murderer of Laius

quiz.question: True or false: Sophocles refines the tragedy inherited from Aeschylus by adding more characters and psychological tension.
quiz.explanation: Sophocles evolves the tragic genre by giving more space to the characters and their inner tension, the chorus remaining a commentator rather than a driving force behind the action.

quiz.question: Who does Oedipus question first in his investigation into the murder of Laius?
quiz.explanation: Oedipus first questions the soothsayer Tiresias, then his wife Jocasta, widow of Laius, before the clues close in on himself.

quiz.question: According to Aristotle, what are the two key effects that he admires in Oedipus Rex?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle admires the peripeteia, the sudden reversal of the situation, and the anagnorisis, the moment when Oedipus understands who he is.

quiz.question: What does Oedipus do when the truth completely comes out?
quiz.explanation: When the truth comes out and Jocasta commits suicide, Oedipus puts out his eyes, he who saw for the city now refusing to look at the world.
options: He immediately exiled himself without a word
He abdicates and appoints a successor

quiz.question: True or false: in Oedipus the King, the more lucidly the hero seeks the truth, the closer he comes to his own downfall.
quiz.explanation: This is the tragic irony of the play: Oedipus's desire to be just and lucid accelerates his loss rather than protecting him from it.

quiz.question: What does Oedipus mean for the city once the truth is known?
quiz.explanation: Oedipus becomes the pharmakos: the plague being the sign of an unpurified crime, he is expelled to purify the city.
options: The pharmakos, the one who is expelled to purify the community
A king who is celebrated as a savior
A judge responsible for punishing other culprits

quiz.question: Which 20th century thinker rereads the myth of Oedipus through psychoanalysis?
quiz.explanation: Freud sees in the Oedipus myth the complex that bears his name, one reading among others of the broader scope of the play.

title: Antigone, Sophocles
description: Antigone buries her brother against the order of King Creon. Between the law of the city and duty to family, Sophocles sets up a conflict that has never aged.
subject: litterature

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Written by **Sophocles** around 441 BC, **Antigone** is undoubtedly the most emblematic Work of ancient theater. Although it is part of the legendary cycle of the Labdacids, it stands out for a striking modernity: it abandons blind fatality to focus on individual moral choice.

[Antigone Creon Greek tragedy painting]

The heart of the play rests on an insoluble dilemma opposing two forms of Legitimacy: the law of the city, necessary for social order, and the law of conscience, imperative for the individual. This text does not just tell of a tragic fall; it founds the millennial debate on civil disobedience and the hierarchy of legal norms.

lessons.title: The legacy of Oedipus still weighs
lessons.content:
The action begins in the aftermath of a bloody civil war in Thebes. Antigone's two brothers, **Eteocles** and **Polynices**, killed each other under the city walls during the expedition of the <Seven Against Thebes>. Their uncle **Creon**, ascending the throne in a climate of extreme instability, must restore order and loyalty to the State.

To mark the difference between the exemplary citizen and the rebel, Creon decrees national funerals for Eteocles, but formally forbids burying Polynices. The latter, having attacked his own homeland with a foreign army, is declared a traitor. His corpse must remain exposed on the sand, delivered to beasts of prey.

In the mental universe of the Greeks, this decision is of unheard-of violence. The deprivation of burial is not only a social blight; it is a metaphysical condemnation. Without funeral rites, the soul of the deceased cannot access <Hades> and remains condemned to wander eternally at the boundaries of the World of the dead. Creon uses here the instrument of the sacred to serve a purely political vision of justice.

{At the time of Sophocles, theater was so powerful that the poet Phrynichos was sentenced to a fine for having written a play that was too sad: the spectators had burst into tears so much that the city was judged destabilized by the emotion.}

lessons.title: Disobeying also means saying “I”
lessons.content:
Faced with the royal decree, Antigone refuses to submit. For her, Polynices, regardless of his political faults, remains her brother and a human being deserving the respect due to the dead. While her sister **Ismene** favors power and submission to the laws of the city, Antigone chooses solitary resistance.

[Antigone burying Polynices painting]

She is captured while covering the body with dust, performing the symbolic gesture of burial. Brought before her uncle, she denies nothing. On the contrary, she opposes the ephemeral decree of a man with the "unwritten and unfailing laws of the gods." It is here that the fundamental distinction between **positive law** (the law of the State) and **Natural law** (a transcendent morality) is born.

{In 1944, during the premiere of Anouilh's version in Paris, German censorship authorized the play because it saw in Creon a defender of necessary public order, while the French public recognized in it the heroism of the Resistance in the Figure of Antigone.}

Creon does not perceive Antigone's religious argument. In his eyes, any citizen who disobeys is an agent of chaos endangering the stability of Thebes. His authority is all the more contested as it is by a woman, in an ultra-codified patriarchal society. The tension worsens when his own son, **Haemon**, Antigone's fiancé, tries to convince his father that flexibility is proof of sovereign wisdom. But Creon locks himself in his pride.

lessons.title: Creon holds too hard: the hubris of power
lessons.content:
The tragedy tips when Creon, deaf to pleas, decides to wall Antigone up alive so as not to have blood on his hands (a ritual hypocrisy). It is then that the blind seer **Tiresias**, spokesperson for the divine will, intervenes. He warns the king that the gods refuse sacrifices because the city is defiled by the rotting corpse of Polynices.

Scared by the threats of imminent misfortunes, Creon finally gives in. This is the moment of the <peripeteia>: he runs towards the tomb to free Antigone. But tragic destiny requires that the reparation be too late. Upon his arrival, he discovers that Antigone has committed suicide. Haemon, drunk with grief, throws himself on his own sword after trying to strike his father.

The tragedy does not stop there. **Eurydice**, Creon's wife, learning of the death of her son, also takes her own life. In a few moments, the king's rigidity has annihilated his entire lineage. The sovereign remains alone on stage, alive but broken, having realized too late that his Law, by wanting to ignore superior forces, has drawn upon him **hubris** and existential nothingness.

lessons.title: A tragedy of values, not a slogan
lessons.content:
What makes Sophocles' Work immortal is the absence of Manichaeism. Contrary to a simplistic vision, Creon is not a monster: he is a head of State who wants to protect his city after a devastating war. Antigone, for her part, can seem fanatical in her thirst for martyrdom. It is the very essence of Greek tragedy: the confrontation of two consciences each being right from their point of view.

The philosopher **Hegel** saw in this play the perfect example of his Theory on tragedy: the conflict between two equally valid, but unilateral rights. For him, Antigone represents family and religious morality, while Creon embodies the rationality of the State. The synthesis of this conflict can only occur in destruction.

Even today, Antigone is invoked whenever a human law comes into contradiction with moral conscience. She remains the symbol of those who dare to say "no" in the name of a superior principle, reminding us that legality is not always synonymous with justice.

|| Antigone poses in 441 BC the fundamental question of civil disobedience: must the law of individual conscience prevail over the law of the State when the latter is judged unjust? ||

quiz.question: What does Creon refuse to grant to one of the two brothers who died killing each other?
quiz.explanation: Creon orders one of the brothers to be honored and the other to be left unburied, which Antigone refuses.

quiz.question: What does Antigone do against King Creon's order?
quiz.explanation: Antigone refuses Creon's decree and herself buries the body of her brother who remains unburied.
options: She demands arbitration from the gods at the temple

quiz.question: True or false: Antigone is the daughter of Oedipus.
quiz.explanation: Antigone belongs to Oedipus' cursed family, which weighs on the entire play.

quiz.question: What conflict of values ​​does Antigone oppose to Creon?
quiz.explanation: Antigone invokes a law older than the royal decree, while Creon defends the positive law he has just decreed.
options: The natural law of duties towards the dead against the positive law of the city

quiz.question: Who is Haemon in the play?
quiz.explanation: Haemon, son of Creon and fiancé of Antigone, begs his father in vain to renounce the sentence.
options: A guard who discovers Antigone's crime

quiz.question: What flaw in Creon does Sophocles highlight through his decision to be stubborn?
quiz.explanation: Creon persists despite pleas, embodying hubris, the excess which blinds and leads to catastrophe.
options: Hubris, the proud excess that blinds
Cowardice in front of the people

quiz.question: True or false: when Creon finally gives in and renounces his decision, there is still time to save everyone.
quiz.explanation: Creon gives in too late: Antigone, then Haemon and Queen Eurydice die despite his change of mind.

quiz.question: How does Antigone's sister, Ismene, react to Creon's decree?
quiz.explanation: Ismene hesitates in the face of the royal ban, while Antigone openly accepts her action.
options: She hesitates, unlike Antigone who chooses the act
She denounces her sister to the king
She buries the body in its place
She takes up arms against Creon

quiz.question: Which 19th century philosopher reads in Antigone a conflict between two equally legitimate rights?
quiz.explanation: Hegel analyzes the play as the confrontation of two legitimate rights, public order and family piety, without either being entirely wrong.

title: The Symposium, Plato
description: Around an Athenian dinner, the guests take turns defining love. Aristophanes tells the story of the androgynes, Socrates lifts desire toward the Beautiful. Plato turns a party into philosophy.
subject: litterature

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The Symposium is undoubtedly the most famous Work of **Plato** on the question of desire. Written around 380 BC, this text does not present itself as an arid treatise, but as a vivid account of Athenian customs.

[ancient Greek symposium banquet painting]

Through an oratorical joust where each guest strives to define Love, the philosopher deploys a revolutionary theory: desire is not just a carnal drive, but a powerful engine of knowledge. This text explores how the aspiration toward a singular being can be transformed into a quest for **absolute Beauty** and the divine, thus durably marking Western thought.

lessons.title: Drinking, talking, competing
lessons.content:
The narrative opens on an <Athenian symposion> organized at the home of the poet **Agathon**. We are in 416 BC, and the young playwright has just won his first competition. To celebrate the Event, he gathers his friends, including the philosopher **Socrates**, for an evening of reflection guided by drink and speech. The guests, still tired from the excesses of the day before, choose to drink moderately and to dedicate the evening to a praise of **Eros**, the god of Love, often neglected by poets.

The structure of the text follows a series of speeches whose depth gradually increases. We first hear classical or medical visions: **Phaedrus** praises the courage that love inspires in lovers, while the physician **Eryximachus** sees in love a force of cosmological balance. However, it is the smashing entry of **Alcibiades**, a brilliant and provocative general, that comes to break the solemnity of the exercise at the end of the text.

[Socrates Alcibiades banquet painting]

Drunk, **Alcibiades** refuses to praise an abstract god. He prefers to tell of his own fascination for **Socrates**, depicting the philosopher as a being of striking external ugliness but housing <within> "divine treasures." This contrast between physical appearance and spiritual value is one of the keys to reading the dialogue.

{Historical irony: although the guests praise philosophy, several participants of The Symposium, like Alcibiades or Agathon, were later involved in religious or political scandals that led indirectly to the trial of Socrates in 399 BC.}

lessons.title: The myth of the androgynes
lessons.content:
Before the intervention of **Socrates**, the comic poet **Aristophanes** proposes a mythological explanation that has remained famous. He tells that originally, human nature was radically different. Men were not simple, but "double" and spherical: they possessed four arms, four legs, and two identical faces turned outward.

These beings were divided into three genders: the double-males (descended from the sun), the double-females (descended from the earth), and the <androgynes> (male and female, descended from the moon). Their power and pride were such that they attempted to scale the heavens to attack the gods. To punish them without annihilating them, **Zeus** decided to cut them in half.

Since this original separation, each half is inhabited by a throbbing desire to find its lost part to restore its wholeness and its former strength. According to **Aristophanes**, love is therefore the pursuit of this integrity, a feeling of deep lack that pushes beings towards one another.

{This myth is at the etymological origin of the word 'symbol'. In Greek, the sumbolon was an object broken in two whose two parts, once reunited, allowed the carriers to recognize each other and prove their bond.}

lessons.title: Diotima and the ladder of love
lessons.content:
When his turn comes, **Socrates** subverts the previous speeches. He claims to report the words of a foreign priestess, **Diotima**. She taught him that Eros is not a perfect and beautiful god, but a <daimon>: an intermediary between the world of men and that of the gods. Son of **Poros** (passage, abundance) and **Penia** (poverty), Eros is by nature indigent, but ingenious and a hunter of beauty.

Love is therefore a constant tension. Since one only desires what one does not have, Eros is lack itself. But this lack is fertile. **Diotima** then describes a methodical ascent that is called the **ladder of love**. The novice begins by loving the beauty of a single body. Then, he realizes that beauty is the same in all beautiful bodies.

Next, he rises towards the beauty of souls, more precious than that of flesh. From there, he contemplates the beauty of laws, sciences, and human actions. At the summit of this progression, the initiate finally accesses the vision of **Beauty in itself**: an eternal, immutable Idea and the source of all other splendors. This is the very essence of philosophy: to use the energy of desire to propel oneself toward the truth.

lessons.title: What “platonic” ended up meaning
lessons.content:
The posterity of The Symposium gave birth to the Concept of **platonic love**. Today, this expression is often reduced, wrongly, to a simple affection without sexuality. In **Plato**, the meaning is much more demanding: love is not an end in itself, but a means. It is a process of "procreation in beauty," both physically (through children) and spiritually (through ideas and virtues).

The ultimate goal of the platonic lover is not to remain fixed in the possession of the loved Object, but to use the romantic emotion to awaken to the intelligible. It is an education of the gaze: learning to see, behind the loved face, the radiance of the Absolute.

The Symposium remains a pivotal Work because it reconciles the body and the spirit. It does not reject desire, but it transforms it into a vector of transcendence. By showing that passion can lead to wisdom, **Plato** defined the foundations of Western aesthetics and mysticism, influencing both the medieval poetry of troubadours and modern psychology.

|| Plato's Symposium defines Love (Eros) as a desire born of lack, which must serve as an engine to rise from sensible physical beauty toward the contemplation of ideal and eternal Beauty. ||

quiz.question: In what context does the dialogue of the Banquet take place?
quiz.explanation: The Banquet takes place during a symposion, a citizen's meal where people drink, discuss and compete in eloquence.
options: A meal of Athenian citizens, a symposion
A temple during a religious ceremony

quiz.question: What theme should the guests of the Banquet address in their speeches?
quiz.explanation: The imposed theme of the evening is Eros, and each guest offers their own theory of love.
options: Death and the immortality of the soul

quiz.question: What do the androgynes say in Aristophanes' speech?
quiz.explanation: Aristophanes says that humans were once double and that Zeus cut them in two to punish them, each seeking their lost half ever since.
options: Humans were once double, before Zeus cut them in two
The gods created humanity from clay
Men are descended from a single immortal ancestor

quiz.question: True or false: Aristophanes' myth of androgynes gave French the expression "soulmate".
quiz.explanation: This story of humans cut in two inspired the French expression “soulmate”, designating the half that we are trying to find.

quiz.question: Who teaches Socrates the theory of love as an intermediary, or daimon?
quiz.explanation: Socrates reports the teaching of Diotima, a wise foreigner, that Eros is a daimon, a go-between who desires what he lacks.

quiz.question: According to the teaching of Diotima, through what stages does the lover progress?
quiz.explanation: The lover starts from the beautiful body, moves on to beautiful souls, then to beautiful actions, before reaching Beauty in oneself: this is the scale of Platonic Eros.
options: From beautiful bodies to beautiful souls, then to beautiful actions, until Beauty in itself
From friendship to hatred to forgiveness
From marriage to solitude then to wisdom
From wealth to poverty to virtue

quiz.question: Who bursts in, drunk, at the end of the Symposium to praise Socrates?
quiz.explanation: Alcibiades, a drunken ambitious young man, bursts in and praises Socrates as a troubling Satyr, showing that philosophical desire does not abolish trouble.

quiz.question: True or false: in everyday language, “platonic” love has the same meaning as for Plato himself.
quiz.explanation: In everyday language, “platonic” means without flesh, while in Plato the body remains a legitimate starting point, not a shame.

title: The Republic, Plato
description: To define justice, Plato imagines an ideal city and the myth of the cave. The Republic is not an election platform: it is an inquiry into the soul and into power.
subject: litterature

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Written around 375 BC, **The Republic** is not merely a political treatise; it is the architectural Work of **Platon**'s thought. Through the Figure of **Socrate**, his teacher, Plato explores a fundamental question: what is a just life? To answer it, he abandons the individual scale to build, through discourse, an ideal city named <Kallipolis>.

This monumental dialogue in ten books intrinsically links morality, education, psychology, and metaphysics. It houses one of the most powerful images in universal culture, the allegory of the **cave**, which still defines our relationship to truth and appearances today.

[Plato Academy Athens painting]

lessons.title: The soul and the city, same blueprint
lessons.content:
The dialogue opens with a confrontation with the sophist **Thrasymachus**, who maintains a provocative thesis: **justice** is nothing other than the interest of the stronger. According to him, laws are Dicté by the dominant for their own profit. To refute this Cynicism, **Socrate** proposes an original method: examining justice "writ large" to better see it "writ small." He therefore decides to design an imaginary city to observe how justice settles within it.

[Plato portrait bust sculpture]

This approach is based on the principle of **isomorphism**: the structure of the state must be the mirror of the structure of the human soul. Plato postulates that the soul is composed of three distinct forces. The first is **epithumia** (sensory desires and primary needs). The second is **Thumos** (the heart, the force of indignation and courage). The third is **Logos** (reason). 

A just soul is one where reason commands desires with the help of courage. By extension, a just city will be one where each social class fulfills the function corresponding to the part of the soul that dominates within it. Justice is therefore not an arbitrary rule, but an internal harmony where everyone is in their rightful place.

 It is said that "Plato" is only a nickname given by his gymnastics teacher because of his athletic build (platos meaning "breadth" or "width" in Greek). His true birth name was Aristocles.

lessons.title: Who should rule?
lessons.content:
To guarantee the balance of <Kallipolis>, Plato divides the population into three rigid orders. The **producers** (craftsmen and farmers), in whom desire dominates, ensure material survival. The **auxiliaries** (warriors), dominated by courage, protect the city. Finally, the **perfect guardians** form the ruling elite. 

This is where the central Figure of **<philosopher-kings>** appears. For Plato, the ills of the city will only cease when political power and philosophy are reunited. The philosopher is the only one fit to govern because he is the only one who has risen to the knowledge of universal truths, escaping personal interests and passions.

This model imposes radical discipline. For the upper classes, Plato advocates the suppression of private property and the nuclear family to avoid nepotism and corruption. Children are raised in common by the state. This vision makes **The Republic** a meritocratic utopia where education, and not birth, determines social position. 

The ideal city must also protect itself from corrupting influences. Plato thus proposes to perform Censorship on poets and artists, accused of flattering the lower emotions of the soul rather than nourishing reason. This mistrust of the arts highlights the demand for intellectual purity in his system.

lessons.title: The cave: getting out of the illusion
lessons.content:
At the center of the Work is the allegory of the **cave**, which explains the journey of education and access to knowledge. Plato imagines prisoners chained in an underground dwelling, turning their backs to the entrance. Behind them, a fire projects the shadows of objects onto the wall they face. For them, these shadows constitute the only reality.

The passage toward the light is a violent process. If a prisoner is released, he suffers from being dazzled. He must first look at reflections in the water, then at the objects themselves, before finally being able to contemplate the **Sun**. The sun represents the Idea of the Good, the source of all truth and all existence.

This metaphor illustrates **Plato's Theory of Ideas**: the sensible World in which we live is only a world of shadows, an imperfect copy of the intelligible world, populated by perfect and eternal forms (the Ideas). The role of the philosopher is to perform this intellectual ascent to then guide his fellow men.

However, the return to the cave is perilous. The philosopher, accustomed to the height, seems clumsy in the darkness of human affairs. His companions, mocking and attached to their illusions, might even seek to kill him, a transparent allusion to the trial and death of Socrates.

lessons.title: Regimes that rot, a book that lasts
lessons.content:
Plato does not settle for describing perfection; he also analyzes corruption. In the final books, he describes the slow degradation of political regimes, which follows the degradation of souls. **Timocracy** (the pursuit of honor) leads to **oligarchy** (domination by money), then to **democracy**. Plato is a fierce critic of the latter, which he sees as the anarchy of desires where the word of the scholar is worth as much as that of the ignorant. 

The ultimate stage of this fall is **tyranny**, where a single man, the slave of his own vilest passions, enslaves the entire city. This cyclic analysis shows that without rigorous education and a government of reason, every society ends up collapsing in violence.

The influence of the Work is immeasurable. While some saw it as the first manifesto of **totalitarianism** in the 20th century, notably <Karl Popper>, others perceive in it an unsurpassable ethical quest. As the philosopher <Alfred North Whitehead> wrote, the European philosophical tradition consists only "of a series of footnotes to Plato." 

Beyond Politics, **The Republic** remains a text on the conversion of the soul: learning no longer to look at the shadows, but to seek the source of the light.

 Although Plato is often criticized for his authoritarianism, he was incredibly progressive for his time by affirming that women possessed the same intellectual capacities as men and could, as such, become guardians and lead the city.

quiz.question: What central question does Plato seek to resolve in the Republic?
quiz.explanation: The Republic starts from a simple question: what is justice? To answer this, Socrates imagines an ideal city.
options: What is the origin of the gods?

quiz.question: How does Plato divide the human soul in the Republic?
quiz.explanation: Plato distinguishes desire (Epithumia), courage (Thumos) and reason (Logos), which he puts in parallel with the three classes of the ideal city.
options: In three parts: desire, courage and reason
In two parts: body and mind

quiz.question: Who should govern the ideal city, according to Plato?
quiz.explanation: The ideal rulers are the philosopher-kings, long trained in mathematics and dialectics, living without excessive private property.
options: The philosopher-kings, who love truth more than power

quiz.question: True or false: Plato trusts Athenian democracy as the best possible regime.
quiz.explanation: Plato, on the contrary, is wary of Athenian democracy, which according to him condemned Socrates, a just man.

quiz.question: What do the chained prisoners see in the myth of the cave?
quiz.explanation: Prisoners of myth only see shadows on a wall, mistaking these illusions for the only reality they know.
options: Only shadows cast on a wall
Their own reflection in the water

quiz.question: What happens when a freed prisoner returns to warn the others, in the myth of the cave?
quiz.explanation: The freed prisoner who returns to announce what he saw to the sun is treated as crazy by those who remain in chains.
options: Everyone immediately follows him towards the exit
He is named king of the cave
The others thank him and go out with him

quiz.question: Which 20th century philosopher accuses the Republic of announcing totalitarianism?
quiz.explanation: Karl Popper accuses the Republic of opening the way to totalitarianism, while others see it more as an educational utopia.

quiz.question: Put these political regimes back in the order of degeneration described by Plato.
quiz.explanation: Plato describes a progressive degeneration of regimes, each one born from the vices of the previous one, from aristocracy to tyranny.
items: Aristocracy
Timocracy
Oligarchy
Democracy
Tyranny

quiz.question: According to the theory of Ideas, what does the sensible world that we perceive represent?
quiz.explanation: For Plato, the sensible world is only a shadow compared to the world of Ideas, which the myth of the cave illustrates.
options: A shadow of the real world of Ideas
A perfect creation of the gods

title: The Apology of Socrates, Plato
description: In 399 BC, Athens put Socrates on trial. Accused of corrupting the young, he refused to plead for pity. Plato fixed the founding scene of Western philosophy.
subject: litterature

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The **The Apology of Socrates, Plato** is not an excuse in the modern sense of the term, but a defense (from the Greek <apologia>). This text by **Platon** recounts the trial of his master, **Socrate**, which took place in **399 BC** in the heart of Athens. This pivotal moment in the History of thought sees the most famous philosopher of Antiquity face a jury of **501 Athenian citizens**. Beyond a simple judicial event, this trial questions the place of truth and individual criticism in the face of the conformism of a city in crisis.

[Socrates trial Athens painting]

lessons.title: Why Athens loses patience
“I know that I know nothing”
lessons.content:
Before his judges, Socrates refuses the traditional codes of the court. Rather than seeking pity by parading his family or crying, he adopts a tone mixing **irony** and radical sincerity. He tells how his friend Chaerephon questioned the **Oracle of Delphi**, who stated that no one was wiser than him. This revelation was the starting point of his mission: to test men reputed to be wise (politicians, poets, craftsmen) to understand what the oracle meant.

From this inquiry, he draws a famous conclusion that founds <Socratic maieutics>: while others believe they know without knowing, he is aware of his own lack of knowledge. This posture, summarized by the sentence **“I know that I know nothing”**, does not aim for stagnation but for the sincere search for truth. Socrates presents himself then as a gadfly sent by the gods to sting a city slumbering in its prejudices.

This paradoxical attitude provokes the hostility of part of the jury. Socrates refuses to consider himself a teacher charging for his lessons, unlike the <sophists>, and claims a poverty that proves his disinterestedness.

{Contrary to idealized representations of philosophers, Socrates was described as physically very ugly, with bulging eyes and a snub nose, which accentuated the contrast between his nobility of spirit and his external appearance.}

lessons.title: The verdict, then the provocation
lessons.content:
At the end of the deliberations, the verdict is delivered: Socrates is found guilty by a narrow majority of 280 votes to 221. According to Athenian procedure, the accused must then propose a counter-penalty against the death penalty sought by the accuser. Here, Socrates pushes the logic of his integrity to the point of absurdity or the sublime: convinced that he has been a benefactor to his country, he proposes to be housed and fed at the **Prytaneion**.

This proposal, which corresponds to the honors reserved for war heroes or winners of the Olympic Games, is experienced as an ultimate insult by the jurors. It seals his fate. In the second vote on the sentence, the majority widens: 360 votes are cast for death. Socrates accepts this sentence with disconcerting serenity, affirming that he prefers to die true to himself rather than live having renounced his mission.

[Death of Socrates Jacques-Louis David painting]

Death is not an evil for him, but either a dreamless sleep or the passage to a Location where he can continue to question the shadows of the great heroes of the past.

lessons.title: The birth of a philosophical myth
lessons.content:
The execution of Socrates by consuming **hemlock** marks the birth of the Figure of the "martyr of philosophy." By dying for his ideas, Socrates transforms his trial into an eternal moral victory over the city of Athens. This moment defines the essence of the philosophical act: the search for justice and truth must take precedence over biological survival or the opinion of the crowd.

Platon, devastated by the death of his master, would dedicate a large part of his Work to rehabilitating his memory and spreading his teaching. The Apology serves as a starting point for this endeavor of transmission. It establishes a clear distinction between technical knowledge and moral wisdom, highlighting that a man of value must never act unjustly, even if it must cost him his life.

The legacy of this text is immense: it has inspired centuries of thinkers on civil disobedience and freedom of thought, from Antiquity to **Henry David Thoreau** or **Martin Luther King**.

{The execution of Socrates was delayed for 30 days because of a religious festival: Athenian Law forbade any execution as long as a sacred ship sent to Delos had not returned to port.}

|| Socrates is condemned to death in 399 BC by an Athenian jury; he refuses compromises, claims the wisdom of ignorance and chooses death by hemlock out of loyalty to his principles. ||

quiz.question: In what year was Socrates tried and sentenced to death in Athens?
quiz.explanation: Socrates was tried and convicted in 399 BC, a trial that became the founding scene of Western philosophy.

quiz.question: What is Socrates accused of during his trial?
quiz.explanation: Socrates is accused of not honoring the gods of the city and of corrupting the youth with his speeches.
options: Not to honor the gods of the city and to corrupt the young
For having insulted a magistrate in public

quiz.question: True or false: in court, Socrates pleads for mercy to obtain clemency from the judges.
quiz.explanation: Socrates refuses to play the repentant accused: he transforms the tribunal into an examination of the city itself rather than pleading for mercy.

quiz.question: What does the oracle of Delphi reveal to Socrates, according to his own account?
quiz.explanation: The Oracle of Delphi states that no one is wiser than Socrates, who then understands that his wisdom consists of knowing that he does not know.
options: That no one is wiser than him
That he must become a sophist

quiz.question: What is Socrates' method of dialogue called, compared to childbirth?
quiz.explanation: Socratic maieutics compares dialogue to childbirth: creating clearer thoughts in the other through successive questions.

quiz.question: What does Socrates propose as a punishment after being found guilty, angering the judges?
quiz.explanation: Rather than careful exile, Socrates suggests being fed to the Prytaneus, a provocation that causes the judges to vote for death.
options: Being fed at the Prytaneum, an honor reserved for benefactors
A fine paid by his disciples

quiz.question: Who wrote the Apology of Socrates?
quiz.explanation: The Apology is written by Plato, a disciple of Socrates, who depicts the trial of his master.

quiz.question: True or false: depending on the course, Socrates is clearly distinguished from the sophists, although public opinion sometimes confuses them.
quiz.explanation: The sophists are paid teachers of rhetoric from whom Socrates stands out, even if Athenian opinion tends to mix them.

title: The Poetics, Aristotle
description: Aristotle analyzes Greek tragedy and coins words that are still everywhere: mimesis, catharsis, peripeteia. The Poetics is the first great instruction manual for storytelling.
subject: litterature

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The **Poetics, Aristotle** is considered the first treatise on systematic literary analysis and aesthetic Theory in Western History. Written in the 4th century BC, this book does not settle for cataloging the works of its time; it seeks to understand the deep mechanisms by which a narrative touches the human soul.

[Aristotle portrait bust sculpture]

By focusing mainly on Greek tragedy, **Aristotle** establishes theoretical pillars - such as <Aristotelian mimesis>, <catharsis>, peripeteia or recognition - which still structure dramaturgical and cinematographic writing worldwide today. This text transformed the perception of fiction, moving from the status of simple entertainment or dangerous lies to that of a tool for knowledge and social regulation.

lessons.title: Imitating is not cheating
lessons.content:
**Aristotle** (384-322 BC), a pupil of Plato and then tutor to **Alexander the Great**, is often described as the first great encyclopedist. His immense Work covers all fields of knowledge, from biology to ethics. To understand **Poetics**, one must grasp his break with his teacher Plato.

Plato condemned poets and mimetic art, believing that imitation was only a distorted copy of reality, itself a copy of the world of Ideas. For him, Art distanced man from the truth. **Aristotle** takes the total opposite view of this vision by affirming that imitation is an innate tendency of the human being from childhood. He proposes the Concept of <Aristotelian mimesis>: Art does not just copy reality, it represents it by structuring it to extract a universal truth.

The imitation then becomes a source of intellectual pleasure: even the representation of painful things can provide joy through the quality of the execution and the learning it allows. The **Poetics** has reached us in an incomplete manner: only book I dedicated to tragedy and epic remains, while the second volume, dedicated to comedy, was lost in the sands of History.

{The lost second volume of the Poetics has so fascinated historians that Umberto Eco made it the pivot of his novel "The Name of the Rose," imagining a librarian monster poisoning the pages of the book so that no one would discover Aristotle's theory on laughter.}

[ancient Greek theater Epidaurus]

lessons.title: Catharsis: fear, pity, relief
lessons.content:
For **Aristotle**, tragedy is not simply a sad play; it is a structure designed to produce a specific psychological effect. He defines it as the imitation of an action that is noble, complete, and of a certain magnitude, featuring acting figures. The ultimate goal of this perspective is to arouse **pity** (at the sight of unjust misfortune striking a fellow human) and **terror** (realizing that such misfortune could happen to us).

The result of this process is <Catharsis>. This medical term, meaning "purification" or "purgation," refers to the relief felt by the spectator at the end of the performance. By experiencing these emotions vicariously within the safe framework of the <Theatre of Epidaurus> or any other scenic space, the citizen is liberated from their own excessive passions.

<Catharsis> thus possesses a social and political function: it regulates the crowd's emotions to maintain the balance of the city. The spectator does not leave overwhelmed by the fate of Oedipus, but internally clarified, having understood something of the order of the World and human fragility without having had to endure the hero's actual suffering.

lessons.title: Plot, reversal, recognition
lessons.content:
Aristotle analyzes the technical structure of the Work through a strict hierarchy of elements. At the top is the **muthos** (the plot). Contrary to a modern vision that sometimes prioritizes the psychology of the figures, **Aristotle** asserts that tragedy is an imitation not of men, but of an action. The plot must possess an organic unity: a beginning, a middle, and an end following logically according to necessity or probability.

Two mechanical drivers ensure the effectiveness of the **muthos**. First, the **peripeteia**, which is the sudden reversal of action by which happiness changes into misfortune (or vice versa). Second, the anagnorisis or **recognition**, the transition from ignorance to knowledge (for example, the moment a hero discovers his real identity or the crime he committed unknowingly).

The Other elements are the **ethos** (character, which must be consistent with the action), the **dianoia** (thought or speeches), then verbal expression, song, and finally the spectacle (staging). For **Aristotle**, a good text must be able to produce its tragic effect even through simple reading, without the artifice of the stage.

lessons.title: An instruction manual that survived
lessons.content:
The History of the transmission of the **Poetics** is a true tale of intellectual adventure. After the closure of the philosophical schools in Athens, the text sank into oblivion in the West. It was the scholars of the Arab-Muslim world who saved it. In the 10th century, **Abu Bishr Matta ibn Yunus** translated the work from Syriac into Arabic, allowing thinkers like <Averroes> to comment on the Work.

It was only during the Renaissance that the text was rediscovered in Europe, becoming the "bible" of 17th-century French & European Classics such as Corneille or Racine. The latter derived rigid rules from it, such as the famous **rule of the three unities** (time, Location, action), although **Aristotle's** original text is far less dogmatic than has been claimed.

Today, the influence of the **Poetics** is omnipresent in Popular culture. The three-act structures used by Hollywood screenwriters and the notions of "climax" or "plot twist" descend directly from **Aristotle's** analysis. The philosopher succeeded in proving that the pleasure of fiction is not mere escapism, but a form of knowledge that teaches us how to be human.

{Did you know that most Disney and Pixar films still follow Aristotle's precepts so faithfully that modern screenwriting manuals, like 'Save the Cat', are often just reinterpretations of the Poetics for the 21st century?}

|| To remember: Aristotle's Poetics (4th century BC) founds Western dramaturgy by defining art as a structured mimesis aiming for the catharsis of emotions through a rigorous plot (muthos). ||

quiz.question: What does Aristotle seek to analyze in the Poetics?
quiz.explanation: Poetics analyzes tragedy and seeks to understand how a story produces fear and pity, and why this effect makes us feel good.
options: How tragedy creates fear and pity, and why it makes us feel good
How to compose a political speech
How to found an ideal city
How to conduct a judicial investigation

quiz.question: How does Aristotle name the artistic imitation that he rehabilitates in the face of Plato's distrust of images?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle rehabilitates mimesis, artistic imitation, which he compares to the way a child imitates to understand the world.

quiz.question: True or false: for Aristotle, tragedy must above all respect the documentary accuracy of real facts.
quiz.explanation: For Aristotle, the criterion is not the true documentary but the probable and the necessary, what had to happen in this story.

quiz.question: What does catharsis mean according to Aristotle?
quiz.explanation: Catharsis refers to the way in which tragedy orders our affects of pity and fear, even if the exact meaning of the term remains debated.
options: A form of purification of the emotions of pity and fear
A memory exercise for the actors
A religious ritual before the performance

quiz.question: According to Aristotle, what constitutes the heart of the drama, more than the characters?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle places the muthos, the intrigue, at the heart of the drama, valuing the adventure and the recognition more than the characters themselves.

quiz.question: Which play does Aristotle cite as a star example of peripeteia and recognition?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle takes Oedipus the King as a star example: the hero discovers too late who he is, in an exemplary reversal.

quiz.question: What type of hero does Aristotle prefer for a successful tragedy?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle prefers an error, hamartia, to pure wickedness: the hero is neither perfectly good nor monstrous, which makes his fall logical and terrible.
options: A hero who makes a mistake, neither perfectly good nor monstrous
A perfectly virtuous hero punished without reason
A totally evil hero who receives his punishment
A hero absent from the main action

quiz.question: True or false: according to Aristotle, poetry says the particular while history says the general.
quiz.explanation: It's the opposite: for Aristotle, poetry speaks of the general, while history speaks of the particular.

title: Works and Days, Hesiod
description: Hesiod speaks to his brother Perses: work, be just, beware of excess. Between the myth of Pandora and a farming calendar, an ethic of labor is born.
subject: litterature

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Written around **700 BC**, *Works and Days* constitutes, alongside the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*, one of the founding pillars of European Literature. If Homer sings of the glory of warriors, **Hesiod** becomes the singer of the ordinary human condition, marked by the necessity of labor and the requirement of justice. 

[Hesiod ancient Greek poet illustration]

This long didactic poem is not just a manual on agriculture; it is a treatise on morals based on the account of the **<five ages of mankind>**, exploring the progressive decline of man from a state of original purity to the misery of the present. Through a complex structure mixing practical advice and cosmogony, Hesiod defines what separates man from the beast: the consciousness of right and redemption through effort.

lessons.title: A poet who speaks from his field
lessons.content:
Contrary to the relative anonymity of Homer, **Hesiod** is the first poet of the Western tradition to place himself on stage. Originally from Ascra, a village in **Boeotia**, he describes himself as a simple shepherd who received the poetic anointing of the Muses while grazing his flocks on Mount Helicon. This rural origin is vital: Hesiod does not speak from royal courts, but from the land.

The poem was born from a deep personal conflict. Hesiod addresses his brother, **Perses**, whom he describes as a great consumer of goods. According to the story, Perses seized the major part of the paternal inheritance by corrupting local dispensers of justice, the "gift-devouring kings." The text then becomes an indictment against injustice and an exhortation addressed to an idle brother so that he understands that only sweat ensures a stable life.

The Work is thus articulated around a double theme: the "Days," which are a religious and superstitious calendar indicating favorable moments for each task, and the "Works," a technical manual on grain cultivation and navigation. Hesiod thus transforms a family quarrel into a universal lesson on the morals of work.

An ancient tradition tells that Hesiod once faced Homer in a poetry contest at Chalcis. Although Homer was judged superior, the king awarded the prize to Hesiod because he sang of peace and agriculture rather than the carnage of war.

lessons.title: Prometheus, Pandora and the decline
lessons.content:
To explain why human life has become an incessant struggle against hunger, Hesiod summons myths. He first relates the crime of **Prometheus**, the Titan who defied the will of Zeus. Having stolen the seeds of fire to offer them to mortals, he allowed humanity to rise through Technique, but triggered celestial anger.

In retaliation, Zeus had Hephaestus forge the first woman: **Pandora**. Endowed with all gifts by the gods, she carried with her a jar - and not a box, a term originating from a late translation error by <Erasmus>. By opening this vessel, Pandora released fatigue, sickness, and death onto Earth, leaving only Hope (**Elpis**) at the bottom. This myth marks the end of direct communication between men and gods.

[Prometheus fire myth painting]

This downfall is theorized by the account of the **five ages of mankind**. Hesiod describes an involution: the Golden Age (under Cronus) where men lived like gods, the Silver Age marked by impiety, the Bronze Age populated by brutal warriors exterminating themselves, the Age of Heroes (that of the Trojan War) which marks a brief improvement, and finally the Iron Age. The latter is ours: an era of total corruption where children are born with white hair and where shame and indignation leave the Earth for Olympus.

lessons.title: Dike against hubris
lessons.content:
At the heart of the poem lies a revolutionary reflection on **justice** (**Dike**). Hesiod affirms that Zeus endowed men with a moral sense that radically distinguishes them from the animal kingdom. Where fish and beasts devour each other according to the Law of the strongest, man must follow the Law of right.

The poet warns the powerful against **<Hubris>**, the excessive pride that leads to the ruin of cities. For Hesiod, the just city prospers, its women give birth to healthy sons and the land produces in abundance, while the unjust city suffers famine and sterility. It is one of the first texts in History to link the economic success of a society to its moral probity.

Work (**Ergon**) then becomes the instrument of this justice. Far from being a contemptible activity reserved for slaves, as would be seen later among certain Athenian philosophers, work is for Hesiod the only way to please the gods. He develops the idea of a "good emulation" (Eris) which pushes neighbors to rival each other's labor to grow rich, contrary to the "bad emulation" which leads to war and pecuniary lawsuits.

lessons.title: The ancestor of poems about the land
lessons.content:
The influence of *Works and Days* is immense. During Antiquity, the poem served as a basis for education, teaching young Greeks not only Mythology, but also the virtues of household economy and perseverance. Hesiod succeeded in making the peasant World a noble subject, worthy of the epic muse, paving the way for the genre of **didactic poetry**.

Later, the Romans would reappropriate this model. Virgil, in the **<Georgics>**, would pay explicit tribute to the "old man of Ascra" by taking up the structure of his treatise to exalt the values of the Italian land. The idea of the Golden Age, for its part, would become a universal literary topos, feeding political utopias and poetic nostalgia until the Renaissance.

Ultimately, Hesiod was the first to understand that if humanity has lost Paradise, its greatness now resides in its capacity to organize the World through right and to transform it through effort. His pessimistic vision of decline is offset by a heroic pragmatism: the iron man can still save his soul through loyalty and the plow.

|| Works and Days (c. 700 BC) defines work (ergon) and justice (dike) as the two pillars allowing the man of the Iron Age to survive with dignity after the end of the Golden Age and the opening of Pandora's jar. ||

quiz.question: To whom does Hesiod address his poem Works and Days?
quiz.explanation: The poem is addressed to Perses, Hesiod's brother, accused of having cheated on the division of an inheritance.

quiz.question: True or false: unlike Homer, a vague figure, Hesiod portrays himself in his poem.
quiz.explanation: Hesiod speaks of his village, his father who came from Asia Minor and his trial against Perses, a personal voice which contrasts with the anonymity of the Homeric bard.

quiz.question: What does Prometheus do in the myth told by Hesiod to explain the harshness of life?
quiz.explanation: Hesiod relates that Prometheus steals fire, a gesture that results in divine punishment and helps explain the harshness of the human condition.
options: He creates the first men in clay

quiz.question: What does Pandora's jar release, according to the myth told by Hesiod?
quiz.explanation: Pandora's jar releases the evils that have since struck humanity.

quiz.question: According to the five ages of humanity described by Hesiod, what age are we living in?
quiz.explanation: Hesiod places his time in the Iron Age, the last and worst of the five ages, where justice falters.
options: The Iron Age, the worst, where justice wavers
The Silver Age, peaceful and long
The age of heroes, glorious and just

quiz.question: What other poem, attributed to Hesiod, tells of the birth of the gods?
quiz.explanation: The Theogony, another poem by Hesiod, tells of the birth of the gods, while Works and Days descend from heaven to the plow.

quiz.question: What moral opposition structures the heart of the poem?
quiz.explanation: The poem opposes Dikè, justice, to Hubris, arrogant excess: unjust kings are threatened by Zeus, while the honest peasant has a chance.
options: Dikè, justice, against Hybris, arrogant excess

quiz.question: Which Latin poet would later draw inspiration from Works and Days in his Georgics?
quiz.explanation: Virgil will remember Hesiod's poem in his Georgics, another great poetic text devoted to agricultural life.

quiz.question: True or false: according to Hesiod, any form of rivalry between neighbors is bad and should be avoided.
quiz.explanation: Hesiod distinguishes the good Eris, a useful rivalry which pushes one to work better, from the bad Eris, that of hatred and trial.

title: Medea, Euripides
description: Jason leaves Medea for a princess. She kills their children. Euripides creates a heroine who is terrifying, brilliant and foreign: passion turns into reasoning.
subject: litterature

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Medea is one of the most terrifying and psychologically complex tragedies of Antiquity. By staging a mother who murders her own children to take revenge for her husband's betrayal, **Euripides** shakes the codes of the city and of morality. This Work, first performed in 431 BC, does not merely tell a bloody myth; it dissects the pain of a displaced woman and the mechanism of fury.

[Medea Delacroix painting]

Through this narrative, Euripide creates a Figure of striking modernity, whose radical Other-ness - woman, foreigner, and sorceress - serves as a mirror to the contradictions of classical Athenian society.

lessons.title: Euripides, the most “modern” of the three
lessons.content:
**Euripides** (480-406 BC) is the last of the three great Greek tragedians. While <Aeschylus> focused on the divine order and <Sophocles> on the solitary greatness of the hero facing fate, Euripides marks a break with his psychological realism.

He is particularly interested in outcasts and the torments of the human soul. His contemporaries perceived this approach as a form of degradation of tragic nobility. The comic poet **Aristophanes**, in his parodies, reproached him for staging "ragged" Figures and women with passions that were too virulent.

Yet, it is this attention to the nuances of feeling that makes his Work timeless. By introducing doubt and internal contradiction in his heroes, he invents what is called **double motivation**: the idea that a Figure acts as much through external forces as through their own psychological impulses.

{During the creation of the play in 431 BC, Euripides finished last in the tragic competition, the public probably having been too shocked by the radical innovation of maternal infanticide.}

lessons.title: The foreign woman whose pact is broken
lessons.content:
The plot is rooted in the mythological past of **Medea**. Princess of Colchis, she is a <Barbarian> in the eyes of the Greeks, endowed with supernatural powers. Out of love for **Jason**, the leader of the <Argonautes>, she sacrificed everything: she betrayed her father, murdered her own brother to facilitate their escape, and stole the Golden Fleece.

[Jason Golden Fleece painting]

Settled in Corinth, she finds herself in a position of total vulnerability. Jason, ambitious, decides to break their union to marry the daughter of King **Creon**. To justify his perjury, he invokes the interest of his children and the superiority of Greek laws over Barbarian oaths.

Jason's abandonment is not just a romantic betrayal; it is a social condemnation. Without male protection, Medea is struck by a decree of exile. It is here that her nature as a sorceress tips toward a destructive rationality. She no longer seeks to convince, but to annihilate everything that constitutes her enemy's future: his new lineage and his current offspring.

lessons.title: Killing her children: reason against passion?
lessons.content:
The heart of the tragedy lies in the famous **monologue of Medea**. Just before taking action, she expresses a profound inner conflict. Contrary to earlier versions of the myth where the children died by accident or were killed by the Corinthians, Euripides makes Medea the conscious author of the crime.

This passage illustrates the struggle between her <Thumos> (her anger, her need for honor) and her maternal love. She hesitates four times, looking at her children, before concluding that her thirst for revenge is stronger than her pain as a mother. For her, the dishonor of seeing her enemies laugh at her misfortune is more unbearable than the death of her sons.

The resolution of the play uses a technical device called the <Deus ex machina>. While Jason believes he can punish her, Medea appears in the sky on a winged chariot sent by her grandfather, the Sun (Helios). She carries away the corpses of her children, refusing Jason even the right to bury them. This finale emphasizes that Medea is not an ordinary criminal subject to human laws, but an irreducible elemental force.

lessons.title: A heroine who keeps disturbing us
lessons.content:
Despite its initial failure, Euripides' Medea has become the most influential Work on posterity. Where Antiquity saw in her mainly the danger of feminine Hubris and foreign irrationality, subsequent centuries have multiplied the interpretations.

In the classical era, painters like **Delacroix** immortalized the dramatic tension of the infanticidal mother, capturing the moment when tenderness transmutes into fury. In the 20th century, the Figure was reappropriated by feminist movements. Medea is no longer just a murderer, but a woman who, faced with the oppression of a patriarchal society and the contempt for her status as a foreigner, has no choice but total destruction to regain her sovereignty.

Her voice still resonates today as a denunciation of the injustices done to the uprooted and the contempt of the powerful. She remains the universal symbol of monstrous resistance: she who prefers to destroy her own World rather than see it enslaved.

{In astronomy, the asteroid (212) Medea, discovered in 1880, bears her name; it belongs to the main belt and testifies to the indelible mark of this Figure in our culture.}

|| Euripides' Medea (431 BC) transforms the myth of the sorceress into a tragedy of interiority where revenge triumphs over maternal instinct to restore broken honor. ||

quiz.question: Why does Jason leave Medea in Corinth?
quiz.explanation: In Corinth, Jason abandons Medea to marry the king's daughter, which triggers Medea's vengeance.
options: To marry the daughter of the king of Corinth
Because she lost her magical powers

quiz.question: What did Medea bring to Jason before he divorced her?
quiz.explanation: Without Medea's spells, Jason would never have obtained the Golden Fleece: Euripides insists on the ingratitude of "civilized" man.
options: His magical help in obtaining the Golden Fleece

quiz.question: True or false: in the eyes of the Greeks, Medea is considered a Barbarian, foreign to the Hellenic world.
quiz.explanation: Medea comes from Colchis, outside the Greek world, and this status as a foreigner becomes central when Jason repudiates her.

quiz.question: How does Euripides represent Medea's decision to kill her children?
quiz.explanation: Medea hesitates, but her decision to kill her children is explained in a lucid speech: it is not a silent act of madness.
options: Like a lucid choice, presented in a thoughtful speech
Like a direct order from the gods
Like an act immediately regretted and canceled

quiz.question: How does the play end for Medea?
quiz.explanation: A deus ex machina allows Medea to escape on a winged chariot sent by her grandfather the Sun, without immediate punishment.
options: She escapes on a winged chariot sent by her grandfather the Sun
It is publicly executed in Corinth
She commits suicide like Jocasta in Oedipus the King
She is forgiven by Jason and remains in Corinth

quiz.question: True or false: depending on the course, Euripides is clearly trying to excuse Medea's action.
quiz.explanation: Euripides does not excuse infanticide, but he forces the audience to hear the voice of the person who commits it.

quiz.question: How is Euripides considered the most “modern” of the three great Greek tragedians?
quiz.explanation: Alongside Aeschylus and Sophocles, Euripides explores the interiority of characters who doubt and contradict themselves, which makes him read as a psychological genius.
options: It explores the interiority of characters who doubt and contradict themselves
He avoids any dialogue in favor of pure action
He abandons the chorus in all his pieces

quiz.question: Beyond personal vengeance against Jason, what does Medea also destroy by killing her children, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: By destroying her own lineage, Medea also harms the future of the city, a political cost that the course underlines.
options: The future of the lineage, with a political cost for the city

title: Les Misérables, Victor Hugo
description: Jean Valjean looks for redemption in a France that refuses to forgive him. Hugo mixes love story, historical chronicle and a plea for the outcast.
subject: litterature

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Published in **1862**, Les Misérables is not only a masterpiece of French literature; it is a universal Epic that explores the depths of the human soul and the flaws of society. **Victor Hugo** deploys a monumental narrative over nearly 1,500 pages, blending a detective plot, a romance novel, a historical chronicle, and a political plea. 

The story revolves around the Figure of **Jean Valjean**, a man broken by the <penal colony and the 19th-century penal system> who seeks redemption in a world that refuses to forgive him. Facing him stands <Inspector Javert>, the embodiment of implacable justice. By recounting this hunt spanning several decades, Hugo paints a portrait of a people in search of dignity and light in the heart of 19th-century France.

lessons.title: Hugo and a book born in exile
lessons.content:
**Victor Hugo** (1802-1885) began writing this titanic project as early as **1845**, initially under the title "Les Misères." His work was violently interrupted by the political upheavals of his time. Witness to the Revolution of 1848, he opposed Napoleon Bonaparte, leading him into exile after the coup d'état of **1851**.

[Victor Hugo portrait photograph]

Taking refuge in the Channel Islands, he resumed his manuscript with new fervor, matured by his own experience of injustice and political isolation. The novel was finally published in **1862** in Brussels, after seventeen years of gestation. Victor Hugo was aware of creating an unprecedented literary Object: a "world-work" meant to speak to all nations, transcending social and geographical boundaries.

The ambition of the text goes beyond simple fiction. Hugo inserts long thematic chapters, called <digressions>, on the Battle of Waterloo, convents, or the system of the <sewers of Paris>. These passages, far from being incidental, serve to anchor the figures in the material and historical reality of their time, making the novel a treatise on social philosophy as much as a work of Art.

 Victor Hugo was so famous that the address on some letters from his admirers simply read: 'To Mr. Victor Hugo, in his avenue, Paris'.

lessons.title: Jean Valjean: from hard labor to grace
lessons.content:
The journey of **Jean Valjean** illustrates the central thesis of the novel: the possibility of redemption. Sentenced to five years of forced labor for stealing a piece of bread to feed his starving nephews, his sentence was multiplied by escape attempts. He ultimately spent **19 years** in the penal colony, an experience that left him full of hate toward a society he held responsible for his downfall.

[French convict galley 19th century]

Upon his release, the **yellow passport** identifying him as a former convict made him a pariah. It was Bishop **Myriel**, a Figure of absolute kindness, who broke this cycle of violence. After Valjean stole his silverware, Myriel claimed to the gendarmes that it was a gift, going so far as to offer him two additional candlesticks while declaring that his soul was henceforth redeemed from evil.

This act of pure grace provoked a crisis of conscience in Valjean. Under the identity of **Monsieur Madeleine**, he became a prosperous industrialist and a philanthropic mayor in Montreuil-sur-Mer. However, he remained haunted by the idea that a criminal could be unmasked. For Hugo, this internal duel between past identity and present virtue is the very engine of the sublime. Charity then becomes the only force capable of defeating social fatality.

 The shortest exchange of telegrams in History took place between Hugo and his publisher: the poet sent '?' to ask about sales, the latter replied '!' to signify the immense success.

lessons.title: Fantine, Cosette and the barricades
lessons.content:
The novel expands to embrace the suffering of the most vulnerable, embodied by **Fantine**. This abandoned worker sinks into poverty to pay the boarding fees for her daughter **Cosette** to the Thénardiers, a malicious couple of innkeepers. Protecting Cosette becomes Valjean's sacred mission after Fantine's death, marking his definitive transition from fugitive to protector.

The narrative then moves to Paris, where individual destinies intersect with History. The major turning point is the insurrection of **June 1832**, triggered during the funeral of General Lamarque. Victor Hugo uses this Event to stage the fire of the republican youth gathered in the <ABC>, a secret society of students fighting for progress.

[Paris barricades 1832 painting]

On these barricades, two figures mark the collective imagination: **Marius**, the idealistic student in love with Cosette, and especially **Gavroche**, the street urchin. Gavroche dies while singing, collecting cartridges under soldier fire, becoming the symbol of innocence sacrificed for freedom. Through this turmoil, Valjean reappears not to fight with weapons, but to save a life, that of Marius, performing an act of total self-sacrifice that binds him definitively to Cosette's future.

 The figure of Gavroche was inspired by a press engraving Hugo saw depicting a child on the barricades of the 1830 Revolution.

lessons.title: A novel that changes minds
lessons.content:
The end of the novel seals the protagonists' fate in a metaphysical dimension. Javert, confronted with the humanity of Valjean who saves his life, sees his dogmatic certainties collapse. Unable to reconcile the rigor of the Law and the evidence of Grace, he takes his own life. Jean Valjean, after ensuring the happiness of those under his care, passes away in the light, fulfilling his promise to Bishop Myriel.

Beyond the story, Les Misérables is a pillar of <socially engaged literature>. Hugo denounces the lack of schooling, sexist oppression, and the inhumanity of prisons. The book fueled debates on the abolition of the death penalty and the improvement of the working-class condition. It is not just a narrative, but a program for social reform through empathy.

Its influence continues through infinite adaptations, notably the famous global musical. Hugo succeeded in his gamble: writing a book that, as long as there is ignorance and misery on earth, may not be useless. The Work invites every reader to believe in the perfectibility of man and the transformative power of <providence>.

 To write the escape scene in the sewers, Hugo researched with the Paris sanitation services and explored the underground galleries himself to capture the stifling atmosphere.

 || An Epic fresco published in **1862**, Les Misérables recounts the redemption of **Jean Valjean** during the July Monarchy. Through the conflict between charity (Valjean) and implacable law (Javert), Hugo denounces social misery and turns the barricades of **1832** into a symbol of the struggle for dignity. ||
