title: The Suez Canal: why it is strategic
description: A 193-kilometer water corridor carries 12% of world trade. One ship ran aground in 2021 and stalled the planet: welcome to **Suez**.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: The **Suez Canal**, located in Egypt, constitutes one of the most strategic crossing points on the planet. By connecting the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, it offers a direct alternative to the long bypass of Africa via the **Cape of Good Hope**, reducing the journey between Europe and Asia by nearly **7,000 km**. Beyond its crucial economic role, this canal is a true barometer of global power relations. From its construction under colonial aegis to its nationalization by Egypt in 1956, up to contemporary maritime tensions, it remains a major issue of sovereignty and international security.

lessons.title: The colonial era: a bridge to empire
lessons.content:
The cutting of the Isthmus of Suez was the culmination of a titanic project led by the French engineer and diplomat **Ferdinand de Lesseps**. Between **1859 and 1869**, tens of thousands of Egyptian workers worked to dig this 193-kilometer waterway.

[Suez Canal inauguration 1869 Lesseps]

At its inauguration in **November 1869**, the canal was managed by the Suez Canal Company, a private company with predominantly French capital. Although **Great Britain** was initially skeptical, it quickly understood the vital importance of this route to secure access to its colonies. Taking advantage of the abyssal debts contracted by the <khedive> of Egypt, the British government bought back his shares in **1875**. London then became the principal shareholder of the canal, transforming the latter into an indispensable imperial artery, affectionately named the "Road to India.”

This foreign domination on Egyptian soil created growing tensions. During most of the 20th century, the canal was perceived by Egyptian nationalists as the symbol of colonial humiliation, a British enclave in the heart of a country seeking to assert its independence.

{At the inauguration in 1869, the composer Giuseppe Verdi was commissioned to write an opera celebrating the Event, which gave birth to the famous Work "Aida," although it was not performed in Cairo until 1871.}

lessons.title: 1956: the nationalization turning point
lessons.content:
The year 1956 marked a historical break. The Egyptian president **Gamal Abdel Nasser**, a leading figure of <pan-Arabism>, decided to nationalize the canal company on **July 26, 1956**. His objective was clear: to retake control of this strategic resource to finance the construction of the **Aswan High Dam**, a massive development project from which Western powers had just withdrawn their funding.

[Gamal Abdel Nasser Egyptian president portrait]

The reaction was immediate. France and the United Kingdom, seeing their interests despoiled, allied with Israel to launch a secret military offensive. The operation was a technical success on the ground: the canal was occupied. However, it triggered the anger of **Dwight D. Eisenhower**, President of the United States, who had not been informed. In the middle of the **Cold War**, Washington feared that this colonial aggression would throw Third World countries into the arms of the **USSR**.

Under American economic pressure and Soviet threats, the European powers were forced into a humiliating withdrawal. This diplomatic defeat sealed the definitive decline of France and Great Britain as first-tier colonial powers and consecrated the political triumph of Nasser, who became the idol of the Arab world.

lessons.title: A vital artery under modern strain
lessons.content:
Today, the Suez Canal remains the lung of global maritime trade, seeing approximately **12% of world trade** and nearly 20,000 ships pass through per year. However, its relative narrowness in the face of the gigantism of modern ships constitutes a major vulnerability. On **March 26, 2021**, the whole world held its breath when the giant container ship **Ever Given** ran aground, paralyzing all traffic.

[Ever Given container ship Suez Canal stuck 2021]

For six days, the obstruction of the canal caused a massive traffic jam of more than 400 ships. The economic consequences were staggering: the paralysis cost approximately **$400 million per hour** to the global economy. This incident highlighted the extreme dependence of globalized production chains on a single narrow passage.

Beyond the technical aspect, regional geopolitics also threatens this stability. Between 2023 and 2024, missile attacks carried out by the <Houthis> from Yemen against commercial ships forced shipowners to divert their fleets via Southern Africa. This three-week detour massively increases transport and insurance costs, proving that control of the canal remains dependent on peace in the Red Sea basin.

lessons.title: Challenges of the 21st century
lessons.content:
To maintain its competitiveness against potential new routes, such as the Northern Sea Route made accessible by the melting of polar ice, Egypt launched the "New Suez Canal" project. Inaugurated in 2015, this widening makes it possible to double passage capacities on certain sections and reduce waiting times. But the canal is no longer content to be a place of transit; it is becoming a special economic zone, attracting Chinese and European investments.

Egyptian management of the canal remains an essential diplomatic lever. Canal revenues constitute one of the main sources of foreign currency for the country, making the Egyptian state extremely vigilant regarding the security of the **Bab-el-Mandeb** strait, the real southern gateway to the Suez system. The vulnerability of the canal is no longer just that of a physical blockage by a ship, but indeed that of a global regional instability that could durably weaken this axis so precious for the energy and industrial supply of Europe.

|| To remember: The Suez Canal, inaugurated in 1869 by de Lesseps, went from a tool of British imperial domination to a symbol of Egyptian sovereignty after the 1956 crisis. Today, it handles 12% of global trade but remains vulnerable to technical incidents and geopolitical tensions in the Red Sea. ||

title: NATO: what is it still for?
description: Founded against the USSR in 1949, **NATO** should have disappeared with the Cold War. It is now bigger and busier than ever.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The **NATO** (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) represents today the most powerful military alliance in modern History. Founded in 1949 in a world fractured by the emergence of the Cold War, it initially aimed to protect Western Europe against Soviet Union expansionism. However, the disappearance of its designated adversary in 1991 did not lead to its dissolution. Quite the contrary, the organization has gone through three decades of searching for identity, transforming from a regional shield into a global actor intervening on several continents. 

The Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 marked a historical turning point, putting an end to doubts about the Alliance's utility and provoking an unprecedented enlargement towards the North. This course analyzes how NATO went from a classic deterrence structure to a sprawling organization confronted with new challenges: the Russian threat at its borders, the budgetary requirements of its members, and the complexity of international interventions.

lessons.title: Origins: a shield against the Eastern bloc
lessons.content:
NATO was officially born on **April 4, 1949** with the signing of the Washington Treaty by 12 pioneering countries. This military alliance responded to an urgent need for collective security in a context where the Red Army occupied Central Europe. The organization's philosophy was then summarized by a famous formula from its first Secretary General, **Lord Ismay**, who stated that NATO's role was to "keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down." This strategy was as much about containing the USSR as it was about ensuring a structural commitment of the United States on the European continent, while reintegrating West Germany into a secure framework.

[NATO headquarters Brussels flags]

{Iceland is the only NATO member country that does not have a standing army; its contribution to the alliance is based on radar sensors, coast guards, and strategically hosting allied aircraft on its soil.}

The nuclear heart of the treaty lies in its **Article 5**, which establishes the principle of collective defense. This clause stipulates that an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all. This is what is called **extended deterrence**: the Soviet Union knew that an offensive on Berlin or Paris would trigger a massive response, potentially nuclear, from the American superpower. Throughout the Cold War, this mechanism of automatic solidarity froze European borders, making any direct conflict too costly to be considered.

Despite this permanent tension, the alliance succeeded in its initial bet for stability, evolving from a simple diplomatic promise to a unique integrated military structure in the World, equipped with permanent commands and forces capable of operating under a common flag.

lessons.title: After the Cold War: enlargement and new missions
lessons.content:
The fall of the Berlin Wall and the dissolution of the USSR in **1991** plunged NATO into a major existential crisis. Without a designated enemy, the alliance seemed to become obsolete. Yet, it chose to reinvent itself through two major strategic axes. The first was the massive **enlargement** towards the East. From 1999, former <Warsaw Pact> countries like Poland or Hungary, then the <Baltic states> in 2004, joined the organization. For these nations, membership represented the ultimate assurance against a possible return of Russian imperialism.

[NATO enlargement Eastern Europe map]

The second axis was NATO's operational transformation into an international policeman. Under American influence, the alliance began to intervene "out of area," that is, outside the territory of its members. It thus carried out its first combat operations during the **Kosovo** war in 1999 to stop ethnic cleansing, and then engaged massively in **Afghanistan** after 2001 as part of the fight against terrorism. These missions showed a NATO capable of projecting its power far from its bases, even if they were sometimes criticized for their lack of political clarity.

{The acronym NATO is one of the few to be commonly used in two inverted forms: NATO in English and OTAN in French, the two official languages of the organization since its creation.}

However, this expansionism fed a sharp resentment in Moscow. <Vladimir Putin> has regularly denounced a breach of oral promises of influence made at the end of the Cold War, considering NATO's approach to Russian borders as an unbearable provocation.

lessons.title: The shock of 2022 and the return of territorial defense
lessons.content:
Russia's invasion of Ukraine on **February 24, 2022** abruptly ended the era of doubts about the Alliance's utility. In a few days, NATO regained its original mission: the defense of European territory. The conflict caused a diplomatic earthquake in Northern Europe, pushing **Sweden** and **Finland**, historically attached to their neutrality, to request immediate membership. Finland joined the organization in 2023, followed by Sweden in 2024, thus doubling the length of the land border between NATO and Russia.

[NATO soldiers tanks Ukraine support 2022]

The alliance, which now has **32 members**, does not participate directly in the fighting in Ukraine to avoid a <nuclear escalation>, but it coordinates unprecedented logistical support. Member states provide heavy weaponry, satellite intelligence, and training to Ukrainian troops. This war also imposed generalized rearmament in Europe. Countries like Germany underwent a historical turning point (the "Zeitenwende") by unlocking massive funds to modernize their armies neglected for 30 years.

Parallel to this resurgence of activity, internal tensions remain. The United States, through the voices of politicians like Donald Trump, demand better burden-sharing of the financial weight. The **2% of GDP** rule dedicated to defense has become the thermometer of allies' credibility. In 2024, a majority of members finally reached this goal, symbolizing an awareness: European security is no longer a free asset but a necessary investment in the face of the high-intensity threat.

lessons.title: NATO and the challenges of the 21st century
lessons.content:
Beyond the conventional Russian threat, NATO must now adapt to a new grammar of conflict. The alliance has integrated <cyberspace> and space as new official domains of operations. Cyberattacks on critical infrastructure or disinformation campaigns are now considered aggressions that can, in certain cases, justify the activation of collective assistance.

{Although NATO is a defense alliance, it possesses its own fleet of AWACS surveillance aircraft, recognizable by their huge circular radar on their backs, allowing them to monitor European skies 24/7.}

The organization is also looking more and more towards Asia. China's rise to power is perceived by Washington as the major systemic challenge of the century, prompting NATO to forge partnerships with Japan, South Korea, or Australia. This evolution creates debates within European members, some fearing that NATO is moving too far from its original geographical area.

Finally, the political balance remains fragile. Between the rise of populism, the ambiguities of countries like Turkey, and the uncertainty over long-term American commitment, NATO is condemned to permanent adaptation. However, 75 years after its creation, it remains the only platform for military dialogue and cooperation capable of uniting both sides of the Atlantic.

|| NATO grew from 12 to 32 members between 1949 and 2024, repositioning itself as the central pillar of European security against the Russian threat while integrating new fields of conflict like cyberspace. ||

title: The UN: powerful or powerless?
description: Created in 1945 to prevent war, the **UN** saves millions of lives every year, yet stays paralyzed in the face of the biggest conflicts.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The **UN** (United Nations) was born on the ashes of the **World War II**, with the ambition to replace force with Law. Founded in 1945 by the **San Francisco Charter**, it succeeded a **League of Nations** which had been unable to prevent the second global conflict. Its mission is clear: to preserve future generations from the scourge of war, protect human rights, and promote social progress.

Yet, from the **Cold War** to contemporary tensions, the **Institution** often seems powerless against the great powers. Between its undeniable humanitarian successes and its repeated political paralyses, the **UN** appears today as a colossus with feet of clay, whose very structure reflects a world balance nearly 80 years old. Understanding the **UN** requires analyzing this permanent tension between universal ideal and national interests.

lessons.title: An architecture inherited from 1945
lessons.content:
The architecture of the **UN** is not the result of a global democracy, but of a compromise between the victors of 1945. The supreme decision-making body, the **Security Council**, is composed of fifteen members, but only **five permanent members** hold the reality of power: the United States, Russia (heir to the **USSR**), China, France, and the United Kingdom. 

[UN Security Council chamber meeting]

These five powers possess the **right of veto**, a tool that allows a single state to block any resolution, even if it is supported by the vast majority of other countries. This mechanism was initially intended to ensure that the great powers did not go to war with each other by forcing them into consensus. However, it has become the instrument of almost systematic paralysis. 

During the **Cold War**, the world witnessed a rain of cross-vetoes between the Eastern and Western blocs. Today, this logic persists: the Russian veto blocks any direct action in Ukraine, while the American veto traditionally protects its allies in the Middle East. This structure freezes global geopolitics in a photograph from 1945, ignoring the emergence of new powers like India or Brazil.

{The **UN** headquarters in **New York** is considered international territory. For its construction, the wealthy John D. Rockefeller Jr. donated $8.5 million to purchase the land, which was previously slaughterhouses and meat-packing plants.}

lessons.title: Quiet effectiveness: the humanitarian arm
lessons.content:
If the political **UN** is often blocked, the operational **UN** records major victories for humanity. This success rests on the **<UN specialized agencies>** and funds acting on the ground, far from the oratory jousts of **New York**. These bodies have their own budgets and expert personnel who intervene in the most disadvantaged areas of the planet.

One of the greatest successes in human History, the **eradication of smallpox** in 1980, was coordinated by the WHO (World Health Organization). Similarly, the WFP (World Food Programme) feeds nearly 100 million people every year during famines or natural disasters. These actions prove that when states put aside their ideological rivalries for **Technique** or humanitarian issues, the UN tool becomes formidably powerful.

[UN peacekeepers blue helmets]

On the security front, the **Blue Helmets** embody the visible face of **UN** intervention. These soldiers, made available by member states, do not have the mission to wage war, but to interpose a neutral force between belligerents after a **ceasefire**. Although criticized during the tragic failures in Rwanda or Bosnia, they remain essential for stabilizing regions like South Lebanon or certain areas of Central Africa, where their simple presence allows the deployment of humanitarian aid.

lessons.title: Sovereignty against international law
lessons.content:
The fundamental limit to the action of the UN lies in the principle of **national sovereignty**. Article 2 of the Charter states that the organization cannot intervene in matters that fall within the internal jurisdiction of a State. This principle protects countries from arbitrary interference, but it also often serves as a shield for dictatorships to commit abuses without fear of legal intervention.

[UN General Assembly hall New York]

To try to compensate for this flaw, a new Concept emerged in 2005: **<Responsibility to Protect (R2P)>**. According to this principle, if a State fails to protect its population against mass crimes, the international community has a duty to intervene. However, the implementation of R2P always requires the approval of the Security Council. In 2011, its application in Libya led to the fall of the regime, but created such a precedent that Russia and China subsequently systematically refused its application in Syria, fearing a new instrumentalization of international law by the West.

The **General Assembly**, where each country has one vote, is the only truly universal Location for debate. Its resolutions do not have binding force (they are not mandatory), but they constitute a powerful barometer of world opinion. When 141 countries condemn the aggression of a neighbor, it creates diplomatic and moral pressure that even the great powers cannot totally ignore.

{It was American President Franklin D. Roosevelt who coined the name "United Nations". He had the idea in 1942 and reportedly announced it to Winston Churchill while the latter was in his bath during a visit to the White House.}

lessons.title: The impossible reform of a frozen system
lessons.content:
The debate on the reform of the UN is as old as the Institution itself. Almost all diplomats agree on the anachronistic nature of the current Security Council. The absence of India (1.4 billion inhabitants), Japan, or any African nation among the permanent members undermines the Legitimacy of UN decisions in the eyes of the "Global South".

However, the procedure for amending the Charter is an almost insurmountable lock: it requires ratification by two-thirds of the member States, imperatively including the five permanent members. Yet, none of these powers is ready to abandon or dilute its veto power. France and the United Kingdom do suggest a framework for the veto in cases of mass crimes, but the United States, Russia, and China firmly oppose it to preserve their strategic freedom of action.

The UN remains this living paradox: it is both indispensable, as it is the only forum for planetary dialogue, and ineffective, as it is a prisoner of the States that compose it. It cannot be stronger than what the great powers allow it to be. As its second Secretary-General, Dag Hammarskjöld, said: "The UN was not created to lead mankind to heaven, but to save it from hell".

|| The veto power of the 5 permanent members of the UN blocks any action in Conflicts involving them - it has been used more than 300 times since 1945. ||

quiz.explanation: The UN was founded in 1945, in the ashes of the Second World War, to replace force with law.

quiz.explanation: The Security Council has fifteen members, but only five of them have veto power.

quiz.explanation: The five permanent members with veto power are the United States, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom.

quiz.explanation: The eradication of smallpox in 1980, coordinated by the World Health Organization, is one of the greatest successes in human history.

quiz.explanation: The World Food Program feeds nearly 100 million people affected by famine each year.

quiz.explanation: The mission of the Blue Helmets is not to wage war, but to intervene between belligerents after a ceasefire.

quiz.question: What principle prevents the UN from intervening in the internal affairs of a state?
quiz.explanation: The principle of national sovereignty protects against arbitrary interference, but it also sometimes serves as a shield against dictatorships.

quiz.question: In what year did the concept of “responsibility to protect” (R2P) appear?
quiz.explanation: The concept of responsibility to protect appeared in 2005 to fill the gap left by the principle of national sovereignty.

quiz.question: True or false: the permanent members' veto power has been used more than 300 times since 1945.
quiz.explanation: The veto has been used more than 300 times since 1945, regularly blocking action in conflicts directly involving major powers.

quiz.explanation: From the name invented by Roosevelt to the appearance of the responsibility to protect, these milestones show the successes and limits of the institution.

title: Putin's Russia
description: In 25 years, a former KGB officer turned a country in crisis into an authoritarian power. A portrait of **Vladimir Putin** and his regime.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: Since his accession to the top of the state in **1999**, **Vladimir Putin** has profoundly reshaped the Russian Federation. In a quarter of a century, he has transformed a country weakened by the collapse of the USSR into a centralized and bellicose power, openly defying the liberal international order. His reign is characterized by a singular trajectory: first perceived as a pragmatic stabilizer, he became the builder of an authoritarian regime based on the control of energy resources, the repression of all internal dissent, and a desire for territorial reconquest based on a nostalgic vision of Russian imperial grandeur.

lessons.title: A meteoric rise in the 2000s
lessons.content:
The rise of **Vladimir Putin** is inseparable from the chaos of the 1990s. A former <KGB> officer stationed in East Germany, he learned his trade in the shadows of the St. Petersburg mayor's office before joining **Boris Yeltsin**'s inner circle in Moscow. His appointment as Prime Minister in **August 1999** occurred in a climate of extreme fear, marked by apartment bombings in Russian cities and the outbreak of the second **Chechen** war. His strongman posture, promising to "flush out terrorists even in the toilets," appealed to a population exhausted by instability.

[Vladimir Putin portrait Kremlin]

{Vladimir Putin was virtually unknown to the Russian general public until August 1999 – his popularity rating was 2%. Terrorist attacks and the war in Chechnya propelled him to 80% in a few months. It is one of the most meteoric political rises in modern History.}

Elected president in March **2000**, he based his first mandate on a tacit "social contract": the restoration of order and the improvement of living standards in exchange for a progressive renunciation of political freedoms. This Period benefited from an exceptional economic situation. Driven by soaring oil and gas prices, the Russian GDP was multiplied by **8** between 1999 and 2008. This financial windfall made it possible to repay external debt and foster the emergence of an urban middle class, anchoring the Legitimacy of the new master of the Kremlin in rediscovered economic prosperity.

lessons.title: Bringing society to heel
lessons.content:
Once economic stability was achieved, Putin set about the systematic neutralization of all autonomous power centers. The first pillar of this strategy was the domestication of the <oligarchs>, those businessmen who had built colossal fortunes during the wild privatizations of the Yeltsin era. The signal was given in 2003 with the arrest of **Mikhail Khodorkovsky**, head of the Yukos oil company, imprisoned for ten years for showing political ambitions. This message was clear: enrichment is permitted as long as it does not challenge the authority of the Kremlin.

At the same time, the regime attacked press freedom. National television channels were gradually placed under the tight control of state enterprises like <Gazprom>, transforming information into a propaganda tool. Repression intensified against the boldest dissident voices. Opponent **Alexei Navalny** embodied this internal challenge: after surviving a **Novichok** poisoning in 2020, he was incarcerated upon his return to Russia. His death in an Arctic penal colony in **February 2024** symbolizes the completion of the regime's authoritarian drift, where any credible political alternative is now proscribed.

[Alexei Navalny Russian opposition]

{Although his official salary is modest, Vladimir Putin is often seen with luxury watches whose total value far exceeds his declared income. One of them, an A. Lange & Söhne, is worth about $500,000 alone.}

The very structure of the State evolved toward a system dominated by the <siloviki>, representatives of the power structures (army, secret services). They occupy the key positions in the administration and major state-owned enterprises, merging the security and financial interests of the Putin clan.

lessons.title: Toward a break with the West
lessons.content:
Putin's geopolitical vision is based on a trauma: the disappearance of the USSR, which he calls the "greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the 20th century." His foreign policy aims to restore an exclusive zone of influence around Russia, frontally opposing the expansion of NATO, which he perceives as an aggression. As early as **2007**, during his speech at the Munich Conference, he denounced American unilateralism and announced a turn toward a diplomacy of confrontation.

The escalation materialized through the use of military force. In 2008, Russia intervened in **Georgia** to support the separatist territories of Abkhazia and South Ossetia. The major breaking point occurred in **2014** when, following the Maidan revolution in Ukraine, Russia proceeded with the annexation of **Crimea** and supported an armed insurrection in the **Donbas**. These acts marked the definitive return of territorial war in Europe and isolated Russia on the international stage.

[Russia Crimea annexation 2014]

{Although Putin is the strongman, Russia experienced a formal hiatus between 2008 and 2012: to respect the constitution, he became Prime Minister and left the presidency to his ally Dmitry Medvedev. But this "tandem" was only a facade, with Putin retaining the reins of real power.}

The intervention in **Syria** from 2015 allowed Putin to assert himself as an essential player in the Middle East, but it was the full-scale invasion of **Ukraine** launched on February 24, 2022, that tipped Russia into a total break with the West. This aggression triggered the most massive economic sanctions in modern history and paradoxically welded European and transatlantic unity in the face of the Russian threat.

lessons.title: The regime's ideology and its grip on power
lessons.content:
To legitimize this confrontation, the Kremlin developed a complex doctrine often referred to as **sovereign democracy**. This ideology advocates a specific Russian path, based on conservative values (traditional family, Orthodox religion) in opposition to a West judged to be decadent. The regime relies on a rewriting of History, glorifying the 1945 victory and trivializing the crimes of the Stalinist era in the name of national power.

Structurally, Putin locked in his stay at the head of the State through a major constitutional reform in **2020**. These changes allow him to "reset" his presidential term clock, offering him the theoretical possibility of remaining in power until **2036**. We are witnessing a growing militarization of society, where the entire economy is now geared toward the war effort, while laws on "foreign agents" are used to liquidate the last <civil society> organizations.

{The cult of personality around Putin gave birth to an official clothing brand called 'Putin Team'. Created by a Russian designer and supported by famous athletes like Alex Ovechkin, it sells sports items glorifying the image of the president.}

|| Putin came to power in 1999 promising stability - in 25 years, he has rebuilt a strong State, muzzled the opposition, and transformed Russia into a bellicose authoritarian regime engaged in a violent challenge to the World order. ||

title: The war in Ukraine explained
description: An invasion meant to last three days became the largest war in Europe since 1945. A look at the causes and the consequences of the conflict in **Ukraine**.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
On **February 24, 2022**, Russia launched a massive military offensive against Ukraine, triggering the most devastating conflict on European soil since the end of the Second World War. This Event did not emerge from nothingness; it is the culmination of tensions accumulated over several decades regarding Ukrainian sovereignty, the European security architecture, and the Russian imperial vision of the 21st century.

[Ukraine war destroyed city 2022]

Beyond the armed clash, this war represents a major systemic shift. It challenges the inviolability of borders, disrupts global energy and food markets, and redefines alliances within the international community. Understanding this conflict requires analyzing its historical roots, the victimhood dynamic developed by Moscow, and the unexpected resilience of the Ukrainian State.

lessons.title: The post-Soviet legacy and a clash of identities
lessons.content:
The roots of the war lie in the dislocation of the **USSR** in 1991. Ukraine's independence is experienced by a section of the Russian elite, and specifically by **Vladimir Putin**, as an unbearable amputation of Russia's "historical heart." For Moscow, Ukraine is not a sovereign nation but a component of Russia's natural "sphere of influence," a vision formalized in a 2021 presidential essay denying the distinctness of Ukrainian identity.

{Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky voiced Paddington Bear in the Ukrainian version of the film, a voice-acting career that illustrates his immense popularity as an actor before entering Politics.}

The security issue crystallizes tensions. Ukraine, which had the third-largest nuclear arsenal in the World in 1991, chose the path of disarmament. Via the <Budapest Memorandum> in 1994, it exchanged its warheads for guarantees of respect for its territorial integrity by Russia, the United States, and the United Kingdom. However, Kyiv's gradual rapprochement with the **European Union** and **NATO**, perceived by the Kremlin as a strategy of hostile encirclement, broke this balance.

The final break occurred in 2014 with the Maidan revolution, where the Ukrainian people ousted a pro-Russian president. In response, Russia illegally annexed **Crimea** and fomented a separatist insurgency in the <Donbas>. This conflict, frozen for eight years, served as a laboratory for the total war of 2022, transforming Ukrainian identity into a force of resistance resolutely turned toward the West.

lessons.title: The turning point of February 2022
lessons.content:
On **February 24, 2022**, the Russian army launched its "special military operation" on three fronts. Moscow's strategic goal was to decapitate the Kyiv government within seventy-two hours to install a puppet regime. This ambition was based on a major intelligence error: the total underestimation of Ukrainian national cohesion and the modernization of its army since 2014.

At the heart of this tipping point, President **Volodymyr Zelensky** refused the evacuation proposed by the United States, declaring: "I need ammunition, not a ride." Through his daily addresses on social media, he became the symbol of a nation that refuses to bend.

[Volodymyr Zelensky Ukrainian president address]

The Battle of Kyiv ended in a stinging Russian failure in the spring of 2022. Faced with failing logistics and mobile Ukrainian resistance using Western anti-tank weapons, Moscow had to withdraw its troops from the north of the country to focus on the east and south. This withdrawal revealed to the World the atrocities committed against civilians in cities like Bucha, hardening international determination to support Ukraine. The conflict then shifted into a war of attrition, characterized by massive artillery duels and a front line of more than 1,000 kilometers.

lessons.title: A global economic and security earthquake
lessons.content:
The shockwave of the invasion spread far beyond Ukrainian borders. In response to the aggression, Western powers deployed an unprecedented arsenal of **economic sanctions**. The objective was to paralyze the Russian war machine by targeting the heart of the financial system.

[economic sanctions Russia SWIFT banking]

The exclusion of Russian banks from the <SWIFT> secure messaging system and the freezing of the Russian central bank's foreign exchange reserves marked a historical break. These measures sought to isolate the Russian economy, but they also caused a disruption of global energy flows. Europe, which depended on Russian gas for 40% before the war, had to undertake a forced and ultra-fast mutation toward other supply sources, such as American Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG).

{At the start of the conflict, the Ukrainian government updated its 'Diia' public services app to allow citizens to report the position of Russian tanks in real-time, transforming every smartphone into a tool for military intelligence.}

The agri-food sector was the other major collateral victim. Ukraine, nicknamed the "breadbasket of Europe," saw its ports blocked, threatening famine in countries dependent on its **grains**, particularly in Africa and the Middle East. This wheat blackmail highlights the hybrid dimension of this war: it is played as much in grain silos and on banking terminals as in the trenches of the Donbas. Finally, the conflict reunited the Atlantic Alliance, pushing Finland and Sweden to abandon their historical neutrality to join **NATO**.

lessons.title: Toward a long war
lessons.content:
After more than two years of combat, the war in Ukraine has mutated into a high-intensity conflict where modern technologies (drones, satellites) sit alongside the methods of 1914. The failure of the major 2023 counter-offensives shows that the terrain has become extremely difficult to conquer due to Russian minefields and constant surveillance of the battlefield.

The challenge is now one of industrial endurance. Russia has shifted its economy toward a total war model, while Ukraine vitally depends on the sustainability of Western military and financial aid. The political debate in the United States and Europe over the cost of this support is becoming a determining factor in the outcome of the conflict.

{The Ukrainian Post issued stamps illustrating the resistance, such as the one depicting a soldier giving the middle finger to the Russian ship Moskva; these stamps were snapped up around the world, becoming collector's items and funding for the army.}

The war also redefines diplomatic balances. Moscow now relies on an axis of "pariahs" (Iran, North Korea) for its military supply, while strengthening its economic dependence on China. On the other side, Ukraine has obtained candidate status for entry into the **European Union**, definitely anchoring its destiny to the West. The end of hostilities seems distant today, with neither side in a position to force a definitive military decision.

|| Ukrainian resilience transformed a lightning invasion meant to last three days into a global war of attrition that redefined Cold War alliances and disrupted global energy and food security. ||

title: How does the price of oil work?
description: No single seller sets the price of oil. It comes out of a **tug of war** between producing countries, financial markets and sudden crises, sometimes to the point of absurdity.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Oil, often described as the "blood of the economy," remains the most consumed primary energy source in the World. Its price is not just a simple figure displayed at the pump; it is a metabolic signal that directly influences inflation, global GDP growth, and the stability of States. 

Understanding how this price is set requires diving into the heart of a hybrid mechanism where the fundamental laws of physical trade, the strategies of geopolitical cartels, and the invisible power of financial markets intertwine. From the North Sea to the Arabian deserts, by way of computer terminals in Chicago, a barrel of oil travels a complex circuit before impacting household budgets.

lessons.title: OPEC against American shale: the battle over supply
lessons.content:
Historically, the price of oil is governed by the balance between global production and global consumption. The particularity of this market lies in its **Inelasticity**: in the short term, demand does not drop proportionally to a price increase, as transport and industrial infrastructures cannot instantly switch to energy alternatives. 

The central actor of supply remains **OPEC** (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries), founded in 1960. By coordinating their production policies through quotas, its members seek to stabilize or support prices. Since 2016, this group has expanded to become **OPEC+**, notably including Russia, in order to carry more weight against the emergence of new producers. Together, they control about **40%** of global extraction.

[OPEC meeting oil ministers]

However, the cartel's dominance has been shaken by the <American shale oil revolution>. Thanks to Techniques like hydraulic fracturing, the United States has moved from being the leading importer to the World's leading producer in a decade. This new supply, more reactive and decentralized, has transformed the market into a more competitive space, limiting OPEC's ability to arbitrarily set prices.

{Oil contains so much energy that a single 159-liter barrel contains the equivalent of the manual labor of 12 people working for a year.}

lessons.title: “Paper” oil: when finance joins in
lessons.content:
Beyond the physical exchange of barrels, the price is today determined on metal and energy exchanges. A distinction is made between physical oil and "paper" oil. The majority of transactions are made via an <oil futures market>, where a barrel is bought today for delivery in one, three, or six months.

[oil futures trading floor markets]

These markets attract **speculators** (banks, hedge funds) who have no intention of taking delivery of the product. They bet on price movements, providing liquidity to the market but also amplifying its **volatility**. In Period of uncertainty, the geopolitical risk premium can cause prices to jump in anticipation of a shortage that has not yet occurred.

The market relies on two global reference standards: **Brent**, from the North Sea, which serves as the basis for about two-thirds of the World's oil, and **WTI** (West Texas Intermediate), the American benchmark. The price gap between these two barrels, called the "spread," reflects logistical constraints or quality differences between producing regions.

lessons.title: Prices that collapse... or explode
lessons.content:
The oil economy operates in brutal cycles. A prolonged rise in prices encourages investment in expensive deposits (such as deep Offshore), which eventually creates an oversupply. Conversely, low prices discourage exploration, sowing the seeds of a future shortage and a new price shock.

The **COVID-19** crisis provided a spectacular illustration of this mechanism. In **April 2020**, the sudden halt of the global economy caused demand to plummet while production continued. Global storage capacities reached saturation. As a result, WTI fell to **-37 dollars**: sellers were willing to pay buyers to take the oil off their hands.

[oil price chart volatility]

In **2022**, Russia's invasion of Ukraine caused the opposite shock. Fear of an embargo on Russian oil, the World's second-largest exporter, propelled Brent to over **130 dollars**. These extreme variations show that oil remains a diplomatic weapon and a barometer of global stability, despite the energy transition underway.

lessons.title: Does oil have a future?
lessons.content:
In the long term, the price of oil faces an existential challenge: the disengagement from fossil fuels. If global demand begins to plateau due to the rise of electric vehicles, producing countries could enter a price war to sell off their reserves before they lose their value. 

However, a paradox haunts the market: the lack of investment in new extractive infrastructure, driven by climate policies, could paradoxically create violent price hikes in the short term if demand does not fall as fast as supply. Oil will not disappear overnight, as it remains essential for petrochemistry (plastics, fertilizers) and heavy transport (aviation, maritime freight).

{It takes about 7 liters of oil to manufacture a single smartphone, counting material extraction, component manufacturing, and international transport.}

|| To remember: The price of oil results from a tug-of-war between OPEC+, American shale production, and speculative financial markets, making prices extremely volatile in the face of global geopolitical crises. ||

title: Tax havens explained
description: About 10% of the world's wealth escapes tax in secretive territories. How does the system work, and why does it survive so well?
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: The **tax havens** constitute one of the most discreet yet most powerful cogs of financial globalization. These jurisdictions, often small in size, allow multinational companies and wealthy individuals to shield their capital from taxation in their home country. It is estimated today that **8 to 10% of global wealth** - about 10 trillion dollars - is held in these opaque territories. This phenomenon represents not only a colossal loss of revenue for public budgets, estimated at 600 billion dollars per year, but also questions the equity of the global economic system and the capacity of States to regulate capital flows in the digital age.

lessons.title: How the money hides
lessons.content:
A **tax haven** is defined by the convergence of three fundamental pillars: negligible taxation, administrative opacity, and a lack of international cooperation. These territories offer tax rates close to zero on profits, income, or assets, creating a pull for capital circulating in the <offshore> economy.

Opacity is guaranteed by <banking secrecy> or by the opacity of the company register. In many tax havens, it is possible to create **shell companies**, legal entities that have no real activity (no offices, no employees) and whose sole purpose is to hide the identity of the **Beneficial owner**. This architecture allows for masking the origin of funds or the identity of their owner.

[Cayman Islands offshore banking paradise]

{The Cayman Islands, with only 65,000 inhabitants, host more than 100,000 registered companies. It is the 5th global financial center in terms of bank deposits, even though its total area is smaller than the city of Paris.}

The diversity of these centers is striking: island territories like the **British Virgin Islands** specialize in creating complex legal structures, while financial centers like **Luxembourg** or **Switzerland** offer sophisticated wealth management services or tailor-made tax agreements, called <tax rulings>.

lessons.title: The art of making a profit disappear
lessons.content:
For multinationals, the goal is not necessarily illegality (fraud), but **tax optimization**, meaning the use of loopholes in different national systems to legally reduce their bill. The primary lever rests on **<transfer pricing>**. This mechanism allows a company to manipulate the prices of internal transactions between its various subsidiaries to locate profits where taxes are lowest.

The most effective strategy concerns intangible assets like **intellectual property rights**. A multinational transfers its patents or brands to a subsidiary located in a tax haven. Then, all its operational subsidiaries located in high-tax countries (like France or Germany) must pay massive royalties to this subsidiary for the right to use the brand. These payments are deductible: they cause taxable profit to drop in taxed countries and inflate profit in the tax haven.

[multinational corporate tax avoidance structure]

{The French term "paradis fiscal" comes from a translation error of the English "tax haven" (refuge fiscal). A phonetic confusion between "haven" (refuge) and "heaven" (paradis) transformed a simple safe harbor into a financial Eden in the French-speaking imagination.}

Famous Edits like the **"Double Irish"** or the **"Dutch Sandwich"** have allowed digital Giants to move their profits through several European jurisdictions before sending them to overseas territories without them ever being taxed. While these schemes are now under pressure, they long allowed companies to pay effective tax rates of less than 1%.

lessons.title: The world reacts (a little)
lessons.content:
Faced with the 2008 financial crisis and the indignation caused by massive leaks like the <Panama Papers>, the international community reacted. Under the aegis of the **OECD** and the **G20**, transparency mechanisms were established, notably **automatic exchange of information**, which now obliges banks to transmit their foreign clients' data to tax administrations.

The most spectacular advance occurred in **2021** with the agreement on a **global minimum tax rate of 15%** for multinationals. Driven by the Biden administration, this project aims to end the "race to the bottom," where States compete by lowering their taxes to attract investment. This floor rate means that if a company pays 5% tax in a tax haven, its home country can tax the remaining 10% to reach the 15% threshold.

[OECD G20 international tax agreement]

Despite this progress, gray areas remain. Assets held in <trusts> or foundations remain particularly difficult to trace. Furthermore, the very definition of a tax haven remains Politics: certain international blacklists omit powerful member countries of the OECD or the European Union to avoid diplomatic tensions.

lessons.title: Fragile progress toward tax fairness
lessons.content:
Beyond the figures, the persistence of tax havens poses a challenge of **social justice**. When the largest fortunes and the most profitable companies exempt themselves from tax, the tax burden rests more on the middle classes and small local businesses. This creates a major distortion of competition and weakens public services (health, education) due to lack of resources.

Today's World is witnessing a mutation toward cyber-taxation. Digital platforms no longer need a physical presence to generate revenue, making fiscal borders increasingly porous. The fight against tax evasion is therefore moving to the technological field: the use of <big data> by administrations to spot anomalies and the implementation of public registers of beneficial owners to break the wall of secrecy.

The transition toward a more transparent economy is a long-term process. While absolute banking secrecy has receded, financial engineering constantly creates new instruments to bypass regulation. The survival of the social contract in Western democracies will depend largely on the ability of international Institutions to impose common rules on capital that has become perfectly mobile.

|| To remember: Tax havens house about 10% of global wealth thanks to banking secrecy and near-zero taxation. Thanks to the impetus of the OECD and G20 in 2021, a 15% global minimum tax rate was adopted to limit multinational optimization and restore the fiscal sovereignty of States. ||

title: Tax avoidance by multinationals
description: The digital giants often pay tiny amounts of tax compared with their profits. It is not always illegal. It is the result of gaps in international law.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: Corporate tax evasion by multinationals, and more specifically that of the **GAFAM** (Google, Apple, Facebook/Meta, Amazon, Microsoft), constitutes one of the major challenges of contemporary globalization. While small and medium-sized enterprises are subject to standard national tax rates, these digital Giants manage to pay derisory taxes compared to their real profits. This phenomenon is not based on pure illegality, but on the sophisticated use of loopholes in international law, a practice known as **tax optimization**. By legally diverting hundreds of billions of dollars from public budgets, these companies erode the fiscal bases of States, accentuate global inequalities, and create a distortion of competition that questions the ability of international bodies to regulate the digital economy.

lessons.title: A tax built for factories, not for the internet
lessons.content:
The current international tax system was designed at the beginning of the 20th century to meet the requirements of the industrial economy. At that time, value creation was closely linked to a physical presence: a company had to own factories, warehouses, and offices in a country to conduct business there. Tax was then based on this permanent establishment.

The emergence of the digital economy has radically broken this geographic link. Today, a multinational can dominate a national market, capture the data of millions of users, and generate colossal revenue without owning any physical infrastructure on the territory. This dematerialization allows companies to disconnect the place where profit is generated from the place where it is declared.

[Google Dublin Ireland headquarters]

To maximize their profits, these firms use **transfer pricing** mechanisms: they bill for intangible services (use of an algorithm, right to use a brand) from a subsidiary located in a low-tax country to their subsidiaries in high-tax countries. These fictitious charges artificially decrease the taxable profit where the activity is real, to make it appear where it will be taxed the least.

{In 2014, the US tax authorities discovered that Microsoft had transferred $39 billion in profits to Puerto Rico using intellectual property rights mechanisms, thus saving more than $6.5 billion in taxes in a single editing.}

lessons.title: Hundreds of billions in lost revenue
lessons.content:
The scale of the loss for public finances is staggering. According to **OECD** estimates, tax base erosion and profit shifting generate an annual loss of between **$100 and $240 billion** on a global scale. These figures represent between 4% and 10% of the total amount of corporate tax collected on the planet. 

[OECD tax avoidance report billion]

In Europe, this issue takes on a sensitive Political dimension. The European Commission estimates the loss at about **50 to 70 billion euros** per year. This budgetary void forces States either to increase tax pressure on households and SMEs or to reduce investments in essential public services such as health or education. 

Beyond the accounting aspect, the fairness of the system is at stake. A local company pays on average a much higher effective tax rate than a multinational. This asymmetry creates an unfair competitive advantage for the digital Giants, allowing them to invest more in research or the acquisition of competitors thanks to the capital saved on tax.

lessons.title: The response: a global minimum tax
lessons.content:
Faced with growing public indignation, a coordinated response has begun to emerge under the aegis of the G20 and the **OECD**. The central pillar of this reform is the historic 2021 agreement aiming to establish a <15% global minimum tax>. This mechanism targets companies whose turnover exceeds 750 million euros, with the goal of neutralizing the advantage of tax havens: if a company pays 5% tax in one country, its country of origin can now collect the remaining 10%.

In parallel, some countries like France have introduced a national **GAFAM tax**, targeting turnover rather than profit, in order to claim a share of the value created by the exploitation of residents' data. These unilateral initiatives have caused diplomatic tensions, particularly with the United States, which sees them as a discriminatory measure against its technology champions.

[digital services tax GAFAM Europe]

Finally, the fight against opacity is progressing with the Concept of **country-by-country reporting**. This measure forces multinationals to make public the location of their employees, their profits, and their taxes. This transparency is a powerful weapon for regulators and NGOs who can thus point out the flagrant gaps between real economic activity and tax declarations.

lessons.title: Ireland, Europe's capital of tax optimization
lessons.content:
Ireland occupies a unique place in this system. By offering an official tax rate of 12.5% and secret arrangements (the <tax rulings>), the country has become the European hub for tax optimization. The case of Apple is emblematic: thanks to a complex structure, the Apple firm benefited from an effective tax rate close to 0.005% in 2014. 

Despite the initial condemnation by the European Commission, which asked Ireland to recover 13 billion euros, the latter long refused to collect this Sum. This refusal illustrates a paradox: for some countries, tax attractiveness is a pillar of economic sovereignty more precious than immediate tax revenues. They fear that harmonization will cause headquarters to move to other regions of the World.

The OECD reform, although beneficial, remains criticized by <tax justice> economists. They point out that the 15% rate is lower than the average for developed countries and that countries in the South, most affected by tax evasion, will receive only a tiny portion of the redistributed revenue. The battle for a taxation system adapted to the 21st century is therefore far from over.

title: The crisis of the welfare state
description: Born after 1945 to protect every citizen against illness, unemployment and old age, the welfare state is now shaken by aging populations and by globalization.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: The **Welfare State** refers to the set of government interventions aimed at guaranteeing a minimum level of well-being for the entire population, notably through a comprehensive social protection system. Born in its modern form in the aftermath of the Second World War, this model is based on a promise of collective solidarity in the face of life's hazards. However, since the late 20th century, this pillar of developed societies has been undergoing an unprecedented crisis of **Legitimacy** and financing. Between the accelerated aging of populations, shifts in work related to **globalization**, and the explosion of public debt, the balance between social protection and economic dynamism is now at the heart of global **politics** debates.

lessons.title: 1945: the birth of a social contract
lessons.content:
The emergence of the modern **Welfare State** cannot be understood without the trauma of the Great Depression and the war. In 1942, British economist **William Beveridge** published a revolutionary **Beveridge Report** that aimed to free the individual from want. His project was based on the "three Us": unity, uniformity, and universality. It involved protecting every citizen against the "five **Giants**" of disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness, and want.

[William Beveridge report welfare state 1942]

At the same time, France established **Social Security** in 1945, the fruit of a political compromise within the <National Council of the Resistance>. This system was initially based on a Bismarckian logic — where protection is linked to work and contributions — but gradually tended towards the universality dear to Beveridge. The State was no longer content with its sovereign functions (police, justice, defense); it became the guarantor of national cohesion.

The **Trente Glorieuses**, a **Period** of exceptional growth between 1945 and 1975, provided ideal ground for this model. Full employment ensured massive contribution revenues, while the age pyramid, very favorable with a young base and narrow top, made it easy to finance the first waves of retirements. In this context, social protection was not seen as a burden, but as a driver of **mass consumption** and social peace.

 Although institutionalized in 1945, the expression "public relief" and the idea of a debt owed by society to destitute citizens already appeared in the French Constitution of 1793.

lessons.title: The demographic shock
lessons.content:
The perfect balance of the post-war years broke under the effect of two environmental groundswells. The first is demographic: the increase in life expectancy, coupled with the decline in the birth rate, radically transformed the structure of society. The **aging of the population** weighs doubly on social accounts: it increases health expenditures (long-term care, chronic diseases) and extends the duration of pension payments.

[elderly retirees demographic aging population]

In France, this effect is spectacular: while there were 4 active workers for 1 retiree in the 1960s, we have dropped to fewer than **2 active workers today**. This ratio mechanically makes pay-as-you-go pension financing run at a deficit, unless contributions are massively increased, pensions are lowered, or the retirement age is pushed back.

The second rupture is economic. The end of rapid growth and the emergence of **structural unemployment** starting from the oil shocks of 1973 reduced the contribution base. Furthermore, the rise of the <gig economy> and the status of self-employed entrepreneurs weakens the historical link between stable salaried employment and robust social protection. Precarious workers contribute less to the system while being more vulnerable to risks, creating a formidable budgetary scissor effect.

 The Welfare State was invented not by socialists, but by the German conservative Chancellor **Otto von Bismarck** in 1883. His objective was purely strategic: to offer social security to workers to dry up support for revolutionary **movements** and strengthen the unity of the German Empire.

lessons.title: Globalization puts the model under pressure
lessons.content:
The opening of borders and market integration pose a challenge of sovereignty to the Welfare State. In a globalized economy, companies and capital are mobile. The compulsory levies (taxes and social contributions) necessary to finance the social model can be perceived as a competitiveness handicap. This is the argument of "social dumping": countries with generous protection systems fear competition from nations where labor costs are much lower.

This pressure pushes many governments to adopt policies reducing the state's scope. The liberal right often advocates a shift from a universal model to a **safety net** (or targeting) model, where aid is reserved only for the most destitute in order to reduce overall tax pressure. Conversely, defenders of the social model point out that collective protection is an investment that promotes stability and the qualification of the workforce.

The most frequently cited counter-example is that of the **Scandinavian model**. Countries like Sweden or Denmark manage to maintain a level of redistribution and public services among the highest in the **World** while remaining extremely competitive on the international stage.

[Sweden Denmark Scandinavian welfare model]

Their secret lies in <flexicurity>: great flexibility for companies regarding layoffs, compensated by very high unemployment benefits and massive support for training. However, even these models had to integrate doses of competition and individual responsibility to remain viable in the face of global mutations.

 Denmark spends about 32% of its GDP on social protection, one of the highest rates in the **World**, while regularly being ranked among the most innovative and business-enabling countries.

lessons.title: Reinventing social protection
lessons.content:
The future of the Welfare State likely lies not in its dismantling, but in its profound mutation to respond to the new risks of the 21st century. If the original system was designed to protect the industrial worker against accidents and old age, tomorrow's system must face the **uberization** of work, the ecological transition, and dependency related to old age.

The 2023 reform in France, setting the legal retirement age at 64, illustrates the difficulty of managing these transitions in a climate of high social tension. The debate is now shifting towards financing: should the bulk of protection continue to weigh solely on labor (contributions), at the risk of penalizing employment, or should it shift towards tax-based financing (like the <CSG>) which is broader and disconnected from professional status?

New paths are emerging, such as universal income to counter the automation of tasks, or dependency insurance to manage the "fifth risk" of life. The challenge is to move from a restorative State, which intervenes after the shock (unemployment, illness), to a social investor State, which bets on education and prevention to limit the occurrence of risks. The viability of the system ultimately rests on the political acceptability of the level of levies required to maintain the cohesion of society.

|| To remember: The Welfare State, a pillar of social stability since 1945, is weakened by a demographic ratio that dropped from 4 active workers for 1 retiree in the 1960s to fewer than 2 today in France, forcing it to reform to survive globalization and aging. ||

title: North-South inequality
description: The richest 10% of the planet take more than half of all world income. And yet extreme poverty is a quarter of what it was thirty years ago.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: The **inequalities between rich countries and poor countries** constitute one of the most persistent challenges of the contemporary World. While globalization promised global economic convergence, the gap between nations remains a striking reality, both in terms of income and access to fundamental rights. If we observe a spectacular reduction in extreme poverty in some regions of the globe, the structural imbalances inherited from the past and exacerbated by modern financial mechanisms continue to fragment the planet. This course analyzes the complex dynamics of these inequalities, from their historical roots to the contemporary issues of sustainable development.

lessons.title: A two-speed world
lessons.content:
The scale of the global imbalance is first measured by the distribution of the value produced. Currently, the **richest 10%** of the world's population saturate the economy by capturing more than **52% of global income**, while the **poorest 50%** share a meager **8%**. This power imbalance illustrates a concentration of wealth unprecedented in human History.

[global inequality rich poor contrast photograph]

Beyond money, this divide translates into biological Inequality in life. **Life expectancy at birth** reveals staggering gaps: it peaks at 83 years in Japan, drops to 72 years in China, plateaus at 65 years in India, and falls drastically to 55 years in the Central African Republic. These figures are not the result of chance but the direct result of unequal access to sanitary infrastructure, drinking water, and stable food supplies. Infant mortality in sub-Saharan Africa, for example, remains 30 times higher than in Europe, testifying to a systemic failure in protecting the South's most vulnerable populations.

{The Concept of the "birth lottery" is a biological reality: an American earns on average as much in one hour of activity as an inhabitant of Niger during an entire day of hard work.}

lessons.title: Historical roots that are still alive
lessons.content:
To understand why some countries stagnate, one must go back to the construction of the modern global economy. **Colonialism** left an indelible mark by structuring Southern territories as peripheries at the service of the Center. This system imposed export monocultures (coffee, cocoa, cotton) to the detriment of food self-sufficiency and slowed local industrialization to protect European manufacturers.

[colonial plantation cash crops Africa historical]

This logic persists today through unequal <terms of trade>. Countries of the South, often dependent on raw material exports, suffer from the volatility of global markets. When the price of oil or minerals drops, their budgets collapse, while they must import manufactured goods or technologies whose price is set by Northern countries and remains constantly increasing. This is what economists call the <deterioration of terms of trade>.

A further mechanism is that of **debt**. Many developing nations find themselves caught in a financial spiral where interest repayments - the debt service - absorb a larger share of their national budget than investments in education or health. This situation creates a dependence on international financial institutions, effectively limiting the economic sovereignty of Southern States.

{Did you know? To secure its resource supplies in the South, China practices "panda diplomacy": it leases these animals to foreign zoos in exchange for strategic trade agreements on raw materials.}

lessons.title: Real progress, unevenly shared
lessons.content:
Despite this dark picture, the last thirty years have been marked by a major transformation. For the first time in modern History, **absolute poverty** (defined as an income of less than $1.90 per day) has recled massively. It went from 36% of the world's population in 1990 to less than 10% before the 2020 health crisis. This leap forward is not the result of charity aid, but the result of the dazzling economic growth of **China and India**.

[extreme poverty reduction chart Asia]

This emergence of Asia has helped reduce inequality <between countries>, but it has often masked an explosion of inequalities <internally> (within countries). This is where Branko Milanovic's <“elephant curve”> comes in. This graph shows that while Asian middle classes have seen their incomes explode, the working classes in rich countries have stagnated, feeling the full brunt of global competition. 

Health successes are also notable: global infant mortality has been halved in three decades. However, these gains remain precarious. Global shocks, such as pandemics or financial crises, primarily hit countries that have not yet consolidated their social protection systems, threatening to plunge millions of people back into precarity overnight.

lessons.title: Climate, the new fault line
lessons.content:
The future of North-South inequalities is now being played out on the terrain of the **climate crisis**. Southern countries, historically the least responsible for greenhouse gas emissions, are paradoxically the most exposed to its consequences: droughts, floods, and rising sea levels. This asymmetry creates a new form of injustice, environmental insecurity, which could generate massive waves of displaced populations.

The question of development is no longer just posed in terms of GDP growth, but in terms of resilience. Economic models based on resource extraction are reaching their ecological limits. To sustainably reduce gaps, the international community is exploring new paths, such as <official development assistance> targeted at the energy transition or debt cancellation for the most fragile countries.

In conclusion, the fight against global inequalities is not a simple work of charity, but a necessity for global stability. As long as the wealth of the richest grows faster than that of the poorest in a world of finite resources, social and geopolitical tensions will remain inevitable. The challenge of the 21st century will be to reconcile poverty reduction with the imperatives of safeguarding the planet.

{Did you know? In 1960, per capita income in the richest countries was about 30 times higher than in the poorest countries; today, this gap has increased to about 80 times, showing that relative inequalities are worsening despite the drop in extreme poverty.}

|| The richest 10% capture 52% of world income - and yet extreme poverty has been divided by 4 in 30 years, falling from 36% to 9% of the world's population.||

title: Global debt
description: World debt has never been higher. Should we worry about it, or is it a normal tool for funding growth and getting through crises?
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
**Global debt**, encompassing the financial commitments of governments, corporations, and households, has reached staggering heights, now exceeding **300% of global GDP**. This figure, unprecedented in economic **History**, raises fundamental questions about the stability of the global financial system. Far from being a mere accounting figure, debt is the instrument that allows for financing growth, responding to health crises, or leading ecological transitions, but it carries the seeds of systemic vulnerabilities.

Understanding **Global debt** requires diving into the mechanisms of sovereign finance, analyzing the disparities between established powers and emerging economies, and confronting the economic visions that clash over the reality of the risk of state bankruptcy. Between a tool for **recovery** and an intergenerational burden, debt is the mirror of the ambitions and fragilities of our **World** today.

lessons.title: How a state goes into debt
lessons.content:
A State enters a spiral of indebtedness when its **public spending**, including investments and service operations, structurally exceeds its **tax revenues**. This imbalance creates a **budget deficit** that the State must fill by borrowing on financial markets through the issuance of debt securities. This process is not necessarily perceived as a drift: according to <Keynesian theory>, borrowing is a legitimate lever to stimulate economic activity during recessions, the idea being that the generated growth will eventually allow for the repayment of the sums owed.

However, political practice shows a blatant asymmetry: while governments easily agree to go into debt to support demand, they struggle to generate surpluses to repay during growth periods. This accumulation transforms a cyclical deficit into a massive structural debt.

The case of **Japan** is, in this regard, the most fascinating in the **World**. With a public debt flirting with **260% of its GDP**, the archipelago should logically be in a state of default. Yet, it faces no crisis of confidence. The key lies in the structure of its creditors: the bulk of the debt is held by domestic actors (Japanese banks and savers), which immunizes the country against foreign pressure and capital flight.

[Japan government debt statistics chart]

{The United Kingdom finished repaying debts in 2015 dating back to the South Sea Bubble of 1720 and the Napoleonic Wars, with some bonds being called 'perpetual'.}

lessons.title: Not all debts are equal
lessons.content:
The danger of debt is not correlated only to its gross amount, but especially to the **nature of the currency** in which it is denominated. Developed countries, such as the United States or France, enjoy an immense privilege: they borrow in their own currency or in international reserve currencies. For these nations, debt is perceived as **sustainable** because investors are certain that these economies are robust or that their central banks can intervene to ensure liquidity.

Conversely, developing countries face a more brutal reality. Not having a currency deemed stable by international markets, they are often forced to borrow in **US dollars** or euros. This situation creates a mortal exchange rate risk: if the national currency depreciates against the dollar, the real amount to be repaid mechanically explodes, regardless of the country's internal budgetary efforts.

This fragility has led to devastating crises, like the **debt crisis of the 1980s** in Latin America, where Mexico and Brazil found themselves unable to honor their commitments following interest rate hikes in the United States. Today, countries like Sri Lanka or Zambia face similar challenges, often aggravated by the opacity of certain bilateral loans.

[developing country IMF debt crisis protest]

During these crises, the intervention of institutions like the <IMF> is frequent, but it is often accompanied by drastic austerity policies that weigh heavily on local populations, triggering massive social protests against imposed reforms.

lessons.title: Can debt be infinite?
lessons.content:
The debate on debt limits today pits two major schools of thought against each other. On one side, proponents of <Modern Monetary Theory (MMT)> argue that a sovereign State cannot go bankrupt as long as it borrows in the currency it issues. According to them, the true debt ceiling is not an arbitrary ratio (like the 60% in the **Maastricht Treaty**), but the level of **inflation**. If the injection of money through debt exceeds the economy's production capacity, prices rise; otherwise, debt can grow indefinitely without immediate peril.

On the other side, so-called **orthodox** economists sound the alarm. They fear that excessive debt levels will lead to a sharp rise in interest rates if markets lose confidence, making debt service (the payment of interest) unbearable. They also point to the **crowding out** effect: money lent to the State is money that is not invested in the private sector.

The **Eurozone crisis** that occurred between 2010 and 2012 served as a severe warning. Countries like Greece or Portugal, no longer having their own national central bank to monetize their debt, saw their interest rates soar, threatening the integrity of the monetary union.

[Greek sovereign debt crisis 2012 Athens protest]

This period demonstrated that a crisis of confidence can transform a budgetary difficulty into a real economic collapse, where the State loses its ability to finance its basic services.

lessons.title: The new faces of debt
lessons.content:
Beyond States, global debt is also carried by the private sector (companies and households). A growing share of this debt is now held in the form of **Shadow Banking**, less regulated non-bank financial entities, which makes monitoring systemic risks more complex. In the event of a rapid rise in rates by central banks to fight inflation, many "zombie companies" (which survive only thanks to cheap money) could collapse.

The challenge of the 21st century is also shifting towards **climate debt**. Many experts advocate for a differentiated treatment of "good" debt — the kind that finances the energy transition — and "bad" debt linked to current consumption. The idea of transforming the debt of poor countries into investments for biodiversity is gaining ground in diplomatic circles.

Finally, the question of **intergenerational justice** remains central. Accumulating debt today technically means drawing from future taxes. However, if this borrowing finances sustainable infrastructure or high-quality education, it can be considered a transmission of wealth rather than a burden.

|| To remember: Global debt exceeds 300% of global GDP, a historical record. Its danger depends less on its gross amount than on the borrowing currency and the confidence of creditors, with Japan proving that a ratio of 260% can be sustainable if it is held locally. ||

{In 1790, Alexander Hamilton, the first US Treasury Secretary, stated that a moderate national debt would be a 'national blessing' because it would force citizens to be interested in the stability of the government.}
